items.title: [Bug] MP connector reports finished_sending for a request vLLM already freed after it was aborted mid-retrieve (EngineCore assert)
items.author: amd-lalithnc
items.body_excerpt:
**Labels**
bug, vllm

**Describe the bug**
With `LMCacheMPConnector` (engine-driven transfer), aborting a request while its KV is still being retrieved can kill EngineCore. Log from vLLM 0.31.0 with LMCache `dev` @ 90a4ae2f:

```
(EngineCore pid=129) ERROR 10-21 05:11:11 [core.py:1435] EngineCore encountered a fatal error.
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File ".../vllm/v1/engine/core.py", line 1419, in run_engine_core
    engine_core.run_busy_loop()
  File ".../vllm/v1/fault_tolerance/engine_core_sentinel.py", line 179, in run_with_fault_tolerance
    busy_loop_func(self)
  File ".../vllm/v1/engine/core.py", line 1478, in run_busy_loop
    self._process_engine_step()
  File ".../vllm/v1/engine/core.py", line 1529, in _process_engine_step
    outputs, model_executed = self.step_fn()
  File ".../vllm/v1/engine/core.py", line 654, in step
    engine_core_outputs = self.scheduler.update_from_output(
  File ".../vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py", line 2271, in update_from_output
    self._update_from_kv_xfer_finished(kv_connector_output)
  File ".../vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py", line 3157, in _update_from_kv_xfer_finished
    assert req_id in self.requests
AssertionError
(APIServer pid=1) ERROR 10-21 05:11:11 [async_llm.py:871] AsyncLLM output_handler failed.
...
vllm.v1.engine.exceptions.EngineDeadError: EngineCore encountered an issue. See stack trace (above) for the root cause.
```

`scheduler.py:3157` is the assert in the `finished_sending` loop:

```python
for req_id in kv_connector_output.finished_sending or ():
    assert req_id in self.requests
```

The API server then fails every in-flight request, and the instance exits.

Sequence:
1. The scheduler issues a retrieve for request R (async load).
2. In `EngineCore.step()`, the worker reports R in `finished_recving`. The abort for R is processed after the worker returns and before `update_from_output()`.
3. vLLM parks R because it finished while its load was unreported. It frees R when it processes the `finished_recving` report.
4. One step later the worker sees R as finished. It cannot tell this apart from a request that loaded and then finished, so it reports R in `finished_sending`.
5. R is no longer in `self.requests`, so the assert fails.

On current `dev`, `finished_sending` is only deduplicated when both reports come in the same call on the server-died path, so this cross-step case is not covered.

**To Reproduce**
Any client that cancels requests whose KV is still loading can trigger it. GuideLLM does this at the end of every rate, because it cancels the requests still in flight.

Setup used (prefix caching in vLLM disabled, so every request goes through LMCache):
1. One LMCache MP server (`dev` @ 90a4ae2f, L1 32 GB) and two vLLM 0.31.0 instances (CPU, 32 cores each) behind NGINX round-robin. Each instance runs `Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B` with `--max-model-len 4096 --no-enable-prefix-caching` and:
   ```
   --kv-transfer-config '{"kv_connector":"LMCacheMPConnector","kv_role":"kv_both","kv_connector_module_path":"lmcache.integration.vllm.lmcache_mp_connector","kv_connector_extra_config":{"lmcache.mp.host":"tcp://<server>","lmcache.mp.port":5555,"lmcache.mp.mp_transfer_mode":"engine_driven"}}'
   ```
2. Run GuideLLM v0.6.0 with a shared-prefix workload and short windows:
   ```
   guidellm benchmark run --target http://<nginx> --profile constant --rate 8 \
     --max-seconds 15 --data "prompt_tokens=64,output_tokens=16,prefix_tokens=2048,prefix_count=64" \
     --processor Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B
   ```
   Then run it again with `--rate 16`.
3. The rate 8 run ends with 121 of 121 requests incomplete (cancelled at the cutoff). The rate 16 run completes 36 requests and cancels 205 at the cutoff. Instance 1 died with the assert above at that cutoff.

A client that cancels streaming requests 5–300 ms after sending them (64 concurrent, 16 shared long prefixes) killed both instances within ~30 s.

Deterministic unit-level repro (attached in the PR): in `tests/v1/test_mp_connector_kv_roles.py`, issue a retrieve, call `request_finished()` before the scheduler sees `finished_recving`, then bind the next step's metadata on the worker. On unfixed `dev` (90a4ae2f) it fails for `[kv_producer-False]` and `[kv_both-False]`, i.e. `lazy_offload=False`.

**Expected behavior**
A request that finishes while its retrieve is unreported is freed by vLLM on `finished_recving`, so the connector must never report it in `finished_sending`. Each request ID is reported at most once.

**Environment**
- LMCache: `dev` @ 90a4ae2f, MP server with SHM transport
- vLLM: 0.31.0+cpu, torch 2.13.0+cpu, zentorch 2.13.0.3, Python 3.12
- Hardware: AMD EPYC 9755 (CPU inference)
- Topology: one LMCache MP server, two vLLM instances behind NGINX round-robin, `engine_driven` transfer
- Model: Qwen3-0.6B (the size doesn't matter; we first hit it with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct). Hybrid models (Qwen3.5) reach the same path through `request_finished_all_groups()`.
- Load: GuideLLM v0.6.0 constant-rate runs with short `--max-seconds`
- The unit repro also fails with vLLM 0.32.0.

**Additional context**
Related: #4938 (same race, reported on vLLM 0.25.x with DeepSeek-V4-Flash on GPU) and #4185. This issue confirms the race is still live on current `dev` and vLLM 0.31.0. It also shows that it is model- and hardware-independent, and that a standard GuideLLM rate sweep is enough to hit it.

#4939 (carried over from #4136) proposes a broader rework: an explicit LOADING state, about 300 lines across 5 files, with no reviews yet and merge conflicts at the moment. We'd like to propose a minimal fix for this specific crash that is independent of that work (+62/−4, 4 files):

- Scheduler side: track the retrieves it issued until they appear in `finished_recving`. If `request_finished()` runs for one of them first, move it to a `finished_while_loading` set.
- Pass that set to the worker in the next step's `LMCacheMPConnectorMetadata.finished_while_loading`.
- Worker side: `skip_finished_sending()` marks

items.title: Vulkan: ~78% decode throughput cliff at 131072 context — suballocation fragmentation; fixed via GGML_VK_SUBALLOCATION_BLOCK_SIZE=4 GiB
items.author: KEndlleas
items.body_excerpt:
# Vulkan: ~78% decode throughput cliff at 131072 context window — default ~1 GiB suballocation fragmentation; fixed via GGML_VK_SUBALLOCATION_BLOCK_SIZE=4 GiB

## Environment

| | |
|---|---|
| GPU | AMD Radeon RX 7900 XTX (24 GB, RDNA3, gfx1100) |
| OS / Driver | Windows 11, AMD proprietary driver |
| llama.cpp | 0.2.0-dev (build **10603**, commit c060ca974), Vulkan backend (ggml-vulkan.dll) |
| Model | Qwen3.8-27B (hybrid linear-attention, 64 layers), `Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf` (16.35 GiB) |
| Context | 131072 · KV cache `q8_0`/`q8_0` · `-fa on` · 4 slots unified pool |

## Summary

Decode throughput collapses from **~40 tok/s to ~8.9 tok/s** when the context window is raised from 98304 to 131072. The cliff is caused by the Vulkan backend's default **~1 GiB suballocation block size** fragmenting the large KV/compute pool into **30+ separate VkBuffers**. Setting `GGML_VK_SUBALLOCATION_BLOCK_SIZE=4294967296` restores full throughput at 131072.

## Reproduction

```powershell
llama-server -m Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf --mmproj mmproj-F16.gguf `
  --ctx-size 131072 -fa on --cache-type-k q8_0 --cache-type-v q8_0 --jinja `
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080
```

Send a single-stream 1200-token completion (prompt ≈ 31 tokens), measure wall time.

## Results (same request, same binary, single GPU)

| ctx | KV dtype | suballoc block size | wall time | throughput |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 65536 | f16 | default (1 GiB) | ~30 s | **40.4 tok/s** |
| 98304 | q8_0 | default | ~29 s | **40.8 tok/s** |
| **131072** | q8_0 | default | **~145 s** | **8.9 tok/s** ← cliff |
| **131072** | q8_0 | **4 GiB** | **~30 s** | **40.3 tok/s** ← restored |

Note: `llama-bench -p 512 -n 128` (small actual KV usage) stays at 40.4 tok/s even with q8 KV, so the cliff is tied to **pool allocation size**, not KV dtype.

## Diagnosis (`GGML_VK_MEMORY_LOGGER=1`)

At 131072, total device allocation is **21.55 GiB — fully in VRAM, no sysmem fallback** (total host = 152 MiB). The largest individual allocations are ≈ **1018 MiB each**, i.e. the pool is split into 30+ sub-blocks. At 98304 the same split stays below a critical block count and performance is unaffected.

No `OOM` / fallback warnings in logs. Memory location is not the issue — fragmentation of the pool into many independent `VkBuffer` objects is.

## Root-cause hypothesis

Decode at batch=1 touches the full KV/compute pool every step. With 30+ separate ~1 GiB sub-buffers, each step incurs per-buffer descriptor binding / submission overhead (and likely suboptimal memory access locality across disjoint buffers), multiplying the per-token cost by ~4.5×. Raising the suballocation block to 4 GiB keeps the pool in contiguous large buffers and eliminates the overhead.

## Workaround

```
GGML_VK_SUBALLOCATION_BLOCK_SIZE=4294967296
```

(before launching llama-server / llama-bench)

## Suggestions for maintainers

1. Consider raising the default suballocation block size, or sizing it relative to the KV pool (e.g. grow block size when the requested buffer exceeds N GiB).
2. Alternatively, allocate the KV cache as one contiguous buffer when it fits in VRAM, instead of splitting through the suballocator.
3. This appears to be a sibling of other "cliff at specific sizes" issues in the same backend: #25356 (fixed 8-token MMV dispatch thresholds) and #16759 (compute buffer jumps at specific context breakpoints).

---

**AI disclosure:** This report was researched and drafted with the assistance of an AI assistant (opencode). All measurements were performed locally on the machine described above; the evidence chain (memory logger output, A/B benchmark table) is reproducible with the commands provided.

## Additional NVIDIA reproduction and profiling

I reproduced a **related block-size-sensitive Vulkan decode regression** on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5070 Ti 16 GB using llama.cpp commit `2cdae802`.

### Environment

| Item        | Value                                      |
| ----------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| GPU         | NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5070 Ti, 16 GB          |
| OS / Driver | Windows 11 / NVIDIA 576.02                 |
| Vulkan      | 1.4.303                                    |
| llama.cpp   | 0.3.0-dev, build 10714, commit`2cdae802` |
| Model       | `Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q2_K_XL.gguf`            |
| KV cache    | `q8_0/q8_0`, Flash Attention enabled     |

### Reproduction

```powershell
llama-server.exe `
  -m Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q2_K_XL.gguf `
  --mmproj mmproj-F16.gguf `
  -ngl 99 `
  --ctx-size 131072 `
  -fa on `
  --cache-type-k q8_0 `
  --cache-type-v q8_0 `
  --jinja
```

For the 4 GiB run:

```powershell
$env:GGML_VK_SUBALLOCATION_BLOCK_SIZE="4294967296"
```

The only changed parameter between the two short-prompt `ctx=131072` runs was `GGML_VK_SUBALLOCATION_BLOCK_SIZE`.

### Runtime results

| Context | Block size | Generation time |  Throughput |
| ------: | ---------: | --------------: | ----------: |
|  98,304 |      1 GiB |         29.38 s | 40.81 tok/s |
| 131,072 |      1 GiB |         49.92 s | 24.02 tok/s |
| 131,072 |      4 GiB |         33.24 s | 36.07 tok/s |

At `ctx=131072` with a short prompt, increasing the block size from 1 GiB to 4 GiB improves throughput from **24.02 to 36.07 tok/s**, about **50%**.

### Nsight Systems profiling

I also collected a control trace for `98304 / 1 GiB` and compared it with the two `131072` traces.

| Configuration   | `vkWaitForFences` total | Median wait |  Max wait |
| --------------- | ------------------------: | ----------: | --------: |
| 98,304 / 1 GiB  |                   3.496 s |     8.43 ms |  342.6 ms |
| 131,072 / 1 GiB |                   5.670 s |    10.00 ms | 1751.4 ms |
| 131,072 / 4 GiB |                   4.599 s |     8.03 ms |  613.5 ms |

The graph structure does not show a corresponding large increase in CPU-side submission work:

| Configuration   | `vkQueueSubmit` | `vkUpdateDescriptorSets` |
| --------------- | ----------------: | -------------------------: |
| 98,304 / 1 GiB  |             5,584 |                    351,009 |
| 131,072 / 1 GiB |             5,662 |                    352,214 |
| 131,072 / 4 GiB |             5,628 |                    351,009 |

All observed `vkWaitForFences` intervals longer than 1 ms overlap WDDM GPU packet activity, with both 3D and Copy queue activity visible during the waits.

This does **not** support a simple explanation based on:

- increased queue submission count;
- increased descriptor update count;
- or the CPU being blocked on fences while the GPU is completely idle.

The fence-wait data by itself does not account for the full runtime difference, so the exact location of the additional GPU/WDDM execution time still needs to be identified.

4 GiB is **not a general workaround**.

With approximately 52.4K prompt tokens at the start of decode, while keeping `ctx=131072`, the result reverses:

| Prompt tokens at decode start | Block size | Generation time |  Throughput |
| ----------------------------: | ---------: | --------------: | ----------: |
|                           ~31 |      1 GiB |         49.92 s | 24.02 tok/s |
|                           ~31 |      4 GiB |         33.24 s | 36.07 tok/s |
|                        52,442 |      1 GiB |         52.64 s | 22.80 tok/s |
|                        52,442 |      4 GiB |        230.05 s |  5.22 tok/s |

The 1 GiB layout changes only slightly between the short- and long-active-KV workloads:

- `24.02 -> 22.80 tok/s` (~5% decrease)

The 4 GiB layout changes dramatically:

- `36.07 -> 5.22 tok/s` (~85.5% decrease)

## Linux / RADV datapoint: the fragmentation reproduces exactly, but neither throughput regression does

Testing this on Linux with the same GPU as the OP, and got a result worth adding to the thread: **the ~1 GiB buffer fragmentation you describe reproduces almost character-for-character, `GGML_VK_SUBALLOCATION_BLOCK_SIZE` fixes it exactly as advertised — and decode throughput does not move, in either direction, at either short or long active-KV.**

### Environment

| | this report | OP (@KEndlleas) | @SG-Amadeus |
|---|---|---|---|
| OS | **Linux (Arch)** | Windows 11 | Windows 11 |
| GPU | RX 7900 XTX 24 GB | RX 7900 XTX 24 GB | RTX 5070 Ti 16 GB |
| Driver | **RADV / Mesa 26.2.3-arch1.1**, Vulkan 1.4.354 | AMD proprietary | NVIDIA 576.02 |
| llama.cpp | **b11065** (0.4.1-dev, `ce8caa6`) | 10603 | 10714 (`2cdae802`) |
| Context | **131072** | 131072 | 131072 |
| KV | **q4_0** | q8_0 / f16 | q8_0 |
| speculative | **MTP on** (`--spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-n-max 2`) | off | off |
| pool | **14.08 GiB device / 301 MiB host** | 21.55 GiB / 152 MiB | — |

Single slot (`-np 1`), `-fa on -dev Vulkan0`, `-t 16`, `GGML_VK_TILE_L=64:256:32`, Qwen3.8-27B IQ3_XXS + MTP.

### Method

Two things, both against `llama-server`:

1. **Allocation structure** via `GGML_VK_MEMORY_LOGGER=1`, parsing the `ggml_vulkan memory:` alloc/dealloc lines keyed by address and keeping only **net-alive** buffers (transients excluded).
2. **Throughput** via `POST /completion`, `n_predict=300`, `cache_prompt=False`, **3 reps per arm** (short KV) and **2 reps per arm** (long KV). Both arms launched with byte-identical cmdlines — the *only* difference is `GGML_VK_SUBALLOCATION_BLOCK_SIZE`.

That yields a **2×2**: `{1 GiB, 4 GiB} × {short KV, long KV}`, so the high-active-KV crossover you found could be tested too.

### Fragmentation: reproduces, and is deterministic

Both arms start at an identical `Total device: 14.08 GiB, total host: 301.07 MiB`, so only the block size varies. Both parsed at the same **startup-only** stage (before either saw probe traffic):

| metric | 1 GiB | 4 GiB |
|---|---|---|
| device buffers | **25** | **16** |
| buffers ≥ ~1000 MiB | **10** | **4** |
| **the ~1000–1024 MiB ring** | **10** | **0** |
| largest single buffer | **1020.52 MiB** | 4.000 GiB |
| distinct sizes | 22 | 14 |

1 GiB arm, largest device buffers:

```
1020.52  1017.51  1016.78  1016.73  1010.63
1009.50  1008.00  1008.00  1005.05  1001.85   MiB
 991.18   887.99   512.00   470.45   448.88   MiB
```

4 GiB arm:

```
4.000  3.990  2.250  1.340 GiB
887.99  512.00  448.88  260.28  248.10  200.02 MiB
```

You wrote *"the largest individual allocations are ≈1018 MiB each."* Here the top ten cluster at **1001.85–1020.52 MiB** — a match within ~2 MiB, on Linux, on RADV. And `GGML_VK_SUBALLOCATION_BLOCK_SIZE=4294967296` does exactly what you say: **the ring goes 10 → 0**, largest 1020.52 MiB → 4.000 GiB.

**It is also fully deterministic, not run-to-run noise:** two independent launches from different shells, 44 minutes apart, produced byte-identical top-3 device allocations (`1020.5 / 1017.5 / 1016.8 MiB`), the same 10-buffer ring, and the same `14.08 GiB` endpoint.

### Throughput: flat in all four cells

```
                short KV     long KV
  1 GiB          76.59        72.93     mean tok/s
  4 GiB          76.60        72.86     mean tok/s
  ratio 1G/4G    0.9999       1.0010
```

- **short KV (~55 prompt tokens):** 76.59 vs 76.60 → **0.01% apart** (reps: 1 GiB 83.54/67.74/78.48, 4 GiB 73.56/72.17/84.06)
- **long KV (56,110 / 58,116 prompt tokens):** 72.93 vs 72.86 → **0.10% apart** (spread only 0.04 and 2.83 — much tighter than short KV)

items.title: [Bug] fast_topk_v2 can silently return wrong top-k sets when a radix threshold bucket exceeds its 4096-entry candidate buffer (k=2048, long rows)
items.author: zkyue
items.body_excerpt:
## Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

## Describe the bug

`sgl_kernel.fast_topk_v2` (`topk_kernel` in `python/sglang/kernels/aot/csrc/elementwise/topk.cu`) can return silently wrong top-k index sets when the coarse-radix threshold bucket of a row contains more than 4096 candidates. No error is raised, the output has the normal shape and exactly `k` valid indices, but some of them are not in the true top-k. In the reproduction below, at 64 rows x 256K columns with k=2048, **all 64 rows return wrong top-k sets, with 6-42 of the 2048 selected entries per row absent from the true top-k** (and 98-157 per row at 64 x 1M). Which selections are wrong is nondeterministic run to run. (Overflow makes corruption *possible*, not certain: if the overflowing bucket is dominated by ties at the k-th value boundary, any k tied candidates are valid and the output may still be correct. For continuous score distributions every measured row past the cliff is wrong.)

### Mechanism

Line numbers are at current main (`6480cce9bc`), file `python/sglang/kernels/aot/csrc/elementwise/topk.cu`:

- The kernel builds a 256-bin coarse histogram over the fp16-high-byte key of each score (pass 1), then re-scans the row (pass 2): scores strictly above the threshold bin go directly to the output; scores *in* the threshold bin are staged into a fixed shared-memory candidate buffer for radix refinement.
- The candidate buffer holds `SMEM_INPUT_SIZE = kSmem / (2 * sizeof(int)) = 4096` entries on CUDA (L38, L96). The sizing comment (L35-L37) records the underlying assumption — "Each radix pass needs at most ~TopK candidates in the threshold bin, so 4K entries per round ... is sufficient" — but for long rows the threshold bucket is much larger than `k`, which is exactly the overflow case.
- Pass 2 stores a candidate only `if (C10_LIKELY(pos < SMEM_INPUT_SIZE))` (L173). Once the threshold bucket exceeds 4096 entries, the remaining candidates are **silently dropped**, and their contributions to the fused refinement histogram are lost with them, so the subsequent threshold selection operates on a truncated population.
- `num_input` is clipped rather than flagged (L192); the refinement rounds carry the same silent-drop guard (L239), though the demonstrated candidate loss happens at the pass-2 staging (L173) — after the clip, the staged population is already at most 4096.
- The kernel still emits exactly `k` valid, duplicate-free indices, so ordinary downstream shape/range/count checks do not detect the corruption. Which candidates survive depends on `atomicAdd` arrival order, so the wrong output is also nondeterministic run to run (repeated calls on the same input changed the selected index sets in roughly 40 of 64 rows in our runs).
- (On CUDA `kSmem` is 32KB. ROCm builds parameterize it via `SGL_TOPK_DYNAMIC_SMEM_BYTES` — 6144 entries on gfx942, 16384 on gfx95x/gfx1250 — so the same defect exists with a later cliff.)

### When it triggers

The coarse key keeps only 2 mantissa bits, so buckets are wide. Whether a given workload overflows depends on how many scores share the bucket containing the k-th value, which grows with row length and with the concentration of the score distribution. With standard-normal synthetic scores at k=2048 that bucket holds ~1.1K candidates at 64K columns (correct output), ~4.3K at 256K columns (every row wrong), and ~5.1K at 1M columns (every row wrong); other smooth distributions sit lower at the same length (in our measurements exponential and logistic scores at 256K columns peaked around ~3.1K candidates and stayed correct), while distributions concentrated near the k-th bucket can cross the cliff earlier. Real-world exposure therefore depends on both the score distribution and on which top-k path a workload routes through.

### Why it matters

- k=2048 is the only k this kernel supports (`TopK = 2048`, L23) and is the DeepSeek V3.2 DSA configuration. In current routing, the affected AOT entry points are reachable as follows: `fast_topk_v2` is the `DSATopKBackend.SGL_KERNEL` unfused path (`topk_func` in `python/sglang/srt/layers/attention/dsa/dsa_topk_backend.py`), taken whenever top-k fusion is off (`SGLANG_DSA_FUSE_TOPK=0` or `force_unfused_topk`); the fused AOT variants are the legacy branches of `topk_transform`, reached only by calls that miss the JIT v2 dispatch predicates (e.g. PAGED calls with `batch_idx_list` set, or the RAGGED prefill-CP path). With all-default settings, eligible PAGED and RAGGED calls route to the separate JIT v2 kernels (`_topk_transform_v2_paged` / `_topk_transform_v2_ragged`) instead — those have a closely related fixed-buffer truncation defect of their own, reported in #35257 (`kMaxNumTie` tie buffer in `topk_impl.cuh`); the bug reported here is in the AOT kernel in `topk.cu`, a separate file and code path, so this is not a duplicate of that report.
- The fused variants `topk_transform_decode_kernel` (L270), `topk_transform_prefill_kernel` (L301), and `topk_transform_prefill_ragged_kernel` (L353) call the same `fast_topk_cuda_tl` device function (L287, L339, L370) and inherit the defect.
- `python/sglang/kernels/aot/tests/test_topk.py` parametrizes `seq_len` only up to 65536, which stays below the cliff, so CI does not catch this.
- The file header notes the adaptation "fix[ed] the potential illegal memory access"; the bounds guard indeed removes the out-of-bounds write, but converts it into silent wrong results.

### Possible directions for a fix

1. Spill overflowing candidates to a global-memory workspace and have the refinement rounds walk both part

items.title: [Bug] Non-causal sliding-window attention is ignored in TorchNativeAttnBackend
items.author: approximated-intelligence
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

 `TorchNativeAttnBackend` currently does not correctly apply sliding-window attention for non-causal models such as encoder architectures.

 The sliding-window mask is hardcoded to causal behavior:

```
(k_pos <= q_pos) & (k_pos >= q_pos - sliding_window_size)
```

 Additionally, `forward_extend` only enables sliding-window attention when `causal=True`.

 As a result, encoder models using bidirectional sliding-window attention silently fall back to **full global attention** instead of respecting their configured local attention window. This can cause significant numerical differences for long sequences and break parity with HuggingFace Transformers.

The BUG is fixed by PR: https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/39298


### Reproduction

 This affects encoder models that use:

 - `causal=False`
- `sliding_window_size` / local attention
- Long-context inputs

 For example, ModernBERT-style architectures require a **bidirectional** sliding-window mask:

```
|q_pos - k_pos| <= sliding_window_size
```

 rather than the causal constraint:

```
k_pos <= q_pos
```

 Without the fix, long-context embeddings can differ substantially from the reference implementation because tokens attend globally instead of only within the configured local window.

 ### Expected behavior

 For causal models:

```
(k_pos <= q_pos) & (k_pos >= q_pos - sliding_window_size)
```

 For non-causal/encoder models:

```
torch.abs(q_pos - k_pos) <= sliding_window_size
```

 Sliding-window attention should also be enabled for encoder models even when `causal=False`.

 ### Proposed fix

 Update `python/sglang/srt/layers/attention/torch_native_backend.py` to:

 - Add a `causal` parameter to `_make_sliding_window_mask`, defaulting to `True` for backward compatibility.
- Generate a bidirectional window when `causal=False`.
- Propagate `causal` through the SDPA extend/decode paths.
- Remove the `causal` requirement from the `forward_extend` sliding-window configuration.

### Validation

 The fix was validated against HuggingFace Transformers using `jhu-clsp/ettin-encoder-17m` on CPU with float32.

 Results after the fix:

 | Test | Cosine Similarity | MSE |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Single | 1.000000 | 0.00000000 |
| Batch | 1.000000 | 0.00000000 |
| Long context (\~1.9K tokens) | 1.000000 | 0.00000000 |
| Longer context (\~3.2K tokens) | 1.000000 | 0.00000000 |

 This confirms that the corrected bidirectional sliding-window mask restores numerical parity with HuggingFace for the tested encoder model.

### Regression considerations

 The new `causal=True` default preserves the existing mask behavior for causal LLMs, so existing causal sliding-window models should remain unchanged.

 No performance benchmark is required because this is primarily a correctness fix for the CPU attention backend.

items.title: [Bug] Anthropic streaming drops a tool call's closing "}" when whitespace text arrives between its arguments (multiple tool calls, qwen3_coder)
items.author: rgrashel
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

`POST /v1/messages` with `stream=true` can return a `tool_use` block whose `input_json_delta` stream is missing the closing `}`. It happens when the model makes more than one tool call in a turn. The aggregated input is invalid JSON, for example `{"path": "a.txt"`. The server logs:

```text
WARNING ... serving.py:1226 Dropping tool_call argument delta with no open tool_use block: '}'
```

| Endpoint / mode | Result (same model, tools and prompt) |
| --- | --- |
| OpenAI-compatible, non-streaming | three valid tool calls |
| OpenAI-compatible, streaming | three valid tool calls (arguments accumulate by `index`) |
| Anthropic-compatible, non-streaming | three valid `tool_use` blocks |
| Anthropic-compatible, streaming | at least one `tool_use` block with truncated JSON (3/3 runs) |

A single tool call is unaffected. Which call loses its brace varies from run to run, because it depends on how tokens are grouped into decode increments.

This is a different failure from #39782, where several calls were merged into one block. Since `force_new=True`, each call gets its own block. Here the block is closed too early instead.

The branch that drops the fragment, and the rule that a text delta closes an open `tool_use` block, both arrived in #25876 (merged 2026-06-12). The same code is on `main` as of 2026-10-02; I compared the files but have not run `main`.

Impact: Anthropic SDK and Claude Code consumers receive invalid tool input for parallel tool calls. In Claude Code the malformed call is rejected as unparseable JSON and the model has to repeat it. In one coding session 10 of 19 batched tool calls were affected.

**Root cause**

Two pieces combine.

1. **Order is lost in the tool-call streaming path.** `Qwen3CoderDetector.parse_streaming_increment` (`srt/function_call/qwen3_coder_detector.py`) returns one `StreamingParseResult` per decode increment, with `normal_text` and `calls` held separately. `OpenAIServingChat._process_tool_call_stream` (`srt/entrypoints/openai/serving_chat.py`) yields `normal_text` first and the tool-call items after it. When one increment spans the end of one call and the start of the next, the `\n` between `</tool_call>` and `<tool_call>` is emitted before the `}` that came earlier in the text. Speculative decoding (DFLASH with 8 draft tokens in this setup) is my suspected reason such increments are common here. I have not verified that the bug disappears with speculative decoding off. Feeding the real detector the increment `"</function>\n</tool_call>\n<tool_call>\n<function=read_file>\n"` returns:

   ```text
   normal_text='\n'  calls=[(0, None, '}'), (1, 'read_file', '')]
   ```

   OpenAI clients don't notice, because they accumulate arguments by tool-call `index`.

2. **The Anthropic adapter closes the open `tool_use` block on any text.** In `AnthropicServing._generate_anthropic_stream` (`srt/entrypoints/anthropic/serving.py`), a text delta calls `_ensure_content_block_events("text", ...)`. That closes the open `tool_use` block and opens a text block. The `}` that follows lands in the "Continuing arguments for current tool call" branch with `content_block_type != "tool_use"`, so it is dropped with the warning above. A closed Anthropic content block cannot be reopened, so the adapter cannot recover once it has closed the block.

**Why the whitespace is formatting, not content**

- **The model's chat template writes it.** Qwen's published template renders every tool call after the first as a newline followed by the next call:

  ```jinja
  {%- else %}
      {{- '\n<tool_call>\n<function=' + tool_call.name + '>\n' }}
  ```

  The line is in the template shipped with this model and in the official ones, for example [Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct/blob/main/chat_template.jinja). The same template tells the model to reply "with NO suffix" and that reasoning may come "BEFORE the function call, but NOT after". So the `\n` between `</tool_call>` and `<tool_call>` is the separator the model was trained to emit, not text it is saying.
- **The Anthropic streaming format expects complete input.** The [streaming documentation](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/streaming) says the deltas are "partial JSON strings, whereas the final `tool_use.input` is always an object", and that a client can "accumulate the string deltas and parse the JSON once you receive a `content_block_stop` event". A block that stops with `{"path": "a.txt"` does not meet that.
- **The non-streaming path already discards it.** The same request without `stream` returns `thinking`, one `text` block (`"\n\n"`), then three `tool_use` blocks with complete input and no text between them.

### Reproduction

Server (image `lmsysorg/sglang:nightly-dev-20260915-8874c51a`, commit 8874c51a9652538fb9f5e2d7650af0f1d91be8fc; model Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4):

```bash
sglang serve --trust-remote-code --model-path /models/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4 --served-model-name qwen3.8-27b-nvfp4 \
  --context-length 262144 --kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3 --mem-fraction-static 0.85 --chunked-prefill-size 2048 \
  --reasoning-parser qwen3 --tool-call-parser qwen3_coder \
  --mamba-full-memory-ratio 1.0 --mamba-radix-cache-strategy extra_buffer --mamba-ssm-dtype float32 \
  --speculative-algorithm DFLASH --speculative-draft-model-path /models/Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2 --speculative-num-draft-tokens 8 \
  --default-chat-template-kwargs '{"reasoning_effort":"medium"}' --enable-metrics --host 0.0.0.0 --port 30000
```

Re

items.title: [Bug] NPU HiCache: MHATokenToKVPoolHost crashes when the device k_buffer is a single tensor (since #40326)
items.author: pingqiu
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

`test/registered/npu/basic_function/HiCache/test_npu_hicache_mha.py` fails on `main` (PR Test (NPU), e.g. runs 37358858354 and 37376161789). The server dies while building the HiCache host pool:

```
File ".../mem_cache/pool_host/mha.py", line 160, in <genexpr>
    for buf in getattr(pool, side, None) or ()
RuntimeError: Boolean value of Tensor with more than one value is ambiguous
```

### Cause

#40326 ("Derive KV row addresses from strides, not shapes (1/7)") added this to `MHATokenToKVPoolHost.__init__`:

```python
self._init_device_row_stride(
    buf
    for pool in (self.device_pool, *self.mtp_draft_device_pools)
    if pool is not None
    for side in ("k_buffer", "v_buffer")
    for buf in getattr(pool, side, None) or ()
)
```

`... or ()` assumes `k_buffer` / `v_buffer` is a list of per-layer tensors (or `None`). The Ascend KV pool with HiCache enabled and FIA off sets them to a single multi-layer tensor (`hardware_backend/npu/memory_pool_npu.py`, `self.k_buffer = self._hicache_k_buffer`), and evaluating that tensor's truth value raises. With FIA on it uses per-layer lists, which is why only some NPU configurations hit it.

### Possible fix

Normalise the attribute before iterating, for example:

```python
def _device_buffers(pool, side):
    bufs = getattr(pool, side, None)
    if bufs is None:
        return ()
    if isinstance(bufs, torch.Tensor):
        return bufs.unbind(0)  # one entry per layer, as with the list form
    return bufs
```

and `for buf in _device_buffers(pool, side)` in the generator. Whether a per-layer view or the whole tensor is the right input to `_init_device_row_stride` on NPU is for the #40326 authors to confirm.

### Reproduction

Run `test_npu_hicache_mha.py` on an Ascend A3 runner (`--attention-backend ascend --enable-hierarchical-cache`, FIA off), as in the PR Test (NPU) workflow.

### Environment

SGLang `main` after #40326 (2026-10-01); PR Test (NPU) `base-b-test-*-npu-a3`.

Found while reading the CI results of #42399, which merged `main` but doesn't touch the host pools.

items.title: [Bug] Qwen3CoderDetector streaming emits unterminated JSON arguments when the model omits `</function>`
items.author: the-Shallow
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug


The streaming parser only closes a tool call's arguments object (`}`) when it sees
`</function>`; `</tool_call>` is treated purely as a region marker. It also does not accept
`</tool_call>` as a parameter terminator. So when a model closes `</tool_call>` but omits
`</function>`, the streamed argument fragments never form valid JSON — they end mid-object
(`{"days": 0`), and if `</parameter>` is missing too the parameter is dropped entirely. The
non-streaming path recovers the arguments correctly in both cases.


### Reproduction


```python
import json

from sglang.srt.entrypoints.openai.protocol import Function, Tool
from sglang.srt.function_call.qwen3_coder_detector import Qwen3CoderDetector

tools = [
    Tool(
        type="function",
        function=Function(
            name="get_current_weather",
            parameters={"type": "object", "properties": {"days": {"type": "integer"}}},
        ),
    )
]

texts = {
    "no </function>": "<tool_call>\n<function=get_current_weather>\n"
    "<parameter=days>\n0\n</parameter>\n</tool_call>",
    "no </function> and no </parameter>": "<tool_call>\n<function=get_current_weather>\n"
    "<parameter=days>\n0\n</tool_call>",
}

for label, text in texts.items():
    oneshot = Qwen3CoderDetector().detect_and_parse(text, tools)
    det = Qwen3CoderDetector()
    streamed = "".join(
        c.parameters
        for ch in text
        for c in det.parse_streaming_increment(ch, tools).calls
        if c.parameters
    )
    print(label)
    print("  oneshot:", oneshot.calls[0].parameters)
    print("  stream :", repr(streamed))

# no </function>
#   oneshot: {"days": 0}
#   stream : '{"days": 0'                <- not valid JSON, missing '}'
# no </function> and no </parameter>
#   oneshot: {"days": 0}
#   stream : ''                          <- argument dropped entirely
```

### Expected behavior and impact

* Both parsing paths in this module are written to tolerate a model that drops closing tags.
  `detect_and_parse` has an explicit fallback alternative for it
  (`r"<function=(.*?)</function>|<function=(.*)$"`), and the streaming parameter scanner
  documents the same intent:

  ```
  # A parameter can end in multiple ways:
  # 1. [Normal] Encounter </parameter>
  # 2. [Abnormal] Encounter next <parameter=
  # 3. [Abnormal] Encounter </function>
  ```

  `</tool_call>` belongs to that same class of abnormal terminators but is missing from the
  candidate list, and there is no corresponding "close the object" handling in section 5.
* The consequence is not a degraded value but a protocol violation: `serving_chat.py` forwards
  `call_item.parameters` verbatim as the `arguments` delta, so the client accumulates
  `{"days": 0` and fails to `json.loads` the finished tool call. `Qwen3CoderDetector` never
  populates `prev_tool_call_arr` / `streamed_args_for_tool`, so
  `_check_for_unstreamed_tool_args` cannot backfill the missing `}` either.
* The same model output parses fine in non-streaming mode, so the request succeeds or fails
  depending only on `stream=True/False`.

### Suggested fix

Treat `</tool_call>` as a parameter terminator, and close an open arguments object when the
tool-call region ends.

```diff
--- a/python/sglang/srt/function_call/qwen3_coder_detector.py
+++ b/python/sglang/srt/function_call/qwen3_coder_detector.py
@@ -314,10 +314,12 @@ class Qwen3CoderDetector(BaseFormatDetector):
                     # 1. [Normal] Encounter </parameter>
                     # 2. [Abnormal] Encounter next <parameter=
                     # 3. [Abnormal] Encounter </function>
+                    # 4. [Abnormal] Encounter </tool_call>
                     # So we need to find the smallest one as the parameter end position.
                     cand_end_param = rest_of_slice.find(self.parameter_end_token)
                     cand_next_param = rest_of_slice.find(self.parameter_prefix)
                     cand_end_func = rest_of_slice.find(self.function_end_token)
+                    cand_end_tool = rest_of_slice.find(self.tool_call_end_token)
 
                     candidates = []
                     if cand_end_param != -1:
@@ -327,6 +329,8 @@ class Qwen3CoderDetector(BaseFormatDetector):
                         candidates.append((cand_next_param, 0))
                     if cand_end_func != -1:
                         candidates.append((cand_end_func, 0))
+                    if cand_end_tool != -1:
+                        candidates.append((cand_end_tool, 0))
 
                     if candidates:
                         best_cand = min(candidates, key=lambda x: x[0])
@@ -405,6 +409,17 @@ class Qwen3CoderDetector(BaseFormatDetector):
             # 5. Tool Call End: </tool_call>
             # -------------------------------------------------------
             if current_slice.startswith(self.tool_call_end_token):
+                if self.current_func_name is not None:
+                    # Model omitted </function>; close the arguments object anyway.
+                    if not self.json_started:
+                        calls.append(
+                            ToolCallItem(
+                                tool_index=self.current_tool_id, parameters="{"
+                            )
+                        )
+                        self.json_started = True
+                    calls.append(
+                        ToolCallItem(tool_index=self.current_tool_id, parameters="}")
+                    )
+                    self.current_func_name = None
score_reasons: 匹配 Serving 与评测、Kernel 与正确性、工程与测试

items.title: [Bug] PD prefill: early cached-prefix send can transfer KV before the HiCache load-back finishes (stale KV on decode)
items.author: mattteochen
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug On a PD **prefill** server with HiCache and the default early cached-prefix send (`SGLANG_DISAGG_PREFILL_EARLY_SEND_CACHED_PREFIX=1`), decode can **silently receive stale KV** for part of a prefix. The trigger is two requests sharing a prefix whose KV is only in host memory, admitted in the **same prefill batch**: 1. The first request queues the HiCache load-back. `commit_load_back` attaches the new device pages to the radix node right away, while the H2D copy is only queued ([unified_radix_cache.py](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/7ff3a112846a3fcc12a27bba09d644885a226e4d/python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/unified_radix_cache.py#L1800-L1823)). 2. The second request is re-matched onto those pages as device prefix (`host_hit_length = 0`). 3. `maybe_send_cached_prefix_chunk` sends them before the forward, while the H2D is still writing them ([prefill.py](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/7ff3a112846a3fcc12a27bba09d644885a226e4d/python/sglang/srt/disaggregation/prefill.py#L1415-L1450)). The range is never re-sent. items.title: [Bug] PD prefill PP8 + HiCache cache mode hangs: PP0–PP3 blocked in the HiCache PP-sync drain
items.author: xiaguan
items.body_excerpt:
## Describe the bug

A P/D-disaggregated prefill server running PP8 with HiCache in cache mode hung after about 35 minutes of serving. The first ~33 minutes were synthetic open-loop load and ran cleanly. The hang came about 2 minutes after a multi-turn agentic workload started. That workload has long contexts (prompts up to ~214k tokens) and many prefix hits.

All PP ranks stopped launching forwards at the same moment, and the scheduler heartbeat stopped. Requests kept piling up in the waiting queue (`#queue-req` 24–32 on every rank), and `/health` failed from then on. At the time of the report the server had been hung for over 8 minutes. The watchdog is set to 3600 s, so it had not fired yet.

The main threads of PP0–PP3 are all blocked in the HiCache PP-sync drain. Each one waits on its previous round's `HICACHE_PP_SYNC` `isend` to the next PP rank, which that rank never receives:

```
Thread (idle): "MainThread"            # identical on PP0, PP1, PP2 and PP3
    _drain_async_work (unified_radix_cache.py:363)
    check_hicache_events (unified_radix_cache.py:3609)
    _process_hicache_events (scheduler.py:3824)
    event_loop_pp_disagg_prefill (scheduler_pp_mixin.py:295)
    decorate_context (torch/utils/_contextlib.py:124)
    _dispatch_event_loop_once (scheduler.py:6105)
    dispatch_event_loop (scheduler.py:6084)
    run_event_loop (scheduler.py:1960)
    run_scheduler_process (scheduler.py:6237)
```

PP0's other threads are idle. These are the `PPConsensusStore` receiver, the mooncake bootstrap thread and the transfer workers. PP4–PP7 run on the second node, and their stacks have not been captured yet; I will add them as soon as I have them. They will show what the ring is waiting on downstream of PP3.

The last scheduler log lines before the hang come from the same second (`08:07:05`). PP0–PP3 each launched one more 16k-token chunk (`#inflight-req` 2–3, `#pending-token` 744k / 325k / 121k / 18k on PP0 / PP1 / PP2 / PP3). Shortly before that, PP4–PP7 had logged a small prefix-hit batch (`#new-token: 291, #cached-token: 64`).

This looks like the failure described in #42433, although no storage backend is configured here. That PR reports the same `cache`-mode PP prefill setup getting stuck with PP0 in its send and one follower draining a HiCache queue whose length had diverged from PP0's. The single-round drain this hang sits in is also discussed in #45351, a performance report on the same code path.

## Reproduction

- Image: `lmsysorg/sglang:nightly-dev-cu13-20261020-ab580b2e`. It includes #38959 (`PPConsensusStore`). The build adds a timing-only probe to the PD prefill loop (CUDA events and `perf_counter` around the loop steps). The probe changes no communication or control flow, but it does shift `scheduler_pp_mixin.py` line numbers relative to upstream.
- Model: Kimi-K3, 1.5T, MXFP4 MoE.
- Prefill: one server with PP8 × TP1 over two 4-GPU GB300 nodes.

  ```
  --disaggregation-mode prefill --pp-size 8 --tp-size 1 --nnodes 2
  --chunked-prefill-size 16384 --max-prefill-tokens 16384 --pp-async-batch-depth 4
  --enable-hierarchical-cache --hicache-size 60 --hicache-write-policy write_through
  --hicache-io-backend kernel --hicache-mem-layout page_first   # host memory mode: cache (default), no storage backend
  --page-size 64 --kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3 --mem-fraction-static 0.88 --mamba-full-memory-ratio 0.5
  --moe-a2a-backend none --moe-runner-backend flashinfer_mxfp4
  --prefill-attention-backend trtllm_mla --decode-attention-backend cutedsl_mla
  --cuda-graph-backend-prefill disabled --context-length 524288
  SGLANG_PP_COMM_OVERLAP=1 SGLANG_PP_LAYER_PARTITION=11,11,12,12,12,12,12,11
  ```
- Decode: a separate TP4 / EP4 server. The P/D router sits in front of both.
- Load before the hang, all of which ran cleanly for ~33 minutes:
  - synthetic unique-prompt prefill (2k-token prompts, and a mix of 2k and 128k), up to ~31k tok/s;
  - `/flush_cache`;
  - then an `aiperf` multi-turn agentic trace replay at 32 concurrent sessions, which hung within about 2 minutes.

## Environment

4× GB300 per node, CUDA 13; the nightly image above.

items.title: [RFC]: Bounded-memory video sessions — KV retention for long-running streaming-input requests
items.author: nvbfalk
items.body_excerpt: ### Motivation. Continuous video understanding - a model that watches a live camera and emits a short reply per frame for hours (captioning, alerting, counting objects over time) - has no good shape in vLLM today. Each frame's reply has to be produced *in the context of the frames before it*, and with request-at-a-time serving the only way to supply that context is to resend it. That leaves two options, and both fail: - **One request per frame carrying the history.** Every frame re-uploads and re-processes everything the model has already seen. Work per frame grows with the age of the stream; the feed falls behind within minutes. Bounding the resent window caps the growth but pays a full window prefill on every frame. - **One long-lived request that never ends.** Two resources then grow without bound: GPU memory, since everything the model has seen stays resident for the life of the request (video is token-hungry - an hour at 2 fps is on the order of a million tokens of context); and sequence length, since the stream crosses the model's trained horizon within minutes to hours and output quality degrades past it. **vLLM already has the mechanism the second option needs.** Streaming input (#28973), introduced to power the realtime audio API and described in [Streaming Requests & Realtime API in vLLM](https://blog.vllm.ai/2026/01/31/streaming-requests-realtime-api.html), keeps one long-lived request alive while input arrives in chunks: context stays live in GPU memory between chunks, so appending a chunk costs only that chunk. That solves cost-per-frame. What it does not solve is what happens when a session runs for hours. The session's KV grows with every chunk and is released only when the session ends, and its position counter keeps climbing. The blog post says as much: > "additional care must be taken to avoid holding sessions open as they will be > blocking the corresponding memory from being used by other requests… > Currently, vLLM will not preempt "idle" streaming input sessions - this > behaviour will be improved in a future update." For audio-conversation lengths that is tolerable. For an always-on camera it is the whole problem. **Sessions exist; memory management for sessions does not.** This is not hypothetical demand. #50570 (RTSP live-stream captioning via a DeepStream/NVDEC backend) brings continuous streams into vLLM at the ingest layer and emits one caption per decoded segment; how context is carried across segments is left open. Ingest and session memory are the two halves of the same feature: that PR gets frames in, this proposal lets the model keep watching without unbounded memory. We would like to converge with it rather than build a second path. The design is a serving-side adaptation of [StreamingVLM](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.09608) (bounded KV, windowed inference over an unbounded stream) that fits vLLM's existing scheduler and KV manager - no attention-kernel changes and no model changes. ### Architecture A bounded streaming session is a long-lived autoregressive request that accepts successive multimodal updates. Each update contains a complete visual input, such as an image or short video clip. For every update: 1. The vision encoder processes the new visual input. 2. Its visual embeddings are appended to the existing decoder sequence. 3. The causal language decoder reuses the KV state produced by earlier updates. 4. The generated response is appended to the same session. The vision encoder is not itself streamed across updates. An update is treated as an atomic visual input: visual attention may operate across all patches or frames within that update, but a later update does not extend a previous vision-encoder invocation. The session therefore grows at the decoder level: instructions → visual update 1 → response 1 → visual update 2 → response 2 → visual update 3 → response 3 → ... Without retention, the decoder KV grows with every update. This RFC bounds that state by retaining the session instructions, recent visual and text segments, and selected generated history. Older decoder-KV ranges are evicted while the request remains live. Surviving tokens retain their original positions, avoiding modification of their cached keys. As positions approach the model's supported range, the remaining session context is consolidated through a fresh prefill with compact positions. This architecture provides bounded, stateful inference across independently encoded visual updates. It does not provide incremental execution inside a single vision-encoder invocation, and it does not apply to a model path that must jointly re-encode earlier visual inputs when a new update arrives. ### Model compatibility The architecture requires an append-stable model execution path: 1. The language decoder is autoregressive and causal. 2. Visual updates can be encoded independently, as described above. 3. The model runner and attention backend honor explicit logical positions after physical KV compaction, including potentially non-contiguous 1D-RoPE or mRoPE positions. 4. The retained session context can be reconstructed and replayed during consolidation. A path is not currently compatible if new visual input changes previously committed visual representations. Streaming-specific fine-tuning is not required to execute this mechanism on a compatible model path. ### Proposed Change. Give a streaming-input session a constant memory footprint no matter how long it runs. The design mirrors how a person watches a feed: keep the

items.title: [RFC]: fp8 KV cache gives little to no memory benefit on Mamba/GDN hybrid models
items.author: shivasathishs-rp
items.body_excerpt:
**TL;DR**
- `--kv-cache-dtype fp8` roughly doubles KV cache capacity on attention-only models (measured 2.00x), but on Mamba/GDN + attention hybrids it gives 1.84x at 32k context and 1.00x (no gain) at short context.
- Root cause is the known hybrid page-pinning behavior (#37121, #40696): the Mamba state is not quantized by `--kv-cache-dtype` and all groups share one uniform page, so the bf16 Mamba page pins bytes-per-block and the fp8 attention page cannot shrink the pool.
- Fix is parity work: quantize the Mamba state too (SGLang already does this at int8) and/or decouple per-group page size (SGLang/TRT-LLM/llama.cpp already use separate pools). This RFC contributes the fp8-capacity characterization plus wiring a fix into vLLM.

### Motivation.

fp8 KV cache is advertised as a ~2x capacity/concurrency lever. On Mamba/attention hybrids (Falcon-H1, Qwen3-Next, Granite-4, Jamba, Nemotron-H) that lever is mostly or entirely dead, and there is no caveat in the docs. Numbers below are from vLLM's own `get_kv_cache_configs`/`get_kv_cache_capacity` (offline, no forward pass; `gpu_memory_utilization=0.85`, `max_model_len=32768`, default `block_size`, A10G). For Qwen2.5-3B and Falcon-H1 the offline bf16 result reproduces the live-served `GPU KV cache size` exactly, which validates the method; gpt-oss-20b is offline-computed and not anchored to a live run.

| model | bf16 KV tokens | fp8 KV tokens | ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen2.5-3B (attention only, live-anchored) | 334,256 | 668,512 | **2.00x** |
| gpt-oss-20b (sliding-window + full, offline/unanchored) | 562,283 | 1,124,567 | **2.00x** |
| Falcon-H1-1.5B (Mamba + attention, live-anchored) | 603,229 | 1,111,381 | **1.84x** |

Falcon-H1 by context length: 512 tok 1.00x, 1024 tok 1.00x, 2048 tok 1.51x, 8192 tok 1.76x, 32768 tok 1.84x. Sliding window alone does not cause this (gpt-oss gets a clean 2.00x); the effect requires a non-attention group co-resident in the pool.

The mechanism is already filed. #37121 reports the ~7x KV memory over-estimation on hybrids: the attention block size is inflated up to the larger Mamba page, and the Mamba state is padded to match, so both grow to a common page. #40696 reports the prefix-caching consequence of the same block-size pinning. This RFC adds the fp8-capacity consequence and proposes the fix.

Why fp8 fails to help, concretely:
1. `get_mamba_state_dtype_from_config` returns bf16 regardless of `--kv-cache-dtype`, so the Mamba page is a fixed ~1.59 MB.
2. `get_uniform_page_size` asserts one page across all groups, and `_align_hybrid_block_size` (`vllm/platforms/interface.py`) enforces `attention_page >= mamba_page` by inflating the attention `block_size` (Falcon-H1: 1568 tokens at bf16, 3120 at fp8). The per-token attention page halves exactly under fp8 (1024 -> 512 B), so the block size roughly doubles (it lands one alignment step short of 2x), leaving the product pinned to the Mamba page.
3. Once pages are unified, `num_blocks` is effectively `available_memory // (uniform_page * num_groups)` (in code, `available_memory // bytes_per_block` where `bytes_per_block` is the max over groups of the summed page size). That uniform page is 1,605,632 B (bf16) vs 1,597,440 B (fp8) — essentially unchanged, so `num_blocks` moves only 405 -> 407. fp8's only gain comes from the larger block, dragged below 2x by the never-shrinking Mamba group and coarse block quantization (a short request fits in one attention block either way — the 1.00x rows).

### Proposed Change.

Two independent levers; either helps, together they recover the full 2x. Neither is novel — both exist in other engines — so the deliverable is the vLLM implementation plus the characterization above.

1. **Quantize the Mamba state alongside attention KV.** vLLM already exposes `--mamba-cache-dtype` / `--mamba-ssm-cache-dtype`, but the allowed values are only `auto/float32/float16/bfloat16` (no fp8 or int8), so today the state cannot be shrunk at all. This is the natural insertion point. SGLang ships state quantization at int8 (`--enable-int8-mamba-checkpoint`, `Int8CheckpointStore`, cited as ~2x prefix capacity), and Quamba2 (arXiv:2503.22879) quantizes the ssm_state at int8. Not yet done anywhere: fp8, and the conv_state (not just ssm_state). The recurrent path is the most quantization-sensitive component (Q-S5, arXiv:2406.09477), so this must ship with its own accuracy check (perplexity + one downstream task), not on an assumption of safety. Larger change: needs a quantized Mamba kernel path.

2. **Decouple per-group page size.** Relax the single-uniform-page invariant so an attention group keeps its smaller fp8 page instead of being inflated to the Mamba page; the pool tracks per-group bytes. This is what SGLang (separate `MambaPool`), TensorRT-LLM (separate cache managers), and llama.cpp (`llama_memory_hybrid`) already do via separate pools; academic cover in Jenga (SOSP 2025) and AVMP (preprint, arXiv:2605.22416). KV-cache-manager change only, no kernels.

Suggested phasing: (2) first as a self-contained KV-cache-manager PR that removes the pinning for the attention group (recovers most of the long-context gain, kernel-free). (1) as a follow-up that also shrinks the Mamba group, gated on the accuracy check. The characterization/probe can land as a test that asserts fp8 recovers ~2x on a small hybrid.

Out of scope: the sliding-window in-flight admission reserve (#54703, different mechanism) and block-pool logging (#54840).

### Feedback Period.

One week.

### CC List.

@heheda12345 @tdoublep

### Any Other Things.

Honest severity: the 1.00x rows are at short context, where KV is not the bottleneck, so the practical impact there is small. The impact that matters is long context, where fp8 under-delivers by ~8-16% on Mamba hybrids (1.84x vs 2.00x at 32k). Real and fixable, on a growing model class; not a crash or correctness bug.

Limitations of the measurement: one anchor hybrid (Falcon-H1) plus two attention-only controls. The mechanism is a

items.title: [RFC]: Programmable KV Cache: Composable Policies for Agentic Serving
items.author: zhhangBian
items.body_excerpt:
## TL;DR

This RFC defines a provider-neutral Programmable KV Cache abstraction in which routers supply session lifecycle and placement intent, composable engine policies propose retention, movement, and quota actions against a shared pressure snapshot, and the engine provides unified resource approval and completion contracts above existing connectors.

## Motivation

Agentic applications are not one continuous generation. A task can:

1. generate one model response;
2. call an external tool and pause;
3. create several child agents from the same context;
4. complete or abandon a branch;
5. resume on the same or another engine.

During a pause, the KV is often the most valuable prefix for the next request, yet it may have no active request reference and enter an ordinary LRU eviction order. During spatial contention, a non-critical request can consume capacity and evict a critical-path prefix. The next turn needs to load an external copy or recompute the context if no usable copy is available.

The [vLLM AgentX post](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-09-08-vllm-agentx) describes representative traffic: a median of 43 turns per session, a median 142K-token input and 444-token output, prefix-cache hit rates above 96%, and subagents in 44% of sessions. These patterns require a cache policy that can combine lifecycle information with local resource state.

## Existing foundations and related RFCs/PRs

### 1. Identity and events: associating multiple requests

[Identity RFC #48049](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/48049) separates session_id from request_id: the former persists across calls; the latter retains per-request output, cancellation, and scheduling semantics. Its implementation [#48048](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/48048) is merged and supplies typed session identity through the request path.

[Event PR #51381](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/51381) is merged. It adds the triggering session_id to GPU BlockStored and supports full reporting of prefixes hit by the current request. [#54325](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/54325) is also merged and corrects SimpleCPU offload event metadata and tier labels. These report cache activity; they do not automatically provide a complete session↔block index. [#50732](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/50732) still proposes BlockInactive to distinguish active references from reclaimable cache; inactivity does not mean session completion.

[#48501](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/48501) extends this direction with session-centric orchestration, continuation_id coordinates, event attribution, and publisher epochs. Logical coordinates help upper layers interpret cache activity, but must remain distinct from content hashes and physical copies. The first session triggering an event is not the exclusive owner of shared content.

### 2. Programmatic KV: existing actions, indexes, and execution boundaries

[#51428](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/51428) is the overarching architecture proposal. It defines Share, Prefetch, Demote, Pin, and Retain, and explicitly allows engine acceptance, clipping, deferral, and rejection. It considers both engine-local SessionPrefixIndex and external orchestrator resolution, including many-to-many associations, cache-hit membership, and bidirectional outcomes.

This establishes important foundations. We do not claim engine authority or action results as unique additions. The remaining contract is how multiple local policies use common observations, produce executable plans, share finite capacity, and connect those plans to existing connectors.

[#52113](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/52113) starts from application events. It proposes agent_hint, a SessionAwareManager (SAM), parent/child sessions, TTLs, and context management. SAM owns detailed associations and updates block metadata through a guarded KVCacheManager interface; the proposal also discusses a remote SPM adapter and a direct connector-capability direction. It provides a broader lifecycle model than a retention parameter and already recognizes remote observation and completion.

The coordination question is not whether a separate manager is valid. It is whether agent_hint and KvHintsEnvelope become competing ingress contracts, whether SAM and another session index duplicate tracking, and whether concrete fields, timers, or adapters unnecessarily constrain the public interface.

### 3. Retention: expressing value over token ranges

[#37003](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/37003) proposes token-range priority/duration to distinguish shared prefixes, tool-wait contexts, and lower-value tails. Its implementation [#38514](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/38514) remains open. It keeps the existing LRU and adds a priority queue and TTL handling for annotated blocks, with retention_scope semantics.

Its strength is separating cache priority from request scheduling priority and directly addressing victim order. Its scope is primarily GPU retention; it does not independently choose request-free prefetch timing, a retention backend, or competition with future request capacity. This RFC adopts range/priority/TTL semantics, permits replacement algorithms as policy implementations, and retains independent declarations for different sessions’ lifetimes.

### 4. Common envelope: unified ingress without rebuilding transport

[#53421](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/53421) defines KvHintsEnvelope and KvHintAction. The envelope carries protocol_version, message_id, and actions; actions carry identity, type, version, and payload. [#53423](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/53423) remains open and provides Python/Rust typed plumbing and kv_hints propagation. Its description includes public HTTP/gRPC fields, but it neither defines nor executes individual actions.

That is an intentional transport boundary. We reuse it and define the cache-operation, policy-input,

items.author: nerminekabadou
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment

<details>
<summary>Environment</summary>

```text
vLLM: main @ 775fefa (2026-10-14), run from source
Python: 3.13.7, PyTorch 2.14.1+cpu, transformers 5.19.0
OS: Windows 11 (CPU only)
```

`collect_env.py` asserts Linux, so I couldn't run it here. The bug is in pure-Python parsing code (`vllm/tool_parsers/olmo3_tool_parser.py`) and doesn't depend on hardware.

</details>


### 🐛 Describe the bug

`Olmo3PythonicToolParser.extract_tool_calls` strips the wrapper tags with a non-greedy regex:

```python
match = re.search(r"<function_calls>(.*?)</function_calls>", model_output, re.DOTALL)
```

If a string argument contains `</function_calls>`, the match stops there. What's left isn't valid Python, so the parser returns the whole output as `content` and no tool call is made. Streaming parses the same output correctly, so the two modes disagree.

A realistic trigger is an agent writing docs or a prompt template that mentions the tag:

```python
from vllm.tokenizers import get_tokenizer
from vllm.tool_parsers import ToolParserManager
from tests.tool_parsers.utils import run_tool_extraction

tok = get_tokenizer("Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B")  # tokenizer only matters for streaming
out = ("<function_calls>write_file(path='README.md', "
       "content='Calls are wrapped in <function_calls>...</function_calls>.')"
       "</function_calls>")
for streaming in (False, True):
    parser = ToolParserManager.get_tool_parser("olmo3")(tok)
    print(streaming, run_tool_extraction(parser, out, streaming=streaming))
```

Output:

```
False -> content = the whole output, tool_calls = []
True  -> content = None, tool_calls = [write_file(path="README.md", content="Calls are wrapped in <function_calls>...</function_calls>.")]
```

Same bug class as #45167 (Hermes, `</tool_call>` inside a JSON string). I'll send a fix.

items.title: [Bug]: v0.25.1 streaming input beyond max_model_len produces negative scheduled token counts and crashes V2 runner
items.author: Adeshen
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment

Recorded environment from the GPU runs on 2026-10-19 (this is a summary of saved evidence, not newly collected `collect_env.py` output):

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| vLLM | 0.25.1; recorded commit `752a3a504485790a2e8491cacbb35c137339ad34` |
| Model runner | V2, selected by the installed configuration; logs say `Using V2 Model Runner` |
| GPU | One NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090, 24564 MiB |
| Driver | 595.80; `nvidia-smi` reports CUDA compatibility 13.2 |
| Python | 3.12 (patch version not captured in these artifacts) |
| PyTorch | 2.11.0+cu130, from the same host/environment's earlier run that day |
| Model | Qwen3-0.6B, local directory `/model/ModelScope/Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B` |
| Engine settings | `max_model_len=64`, `enforce_eager=True`, `gpu_memory_utilization=0.3`, TP=1 |
| Sampling | `temperature=0`; no speculative decoding |

The installed Python sources were checked against the recorded source snapshot. Native binaries were not rebuilt for this report. The engine logs record `revision=None`; this report does not claim an explicitly pinned model revision argument.

### Describe the bug

On vLLM 0.25.1, a single request supplied through `AsyncLLM.add_request` with an async generator of `StreamingInput` chunks can exceed the accumulated session length limit. The scheduler then emits **negative scheduled token counts** (`-14` and `-36` in two saved GPU runs). The V2 runner fails at `assert num_tokens > 0`, EngineCore reports a fatal error, and the caller receives `EngineDeadError`.

Each input chunk is individually shorter than `max_model_len`. The failure occurs after the second chunk is submitted to the same request, after the first output has been received. This is a real model execution, with no monkeypatch of the production scheduler or runner.

#### Related issue and proposed fix

- Related issue: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/42489 — previously reported accumulated resumable-session prompt overflow, with a different failure in `gpu_input_batch.add_request`.
- Related fix PR: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/42502 — proposes guarding resumable streaming updates against `max_model_len` overflow.

This report adds **v0.25.1 + V2 runner evidence and the negative scheduler counts** for the same apparent defect family. It does not claim a newly discovered independent root cause. PR #42502 has **not** been applied or tested in these runs; this is not evidence that the proposed fix fails.

### Reproduction

The exact executed runner, its helper, both configurations, and the full stdout/stderr logs are included below. Save `probe.py`, `prepared_probe.py`, and one configuration as `cases.json` in the same directory. Set `cases.json`'s `model` to an existing local Qwen3-0.6B directory.

Run once with configuration A, then run a **fresh Python process/engine** with configuration B:

```bash
RQ4_E2E_AUTHORIZED=1 python -u probe.py --execute
```

`RQ4_E2E_AUTHORIZED` is only a local guard in the supplied test harness, not a vLLM setting.

The essential sequence is:

1. Construct `AsyncLLM` with `max_model_len=64` and eager execution.
2. Encode `"The capital of France is"` without special tokens and repeat the token sequence.
3. Yield the first token chunk for one request.
4. Wait until `collector.get()` returns the first output, then release an `asyncio.Event` so the generator yields the second chunk.
5. Let the input generator finish and collect outputs/errors.

### Observed results

| Run / case | First chunk | Second chunk | `max_tokens` | Final outcome | Scheduler dump at failure |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|---|
| A / baseline | 20 | 10 | 4 | Completed; client reports 30 prompt tokens and 8 output tokens | No failure |
| A / target | 40 | 30 | 8 | `EngineDeadError` after second chunk | `num_computed_tokens=[77]`, `total_num_scheduled_tokens=-14` |
| B / larger overflow, fresh engine | 50 | 40 | 10 | `EngineDeadError` after second chunk | `num_computed_tokens=[99]`, `total_num_scheduled_tokens=-36` |

The third case listed in configuration A was **not run** because the target had already killed that engine. Configuration B executes that case separately. These are two failing configurations across two engine launches, not a statistical reliability estimate.

The client-side prompt/output lengths and the scheduler's internal computed-token count are different observations and should not be conflated.

The core failure in both runs is:

```text
vllm/v1/worker/gpu/model_runner.py:1174, in execute_model
    input_batch = self.prepare_inputs(scheduler_output, batch_desc)
vllm/v1/worker/gpu/model_runner.py:845, in prepare_inputs
    assert num_tokens > 0
AssertionError

vllm.v1.engine.exceptions.EngineDeadError:
    EngineCore encountered an issue. See stack trace (above) for the root cause.
```

Full tracebacks, scheduler dumps, startup configuration, and final result records are in the raw logs below.

### Expected behavior

Reject the accumulated over-limit update, or finish the affected request with the appropriate length outcome, while keeping the engine healthy. No negative token count should reach the model runner.

### Source-level explanation

At the tested commit:

- [`_update_request_as_session`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/752a3a504485790a2e8491cacbb35c137339ad34/vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py#L1209-L1254) folds the session state and appends the new prompt without an accumulated `max_model_len` check inside that function.
- The [running-request scheduling cap](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/752a3a504485790a2e8491cacbb35c137339ad34/vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py#L482-L489) uses `max_model_len - request.num_computed_tokens - num_sampled_tokens_per_step`.
- The following [zero-token check](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/752a3a504485790a2e8491cacbb35c137339ad34/vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py#L514) checks `== 0`, which does not catch a negative result.

For these non-diffusion runs, the cap arithmetic matches

items.title: [Bug]: Hermes tool parser streaming silently drops all content after a stray <tool_call> marker in prose
items.author: xiaohaifeng1999
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment
The output of python collect_env.py ```text vLLM `main` @ `2d40c0609f` (2026-10-23). Parser-level reproduction: CPU-only, no GPU or model weights needed (`hermes_tool_parser.py` is unchanged on main since the Oct 10 file move in #60522). ```
### 🐛 Describe the bug When serving with `--tool-call-parser hermes` and `stream=true`, all text after a literal `` in ordinary prose is silently dropped — e.g. when the model quotes the tag while explaining or demonstrating the tool-call format. The non-streaming path returns the full text as content, so the two paths disagree. Model output (reaches the parser verbatim): ``` The literal tag opens a call. Done. ``` | path | content | tool_calls | |---|---|---| | non-streaming | `The literal tag opens a call. Done.` | none | | streaming | `The literal ` | none | `' tag opens a call. Done.'` never reaches the client. ### To Reproduce From a vllm checkout (`PYTHONPATH=.`): ```python from tests.tool_parsers.utils import run_tool_extraction from vllm.tokenizers import get_tokenizer from vllm.tool_parsers.hermes_tool_parser import Hermes2ProToolParser tokenizer = get_tokenizer("Qwen/Qwen3-32B") # any tokenizer works model_output = "The literal tag opens a call. Done." # The text round-trips through the tokenizer, i.e. it can reach the # parser verbatim as decoded deltas from a real model. assert tokenizer.decode(tokenizer.encode(model_output)) == model_output for streaming in (False, True): parser = Hermes2ProToolParser(tokenizer) # fresh state per path content, tool_calls = run_tool_extraction( parser, model_output, streaming=streaming ) print(f"streaming={streaming}: content={content!r} tool_calls={tool_calls}") ``` Output: ``` streaming=False: content='The literal tag opens a call. Done.' tool_calls=[] streaming=True: content='The literal ' tool_calls=[] ``` ### Root cause Streaming path of `vllm/tool_parsers/hermes_tool_parser.py`: 1. `_extract_content` ends the sendable-content window at the first start token (`sendable_idx = current_text.index(self.tool_call_start_token)`); everything after it is held back as a prospective tool-call region. 2. `_extract_tool_call_jsons` treats that region as a call body; since it contains no `"name"`, no deltas are ever produced for it. 3. There is no end-of-stream recovery: other parsers implement a `finish_streaming` flush hook (e.g. `k2_horizon_tool_parser.py` and the engine `Parser` base class), but `Hermes2ProToolParser` does not, so the held-back text is never returned. Non-streaming is unaffected: the region fails `json.loads` and the parser falls back to returning the whole output as content (pinned by `test_hermes_parser_non_streaming_tool_call_invalid_json`). ### Expected behavior When no tool call is extracted, streaming should agree with non-streaming and return the full text as content. At minimum, text after a stray marker must not be silently dropped. ### Related - #58227 — identical failure mode in the Qwen3 **engine** parser (unclosed opener in prose holds tool state); fixed there in October. The legacy Hermes parser is a separate implementation and got no such recovery. - #47903 — same parser, adjacent divergence when a call is truncated by `max_tokens` (still open). This report is the prose variant: non-streaming is correct here, so it is pure content loss on the streaming path. - #45167 (+ PRs #45310 / #48353 / #55848) — closing marker inside JSON strings. Start-tag detection stays a plain `str.find` in all of them (explicitly so in #55848), so this bug survives every in-flight fix. - Same class in other parsers: #56658 (Qwen3), #60703 (GLM-4.7), #57541 (fenced blocks). - The `streaming`-parametrized `run_tool_extraction` pattern from #56270 is the natural regression-test template. ### Suggested direction Flush held-back text that never became a tool call as content at end of stream (a `finish_streaming`-style hook for Hermes), mirroring the finish-time recovery taken for the engine parsers in #58227. Happy to submit a PR once the desired behavior is confirmed. AI assistance was used to build the differential harness that found this and to draft this report; I reviewed the findings and ran the reproduction myself on main @ 2d40c0609f. ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.
