items.author: mikicvi
items.body_excerpt:
### Name and Version

./llama-server --version
version: 0.4.0-dev (build 254, commit 6a1a922)
built with GNU 13.3.0 for Linux x86_64


### Operating systems

Windows, Linux

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

llama-server, libllama (core library)

### Command line

```shell
# Linux server
cmake -B build -DGGML_CUDA=ON -DGGML_RPC=ON && cmake --build build --config Release -j$(nproc)

llama-server \
  --model Qwen3.8-27B-UD-IQ4_XS.gguf \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8081 \
  --ctx-size 98304 -ngl 99 \
  --spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-ngl 99 --spec-draft-n-max 2 \
  --cache-type-k q8_0 --cache-type-v q8_0 \
  --spec-draft-type-k q8_0 --spec-draft-type-v q8_0 \
  --flash-attn on \
  --rpc <windows-host>:50052 -dev RPC0,CUDA0 -ts 0.49,0.51 \
  --threads 8 --jinja -b 2048 -ub 1024

# Windows server
cmake -B build -DGGML_CUDA=ON -DGGML_RPC=ON -G 
cmake --build build --config Release

./ggml-rpc-server.exe -H 0.0.0.0 -d CUDA0 -p 50052
```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

After updating both ends from bb4caa7 (21-08-2026) to 6a1a922, generation with draft-mtp over an RPC tensor split dropped ~25–30%. Isolation measurements (same 1209-token prompt / 1024-token generation benchmark throughout)
| Config | `bb4caa7` | `6a1a922` |
|---|---|---|
| draft-mtp depth 2 (flags above) | 27–32 tok/s | 21.3 tok/s |
| draft-mtp depth 1, re-tuned split 0.52/0.48 | — | 22.6–24.4 tok/s |
| no MTP (raw dense decode, same split) | ~17–18 tok/s | 17.5 tok/s |
| draft acceptance (server stats) | ~0.68–0.80 | 0.737–0.832 |
| mean accepted length | ~1.7–1.8 | 1.74–1.83 |

Control point:  a 31B dense model (Muse Glimmer) (no speculative decoding) on the identical RPC split, flags, and both commits measures 17.66 tok/s before and after so that part seems fine to me. This should rule out the RPC transport for single-forward decode, the tensor split, and sampling.

Repro: run the commands above on both commits (both ends must be same-era due to the RPC protocol bump), generate 1k tokens, compare `eval time` in slot timings and the `draft acceptance` stats. 
- From what I can tell, acceptance and raw decode are unchanged, so i think the finger can be pointed at MTP changes. 
- Possibly related: graph/compute buffer sizing grew in the same window - ctx 98304 with `-b 2048 -ub 1024` loaded on `bb4caa7` on a 12GB device but fails graph reserve with CUDA OOM on `6a1a922` until the tensor split is re-tuned, or CTX made smaller.


I am happy to test/build any specific build/version.

Model: unsloth Qwen3.8-27B UD-IQ4_XS GGUF (14.25 GB) with embedded MTP heads. 
Hardware: Linux = i5-12600H, RTX A2000 12GB, 96GB DDR5 5600Mt; windows = RTX 3080 10GB, AMD 5800x3d, 32gb DDR4, 2.5GbE LAN between both.
Linux server is only used as AI server, windows desktop is used only to supplement gpu compute for dense models. 

### First Bad Commit

Not bisected-windows builds take over 30 minutes :( . Regression window is `bb4caa7` (21-08-2026 good) to `6a1a922` (05-09-2026 bad). 

Some candidates in the window, but I can't confirm yet.
- `2c6b141` 2026-08-22 `common : fix draft-mtp with embeddings (#26352, #27299)` this one touches the draft-MTP loop directly and the timeline fits
	- RPC protocol bump to 6.0.0 landed during this time and per-call overhead would be amplified by the speculative loop's higher exchange count
- `662a0b0` 2026-08-31 `spec : fuse the DFlash encoder into the KV cache injection (#27310)`

### Relevant log output

items.title: Eval bug: [SYCL][mtmd] llama-mtmd-cli aborts with 0xC0000409 after threadpool init on Intel Arc Pro B70 (Windows) — before image encode
items.author: matthew-rutledge-dev
items.body_excerpt:
### Name and Version

Official Windows SYCL binary **b11064** (`llama-b11064-bin-win-sycl-x64` / local tree `E:\llama-cpp-sycl\b11064`).
Binary used: `llama-mtmd-cli.exe`.

### Operating systems

Windows 11

### GGML backends

SYCL (Level Zero)

### Hardware

Intel Arc Pro B70, 32 GB VRAM (Xe2 / Battlemage). Dual-GPU host also has an NVIDIA RTX 5080; Arc runs were launched with:

```
ONEAPI_DEVICE_SELECTOR=level_zero:0
ZES_ENABLE_SYSMAN=1
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=-1
```

### Models

- `gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf` (Unsloth)
- `mmproj-BF16.gguf` (same model set)

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

`llama-mtmd-cli` on Windows SYCL **aborts with `STATUS_STACK_BUFFER_OVERRUN` (`0xC0000409` / exit `-1073740791`)** roughly **12s after** logging `llama threadpool init, n_threads = 24`, **before any image encode**, with **empty stdout**.

**Text `llama-cli` on the same GGUF (no mmproj) passes** on this B70 SYCL build.

Reproduced on a dedicated re-run (2026-09-21) with the same fixture + prompt; wall ~18.15s; abort reproduced yes.

Minimal shape used:

```text
llama-mtmd-cli.exe ^
  -m gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf ^
  --mmproj mmproj-BF16.gguf ^
  --image phase-b-shapes-42.png ^
  -p "Describe this image in one short sentence. Name colors and any numbers you see." ^
  -ngl 99 -n 128 --perf
```

Also failed previously with `--no-mmproj-offload` (same abort signature).

### Closest known issue

Closest match by **exit code + post-threadpool timing**:

- https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/issues/27128 — Win SYCL, dies right after threadpool init, exit `-1073740791`. That report shows Level Zero `UR_RESULT_ERROR_INVALID_VALUE` on VMM `phys->map`. **Our stderr is quieter**: no UR/SYCL error line — only load warnings, then threadpool init, then silent abort.

**Question for maintainers:** do the workarounds suggested on #27128 apply to the **mtmd** path as well?

- `GGML_SYCL_ENABLE_VMM=0`
- `--no-mmap` / `--load-mode none`

We have **not** re-tested those env/flags yet on this mtmd lane (filing first). Happy to try and report back.

Related B70 SYCL context (different symptom — garbage output, not this abort):
- https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/issues/21893 (`GGML_SYCL_DISABLE_OPT=1`)

### First Bad Commit

Unknown — observed on official **b11064** win-sycl. Not bisected.

### Relevant log output

```console
0.01.491.674 W load: control-looking token:      1 '<eos>' was not control-type; this is probably a bug in the model. its type will be overridden
0.01.491.986 W load: control-looking token:     50 '<|tool_response>' was not control-type; this is probably a bug in the model. its type will be overridden
0.01.493.022 W load: control-looking token:    212 '</s>' was not control-type; this is probably a bug in the model. its type will be overridden
0.01.543.326 W load: special_eog_ids contains '<|tool_response>', removing '</s>' token from EOG list
0.12.395.642 I cmn          init: llama threadpool init, n_threads = 24
```

(process then exits `-1073740791` / `0xC0000409`; stdout empty)

### Run card (local bakeoff)

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Experience | bakeoff img_describe (one short sentence: colors + numbers) |
| Harness | llama-mtmd-cli (one-shot CLI) |
| Tools | `--image` fixture (no tool-calling) |
| Gateway | none (direct CLI) |
| Serving | llama.cpp CLI |
| Engine | llama.cpp SYCL b11064 |
| Weights | gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf + mmproj-BF16.gguf |
| Hardware / Silicon | Intel Arc Pro B70 (`level_zero:0`; `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=-1`) |
| load_s | ~12.4 to threadpool init log; died before usable load complete |
| ttft / tok/s / VRAM | n/a / n/a / unknown |
| score | **fail** — empty stdout; crash |
| abort_reproduced | **yes** — exit `-1073740791` (`0xC0000409`) |
| wall_s | 18.15 |
| notes | Same signature as prior abort. Text lane on same GGUF historically pass. Co-resident llama-server + ollama left running on host. |

comments.author: matthew-rutledge-dev
comments.body:
Update: tried the #27128 workaround on this **mtmd** path.

Env added (otherwise identical to the report):
```
GGML_SYCL_ENABLE_VMM=0
ONEAPI_DEVICE_SELECTOR=level_zero:0
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=-1
```

Result: **abort reproduced**. Exit still `-1073740791` / `0xC0000409`. Wall ~12.5s. Empty stdout. Same stderr ending at `llama threadpool init, n_threads = 24` (~7.95s into the log timestamps). `GGML_SYCL_ENABLE_VMM=0` did **not** change the failure on `llama-mtmd-cli` + gemma-4-26B-A4B + mmproj-BF16 on Arc Pro B70 / b11064 win-sycl.

comments.author: matthew-rutledge-dev
comments.body:
Update: co-resident isolation + mmap-off attempt.

1. Stopped `llama-server` + Ollama before the run.
2. `--no-mmap` is **not accepted** on `llama-mtmd-cli` b11064 win-sycl (`error: invalid argument: --no-mmap`). Used the documented replacement `--load-mode none` (`-lm none`).

Result: **abort reproduced**. Exit `-1073740791` / `0xC0000409`, wall ~9.3s, empty stdout. Same stderr ending at `llama threadpool init, n_threads = 24`.

So neither co-resident contention nor `--load-mode none` changes this mtmd/SYCL crash on Arc Pro B70.

items.title: [RFC]: Hot Standby Mode for Master Service Metadata High Availability
items.author: Libotry
items.body_excerpt: ## Introduction To address the issue where all metadata is lost after a master service failure and recovery, this solution proposes a **hot-standby synchronization mechanism** and a **hybrid approach** combining hot standby with snapshots, ensuring rapid data recovery following a master service failure. ## Motivation The current HA (High Availability) mode only supports rapid restart of the master service after a failure but cannot guarantee fast data recovery. The pain points of the current HA mode are as follows: | Issue | Impact | Severity | | -------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ | ---------- | | **Complete loss of metadata after Leader failure** | All KV cache location information is lost and must be rebuilt | 🔴 Critical | | **Follower lacks data pre-warming** | After successful election, the new Leader must start serving from scratch | 🟠 Medium | | **Long recovery time** | Relies on clients to re-register; may take several minutes to tens of minutes | 🟠 Medium | | **Service unavailability window** | Requests cannot be processed during Leader failover | 🟡 Low | ## Goals: 1. **Near-zero RPO**: Minimize the data loss window 2. **Fast failover**: Achieve second-level RTO (Recovery Time Objective) 3. **Data consistency guarantee**: Ensure correct synchronization between primary and standby 4. **Verifiability**: Include mechanisms to validate data integrity 5. **Low performance overhead**: Avoid impacting normal business operations ## Proposal ### 1. Core Design Approach **Use etcd as an intermediate reliability component to implement OpLog primary-standby synchronization**: - **OpLog Mechanism**: Primary Master records all state change operations to OpLog - **etcd Storage**: OpLog is written to etcd, leveraging etcd's strong consistency and persistence capabilities - **Watch Mechanism**: Standby Master receives OpLog in real-time through etcd Watch mechanism - **Ordering Guarantee**: Guarantee operation order through global sequence_id and key-level key_sequence_id ### 2. Architecture Design #### (1) Overall Architecture The overall architecture diagram shows the interaction relationships between Primary Master, etcd Cluster, and Standby Master: **Architecture Description**: - **Primary Master**: Handles client requests, records OpLog and writes to etcd - **etcd Cluster**: Acts as intermediate storage, providing strong consistency and Watch mechanism - **Standby Master**: Receives OpLog in real-time by watching etcd and applies to local metadata store #### (2) Data Flow Diagram The data flow diagram shows the complete flow from Client request to Standby synchronization: **Flow Description**: a. Client sends `PutEnd` request to Primary Master b. Primary Master records operation through `OpLogManager`, generating sequence_id c. `EtcdOpLogStore` writes OpLog to etcd d. etcd notifies Standby Master through Watch mechanism e. `OpLogWatcher` receives events and passes to `OpLogApplier` f. `OpLogApplier` checks order and applies to Standby's metadata store #### (3) Failover Sequence The failover sequence diagram shows the complete process from Primary failure to Standby promotion to Primary: **Flow Description**: a. **Normal Operation**: Primary maintains Lease, Standby continuously synchronizes OpLog through Watch b. **Primary Failure**: Primary's Lease expires, etcd notifies Standby c. **Standby Promotion**: Stop Standby service, initialize Lease, clean expired metadata, start leader election ### 3. Core Component Design #### (1) OpLogManager (Primary Side) **Responsibilities**: - Record all state change operations (PUT_END, PUT_REVOKE, REMOVE) - Generate global sequence_id and key-level key_sequence_id - Maintain memory buffer (for fast queries) **Key Methods**: ```cpp class OpLogManager { uint64_t Append(OpType type, const std::string& key, const std::string& payload = ""); std::vector GetEntriesSince(uint64_t since_seq_id, size_t limit = 1000) const; uint64_t GetLastSequenceId() const; }; ``` #### (2) EtcdOpLogStore (Primary Side) **Responsibilities**: - Write OpLog to etcd - Update latest sequence_id - Record snapshot corresponding sequence_id - Clean up old OpLog **etcd Key Design**: - OpLog Entry: `mooncake-store/oplog/{cluster_id}/{sequence_id}` - Latest Sequence ID: `mooncake-store/oplog/{cluster_id}/latest` - Snapshot Sequence ID: `mooncake-store/oplog/{cluster_id}/snapshot/{snapshot_id}/sequence_id` #### (3) OpLogWatcher (Standby Side) **Responsibilities**: - Watch etcd OpLog changes - Read historical OpLog (for initial synchronization) - Process Watch events and pass to OpLogApplier **Key Methods**: ```cpp class OpLogWatcher { void Start(); void Stop(); bool ReadOpLogSince(uint64_t start_seq_id, std::vector& entries); }; ``` #### (4) OpLogApplier (Standby Side) **Responsibilities**: - Apply OpLog Entry to local metadata store - Check global and key-level order - Handle sequence number discontinuities and out-of-order cases - Periodically clean up key_sequence_map_ (memory optimization) **Key Methods**: ```cpp class OpLogApplier { bool ApplyOpLogEntry(const OpLogEntry& entry); bool CheckSequenceOrder(const OpLogEntry& entry); void CleanupStaleKey

comments.body: ### 1. Problem & Assumptions #### 1.1 Problem After a `Delete` (or eviction) on the primary master: - The primary frees a replica’s memory (returns buffer to allocator’s free list). - The `Delete` event is **not** replicated to the standby master. - The primary then crashes; the standby is promoted to new master. - The new master still believes that this replica exists, and returns its address to clients. - That buffer may already have been **reused by another object**, or may still contain **logically deleted data**. We must **never** return data that belongs to some other key/object/tenant due to buffer reuse, even if we allow some metadata loss. #### 1.2 Accepted Semantic Constraints We explicitly accept the following semantics: - **Metadata / delete operations may be lost across failover**: - A delete acknowledged by the old master may be “rolled back” after failover. - That is acceptable because the KV cache can be recomputed. - **Hard safety requirement**: - It is strictly forbidden to read data that **belongs to another key/object/tenant** as if it were the requested key. - In other words: buffer reuse must not cause **cross-key contamination**. Under these constraints, it is acceptable that: - A key that was “deleted” on the old master may reappear after failover (logical delete rolled back). - But it is **not** acceptable to read someone else’s data due to buffer reuse. --- ### 2. Idea We upgrade each replica from a “raw pointer” into a **versioned capability**: - In-memory layout of a replica buffer becomes: - The master generates a **64-bit version** for each successful `Put` of a key. - This `version` is stored: - In `ObjectMetadata` on the master. - In the `ReplicaDescriptor` returned to clients. - In the first 8 bytes of the actual buffer in the KV store. - On **Get**, the client always verifies: - Read the first 8 bytes of the buffer. - Compare with the expected version from `ReplicaDescriptor`. - If versions match → buffer still belongs to this key/epoch → safe to read payload. - If versions differ → buffer was reused by someone else → mark this replica invalid, do not use it. Thus, even if the physical address is reused for a different object, the client will detect it and reject the replica. --- ### 3. Data Model Changes #### 3.1 Version Type ```cpp using Version = uint64_t; ``` Version can be constructed as: - High bits: timestamp (e.g., microseconds since epoch). - Low bits: per-node monotonic sequence ID. Requirements: - For a single master process, each successful `Put` for a given key gets a **unique, monotonically increasing** version. - Version collisions are practically impossible within a process lifetime. #### 3.2 Replica Descriptor Extension Extend `Replica::Descriptor` (or equivalent) to carry version information: On `PutStart`, the master generates `version`, stores it in metadata, and includes it in each replica descriptor. --- ### 4. Write Path (Put) Design #### 4.1 Master: PutStart 1. Client invokes `Put(key, slices, config)`. 2. `MasterService::PutStart(key, slice_lengths, config)`: - Validates input. - Allocates replicas as it does today (segments, buffers, etc.). - Generates a new `Version version = MakeVersion()` for this key. - Stores `version` in `ObjectMetadata` for this key. - Fills `ReplicaDescriptor.version = version` for each allocated replica. - Returns the list of descriptors to the client. All replicas of the same key for this `Put` share the same version. #### 4.2 Client: Writing to Store We enhance `TransferWrite` to enforce the following **write order** per replica: 1. Write **8-byte version header** at `buffer_address`. 2. Write **payload** at `buffer_address + 8` for length `size`. There are two implementation options: - **Option A: Two-step write** (simpler): - First,

comments.author: ykwd
comments.body:
Thanks for sharing the proposal. Unfortunately, this approach is not safe and does not actually guarantee the hard safety requirement you described, for two reasons:

First, RDMA reads and writes do not provide ordering and atomicity guarantees, which breaks the version-only validation scheme. In your design, correctness relies on the assumption that the first 8 bytes (the version) and the payload are written and observed atomically and in order. That assumption does not hold.

Second, the allocator does not guarantee alignment between successive allocations, which makes the embedded-version assumption invalid. Your scheme assumes that when a buffer is freed and later reused, the next allocation will reuse the same start address and layout, so that the version stored in the first 8 bytes corresponds exactly to the logical object boundary.

items.title: [Roadmap] SGLang dLLM Serving
items.author: rwang5203
items.body_excerpt:
# Goal

This roadmap continues #14199, initiated by @ClawSeven, and builds on the community's work toward robust, efficient block-diffusion serving in SGLang.

Fixes for crashes and wrong results on main come before new features. Full-sequence models get baseline compatibility. Checked items record merged work. Unchecked items track remaining work or evaluation. Phases can overlap.

# Roadmap

### Phase 1: Correctness and request lifecycle

- [ ] Fail early on unsupported configurations.

  - [ ] Refuse speculative decoding, two-batch overlap, unsupported deterministic backends, and logprob requests. #43452
  - [ ] Reject unknown algorithm configuration keys. #44385
  - [ ] Refuse or support attention data parallelism, which crashes today.
  - [ ] Refuse or fix the FA3 attention backend, which crashes on the first request.
  - [ ] Reject sampling and grammar fields that the selected algorithm does not apply.

- [ ] Harden request lifecycle and caching.

  - [x] Block-level radix caching. #18724
  - [x] Retain block KV and request slots. #27877
  - [x] Keep one request row across FDFO blocks. #42846
  - [x] Preserve prompt tails and literal mask tokens across prefix reuse. @0z5a #39592
  - [ ] Retract requests held between blocks on a retracting pause. #45227
  - [ ] Apply the waiting timeout to requests queued for dLLM scheduling. @lsnchow #42453
  - [ ] Apply the running timeout between denoising rounds. @lsnchow #43560
  - [ ] Bound staging admission by block size and available capacity. #32992
  - [ ] Fix the radix double count that stops an idle scheduler. #35781
  - [ ] Qualify aborted FDFO cleanup and retained KV recovery.
  - [ ] Qualify committed streaming, EOS/stops, cancellation, and final assembly. @zxr-creator
  - [ ] Define opt-in provisional output separately from committed streaming.

### Phase 2: Scheduling, prefill, and CUDA graphs

- [ ] Complete shared scheduling support.

  - [x] Dynamic batching. #14883
  - [x] Prefill/decode separation. #17484
  - [x] Algorithm-independent FDFO and early block departure. #27551
  - [ ] FDFO + LowConfidence overlap scheduling. @Betelgeu #40756
  - [ ] Extend overlap to other algorithms after state-lifetime qualification.
  - [ ] Mixed prefill/decode rounds. #33196
  - [ ] Derive the default running-request count and graph capture sizes from available memory instead of serving one request at a time.
  - [ ] Refine scheduling interfaces and isolate model behavior.

- [ ] Expand attention and prefill support.

  - [ ] Multi-block pure prefill in eager mode. #31586

  - [ ] CUDA graphs for multi-block prefill through generic padded buckets.
  - [ ] Custom and block-causal masks across backends.
  - [ ] Native block-extend attention. FlashInfer #2722

- [ ] Extend CUDA graph coverage.

  - [ ] Piecewise prefill graphs on compatible backends.
  - [ ] Qualify variable-length prefill and graph buckets.

### Phase 3: Models, decoding, and backends

- [ ] Expand model support.

  - [x] LLaDA2.0 model family. #12588
  - [x] SDAR dense and MoE models. #19044
  - [x] LLaDA2.2 block routing. #31768
  - [x] LLaDA2.2 insertion/deletion decoding. #31773
  - [ ] LLaDA2.2 routing and editing on Ascend. #32280
  - [ ] Qualify LLaDA2.2 mini and 128K context with a documented launch command.
  - [ ] Read block size, mask id, and default algorithm from checkpoint metadata.
  - [ ] Route `sglang serve` dLLM launches to the LLM runtime. #40942
  - [ ] Nemotron Labs Diffusion with its autoregressive, block-diffusion, and LinearSpec modes.
  - [ ] Dream full-sequence baseline. #36881
  - [ ] Qualify the Fast-dLLM v2 continuation and batching support. @SensenGao #22156
  - [ ] GFusion model support. #29776

- [ ] Complete DiffusionGemma serving.

  - [x] Text and image-input serving. #34061
  - [x] FA4 and CUDA graphs on Blackwell. #42239
  - [ ] Radix cache and chunked prefill.
  - [ ] Quantized checkpoints, FP8 first.
  - [ ] Output token logprobs. @Hangzhi #41232
  - [ ] Choice, yes/no, and ordinal answers on the shared decision endpoints. @Hangzhi #43752
  - [ ] Fix the answer-header mismatch on the reproduced decision cases. @Hangzhi #43767
  - [ ] Shared dLLM runtime walkthrough. @Hangzhi #43940

- [ ] Extend decoding support.

items.title: [Bug] A silent DP rank leaves /flush_cache waiting without a deadline and blocks subsequent flush calls
items.author: Adeshen
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] Searched related issues and PRs; related work and limitations are noted below.
- [ ] Reproduced on the latest version. The service observations are from the pinned v0.5.17 image; current main was inspected as source only.
- [x] Included reproduction steps and the available environment information.
- [x] Report written in English.

### Describe the bug

In the pinned v0.5.17 deployment with DP=2, suspending one scheduler rank leaves `/flush_cache` without an HTTP response until the client times out. `FanOutCommunicator.queueing_call` waits for all expected replies while holding its queueing lock, without an internal wait deadline. Subsequent calls on the **same communicator** cannot dispatch until the active call finishes.

This is a worker-failure/deadline limitation of an existing all-rank collection contract. Related PRs already discuss the trade-off; this report adds a real-service reproduction and the observed health behavior, rather than claiming the mechanism was previously unknown.

### Reproduction

Use a dedicated test service in the image below with two NPUs:

```bash
python3 -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path /models/qwen3-0.6b --served-model-name qwen3 \
  --host 0.0.0.0 --port 30130 \
  --device npu --attention-backend ascend --trust-remote-code \
  --context-length 4096 --mem-fraction-static 0.4 \
  --dp-size 2 --tp-size 1
```

1. After readiness, confirm `POST /flush_cache`, `GET /health` and a short generation request succeed.
2. In that test container's PID namespace, identify one scheduler rank with `ps -eo pid,stat,args`. Suspend that specific scheduler PID with `kill -STOP <scheduler-pid>`; keep the other rank and HTTP/tokenizer process running.
3. Run:

```bash
curl -sS --max-time 45 -X POST \
  -w '\nHTTP_CODE=%{http_code} TIME=%{time_total}\n' \
  http://127.0.0.1:30130/flush_cache
```

4. Resume the same PID with `kill -CONT <scheduler-pid>`, and check that a new flush succeeds. For the recovery observation, another flush was started while the rank was still stopped and allowed to remain pending across SIGCONT.

### Recorded results

These are measured real-service observations, not a model of the scheduler:

| Observation | Result |
|---|---|
| Baseline flush | HTTP 200, 0.006699 s |
| One rank stopped, flush | curl exit 28, HTTP code 000, 45.000981 s |
| Health probes during the quiet stopped-rank period | 503 / 200 / 503 |
| Four health probes with paced generation traffic during the same stopped-rank window | all 200 |
| Eight paced generation requests in that window | six HTTP 200 in under 0.1 s; two client timeouts |
| Flush started while stopped and spanning recovery | HTTP 200, total request time 41.384738 s |
| New flush after recovery | HTTP 200, 0.004737 s |

The 41.38 s figure includes waiting before SIGCONT; it is **not** a post-resume recovery latency. A second real-service variant stopped both ranks and also observed a 45 s flush timeout, with health checks returning 503.

A separate CPU integration test of the real communicator and control path supplied only one reply for fan-out 2: the first call stayed pending and a second caller did not dispatch (`dispatch_count=1`). Its transport/rank replies were declared fixtures. This is the direct measurement of same-communicator head-of-line blocking; no claim is made that every other control endpoint shares that lock.

### Code path and expected behavior

The relevant structure is:

```python
async with self._queueing_lock:
    # dispatch and initialize the per-call collector
    ...
    await self._result_event.wait()
    ...
```

The event is set when the expected reply count is reached. With a missing rank, the wait itself has no deadline. **Changing the count comparison from == to >= would not fix missing replies**; fewer than the expected count satisfies neither comparison.

On 2026-10-21, main at [`573b5716f5b4`](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/573b5716f5b47c77a5fb5f2c24ae9b0e596dc3d1/python/sglang/srt/managers/communicator.py#L41-L57) still has the bare event wait inside the lock. This is source inspection, not a fresh full-service reproduction.

Expected behavior to discuss: an explicit control-call deadline and a defined worker-failure/recovery outcome, rather than relying solely on the HTTP client's timeout. Any solution needs to preserve response ownership: simply releasing the lock after timeout can allow late replies to be consumed by a later call. Partial results must not be reported as successful all-rank completion.

### Related work and limits

- #30022 explicitly acknowledged that a scheduler which never replies can keep a control slot held.
- #30606 addresses FIFO serialization.
- #42694 addresses cancellation and late-reply ownership; its description explicitly states that it does not add worker-failure recovery or a drain timeout.
- #39562 concerns aggregating flush results; #40119 and #36152 concern exposing/forwarding the scheduler-side flush timeout. These are distinct from bounding the tokenizer-side reply wait when a rank cannot respond.

SIGSTOP is deliberate fault injection. No production frequency, irreversible deadlock, or permanent whole-service failure is claimed: resuming the rank allowed progress. Other control operations, real client-disconnect cancellation, and gateway behavior were not validated by this real-service run. Healthy responses occurred in the observed traffic window, not under all possible loads.

### Environment

Historical real-service runs were performed on 2026-10-11 with:
- SGLang v0.5.17, recorded commit `29481685462732237d80d86076d6563e1f658102`.
- Image: `quay.io/ascend/sglang:v0.5.17-cann9.0.0-910b`.
- Resolved image digest: `sha256:35852210819ac0d388bce69c24960189c0412a300dc3add13234b549ba00abda`.
- Ascend 910B3; Python 3.11.15; model: Qwen3-0.6B, mounted at `/models/qwen3-0.6b`.
- Full `python3 -m sglang.check_env` output was not captured in the historical archive; the information above is from the recorded i

items.title: [Bug][function_call] GLM tool-call parsers turn JSON null into the string "None"/"null"
items.author: linkedlist771
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

**Framework bug in the GLM tool-call parsers, not a model bug.** When a tool schema uses `anyOf: [{type: string}, {type: null}]` (or anything that makes `infer_type_from_json_schema` resolve to `"string"`) and the model emits a bare JSON `null` inside `<arg_value>`, the detector first parses it correctly as Python `None`, then corrupts it while coercing to a string.

| Path | Expected | Actual |
|---|---|---|
| Non-streaming (`Glm4MoeDetector`) | JSON `null` | string `"None"` |
| Streaming / `Glm47MoeDetector` string branch (upstream) | JSON `null` | string `"null"` |

Both paths disagree with each other and with the model output.

## Affected code

- `--tool-call-parser glm4_moe` → `python/sglang/srt/function_call/glm4_moe_detector.py` (`_parse_argument_pairs`, `str(parsed_value)` fallback)
- `--tool-call-parser glm47` → `python/sglang/srt/function_call/glm47_moe_detector.py` (string branch falls back to raw text `"null"` when `parsed_value` is `None`)

## Root cause (three steps)

1. **Type inference**: `infer_type_from_json_schema` treats `anyOf: [string, null]` as primary type `"string"` (`python/sglang/srt/function_call/utils.py`).
2. **Value parse**: `parse_arguments` / `json.loads("null")` correctly yields Python `None`.
3. **Bad coerce**:
   - **glm4**: `arg_type == "string"` and `parsed_value is None` hits `arguments[arg_key] = str(parsed_value)` → `"None"`.
   - **glm47** (upstream): same branch uses the raw `arg_value` text → `"null"` string.

The parser recognizes JSON null, then throws it away.

## Reproduction (no model required)

Feed this text directly to `Glm4MoeDetector.detect_and_parse` / `Glm47MoeDetector.detect_and_parse`:

```xml
<tool_call>api_fetch<arg_key>body</arg_key><arg_value>null</arg_value><arg_key>method</arg_key><arg_value>GET</arg_value><arg_key>params</arg_key><arg_value>null</arg_value><arg_key>url</arg_key><arg_value>https://example.com</arg_value></tool_call>
```

with tool schema:

```json
{
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "method": {"type": "string"},
    "url": {"type": "string"},
    "params": {"anyOf": [{"type": "string"}, {"type": "null"}]},
    "body": {"anyOf": [{"type": "string"}, {"type": "null"}]}
  },
  "required": ["method", "url", "params", "body"]
}
```

Expected `arguments`:

```json
{"body": null, "params": null, "method": "GET", "url": "https://example.com"}
```

Actual (glm4 non-stream): `{"body": "None", "params": "None", ...}`.

The same corruption shows up on `/v1/chat/completions` when the model emits the XML above (confirmed via `/generate` that the raw model text is correct).

## Proposed fix (minimal)

- **glm4**: keep `None` instead of `str(None)`:

```diff
                 else:
-                    arguments[arg_key] = str(parsed_value)
+                    arguments[arg_key] = None if parsed_value is None else str(parsed_value)
```

- **glm47**: when `parsed_value is None` in the string branch, keep `None` instead of the raw text `"null"`.

Ordinary string args (`"GET"`, URLs) and “schema says string, model emitted a number → stringify” behavior stay unchanged. Known behavior change: a strict `string` schema with a bare `null` from the model yields JSON `null` rather than `"None"` / `"null"` (neither matches the schema, but null matches the model).

Streaming state-machine handling for the same case can be a follow-up if anything remains after the non-stream / detect_and_parse fix.

## Related

- Opposite direction (string `"null"` rewritten to JSON null) in dots / Muse Glimmer: https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/43017
- Same “preserve null / don’t over-coerce string args” principle as https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/42992
- Similar report on vLLM: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/40195

Happy to open a PR with the one-line fixes + regression tests.

items.title: [Feature]: Allow pooling tasks (token_embed / token_classify) to reuse prefix cache while returning full hidden-state sequences
items.author: xxyyy
items.body_excerpt:
### The problem

On vLLM 0.29.0, pooling requests with `task="token_embed"` or `task="token_classify"` are **forcefully excluded from prefix-cache reads**, even when prefix caching is explicitly enabled and the caller explicitly requests it.

The mandatory behavior is in `vllm/pooling_params.py` (`_merge_default_parameters`, present in v0.29.0 through current `main`):

```python
if self.skip_reading_prefix_cache is None:
    # If prefix caching is enabled,
    # the output of all pooling may less than n_prompt_tokens,
    # we need to skip reading cache at this request.
    if self.task in ["token_embed", "token_classify"]:
        self.skip_reading_prefix_cache = True
    else:
        self.skip_reading_prefix_cache = False
```

When the caller leaves `skip_reading_prefix_cache` as `None` (the default), it is forced to `True` for these two tasks. There is no supported way for an application to opt in to cache reads while keeping the pooling task.

### Why full hidden states + prefix caching are needed together

Our workload is multi-candidate classification with a sequence-classification adapter (`vllm-jev`, serving Open-Jev-2B style decision heads). For each HTTP request:

1. The prompt is built as `fixed instructions + fixed candidate list (up to ~18 candidates) + per-request state`, so **the leading ~400+ tokens are identical across requests** and only the trailing state differs.
2. The adapter submits one pooling request per candidate (or a deduplicated set of shared-prefix sequences) with `task="token_embed"`, because the decision head needs **the hidden states at specific readout positions** of the full sequence — a scalar `classify` output is not sufficient.
3. Many candidates share the same leading tokens, and the fixed instruction/criteria block is repeated across every request. This is exactly the workload prefix caching is designed for.

With the forced skip, every request recomputes the entire prompt. Measured on an RTX 4090 (vLLM 0.29.0, prefix caching enabled, same `cache_salt`, identical prompts re-submitted back-to-back):

- `metadata.cached_tokens` is always `0` for both `token_embed` and `classify` pooling requests;
- the engine-level `Prefix cache hit rate` metric does occasionally report small non-zero values (2.6%–5.1%), so the cache subsystem itself is alive — but per-request `num_cached_tokens` stays 0 and our throughput matches the "no reuse" expectation;
- using `--decision-template` style reordering so that the fixed text truly leads the prompt does not change this (the skip happens before any block matching).

With the forced skip, every request recomputes the entire prompt. Measured on an RTX 4090 (vLLM 0.29.0, prefix caching enabled, same `cache_salt`, identical prompts re-submitted back-to-back):

- `metadata.cached_tokens` is always `0` for both `token_embed` and `classify` pooling requests;
- the engine-level `Prefix cache hit rate` metric does occasionally report small non-zero values (2.6%–5.1%), so the cache subsystem itself is alive — but per-request `num_cached_tokens` stays 0 and our throughput matches the "no reuse" expectation;
- using `--decision-template` style reordering so that the fixed text truly leads the prompt does not change this (the skip happens before any block matching).

If prefix-cache reads were allowed for `token_embed` requests, the shared leading blocks (instructions + candidate list ≈ 400+ tokens per request, ×18 candidate variants deduplicated by shared prefixes) would be served from cache, which for our benchmark shape roughly halves the per-request prefill compute.

### Why full hidden states + prefix caching are needed together — the general pattern

The pattern behind this request is **"encode once, read out at many positions"**: a decoder runs the prompt once, and lightweight heads (linear probes, small MLPs) read the hidden states at one or more token positions to produce decisions. This is how a growing family of classification/routing models works on top of decoder backbones. For these models:

- a scalar `classify` output is insufficient — the head needs hidden vectors at specific positions;
- the prompts typically share a large fixed prefix (instructions, schema, candidate definitions) with only a small varying payload;
- request rate is high (classification/routing/moderation workloads), so prefill compute dominates.

All three properties make prefix-cache reuse the single biggest performance lever for this model class, which is why the current forced skip hurts disproportionately.

### Why simply forcing `skip_reading_prefix_cache = False` breaks today

We understand the guard exists for a reason. With cache hits, the scheduler marks the hit tokens as already computed, and the pooling runner processes only the non-cached tail — so `token_embed` would return hidden states for fewer positions than the prompt has tokens, while downstream consumers (decision heads over readout positions, token-level classifiers) require **one hidden vector per prompt token, position-aligned**.

So the missing piece is not just the flag: the V1 pooling path (`vllm/v1/worker/gpu/pool/pooling_runner.py`) has no mechanism to reconstruct position-aligned full-sequence hidden outputs when part of the prompt was served from cache.

### Proposed solutions (any one would unblock this workload)

1. **Fill the gap in the pooling runner**: when a `token_embed`/`token_classify` request has prefix-cache hits, still run (or reconstruct) the hidden states for the cached prefix positions so the output remains position-aligned with the full prompt. Conceptually the KV cache already contains the states for those tokens; the runner would need to re-emit their hidden activations from cache rather than skipping them.
2. **Opt-in flag**: expose `skip_reading_prefix_cache=False` as a documented, caller-owned choice for pooling tasks (as it already is for generation tasks), with a clear caveat that the caller must tolerate/align partial hidden outputs. Applic

items.title: KV-Cache Persistence Issue with SSD Offloading
items.author: LiuQW519
items.body_excerpt:
**Description:**  
follow the SSD offload guide in :

> https://docs.lmcache.ai/kv_cache/local_storage.html

experimentation with vLLM  and LMCache, we observed that the KV-Cache offloading to SSD works partially but lacks persistence across server restarts.  

**Steps to Reproduce:**  
1. Configure vLLM server with SSD offloading for KV-Cache  
2. Run inference scripts with a specific prompt 
3. Observe 2.4GB `.pt` file generated in the SSD cache directory  
4. Restart the vLLM server process  
5. Query the same prompt again  
6. the kv-cache regenerated in SSD

**Expected Behavior:**  
The existing KV-Cache files should be reused, avoiding redundant computation and disk I/O.  

**Actual Behavior:**  
New identical KV-Cache files are regenerated instead of reusing the existing ones

This optimization would significantly improve latency for recurring queries in production scenarios. I would appreciate guidance on recommended methods to achieve proper KV-Cache persistence across server restarts in this workflow.

Which version of vllm and lmcache are you using? Can you show us sample of file names that regenerated time of time?

Latest lmcache has changed data type of hash from str to int and use seed from vllm's NONE_HASH. Such change results in the change of filename in local disk.
If PYTHONHASHSEED is not set, vllm's NONE_HASH changes every time.
see vllm's code
```
def init_none_hash(hash_fn: Callable):
    global NONE_HASH

    hash_seed = os.getenv("PYTHONHASHSEED")
    if hash_seed is None and hash_fn is sha256_cbor_64bit:
        logger.warning(
            "PYTHONHASHSEED is not set. This will lead to non-reproducible "
            "block-hashes when using sha256_cbor_64bit as the hash function."
            "Consider setting PYTHONHASHSEED to a fixed value for "
            "reproducibility.")

    NONE_HASH = (int.from_bytes(os.urandom(32), byteorder="big")
                 if hash_seed is None else hash_fn(hash_seed))
```

You can try to set PYTHONHASHSEED to a fixed value to see if file names are different once you restart vllm and re-query

items.title: [Bug] fs L2 adapter: every store fails at os.open() in _write_with_odirect when use_odirect=true
items.author: h1manshu23
items.body_excerpt:
**Describe the bug**
With the `fs` L2 adapter and `use_odirect: true`, **every** chunk store fails. `FSL2Adapter._write_with_odirect` raises at the `os.open()` call, and each store is logged as failed:

```
[2026-07-31 12:39:27,361] LMCache ERROR: FSL2Adapter failed to store
/mnt/nvme0/-SEP-data-medium-SEP-text-generation-models-SEP-gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-FP8-dynamic-SEP-@0x01000100@1@246ba704d24a7690450504e0a607656c195b4e247501896d103d7d293f9b63dc.data
(fs_l2_adapter.py:629:lmcache.v1.distributed.l2_adapters.fs_l2_adapter)
```

Nothing is ever persisted to L2, so the disk tier is effectively dead while the server continues running and reporting no fatal error.

**This is not an unsupported-storage case.** `base_path=/mnt/nvme0` is a real block-backed filesystem on a 4-device NVMe RAID0 array:

```
md0 : active raid0 nvme3n2[3] nvme2n2[2] nvme1n2[1] nvme4n2[0]
```

Two distinct problems here:

1. **The failure itself.** O_DIRECT should be usable on this mount. Whatever LMCache passes to `os.open()` — flag combination, mode, or path — is being rejected on a filesystem/device stack that otherwise accepts direct I/O.
2. **The failure is undiagnosable and unrecoverable.** The log line prints the target path but not the underlying `OSError`/errno, so there's no way to tell EINVAL from EACCES from ENOENT without reading LMCache's source. And there is no fallback: rather than degrading to buffered I/O or refusing at startup, the adapter fails silently-but-endlessly, once per chunk, for the lifetime of the server.

Note the failure is at **`os.open()`**, not at the write — so this is not an O_DIRECT buffer/offset/length alignment issue, which would surface later in `_write_with_odirect`.

**To Reproduce**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. `base_path` sits on a 4× NVMe md RAID0 (512k chunk) mounted at `/mnt/nvme0`.

2. Start the LMCache server with the `fs` L2 adapter and O_DIRECT enabled:

```bash
lmcache server --host localhost --port 9000 \
  --l1-size-gb 128 --eviction-policy LRU --chunk-size 256 \
  --l2-adapter '{"type": "fs", "base_path": "/mnt/nvme0", "use_odirect": true, "num_workers": 32}' \
  --http-port 8081
```

3. Start vLLM against it on a single GPU:

```bash
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 vllm serve /path/to/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-FP8-dynamic/ \
  --port 9001 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.95 \
  --enable-prefix-caching --enable-chunked-prefill \
  --max-model-len 16384 \
  --kv-transfer-config '{"kv_connector":"LMCacheMPConnector","kv_role":"kv_both","kv_connector_extra_config":{"lmcache.mp.host":"tcp://localhost","lmcache.mp.port":9000}}' \
  --max-num-batched-tokens 8192 --max-num-seqs 12
```

4. Send any request. Every L2 store fails with the traceback below; `/mnt/nvme0` stays empty.

**Expected behavior**

On a direct-I/O-capable filesystem like this one, stores should succeed with `use_odirect: true` — that's the whole point of running the cache on NVMe RAID0.

Failing that, LMCache should:
- include the underlying errno / `OSError` message in the `failed to store` log line, and
- probe `O_DIRECT` support on `base_path` **once at startup**, then either fail fast with an actionable message or fall back to buffered I/O — instead of raising per-chunk for the lifetime of the process.

**Screenshots**
If applicable, add screenshots to help explain your problem.
```
[2026-08-02 14:09:16,887] LMCache ERROR: FSL2Adapter failed to store /mnt/nvme0/-SEP-data-medium-SEP-text-generation-models-SEP-gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-FP8-dynamic-SEP-@0x01000100@1@2fd0d18a24695cedc65b54957836c1ddcde16bfbe2208c8c8425e4fec9c93441.data (fs_l2_adapter.py:629:lmcache.v1.distributed.l2_adapters.fs_l2_adapter)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/miphi/vllm_lib/lib/python3.10/site-packages/lmcache/v1/distributed/l2_adapters/fs_l2_adapter.py", line 611, in _execute_store
    await self._loop.run_in_executor(

items.title: Restart-proof KV cache for llama-server: 40K-token TTFT 155s to 6s after reboot
items.author: qqkzlm
items.body_excerpt:
Every restart wipes your prefill. Server crash, box reboot, model reload — a 40K-token agentic prompt pays the full ~155s prefill again before the first token.

I patched llama-server to persist KV-cache prefix checkpoints to disk and auto-restore the longest matching prefix on boot. Same prompt after a restart: **first token in ~6s instead of ~155s** (2.1s disk read once + decode). No client changes, no re-architecture — the server just remembers.

Measured on GTX 1080 8GB, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, `-c 92160`:

- Cold: 151s prefill → first token at ~155s
- Warm (post-restart): 2.1s disk read (first request only) → first token at ~6s
- Checkpoints keyed by model + ctx + KV quant (wrong config = ignored, never corrupted); disk-budget eviction included

Single-commit patch (86KB): https://github.com/qqkzlm/llama-cpp-prompt-disk-cache — `git am` onto the PrismML `prism` branch, four flags (`--slot-save-path`, `--checkpoint-min-step`, `--ctx-checkpoints`, `--prompt-cache-disk-budget`).

One MoE lesson from the same box: keep experts on GPU, let KV follow the layers — pushing 20 MoE layers to CPU collapsed prefill 265→30 tok/s, which no cache can fix.

Happy to upstream behind a flag if maintainers are interested.

comments.author: qqkzlm
comments.body:
Update to the README since this went up — three things worth calling out for anyone trying it:

**1. Prebuilt CUDA binaries exist for both platforms.** The `v0.2.3` release ships `llama-server-win-cuda-v0.2.3.zip` and `llama-server-linux-cuda-v0.2.3.tar.gz`. The Linux package is built for `sm_61`/Pascal, so it also runs on GTX 10-series. No build needed:

```bash
./llama-server -m model.gguf -c 32768 --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 \
  --slot-save-path /var/tmp/kvstore/model \
  --prompt-cache-disk-budget 20 --checkpoint-min-step 2048 --ctx-checkpoints 64
```

**2. Only one flag is actually required.** `--slot-save-path` is the only one you must pass — `--prompt-cache-disk-budget` and `--prompt-cache-disk-path` are silently ignored without it, and entries land in `<slot-save-path>/pdcache`. `--prompt-cache-disk` is **enabled by default**, so passing it is optional; use `--no-prompt-cache-disk` to turn the cache off.

**3. Cache hits require a byte-identical prompt prefix.** Only the common prefix from token 0 onward is reused. If you prepend a timestamp or a random ID, everything after it misses and the cache is effectively unused. Put stable content first (system prompt, tool definitions, long docs) and per-turn content last — opencode / Claude Code already do this, so it works out of the box.

The README now has a "when does the cache hit / when does it miss" section covering this, a flag-duty table, and a Chinese-first three-step guide (the repo README is now Chinese-primary). A Windows `start-llama-server.bat` is included in the zip if you want a prompt-driven launcher instead of a command line.

Still happy to upstream this behind a flag if maintainers are interested — the whole feature is one commit touching `tools/server/server-prompt-disk.cpp` (~900 lines) plus slot/task integration.

items.author: farouk09
items.body_excerpt:
Hi everyone! 👋

I'm trying to run the model Qwen/Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct-1M on an NVIDIA RTX A6000 (49.1 GB VRAM) using vllm serve with the --dtype auto option. However, I'm getting the following error:

_`ValueError: The model's max seq len (1010000) is larger than the maximum number of tokens that can be stored in KV cache (73792). Try increasing `gpu_memory_utilization` or decreasing `max_model_len` when initializing the engine.`_

From my understanding:

- The model has ~14B parameters, so in FP16 it should use ~28GB of VRAM (please correct me if that’s inaccurate).
- Running in auto mode (which defaults to FP16), the weights should take ~14GB.
- That leaves ~36GB, which I thought would be enough for the KV cache for a 1M context length. But apparently not?

So I have two questions:

1. Is my assumption about the memory breakdown (weights vs KV cache) correct?
2. How can we estimate the required VRAM for a given number of context tokens? Is there a formula or rule of thumb to calculate the KV cache size needed based on context length and model size?

More broadly, I'd really appreciate if someone could explain how to estimate the total VRAM usage in `vllm serve`, including weights, KV cache, context window, etc.

Thanks in advance!

Drop model support in vLLM

I've dug into why this was dropped — \`Phi4FlashForCausalLM\` was removed in v0.10.2 during the V0 deprecation sweep because it explicitly declared \`SupportsV0Only\`, using the old \`MambaCacheManager\`/raw SSM ops plus a manual KV-cache-tensor hack for its YOCO cross-layer attention sharing.

- Re-register the model and drop it from \`_PREVIOUSLY_SUPPORTED_MODELS\`

Will keep prefix-caching/chunked-prefill disabled for this model initially (matching the old V0 behavior) to scope a correctness-first first PR. Flagging the approach here in case a maintainer has opinions before I go deep — happy to adjust. Could I get this assigned?

items.title: Agentic Cache Scheduling System Roadmap (Q4)
items.author: hzh0425
items.body_excerpt:
## 1. Agentic Cache Scheduling

- Supernode-wide KV Cache Sharing @hzh0425  @Shunkangz @zhengd-nv 
	- Enable sharing of GPU-resident (L1) and host-resident (L2) KV caches across engines within the same super-node domain.
	- Add cache location awareness to the Router to coordinate request placement and KV transfers based on cache availability and engine load.
	- Extend HiCache linker integration to support GPU-to-GPU KV transfers over (NVLink @Shunkangz、AMD UALoE @TianDi101、SAIL's card-to-card interconnect @Vinsmoke86) and remote Grace DRAM access through EGM.
	- Optimize small KV-page transfers and NUMA placement; validate correctness, cache hit rate, and TTFT/TPOT on GB NVLink72、 AMD MI455X Helios Rack、and SAIL clusters.
- Build a KV cache orchestrator across the router and engine @ZhaiFeiyue @stmatengss 
	- Identify sessions, sub-agents, and tool calls, and expose `PREFETCH`, `DEMOTE`, and `PIN` hints for global cache scheduling. Align this work with the [[router roadmap](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/25760)](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/25760). 
	- Add session-aware scheduling to the router
- Enhance HiCache Linker Mode @hzh0425 @alphabetc1 @huangtingwei9988 
    - [[PR #40896](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/40896)](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/40896): Support fast failover and recovery.
    - [[PR #41343](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/41343)](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/41343): Extend support to hybrid models with Mamba and SWA.
    - [[PR #44526](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/44526)]((https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/44526)): Support runtime attach and detach of the unified cache external linker through the HiCache storage-backend API.
    - [PR #43831](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/43831): Skip redundant write-through of KV pages just loaded by the external linker to reduce storage existence queries and offload overhead.
    - [PR #44623](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/44623): Support DeepSeek-V4.1 external linker pools with shared C1/C2 KV and indexer mappings, SWA storage, and packed draft mappings in UMBP.
    - [PR #44977](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/44977): Support FULL + MAMBA MLA models such as Kimi-K3 in the direct external linker, including DSPARK sidecar draft KV.
    - Improve reliability and observability for production deployment.
    - Refactor `hybrid_pool_assembler.py`：Simplify pool assembly and improve extensibility across model architectures.
    - Support GDR Prefetch For Linker Mode @huangtingwei9988 
- Support a [[unified KV cache layout](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/33651)](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/33651) for host cache and L3 storage: @Shunkangz @huangtingwei9988 
    - [[PR #39727](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/39727)](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/39727): Add a page-unified host KV layout and topology-independent L3 keys.

items.title: [Bug] Ordinary API key can clear persistent HiCache storage
items.author: JPengLi
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

`POST /hicache/storage-backend/clear` performs a destructive HiCache storage operation but is only marked `AuthLevel.ADMIN_OPTIONAL` and has no explicit `admin_api_key` check:

```python
# python/sglang/srt/entrypoints/http_server.py:1072-1081
@app.api_route("/hicache/storage-backend/clear", methods=["POST"])
@auth_level(AuthLevel.ADMIN_OPTIONAL)
async def clear_hicache_storage_backend():
    """Clear the hierarchical cache storage backend."""
    ret = await _global_state.tokenizer_manager.clear_hicache_storage()
    return Response(
        content="Hierarchical cache storage backend cleared.\n",
        status_code=200 if ret.success else HTTPStatus.BAD_REQUEST,
    )
```

The neighboring runtime attach route treats the same backend family as administrator-only and rejects requests when no admin key is configured. The clear route does not.

For the file backend, the underlying operation deletes every regular file in the configured backend directory:

```python
# python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/hicache_storage.py:725-735
def clear(self) -> bool:
    for filename in os.listdir(self.file_path):
        file_path = os.path.join(self.file_path, filename)
        if os.path.isfile(file_path):
            os.remove(file_path)
```

Consequently, in a common deployment with only `--api-key`, every ordinary inference client can erase the persistent hierarchical cache backend.

### Reproduction

### Reproduction

Launch an isolated server with HiCache enabled, a dedicated file backend, and only an ordinary API key:

```bash
mkdir -p /tmp/isolated-hicache
echo hicache-sentinel > /tmp/isolated-hicache/audit-sentinel.bin

SGLANG_HICACHE_FILE_BACKEND_STORAGE_DIR=/tmp/isolated-hicache \
python3 -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path /models/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct \
  --host 127.0.0.1 \
  --port 30200 \
  --api-key user-secret \
  --enable-hierarchical-cache \
  --hicache-write-policy write_through \
  --hicache-storage-backend file
```

First use an incorrect key:

```bash
curl -i -X POST http://127.0.0.1:30200/hicache/storage-backend/clear \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer wrong-secret' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{}'
```

Observed:

```text
HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
```

Then use the ordinary API key:

```bash
curl -i -X POST http://127.0.0.1:30200/hicache/storage-backend/clear \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer user-secret' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{}'
```

Observed:

```text
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Hierarchical cache storage backend cleared.
```

Before the request:

```text
/tmp/isolated-hicache/audit-sentinel.bin exists
```

After the request:

```text
/tmp/isolated-hicache/audit-sentinel.bin does not exist
remaining files: none
```

The scheduler log included:

```text
Cleared all entries in HiCacheFile storage.
Hierarchical cache storage backend cleared successfully!
```

### Evidence

Source on commit `51686cf8e7fee0ae773c5c9b8ede356507abef7b`:

```python
@app.api_route("/hicache/storage-backend/clear", methods=["POST"])
@auth_level(AuthLevel.ADMIN_OPTIONAL)
async def clear_hicache_storage_backend():
    ret = await _global_state.tokenizer_manager.clear_hicache_storage()
```

The adjacent attach operation includes:

```python
if not get_serving().admin_api_key:
    return _admin_api_key_missing_response()
```

The file backend clear implementation removes every regular file under `self.file_path`.

Dynamic v0.5.19 observations:

```text
wrong bearer key  /hicache/storage-backend/clear -> HTTP 401
ordinary API key  /hicache/storage-backend/clear -> HTTP 200
dedicated sentinel file before request          -> exists
dedicated sentinel file after request           -> removed
```

This test used a disposable file backend. No production or shared cache was cleared.

### Impact

- **Integrity: High** An ordinary API-key holder can invalidate or delete a shared persistent KV-cache backend. Consequences include:

  - loss of cached KV entries across workers or restarts;
  - a sudden cold-cache thundering herd;
  - increased origin/model computation and latency;
  - increased backend storage or object-store traffic and cost;
  - temporary denial of service under load.

- **Availability: High.** Clearing a shared cache can force a cold-cache thundering herd, increase latency and model computation, consume backend bandwidth, and temporarily deny service under load.

If the server has no API key configured, the destructive operation is reachable without authentication. If both `api_key` and `admin_api_key` are configured, `ADMIN_OPTIONAL` requires the admin key and blocks an ordinary key.

Prerequisites:

- hierarchical cache/storage backend is enabled;
- the caller can reach `/hicache/storage-backend/clear`;
- no admin key is configured, or the caller holds admin authorization.

Clearing shared persistent storage should be an explicitly administrator-only operation. The route should use `ADMIN_FORCE` or perform the same explicit admin-key check as attach, and destructive confirmation or scoped invalidation should be considered for multi-tenant deployments.

### Environment

```
$ docker exec sglang-v0519-prefill-134 python3 -m sglang.check_env
Python: 3.12.3 (main, Jul 15 2026, 23:46:41) [GCC 13.3.0]
CUDA available: True
GPU 0: NVIDIA A100 80GB PCIe
GPU 0 Compute Capability: 8.0
CUDA_HOME: /usr/local/cuda
NVCC: Cuda compilation tools, release 13.0, V13.0.88
CUDA Driver Version: 590.48.01
PyTorch: 2.13.0+cu130
sglang: 0.5.19
sglang-kernel: 0.4.6.post1
flashinfer_python: 0.6.18
flashinfer_cubin: 0.6.18
flashinfer_jit_

items.title: [Bug] HiCache on hybrid GDN model: host-tier hits drop to zero once evicted working set exceeds ~3 long prefixes (host mamba pool exhausted while KV stays on host)
items.author: jhsmith409
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] Please use English.

### Describe the bug

On a hybrid GDN model (Qwen3.8-27B) with `--enable-hierarchical-cache`, the host tier stops producing hits once the evicted working set is a bit larger than the device pool. The KV pages are still on host (`hicache_host_used_tokens` is about 354k), but byte-identical requests get `cached_tokens: 0` and a full recompute. The host mamba pool seems to be the limit. Its fixed slot capacity (56 here) is much smaller than the number of mamba states backed up, so the KV on host is left with no matching mamba state.

Fresh server for each row; each document is about 89k tokens; the device pool is 262,144 tokens; the host pool is 704,746 KV tokens and 56 mamba slots:

| documents cycled | identical re-ask: `cached_tokens` / TTFT | `prefill_effective_tokens_total{mode="host_hit"}` | `hicache_backup_tokens_total{pool="mamba"}` | `hicache_host_used_tokens` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 3 (267k total) | 89280 / **0.29 s** for all 3 | 267520 | 263 | 267514 |
| 4 (357k total) | **0 / 23 s** for all 4 | **0** | 702 | 354423 |

With 4 documents, the cold pass and the re-ask pass take the same time, so HiCache gives no benefit. Answers are correct in every case. This is not the wrong-output symptom of #39830.

The default `--mamba-max-states-per-path=-1` is worse. With it, even the 3-document cycle gets no host hits: 394 mamba states were backed up for about 300k KV tokens, and `host_hit` stayed at 0. Setting `--mamba-max-states-per-path=5` makes the 3-document case work, but as the table shows, about 175 mamba states per 89k document are still backed up. That is far more than 5 per path, and more than the 56 host slots.

What I'd expect: host KV that is still resident stays usable. For example, the latest mamba state of each path could be pinned and preferred when host mamba slots are evicted, or host mamba capacity could be sized against the KV host pool. At minimum, a warning when the host mamba pool can't cover the host KV pool would help.

Not tested: whether this reproduces without PP or without speculative decoding. Our setup needs both to fit on 2x16 GB, together with local patches that move the BF16 embedding tables to pinned host memory (memory placement only, no change to cache logic).

### Reproduction

Server (Docker `lmsysorg/sglang:v0.5.22`, env `SGLANG_ENABLE_PP_SPEC=1`, `SGLANG_PP_LAYER_PARTITION=35,29`):

```
sglang serve --model-path nvidia/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4 --trust-remote-code --port 8007 \
  --tp-size 1 --pp-size 2 --json-model-override-args '{"language_model_only": true}' \
  --context-length 262144 --kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3 --attention-backend flashinfer \
  --chunked-prefill-size 1024 --mem-fraction-static 0.95 --max-total-tokens 262144 \
  --max-running-requests 4 --cuda-graph-bs-decode 1 2 3 4 --cuda-graph-backend-prefill disabled \
  --mamba-radix-cache-strategy extra_buffer --mamba-ssm-dtype bfloat16 --max-mamba-cache-size 16 \
  --speculative-algorithm EAGLE --speculative-num-steps 3 --speculative-eagle-topk 1 \
  --speculative-num-draft-tokens 4 --enable-linear-replayssm-spec \
  --enable-hierarchical-cache --hicache-size 15 --mamba-max-states-per-path 5 \
  --enable-cache-report --enable-metrics
```

Startup log: `Allocating kv hierarchical KV host pool: 704747 tokens`, `Allocating 1.96 GB / 2.52 GB host memory for hierarchical Mamba cache`, `Sync fixed-size HiCache host token capacity from 58 to 56`.

Client (`python repro.py 3` gives host hits; `python repro.py 4` gives none):

```python
import json, random, sys, time, urllib.request
URL = "http://localhost:8007/v1/chat/completions"
W = "alpha bravo charlie delta echo foxtrot golf hotel india juliet kilo lima".split()
N = int(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else 4

def doc(i, k=100):
    r = random.Random(1000 + i)
    p = [" ".join(r.choice(W) for _ in range(100)) for _ in range(int(k * 1000 / 151))]
    p.insert(len(p) // 2, f"IMPORTANT: The secret passphrase is 'pass-{i}'.")
    return "\n".join(p) + "\n\nWhat is the secret passphrase? Reply with just the passphrase."

def ask(label, text):
    body = {"model": "qwen3.8-27b", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": text}],
            "max_tokens": 24, "temperature": 0, "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": False}}
    t = time.time()
    d = json.load(urllib.request.urlopen(urllib.request.Request(
        URL, json.dumps(body).encode(), {"Content-Type": "application/json"}), timeout=3600))
    u = d["usage"]
    print(label, u["prompt_tokens"], round(time.time() - t, 2), u["prompt_tokens_details"]["cached_tokens"])

docs = [doc(i) for i in range(N)]
for i, d in enumerate(docs):
    ask(f"doc{i} first", d)
for i, d in enumerate(docs):
    ask(f"doc{i} again (identical)", d)
```

Output with N=4 on a fresh server:

```
doc0 first 89294 23.54 0
doc1 first 89200 23.25 0
doc2 first 89117 23.23 0
doc3 first 89195 23.27 0
doc0 again (identical) 89294 23.12 0
doc1 again (identical) 89200 23.03 0
doc2 again (identical) 89117 23.01 0
doc3 again (identical) 89195 23.05 0
```

The same happens for multi-turn continuations (turn 1 + assistant reply + new user message) across 4 conversations of about 100k tokens each: turn 2 gets `cached_tokens: 0`.

### Environment

- SGLang 0.5.22 (`lmsysorg/sglang:v0.5.22`), torch 2.14.1+cu130, NVIDIA driver 615.71.10
- 2x RTX 5070 Ti 16 GB (SM120), PP=2, no P2P
- Model `nvidia/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4` (hybrid GDN + full attention), EAGLE over the in-checkpoint MTP head, ReplaySSM spec verify

items.title: [Bug] GLM-5.3 FP8 inference hangs after sustained workload with KV cache full (TP8, EAGLE, H200)
items.author: BrynnR
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist - [x] I searched related issues but found no solution. - [x] The bug persists in the latest version. - [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback. - [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed. - [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed. ### Describe the bug

Summary

We encountered a persistent inference hang while serving GLM-5.3 FP8 with SGLang on 8× NVIDIA H200 GPUs (TP=8, EAGLE speculative decoding).

The instance initially worked normally and served requests under sustained workload conditions, including high concurrency and long-context requests. After approximately two days of operation, inference stopped making progress.

The HTTP server remained responsive, but all inference requests stopped returning responses.

Key observations:

  • /v1/chat/completions stopped responding, including simple requests containing only a few tokens.

  • The issue persisted when requesting 127.0.0.1:8080 directly inside the container, bypassing Kubernetes Service and Istio.

  • /health, /v1/models, and /model_info continued returning HTTP 200.

  • All eight Scheduler processes remained alive.

  • All eight GPUs showed 0% utilization during repeated sampling.

  • The last observed Scheduler log showed token usage: 1.00, with one request still running.

  • No further Prefill or Decode logs appeared afterward.

  • No fatal Scheduler exception or process exit was observed.

We suspect a possible Scheduler stall related to KV cache exhaustion, request scheduling, or resource reclamation. However, the root cause remains unconfirmed.

Environment

Component | Configuration -- | -- Model | GLM-5.3 FP8 Model architecture | GlmMoeDsaForCausalLM SGLang version | 0.0.0.dev1+g7760d5264 SGLang Git revision | 7760d52 GPU | 8 × NVIDIA H200 Tensor parallelism | TP=8 NVIDIA Driver | 580.159.03 CUDA version reported by nvidia-smi | 13.0 NCCL version reported by SGLang | 2.30.7 Deployment | Kubernetes Attention backend | DSA DSA prefill backend | flashmla_sparse DSA decode backend | fa3 KV cache dtype | BF16 Configured context length | 524288 Actual KV capacity | 303616 tokens KV cache page size | 64 Chunked prefill size | 8192 Max prefill tokens | 16384 Max running requests | 48 Tokenizer workers | 1 Speculative decoding | EAGLE Metrics | Disabled

An HTTP log also showed:

[2026-10-22 02:28:13]
[http_server] Error:
Request is disconnected from the client side (type 1).
Abort request obj.rid='...'

This appears consistent with the client disconnecting after waiting for inference. It is not necessarily the root cause.

GPU and Scheduler State During the Hang

All eight NVIDIA H200 GPUs retained their allocated memory.

Typical observed utilization:

GPU 0: 140698 MiB / 143771 MiB, GPU-Util 0%
GPU 1: 140926 MiB / 143771 MiB, GPU-Util 0%
GPU 2: 140926 MiB / 143771 MiB, GPU-Util 0%
GPU 3: 140926 MiB / 143771 MiB, GPU-Util 0%
GPU 4: 140926 MiB / 143771 MiB, GPU-Util 0%
GPU 5: 140926 MiB / 143771 MiB, GPU-Util 0%
GPU 6: 140926 MiB / 143771 MiB, GPU-Util 0%
GPU 7: 140828 MiB / 143771 MiB, GPU-Util 0%

Repeated sampling using:

nvidia-smi dmon -s puc -d 1 -c 10

also showed 0% GPU SM utilization.

All eight Scheduler processes were still alive:

PID   STAT  CPU%   Process
238   RLl   92.5   sglang::scheduler_TP0
287   RLl   83.6   sglang::scheduler_TP1
337   SLl   81.3   sglang::scheduler_TP2
387   SLl   80.0   sglang::scheduler_TP3
437   SLl   76.7   sglang::scheduler_TP4
489   RLl   76.1   sglang::scheduler_TP5
539   SLl   76.4   sglang::scheduler_TP6
591   RLl   75.8   sglang::scheduler_TP7

These CPU percentages are process-level observations and do not independently establish an active CPU spin loop.

No GPU computation was observed during our sampling, despite the Scheduler processes remaining alive.

Expected Behavior

When KV cache pressure becomes high, SGLang should either:

  • Continue making inference progress by scheduling or reclaiming resources appropriately.

  • Retract or reject requests when resources are insufficient.

  • Recover scheduling after resource pressure is relieved.

  • Return an appropriate error instead of leaving new inference requests indefinitely pending.

An individual long-context request should not permanently prevent subsequent short requests from being processed.

Actual Behavior

Once the instance entered the problematic state:

  • New inference requests remained unresponsive.

  • Even short prompts failed to produce a response.

  • HTTP informational and health endpoints continued working.

  • Scheduler processes remained al

items.title: Question: long-context generation stops mid-sentence with finish_reason=stop (final token = <|im_end|>) on Qwen3.8-27B with fp8 KV cache
items.author: superniker
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

Occasionally a long-context request ends **mid-sentence**, and on the server side it looks like a perfectly normal completion: `finish_reason="stop"`, `stop_reason=null`, no abort/error counters. With `return_token_ids: true` the final token is `248046` (`<|im_end|>`), i.e. the model itself ended the turn. Clients just see a truncated answer with no error, which is very confusing for an agent workload.

I would like to understand whether this is expected behaviour at very long context, and which knob (if any) reduces it. Happy to run any A/B you suggest.

### Environment

- 2x RTX 2080 Ti 22 GB (SM75), driver 595.99.02, NVLink, no NVSwitch
- vLLM `0.2.3.dev1190+gf45f7bac0` (base commit `f45f7bac0`), with local SM75 patches only (`--disable-custom-all-reduce`, FlashQLA backend for GDN prefill); no changes to sampling / KV cache / EOS paths
- torch 2.13.0+cu130, CUDA 13.0, transformers 5.18.0
- Model: Qwen3.8-27B-AWQ-INT4 (`Qwen3_5ForConditionalGeneration`, hybrid GDN + full-attention layers), TP=2, `--dtype float16`
- Flags:

```
--max-model-len 262144 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.90 --max-num-seqs 8
--max-num-batched-tokens 2560 --enable-chunked-prefill --enable-prefix-caching
--kv-cache-dtype fp8
--speculative-config {"method":"mtp","num_speculative_tokens":4}
--compilation-config {"cudagraph_mode":"PIECEWISE","cudagraph_capture_sizes":[5,10,15,20,25,30,35,40],"max_cudagraph_capture_size":40}
--enable-auto-tool-choice --tool-call-parser qwen3_xml --reasoning-parser qwen3
--generation-config vllm
```

- KV pool at startup: `num_gpu_blocks=269`, `block_size=1616`, `kv_cache_size_tokens=389595`, `kv_cache_max_concurrency=1.486` (for 262,144-token requests)

### Evidence from one real request

- `prompt_tokens=123033` (cached 119,584), `completion_tokens=696`, request `max_tokens=32768`
- final SSE chunk (verbatim):

```json
{"choices":[{"index":0,"delta":{"content":" (1"},"finish_reason":"stop","stop_reason":null,"token_ids":null}]}
```

- text ends mid-word (`...**Batch 1: Procurement** (1`)
- final token id (from `return_token_ids: true` in a reproduction): `248046` = `<|im_end|>`
- engine counters after the event: `request_success_total{finished_reason="stop"}` only; `finished_reason="abort"=0`, `"error"=0`, `"length"=0`

### Frequency (self-measured, same engine)

| workload | prompt size | early stops |
|---|---|---|
| real agent traffic (21 tools, long history) | 91k–198k tokens | 1 / 19 requests |
| synthetic, default sampling, 1024–2048 output tokens | ~39k tokens | 2 / 13 |
| synthetic, greedy (`temperature=0`), 1024 output tokens | ~102k tokens | 0 / 3 |
| sampling A/B: `t=0.7/top_p=0.95/top_k=20` vs vLLM defaults | ~39k tokens | 1 / 6 vs 1 / 6 |

Short contexts (~2k tokens) never showed it (0 / 6+).

### What I ruled out

- client / gateway disconnects: `abort=0`, and the client-side log shows the stream closed *after* the `finish_reason=stop` chunk
- `max_tokens` truncation: `finished_reason="length"=0`; the aborted request used only 696 of 32,768 tokens
- user stop strings: `stop_reason=null`; when a stop string does hit, the engine reports it (`stop_reason="，"`), so this path is distinguishable
- deterministic greedy degeneration: greedy at ~102k tokens completed 3/3 (hit `max_tokens`)

### Secondary observation (probably unrelated, but surprising)

The model's `generation_config.json` contains `eos_token_id: [248046, 248044]`, where 248044 is `<|endoftext|>` and also `pad_token_id`. `SamplingParams.update_from_generation_config` (called from `vllm/v1/engine/input_processor.py`, body in `vllm/sampling_params.py`) discards the primary EOS supplied by the tokenizer (248046) and adds the remaining 248044 to `stop_token_ids`, so **every request silently also stops on `<|endoftext|>`**. In all truncations I captured the final token was 248046, so this is very likely not the trigger here — but it might surprise other users of this model family.

### Questions

1. Is a premature `<|im_end|>` at 100k+ token context a known effect of `--kv-cache-dtype fp8` (KV quantization error accumulating over a long context)? The operator reports never seeing this with fp16 KV, but I have not A/B-tested fp16 myself.
2. Which knob is most likely to reduce it: fp16 KV (costs ~half the KV pool), `--calculate-kv-scales`, smaller `--max-num-batched-tokens`, or disabling the MTP spec decode?
3. Has anyone measured EOS-rate vs context length with fp8 KV on hybrid (GDN/Mamba) models?

I can run a controlled fp16-vs-fp8 KV A/B at ~100k token context and post the numbers, and I have per-request JSONL logs (finish reason, final token id, prompt/completion tokens, TTFT) for every request if that helps.

items.title: [RFC][MP] L1 backend extension points
items.author: jooho-XCENA
items.body_excerpt:
Hi all, following up on #3262 . We agreed there that L1 basically means memory the xPU can access directly, without staging.

This is now happening in code: the CPU path, GDS (#3589, merged), DAX (#3584, in review), Maru (in progress). What's interesting is that each backend ended up needing a different part of the stack — which I think tells us something about where the extension points should be. 

Before more backends show up, it seems like a good time to step back and agree on that picture. Longer term, what I'd really like is for L1 to host multiple backends at once — local and distributed backends side by side — and getting the extension points right now would make that a lot easier later.

I'm not proposing a specific first PR here; I'd rather agree on the overall picture first, and discuss the starting point together.

### What each backend actually needed

**DAX** (#3584 , local L1 target): only the allocation side. It adds a new allocator (DRAM primary + DAX overflow), registers the mmap with cudaHostRegister so the normal copy path just works, and touches nothing else.

**GDS** (#3589 , local L1 target): allocation + data path. The slab manager plugs in behind the memory-manager seam that the PR introduced, and gpu_ops got a cuFile branch for GDS objects.

**Maru** (upcoming, distributed L1 target): allocation + control. The backend owns the key state and lifecycle — store, pin, and retrieve are calls to its own server, not local cache-engine operations. Upstream has no L1-level seam for this today, so a backend like this would have to land as backend-specific special cases inside the L1 manager — which I'd like to avoid.

So a backend may replace up to three separate things, and a fourth shows up once you run more than one L1:

1. Allocation — where the bytes live and how slots are handed out (DRAM, NVMe slab, DAX, CXL pool). #3589 already introduced a seam here, so this level is mostly covered.

2. Data movement — the copy between the GPU and the backing memory. gpu_ops hardcodes one isinstance branch per backend today (cuFile for GDS, memcpy for DRAM, …). Dispatch is already per-object so this isn't urgent, but the object or allocator could eventually own its copy function so gpu_ops stops growing a branch per backend.

3. Control plane — which keys are resident, and the lifecycle around them. This is the missing one. The current L1 manager is a single fixed implementation, which is fine as long as the cache engine owns that state itself. A backend that keeps it in an external server (Maru, for example) simply can't be expressed. The ask here: extract the lifecycle surface (reserve_write / finish_write / reserve_read / finish_read / delete / usage / close...) into an interface, with the current implementation as the default. Existing CPU/GDS/DAX behavior stays exactly where it is.

4. Placement policy — only matters once several L1s coexist: which L1 stores a chunk, and in what order reads probe them. L2 already solved this exact problem with StorePolicy / PrefetchPolicy over an adapter list, so we can probably lift that pattern when the time comes. Not needed yet; I mention it mainly so the interface in (3) doesn't accidentally rule it out.


Does this breakdown match how you think about L1? 
It would also be great to discuss in what order to implement the pieces above — for example, starting with an opt-in interface and registry for new backends, then folding the current L1 manager in as the default implementation later. 

Hopefully we can land on a good design together!
