items.title: Timeout for process termination upon receiving sigterm should be a user configurable parameter
items.author: Shikib
items.body_excerpt:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

I'm trying to implement graceful exit on SLURM pre-emption. SLURM gives 10 minutes upon pre-emption (i.e., SIGTERM; sleep 600; SIGKILL), but it seems that torchrun will send a SIGKILL from the launcher to all the child processes after 30 seconds (based on [this PR](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/61602)). Since graceful termination (e.g., saving checkpoint) can take >30seconds when working with large models, the default 30s timeout should be a user-configurable parameter.

Minimal example/reproduction of this issue:

```
import time
from pathlib import Path
import signal

def ignore(s,f):
    print('!')

signal.signal(signal.SIGTERM, ignore)

p = Path("/tmp/finished")
p.touch()
p.unlink()
time.sleep(200)
p.touch()
```

1. Launch with `python -u -m accelerate.commands.launch --num_processes 1 test.py`
2. Send sigterm `kill -TERM <pid>`
3. Process receives `SIGKILL from launcher (torch.distributed.elastic.multiprocessing.api: [WARNING] Unable to shutdown process 719448 via Signals.SIGTERM, forcefully exiting via Signals.SIGKILL)` -- from this [line](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blame/cd51d2a3ecc8ac579bee910f6bafe41a4c41ca80/torch/distributed/elastic/multiprocessing/api.py#L551)

Tagging based on Slack discussion: @kurman @wconstab 
Slack thread: https://pytorch.slack.com/archives/C3PDTEV8E/p1707866755665289

comments.author: dwan-ith
comments.body:
Hi,
I noticed that #172596 implemented the configurable shutdown timeout for signal-triggered shutdown and final cleanup.
On current main, LocalElasticAgent._stop_workers() still calls _shutdown() without passing self._shutdown_timeout. hence, worker-stop paths used during failures and elastic restarts fall back to the 30-second default, even when the user configured another value.

I have a small follow-up patch that changes this to:
self._shutdown(timeout=self._shutdown_timeout)

and adds a regression test covering _stop_workers().

One tradeoff is that a long user-configured timeout would then also apply during restart-triggered shutdowns, (potentially) delaying elastic recovery from unhealthy workers. The current CLI documentation describes this as the graceful worker-shutdown timeout generally, but I could not find documentation indicating whether restart paths should intentionally retain 30 seconds.
Is applying the configured timeout to _stop_workers() the remaining work intended by the recently added good first issue label? 

If so, I’d be happy to open the follow-up PR.

comments.author: aron-intframe
comments.body:
On nightly `2.16.0.dev20261021+cpu`, single node, CPU, 2 workers, rank0 ignoring SIGTERM.

Signal path is fixed: SIGTERM to the launcher kills at 30.4s by default, 5.5s with `--shutdown-timeout=5`.

The worker-failure path is not. Same flag, `--nproc-per-node=2 --max-restarts=0 --shutdown-timeout=5`, rank1 exits 1 (paths trimmed):

```
W1022 02:57:05.976000 2164000 torch/distributed/elastic/multiprocessing/api.py:1033] Sending process 2166363 closing signal SIGTERM
W1022 02:57:35.977000 2164000 torch/distributed/elastic/multiprocessing/api.py:1052] Unable to shutdown process 2166363 via 15, forcefully exiting via 9
```

30.001s, not 5.

@dwan-ith the line you named is already fixed by #192815 (a9688bae); the remaining 30s sits earlier. `SubprocessContext._poll()` kills the surviving workers itself with a bare `self.close()` (`multiprocessing/api.py:995`), taking the signature default `timeout=30`, before `_stop_workers` runs. Patching only that call to `close(timeout=5)` gives 5.001s. #192815's regression test asserts `_pcontext.close` was called with 150 on a `MagicMock`, so it stays green while the real timing doesn't move.

Not measured: multi-node, and `MultiprocessContext._poll`, same bare `self.close()` at lines 825 and 852.

Should `_poll` use the configured timeout (plumb `shutdown_timeout` into `PContext`), or is the failure path meant to stay at 30s so a crash can't be held open by a user timeout?

---

items.title: [Bug]: ModelOpt Llama-4 Checkpoints Take 5+ minutes to load
items.author: robertgshaw2-redhat
items.body_excerpt:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

In working on some MoE refactors, I discovered that L4 for ModelOpt takes 5+minutes to load weights even from CPU page cache. 
- https://huggingface.co/nvidia/Llama-4-Scout-17B-16E-Instruct-FP8

The root cause is basically this hack logic to load the state dict that ModelOpt uses
- https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/model_executor/models/llama4.py#L439-L523 [modelopt is the fused case] 

What happens is that the CPU tensor (loaded weight) that we are going to load into the GPU tensor (param) becomes non-contiguous due to this logic. As a result, when we eventually call `_copy()` from CPU->GPU we are calling this on a non-contiguous cpu tensor which takes 3-4s per weight.

To hack around this for local R&D, I simply immediately move the loaded_weight to the GPU. This makes the gather happen on the GPU which accelerates things a lot. This isn't reasonable as an actual solution though

We should investigate where the logic in the weight loader can avoid creating non-contiguous CPU tensors


### Alternatives

_No response_

comments.author: robertgshaw2-redhat
comments.body:
> [@robertgshaw2-redhat](https://github.com/robertgshaw2-redhat) tested on H200 with `nvidia/Llama-4-Scout-17B-16E-Instruct-FP8`:
> 
> Approach	Load Time
> Original (buggy)	78 sec
> `.contiguous()` on CPU	88 sec (slower - adds CPU alloc overhead)
> **GPU-first** `.to('cuda').transpose()`	**37 sec (2.1x faster)**
> The GPU-first approach works well. You mentioned it's "not reasonable as an actual solution" - what are the specific concerns? Is it GPU memory during loading, or multi-GPU compatibility?
> 
> Happy to implement a different approach if preferred.

I thought it was a hack because we have:
- the param, which is loaded into gpu memory (empty tensor)
- the loaded_weight, which is coming from disk and is mapped into cpu memory

Right now, we have a simple trustworthy process where we never have a copy of `loaded_weight` in GPU ram. We simply call `._copy()` which copies the loaded wieight into the param. This guarantees that we do not have any straggling gpu memory from weight loading

If we move the loaded weight in to gpu memory, we have to be 100% certain that we put it back. This is kind of a can of worms IMO and I don't think we should do something like this to solve an edge case like a single model with a single quant framework (especially for a model that has limited usage like this)

So my preference would be to figure out if its possible to ensure that the cpu weights remain contiguous rather than moving them to the gpu unless we have a clean way to manage the lifecycle of the weight

comments.author: rohithputha
comments.body:
Hi, 
I have analyzed the possible causes for this issue. 
I have found some to be:
1. I believe there are two types of expert placement strategies: Linear and Round Robin. Linear is better for memory movement between CPU and GPU. I suspected that this problem might have been caused by the use of round-robin placement which causes multiple DMAs. But it turns out that the default is linear and mostly likely linear placement is being used.
2. One more root cause that I learnt might be that .transpose() in torch. PyTorch just Performs metadata remapping for transposing and hence this causes non contagious tensors and hence multiple DMA invokes.

These are some theories. I would like to test some solutions like performing indexing first, transferring to GPU and then performing transpose operations. 

I am new to contributing to vLLM and open source in general. If this approach works for you, I would like this to be assigned to me. Also, one note that I don't have Nvidia gpu to test and benchmark the changes. any leads or help or guidance regarding that would be appreciated.

Hey @rohithputha - thanks for your contribution. I think it will be tough to contribute to this type of feature without a GPU. There are many clouds you can rent them from. Otherwise, I would suggest looking into a different feature.

This does not have anything to do with linear vs round robin. The root cause of the issue is that the model opt checkpoints on disk are in a different "fused" format which require reshaping to get into the runtime format. The indexing associated with this casues the issue. The ideal solution here could be to figure out if its possible to avoid making things non-contiguous. It very well may not be possible and so we might have to hack around it by moving things to the gpu first, whihc as I said above is not ideal

Hi, was looking into this issue for a while. After scanning through the code and comments. I believe that the .contiguous() call should be done right before the weight_loader() call, after all the slicing/transposing is done

comments.author: jadechip
comments.body:
Ran a few experiments against this issue and wanted to share the results in case they are useful.

- I was able to reproduce the slow post-warmup load: ~`495s` on 2x RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell.
- The trace supports the issue hypothesis: the hot path is CPU -> GPU copies from non-contiguous CPU tensors in the Llama-4/ModelOpt MoE loader.
- Tried two fixes but did **not** help:

1. Make routed expert source tensors contiguous before copy:

```text
measured load: 532.63s
routed_experts.copy: 4080 ms
make_contiguous: 609790 ms
```

This made the copy cheap but made total load time worse -_-

2. Slice the local TP shard first, move only that shard to GPU, transpose on GPU, and skip the later TP narrow:

```text
measured load: 494.73s
routed_experts.copy: 0 measured events
local shard -> device: 465178 ms
```

This removed the `routed_experts.copy` hotspot, but did not improve wall-clock time.

I guess the expensive part is repeatedly consuming these non-contiguous CPU views. The simple fixes above mostly move the cost around. A better fix probably needs to avoid creating those views, or load/reshape the checkpoint tensors in an order closer to the final parameter layout?

comments.author: ishrith-gowda
comments.body:
@guptapiyush16 @LeonxLJX heads up before you start, there are 3 open PRs against this issue already.

| PR | author | approach | file |
|---|---|---|---|
| #46766 | @pratheeknathani | `.contiguous()` before the copy | `models/llama4.py` |
| #50227 | @Dev-with-Mouzan | same, inline at the weight_loader call | `models/llama4.py` |
| #47580 | me | flip the strided side to the destination, no CPU gather | `layers/fused_moe/routed_experts.py` |

#46766 and #50227 are the same fix. `.contiguous()` is a no-op if already contiguous, so the conditional in #46766 and the unconditional call in #50227 do the same thing. #46766 was first, 2026-06-25.

That fix works but it makes the strided CPU gather explicit instead of removing it: `.contiguous()` still walks non-contiguous host memory element by element, then transfers the result densely. Same shape as #32081 (~68s to ~60s above), matches @jadechip's traces showing the cost moving, not disappearing.

#47580 removes the gather. Undoing the transpose recovers the contiguous on-disk slab for free, so the H2D transfer is dense with no CPU-side gather, and the layout change happens as a strided write on the device instead. No loaded weight ever sits in GPU memory, so it doesn't hit @robertgshaw2-redhat's lifecycle concern with GPU-first approaches. TP-narrowed slabs degrade to row-run memcpys instead of elementwise gathers.

Numbers: fp8 62.8ms to 4.0ms (15.8x), bf16 93.4ms to 7.5ms (12.4x) per copy on an A100-80G. End to end on a 24-layer truncation, 18.8s to 12.5s. @eric1932 then ran the full 48-layer model on 1x H200 with source-hash-verified builds and paired runs: 102.58s to 23.63s median, 4.34x, identical output tokens across all six runs. Thanks for that, it's exactly the full-model H200 datapoint this needed.

Two tradeoffs worth naming. It's in `routed_experts.py`, not `llama4.py`, so it covers any fused-MoE checkpoint that arrives transposed, not just Llama-4/ModelOpt. It's also bigger: +145/-3 vs +8/-0 and +5/-1, mostly a test file covering contiguous/transposed/TP-narrowed layouts across fp8/bf16/fp32; the fix itself is about 35 lines. If a maintainer wants the one-liner now and the general fix later, that's a fine call, I'd rather see this issue closed than fight for the merge.

Happy to rebase (it's ~2200 commits behind, still conflict-free) or split out the test file if that helps review.

items.title: [Bug]:  Streaming reasoning content misrouted to `content` when `stop` parameter is set (stop buffer desynchronizes `delta_text` from `delta_token_ids`
items.author: huanghuan3
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment
The output of python collect_env.py ```text Your output of `python collect_env.py` here ```
### 🐛 Describe the bug ## How you would like to use vLLM Using the OpenAI-compatible streaming API with a Qwen3 reasoning model, a `stop` parameter, and `include_stop_str_in_output=false` (the default). When the model's output crosses the `` boundary within a single batch of tokens (e.g. under MTP / speculative decoding / async output), the reasoning tail and `` marker leak into `content` instead of being correctly split between `reasoning_content` and `content`. ## The bug ### Summary When a streaming request carries a non-empty `stop` list and `include_stop_str_in_output=false`, the V1 detokenizer holds back up to `max(len(stop)) - 1` characters of visible text in a **stop buffer** to avoid prematurely emitting a stop string. However, the corresponding `delta_token_ids` are **not** buffered — they reflect all tokens generated in the current round. This creates a desynchronization between two inputs that the reasoning parser receives simultaneously: | Input | Source | Buffered? | |---|---|---| | `delta_text` | `detokenizer.get_next_output_text()` → `output.text` | **Yes** (stop buffer holds tail) | | `delta_token_ids` | `output.token_ids` (raw incremental token IDs) | **No** | The Qwen3 reasoning parser uses `delta_token_ids` to detect `` and `delta_text` to split the string. When the stop buffer delays the `` text but the token IDs already report it, the parser's state machine advances prematurely, and the subsequently released text is routed entirely to `content`. ### Concrete example Suppose the model generates in one batch: ```text 我已经想好了你好 ``` With `stop=["你好"]` and `include_stop_str_in_output=false`, `stop_buffer_length = len("你好") - 1 = 1`. **Round 1** — stop buffer holds back the last character(s): | | Value | |---|---| | `delta_text` (after stop buffer) | `我已经` | | `delta_token_ids` | tokens for `我已经想好了你好` | Parser (`qwen3_reasoning_parser.py:123`): `end_token_id in delta_token_ids` → **True**, but `delta_text.find("")` → **-1** (text not yet visible). Parser returns `None` (line 136). The reasoning text `想好了` is silently dropped. **Round 2** — stop buffer releases the remaining text: | | Value | |---|---| | `delta_text` | `想好了你好` | | `delta_token_ids` | `[]` (no new tokens) | Parser (line 142): `end_token_id in previous_token_ids` → **True** (it was in round 1's tokens). Parser returns `DeltaMessage(content="想好了你好")`. Everything — including `` — goes to `content`. **Result:** ```json { "reasoning_content": "我已经", "content": "想好了你好" } ``` **Expected:** ```json { "reasoning_content": "我已经想好了", "content": "你好" } ``` ### Why MTP / speculative decoding amplifies this MTP and async output make it more likely that a single returned batch spans the `reasoning tail → → content head` boundary. Combined with the stop buffer delaying `delta_text` by one or more rounds, the text window and the token window become misaligned precisely at the `` boundary — the worst possible place for the parser. ## Root cause analysis ### 1. Stop buffer in the detokenizer `vllm/v1/engine/detokenizer.py`: ```python # Line 86-89: stop buffer length if self.stop and not self.include_stop_str_in_output: self.stop_buffer_length = max(len(s) for s in self.stop) - 1 else: self.stop_buffer_length = 0 # Line 148-164: get_next_output_text holds back tail characters def get_next_output_text(self, finished: bool, delta: bool) -> str: buffer_length = 0 if finished else self.stop_buffer_length ... length = len(self.output_text) - buffer_length last_offset = self._last_output_text_offset if last_offset < length: self._last_output_text_offset = length return self.output_text[last_offset:length] return "" ``` When `finished=False` and `stop` is set, the last `stop_buffer_length` characters are withheld from `delta_text`. ### 2. Token IDs are NOT buffered `vllm/entrypoints/openai/chat_completion/serving.py`: ```python # Line 755: delta_text comes from detokenizer (stop-buffered) delta_text = output.text # Line 776-780: current_token_ids from raw output.token_ids (NOT buffered) current_token_ids = previous_token_ids + as_list(output.token_ids) ``` `output.text` has passed through `get_next_output_text()` and is stop-buffered. `output.token_ids` is the raw incremental token IDs for this round — no buffering applied. ### 3. Qwen3 parser uses token IDs for state, text for splitting `vllm/reasoning/qwen3_reasoning_parser.py:95-147`: ```python def extract_reasoning_streaming(self, previous_text, current_text, delta_text, previous_token_ids, current_token_ids, delta_token_ids): ... if self.end_token_id in delta_token_ids: # line 123: token-based detection end_index = delta_text.find(self.end_token) # line 125: text-based split if end_index >= 0: reasoning = delta_text[:end_index] content = delta_text[end_index + len(self.end_token):] ... return DeltaMessage(reasoning=..., content=...) # line 136: end_token_id in IDs but not in text → return None ← BUG return None if not delta_text: return None elif self.end_token_id in previous_token_ids: # line 142: already ended return DeltaMessage(content=delta_text) # ← everything → content else: return DeltaMessage(reasoning=delta_text) ``` The desynchronization scenario: 1. **Round 1**: `end_token_id in delta_token_ids` is True (token is present), but `delta_text.find(end_token)` is -1 (text held by stop buffer). Falls through to `return None` — reasoning tail is lost. 2. **Round 2**: `end_token_id in previous_t

items.title: [Bug][MP] Qwen3.8-Flash-Next FP8 at TP=4: subpaged-attention-view never applied to the QSA attention group; RawCudaIPCWrapper rejects non-contiguous attention KV under isolated IPC
items.author: anjosluc
items.body_excerpt:
**Correction (2026-10-23, after filing).** My initial diagnosis was wrong on one point: I treated the zero-token KV group as the cause. It isn't. The [LMCache Qwen3.8-Flash-Next recipe](https://docs.lmcache.ai/recipes/qwen3_8_flash_next.html) states that the `0` entry in `group_tokens_per_block` is the QSA `CircularBufferSpec` ring and is expected, and that text is present at the `v0.5.6rc2` tag. I also confirmed in vLLM v0.31.0 that the ring is a `CircularBufferSpec` (`vllm/models/qwen4_exp/qsa_cache.py`) and the compressed key cache is an `MLAAttentionSpec(tokens_per_state=compress_ratio)`, which is the documented compression path. The description below has been rewritten accordingly.

**Label**
`bug`, `mp`

**Describe the bug**

With `LMCacheMPConnector` on Qwen3.8-Flash-Next FP8 (`Qwen4Exp`), KV registration fails on all 4 TP ranks at every startup. The same vLLM/LMCache versions and the same LMCache server work end to end on Qwen3.8-27B NVFP4 at TP=1, where the vLLM log shows `KV cache group edits applied: {'mamba-unified-view': 48, 'subpaged-attention-view': 17}` and retrieves return correct output.

On Flash-Next the log shows only `mamba-unified-view`; `subpaged-attention-view` is never applied. The attention KV tensors then reach `RawCudaIPCWrapper` as a strided window into a dim-0-padded pool and are rejected:

```
ValueError: RawCudaIPCWrapper requires a tensor that is contiguous
  shape  = (5056, 800, 1, 1024)
  stride = (11315200, 1024, 1024, 1)   # stride[0] ~= 13.8x 800*1*1024
```

Server runs with isolated IPC (operator default).

**Reading of the code (please correct me)**

`_SubpagedAttentionViewEdit.matches` (v0.5.6rc2) needs all of:

- `get_kv_cache_spec_kind(spec) in {FULL_ATTENTION, SLIDING_WINDOW, CHUNKED_LOCAL_ATTENTION, SINK_FULL_ATTENTION}`
- `not _declares_slot_compression(spec)`
- `ndim in (5, 4)` and `shape[2] != spec.block_size`

For this model the main QSA attention layer registers a plain `FullAttentionSpec` with no `tokens_per_state`/`compress_ratio`, so none of those three should exclude it — yet the edit is not applied and the tensor is neither logically paged nor contiguous. So either `shape[2] == spec.block_size` for that group (in which case the padded, non-contiguous registration is the bug), or something upstream of `matches` skips the group. We cannot tell from our logs, which only record the applied edits and the rejected tensor.

**Divergence from the validated recipe**

The recipe validates BF16 at TP8, `N = 400`, `--chunk-size 400`, `--max-num-batched-tokens 799`, no `--enable-expert-parallel`, **MTP off** (listed as "not yet validated"). Ours differs in every one of those: FP8, TP4 (unified block 800), chunk 1600, `--max-num-batched-tokens 8192`, EP on, MTP-3 on.

MTP-3 on is forced on our side, not chosen: MTP off drops the block to 784, which does not divide our shared server's `--chunk-size 1600` (the 27B model on the same server needs 1600). We are moving to a per-model server so we can follow the recipe's chunk, and to a nightly after 2026-10-21 so #5693/#5855 are included.

**What we ruled out**

| Experiment | Change | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Baseline | MTP-3 on, vision encoder loaded | `subpaged-attention-view` not applied; contiguity error on all 4 ranks |
| 1 | `--speculative-config` removed | Same: edit not applied. Fails earlier on the chunk check (784 vs 1600) |
| 2 | MTP on, `--language-model-only` | Same: edit not applied, same contiguity error (shape `(5079, 800, 1, 1024)`) |

**Environment**

```text
Model:    Qwen3.8-Flash-Next FP8 (Qwen4Exp)
vLLM:     v0.31.0
LMCache:  0.5.6rc2 (vLLM side and server, same version)
Hardware: 4x RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell (SM120), single node
TP:       4, expert parallel on, --mamba-cache-mode align
Server:   one per node, isolated IPC, --chunk-size 1600, --separate-object-groups,
          --l1-size-gb 16, LRU
```

Other args: `--enable-prefix-caching --enable-chunked-prefill --enable-expert-parallel
--max-num-batched-tokens 8192 --max-num-seqs 16 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.95
--no-enable-flashinfer-autotune --limit-mm-per-prompt.video 0
--speculative-config '{"method":"mtp","num_speculative_tokens":3}'`.
Env: `PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=max_split_size_mb:512` (no `expandable_segments`), `NCCL_CUMEM_ENABLE=0`.

**Expected behavior**

Either the layout edit is applied to the QSA attention group as it is on Qwen3.8-27B, with registration succeeding and retrieves returning correct output; or registration fails fast naming the unsupported spec/layout, instead of a generic IPC contiguity error.

**Asks**

1. Could the edit's `matches` decision be logged per group (kind, `spec.block_size`, `shape[2]`, which condition failed)? That would answer this in one run.
2. Does MTP-3 change the attention group's registration for this model? The recipe validates MTP off, and vLLM's draft-group annotation (vllm#55390) is in v0.31.0.
3. Does #5693 change anything for us beyond unblocking registration? Without the layout edit we would expect the "compressed" misread in #4870 (1/N of each block transferred), which is silent rather than an error.

Related: #4771, #4966, #4870, #5097/#5693/#5855. We can run a nightly or a patch on this hardware and report back.

items.title: [Bug] NVFP4 KV cache + speculative decoding: extend_prefix_lens_cpu is None in the dequant workspace path
items.author: 0xdespot
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

`--kv-cache-dtype nvfp4` and speculative decoding cannot be used together. Any
target-verify step crashes in the FlashInfer dequant workspace with:

```
TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not subscriptable
```

Reproduced on SM120 (RTX 5090) with native MTP (`--speculative-algorithm NEXTN`)
on `unsloth/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4`. Dropping only `--kv-cache-dtype nvfp4` and
keeping everything else boots and serves fine, so the NVFP4 extend path is the
trigger.

There was an earlier report of this in #36001, but it was closed after the
reporter said it had been filed by an agent using their account. The problem is
real, so here it is again with a clean repro and the call chain.

## Repro

Crashes in two different places depending on whether CUDA graphs are on.

**Graphs on - dies during decode graph capture, before the server is up:**

```bash
python -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path unsloth/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4 \
  --kv-cache-dtype nvfp4 \
  --prefill-attention-backend flashinfer \
  --decode-attention-backend trtllm_mha \
  --disable-radix-cache \
  --speculative-algorithm NEXTN \
  --speculative-num-steps 3 \
  --speculative-eagle-topk 1 \
  --speculative-num-draft-tokens 4 \
  --mamba-ssm-dtype bfloat16 \
  --context-length 131072 \
  --mem-fraction-static 0.93 \
  --cuda-graph-max-bs 2 \
  --max-running-requests 2
```

**Graphs off - starts cleanly, then dies on the first request.** Same command
with `--cuda-graph-max-bs 2` swapped for
`--disable-prefill-cuda-graph --disable-decode-cuda-graph`. It reports
`max_total_num_tokens=73280, max_running_requests=2, context_len=131072`,
logs `Application startup complete`, and then the scheduler dies as soon as a
request arrives.

So this is not specific to graph capture. The runtime target-verify path hits it
too.

## Call chain

```
radix_attention.py:279                       forward
hybrid_linear_attn_backend.py:1185           forward
hybrid_linear_attn_backend.py:1134           forward_extend
hybrid_attn_backend.py:213                   forward_extend
flashinfer_backend.py:1273                   forward_extend
    kv_cache = pool.get_flashinfer_dequant_workspace_kv_buffer(
        ..., forward_batch.extend_prefix_lens_cpu, ...)
memory_pool.py:3879 -> 2565                  get_flashinfer_dequant_workspace_kv_buffer
memory_pool.py:2645                          _prepare_dequant_extend_workspace
    prev_len = int(extend_prefix_lens_cpu[i])     # None
```

Under graph capture the same chain is reached through
`capture_decode_graph -> capture_one_shape -> run_once -> qwen3_vl.py:1482
forward -> general_mm_embed_routine`, since with MTP the decode graph captures a
target-verify step, which is an extend.

## Why the field is None

`ForwardBatch.init_new` populates the `_cpu` mirrors on one path and skips them
on the other, on purpose:

```python
if isinstance(extend_seq_lens, list):
    # Main path: H2D from host lists; populate *_cpu mirrors.
    ...
    ret.extend_prefix_lens_cpu = extend_prefix_lens
    ret.extend_seq_lens_cpu = extend_seq_lens
else:
    # gpu_only: device tensors handed in directly; leave *_cpu unset.
    assert isinstance(extend_seq_lens, torch.Tensor)
    ret.extend_seq_lens = extend_seq_lens
    ret.extend_prefix_lens = extend_prefix_lens
```

Speculative decoding builds its verify batch on the gpu-only path, which avoids
a D2H sync per verify step. `_prepare_dequant_extend_workspace` needs host-side
prefix lengths to pick which pages to dequantize. Those two assumptions collide,
so the field is None whenever spec decode meets an NVFP4 KV pool.

`flashinfer_backend.py:1273` passes the field unconditionally whenever
`prefill_uses_dequant_workspace` is set, which is only true for a quantized KV
pool, which is why nothing else trips over it.

## Notes on fixing it

Populating the `_cpu` mirrors in the spec verify batch is enough to get it
running with CUDA graphs disabled. That costs a D2H sync of a bs-sized tensor per
verify step.

That does not cover the graphs-on case.
`get_flashinfer_dequant_workspace_kv_buffer` is called from inside
`forward_extend`, so it sits inside the captured region. Host values can't be
read there during capture, and capture-time values baked into the graph would
select the wrong pages on replay without raising anything. Making graphs work
looks like it needs the workspace prep moved into the plan/metadata phase, or
the fused NVFP4 extend kernel from #23354, which would drop the host dependency.

Since graphs are worth roughly 2.6x on this model for us, the graphs-off
workaround isn't much use on its own. Flagging it in case it's useful for a
partial fix or a clearer error message in the meantime.

A second thing worth mentioning: `--speculative-draft-attention-backend` takes a
single value applied to both draft prefill and decode
(`model_executor/model_runner_components/attention_backend_setup.py:171`). NVFP4 KV needs `flashinfer` for extend and
`trtllm_mha` for decode, so there's no single value that works for an external
draft model either.

## Environment

```
sglang            0.0.0.dev50+gdb570fe61  (commit db570fe, 2026-08-22)
flashinfer        0.6.17
torch             2.13.0+cu130
triton            3.7.1
transformers      5.12.1
GPU               RTX 5090 (SM120), driver 595.84
model             unsloth/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4
```

items.title: OTel tracing overhead cliffs at c=50 on TP=2 deployments — level/flush tuning has no effect
items.author: wangxf1987
items.body_excerpt:
## Title

OTel trace overhead benchmark on a production-style K8s deployment (TP=2, 2 replicas): throughput loss of 20-33% at c>=50, trace level and flush threshold have negligible effect

## Summary

We benchmarked `--enable-trace` overhead on a production-shaped K8s deployment (RBG + LeaderWorkerSet, not docker-compose), Qwen3.6-27B-CHO on sglang v0.5.18, TP=2 per replica x 2 replicas (4 GPUs total, not an exclusive full node). This complements the larger-scale results already discussed elsewhere for TP=8 exclusive-node setups, and shows the overhead shape is very different at smaller TP.

Full report (charts + tables): attached PDF (`report-en.pdf`). Raw data (`result.csv`, GPU/CPU logs) available on request.

## Environment

- sglang `v0.5.18` (community image), `SGLANG_TRACE_ASYNC=1`
- Deployment: K8s RBG + LeaderWorkerSet, TP=2 per replica, 2 replicas, 4x H20 GPUs
- Trace path: sglang engine -> local OTel Agent (DaemonSet, node-local endpoint) -> Gateway -> backend, i.e. a two-hop agent-gw architecture, not a direct hardcoded Gateway connection
- 4 configs compared:
  | Group | trace level | async | flush threshold |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | G1 baseline | disabled | - | - |
  | G2 | 2 | 1 | default |
  | G3 | 3 | 1 | default |
  | G4 | 2 | 1 | 50 |
- Load generator: fixed-prompt benchmark client, concurrency swept across 1/10/50/100/200, 3 repeats per level (median)

## Findings

1. **Overhead is mild at low concurrency (c<=10)**: ttft_p99 +6~71%, throughput loss only 3~4%.
2. **c=50 is a clear inflection point**: ttft_p99 jumps 4.6x (172ms -> 965ms) going from G1 to G2 — roughly equivalent to the G1 baseline's own c=100 latency level being pulled forward to c=50. In other words, enabling trace shifts the whole latency-saturation curve left by one concurrency tier.
3. **From c>=50 onward, throughput loss is stable at 20~33%**, and grows with concurrency (-20.3% at c=50, up to -33.1% at c=200).
4. **Trace level 2 -> 3 produced no measurable incremental overhead** at c>=10 (all deltas within noise, ±2%).
5. **`SGLANG_TRACE_ASYNC_FLUSH_THRESHOLD=50` vs. default also produced no measurable benefit** at c>=50 (within ±16%, mostly ±2%; one anomalous +132.9% ttft_p99 spike at c=10 looked like a transient one-off, not reproduced at other levels).
6. **Root cause for (4) and (5): CPU was never the bottleneck in this setup.** Host CPU utilization on the GPU node stayed at 2~3% across all 4 groups (vs. GPU sm% rising from 14.8% baseline to 16~19% with trace enabled). Both trace-level and flush-threshold tuning target CPU-side span processing cost — with only 2 TP ranks, span volume is low enough that CPU headroom is never exhausted, so those knobs have nothing to bite on at this scale.
7. This is a **much smaller overhead** than what we see at TP=8 on an exclusive full node (throughput loss there was 75~79%, itl_p99 spiking ~28x, with CPU pegged at 99% — happy to share that data too if useful). The magnitude gap tracks roughly linearly with TP rank count, since span generation scales with the number of ranks, and the TP=8 test used synchronous export while this one used async by default.

## Why we're filing this

- The community advice we've seen elsewhere ("lower `SGLANG_TRACE_LEVEL` to reduce overhead", "tune the async flush threshold") holds at high TP / high CPU pressure, but **doesn't transfer to smaller TP configs** — those knobs are simply inert until CPU saturates. Worth calling out in docs/guidance so users at TP<=2-4 don't spend time tuning a lever with no effect.
- The **c=50 inflection point** (throughput loss going from ~4% to ~20% within one concurrency step) suggests there may be a queueing/lock-contention effect on the trace export path that kicks in once concurrent in-flight spans cross some threshold, rather than a smooth linear cost per request. Might be worth profiling `trace_async.py`'s buffer/flush path under concurrent load to see if there's a lock or queue that serializes once request volume rises (in our TP=8 investigation, we found `trace_req_finish()`/`abort()` and `__getstate__` all trigger unconditional flushes regardless of the configured threshold, and `trace_req_start()`'s `tracer.start_span()` + `propagate.inject()` calls are synchronous OTel API calls on the request path — happy to dig further if maintainers think that's a productive direction).
- Production guidance: for small/mid TP deployments (TP<=2-4), default trace config (level=2, async on) is fine as-is. For TP=8-class deployments, overhead is materially higher and level-tuning is the effective lever — but this should probably be stated explicitly since it's not obvious from the trace docs which regime a given deployment falls into.

## Attachments

- `report-en.pdf` — full benchmark report with charts (ttft_p99 / itl_p99 / e2e_p50 / throughput vs. concurrency, delta% overview, GPU/CPU resource usage)
[Uploading report-en.pdf…]()

items.title: [Bug] Potential hybrid GDN Radix-cache selected-logprob drift on repeated branch scoring
items.author: furedericca-lab

## Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues and did not find an existing report that fully covers this request shape.
- [ ] I have not re-run this on today's latest main; the reproduction was observed on pinned main commit `2f5c9ac43d76eef11e8561c89c55a79db7db715a` (2026-09-25).
- [x] Environment details and a standalone `/generate` reproducer are included below.
- [x] This is a possible correctness issue rather than a general usage question.
- [x] Report is in English.

## Describe the bug

With a hybrid GDN Qwen3.8-27B NVFP4 checkpoint, repeated selected-token logprob scoring is stable when Radix Cache is disabled, but the first Radix-enabled branch scoring pass differs substantially from subsequent identical passes.

The observation is:

| Cache configuration | Max repeated selected-logprob delta | Pattern |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| Unified Radix Cache enabled | `2.551527976989746` | run 1 differs; runs 2 and 3 match exactly |
| Radix Cache disabled | `0.0` | runs 1, 2 and 3 match exactly |

The prefix is explicitly warmed before the repeated branch batches. With Radix enabled, the server log reports `#cached-token: 0` for the first branch batch and `#cached-token: 128` for later identical branch batches. With Radix disabled, the three repeated branch batches are bit-stable.

This strongly correlates the drift with the cache-hit execution path, but I do **not** want to over-attribute the root cause: the current evidence does not prove that a specific GDN recurrent-state checkpoint, restore, split, or other hybrid-cache internal operation is responsible.

This was found while gating a decision workload that consumes candidate-token logprobs directly, so cache-hit equivalence matters even when the top-1 decision itself does not change.

Related work:

- #22935 — Mamba Radix cache prefix/split behavior
- #34899 — bit-exact correctness coverage for Unified Radix Cache
- #38625 — interior/no-buffer checkpoint work

I am not assuming that #22935 or #38625 has the same root cause or fully covers this request shape. In particular, I would like to know whether a shared prefix followed by divergent option branches is expected to preserve selected-token logprobs under deterministic inference when the later identical branch requests hit the hybrid cache.

## Environment

Tested environment:

- SGLang source: `2f5c9ac43d76eef11e8561c89c55a79db7db715a`
- SGLang package: `0.5.21.dev612+g2f5c9ac43`
- Model: `ukisai/Swift-1.5-Qwen3.8-27b-NVFP4`
- Model revision: `332d277a083ca395aa2f822842b82f5f2f3913a2`
- Architecture: `Qwen3_5ForConditionalGeneration`, hybrid GDN / full attention
- Quantization: ModelOpt mixed FP8/NVFP4
- GPUs: 2 × NVIDIA RTX 5090 (SM120), TP=2
- NVIDIA driver: `610.57.04`
- Kernel: `7.0.0-34-generic`
- Python: `3.13.11`
- PyTorch: `2.14.0a0.post20260925` (CUDA 13.4)
- Triton: `3.7.0`
- `sglang-kernel==0.4.7`
- `flash-attn-4==4.0.0b19`

- Deterministic inference: enabled
- Prefill CUDA Graph: disabled
- Decode CUDA Graph: retained
- Unified Radix Cache: enabled for the failing case
- Observed Mamba strategy: `extra_buffer`
- Comparison case: identical server settings plus only `--disable-radix-cache`

A literal `python3 -m sglang.check_env` dump was not retained for this run; the exact pinned runtime versions above are from the same project environment used for the reproduction.

## Reproduction

Launch the candidate server with Radix Cache enabled:

```bash
python -m sglang.launch_server \

items.title: [Feature]  Streamed restore: chunked materialization for oversized storage hits in buffer_only HiCache mode
items.author: R-omk
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] If this is not a feature request but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Motivation


`--hicache-host-memory-mode buffer_only` (PR #34798 + #36345) turned host RAM
into a pure staging buffer between L3 (disk) and L1 (VRAM), which fixed a
whole class of L2/L1 consistency problems. But it introduced a hard sizing
constraint: **a storage hit larger than the empty host arena is rejected
wholesale** (`_reject_oversized_prefetch` → *"declined: cannot fit in an
empty host arena"*), and the entire prompt is recomputed by prefill even
though every one of its pages exists on disk.

In practice this forces `--hicache-size` to be at least as large as the
longest conversation (host RAM ≈ max context), defeating the point of a
"transit buffer" for long-context agentic workloads:

- Qwen3.8-27B hybrid GDN, 524k context (YaRN), TP=4: `hicache-size 6`
  (~24 GiB of pinned host RAM across ranks) just to guarantee that a 500k
  restore never gets declined.
- Cold prefill of a 300k prompt: **~89 s** at ~3.4k tok/s. The same prompt
  is fully written to L3 via `write_through`, yet it is still re-prefilled
  from scratch whenever it exceeds the arena.

What buffer_only is missing is the ability to **stream an oversized hit
through a small arena in chunks**, the same way a download streams through
a bounded socket buffer — the arena should be a throughput knob, not a
capacity ceiling.



## Proposed approach

Split an oversized hit into arena-sized chunks and pipeline them:

1. **Trim** (`_trim_oversized_prefetch`): instead of rejecting, cut the hit
   to the largest page-aligned prefix that fits an *empty* arena
   (anti-livelock: a busy arena still defers the whole hit) and park the
   remainder in a `pending_stream_tails` registry.
2. **Materialize** (`_materialize_stream_chunk`): an intermediate chunk is
   published straight to the device tree as a **KV-only leaf** (evict →
   `cc.load` H2D → root-relative insert with the stock ownership
   choreography and a fail-stop post-insert check). The mamba state is
   not needed mid-span: the tree keeps FULL-only leaves valid, and the
   joint match excludes them until the endpoint checkpoint lands.
3. **Continue** (`_finish_stream_chunk` at the H2D ack): free the bounce,
   unpin the leaf, settle the chunk's share of the storage-hit accounting,
   and re-issue the parked tail as a fresh prefetch into the hit drain —
   which may trim again for 3+ chunk spans.
4. **Admit**: the *final* chunk rides the normal staged-admission path; by
   then the device tree holds every earlier chunk, `prepare_staged_prefetch`
   plans from the FULL match over the whole span, and the mamba endpoint
   checkpoint arrives with the tail's TRAILING_PAGES fetch.

The main invariants the implementation must preserve: the admission gate
has to hold the request across the whole chunk cycle (it spans scheduler
ticks where `ongoing_prefetch` is empty); each chunk's H2D needs an explicit
`start_loading()` (stock only submits loads during admission, which the
gate withholds) plus a `has_free_load_back_slot()` check; and the Rust
TreeCore currently expects a donated `mamba_value` on every insert
(`rust/sglang-radix-tree/src/components/mamba.rs`), so KV-only leaves today
require `SGLANG_UNIFIED_RADIX_TREE_CORE_BACKEND=python` or a Rust-side
change. The full lifecycle rules (anchor pins, stale-tail rebasing,
accounting) are documented in the patch header linked below.

## Measured results

TP=4 RTX 5090, Qwen3.8-27B NVFP4 hybrid GDN, 298,567-token prompt, L3 on
PCIe Gen5 NVMe RAID0, sglang main `ed8c3139f1` (2026-10-16). `hicache-size`
is per-rank GiB (TP=4): size 6 ≈ 24 GiB total, size 2 ≈ 8 GiB total.

| Metric | Before (size 6, whole-hit-or-decline) | After (size 2, streamed) |
|---|---|---|
| Host staging RAM (TP=4 total) | 24 GiB (arena 647k > max ctx — streaming never triggers) | **8 GiB** (arena 216k) |
| Warm restore from disk (L1 empty) | n/a at size 2 — would decline & re-prefill **~89 s** | **15.5 s** (2 chunks: 215,680 + 82,880; 298,560/298,567 tokens from storage = 99.998%) |
| Repeat hit after restore | 0.4 s (L1) | 0.4 s (L1) |
| Decode / EAGLE over restored ctx | 144 tok/s, accept 0.68 | unchanged |

Server flags for the "After" column (full setup in the Gist):

```bash
--enable-hierarchical-cache --hicache-host-memory-mode buffer_only \
--hicache-size 2 --hicache-mem-layout page_first --hicache-io-backend kernel \
--hicache-write-policy write_through --hicache-storage-backend file \
--hicache-storage-prefetch-policy timeout --page-size 64 --tp 4
```

RAM cost drops 3× while keeping the zero-recompute guarantee for any
conversation length; `--hicache-size` becomes a throughput/parallelism knob
instead of a correctness constraint.



### Related resources


- **Working patch (Gist)**: [`streamed-restore.patch` ](https://gist.github.com/R-omk/5ea76d1317147af28393654f58ebd859) 
  against sgl-project/sglang@ed8c3139f1 (main, 2026-10-16), three files
  (`buffer_mode/pipeline.py`, `unified_radix_cache.py`,
  `unified_cache/components/mamba.py`), ~1,100 diff lines.
  Self-contained header documents scope: TP lockstep preserved, SWA models
  excluded (declined as before), PP prefetch excluded (asserted), requires
  the Python TreeCore today.
- The decline being removed: `_reject_oversized_prefetch` in
  `python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/buffer_mode/pipeline.py`.
- Buffer-only mode foundation: #34798, #36345 (Mamba support).
- Adjacent open work the patch builds on: #41453 (in-flight storage prefetch
  retry helper — the tail re-issue reuses the same retry set),
  #44344 (write-backlog throttle — orthogonal, write side).

The patch has been exercised on single-request cold and warm restores,
modified-tail requests, and mid-cycle aborts, with correct decode output
over the restored context

items.title: [Bug] HiCache NIXL L3: under O_DIRECT the DSA indexer sidecar is never written, and the 0-byte objects are restored as hits, so restored prefixes get zero index-K (silent output change, EAGLE accept collapse)
items.author: schroderfernando16
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

With `--hicache-storage-backend nixl` (POSIX plugin, default O_DIRECT) on a DSA model (GLM-5.3), the INDEXER hybrid pool takes the bounce-buffer path, because its page (667,392 B) is not 4096-aligned. Bounce slots are unpadded, so every O_DIRECT indexer write fails with `EINVAL`. The file still exists, because path-mode registration opens it with `create`.

On restore:
- `_query_keys_exist` counts the 0-byte object as a hit (stat only);
- the O_DIRECT read at EOF returns 0 bytes, which NIXL 1.4.x reports as success;
- `batch_get_v2` copies the zero-filled bounce slots into the host indexer pages;
- the DSA clamp commits the full prefix.

The restored prefix then has correct MLA KV but **all-zero index-K and scales**. That changes the target's sparse top-k, and the packed MTP layer's. Nothing is logged at error level on the read side.

Under DP attention it hits at the start of every run. All DP ranks share MLA keys (storage `tp_rank = attn_tp_rank = 0`, suffix `_{model}`), so sibling ranks restore the shared system prompt from L3 instead of prefilling it.

Related open PRs fix parts of this: #35231, #42491, #36524, #37690, #39550. This issue documents the user-visible consequence (silent wrong output) on DSA + DP attention, and asks for a minimal fix and a size check to land.

## Environment

- SGLang `0.5.18` inside the NVIDIA Dynamo `sglang-runtime:1.5.1` container.
- NIXL `1.4.0` (`pip show nixl nixl-cu13` in the running container).
- Hardware: 1x p6-b200.48xlarge (8x B200), L3 on an instance-store NVMe RAID0 (`md127`).
  - FS: `xfs`.
  - Logical / physical sector size: 512 / 512 B (`/sys/block/md127/queue/*_block_size`).
  - Kernel: `6.12.110` (Bottlerocket, EKS Auto Mode).
- Model: `RadixArk/GLM-5.3-NVFP4` (`GlmMoeDsaForCausalLM`: 78 layers + 1 nextn, `index_head_dim` 128, `index_topk` 2048), KV `fp8_e4m3`.
- Args, per engine (2 engines on the node, 4 GPUs each):

```
--tp 4 --dp 4 --enable-dp-attention --page-size 64 --kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3
--speculative-algorithm EAGLE --speculative-num-steps 3 --speculative-eagle-topk 1 --speculative-num-draft-tokens 4
--enable-hierarchical-cache --hicache-size 100            # defaults: write_through, kernel, page_first
--hicache-storage-backend nixl
env SGLANG_HICACHE_NIXL_BACKEND_PLUGIN=POSIX SGLANG_HICACHE_NIXL_BACKEND_STORAGE_DIR=/kvcache/l3   # one dir per engine
```

## Reproduction

Minimal recipe (not yet run in isolation; the evidence below comes from 900 s benchmark replays):


1. Start one engine as above, with an empty L3 directory.
2. Send one request with a long shared prefix: a 5,632-token system prompt (88 pages) plus suffix A. `round_robin` places it on DP rank 0, which prefills it and writes the pages to L3.
3. Send 3 more requests with the same prefix and different suffixes. Ranks 1-3 each issue an L3 prefetch of 5,632 tokens (`sglang:prefetched_tokens_total` +5,632 each), then a load-back.
4. Greedy check: send an identical request (`temperature=0`) 4 times so it lands on each rank once, and compare outputs and `sglang:spec_accept_length` per `dp_rank`.
5. Inspect L3: `find $SGLANG_HICACHE_NIXL_BACKEND_STORAGE_DIR -iname '*indexer*' -size 0 | wc -l` and `ls -l` on a KV object and on an indexer object.

Kernel-level check, no GPU needed: `dd if=/dev/zero of=$DIR/t bs=667392 count=1 oflag=direct` fails with `Invalid argument`.

## Expected

- Indexer objects hold 667,392 B, and restored prefixes behave like a local prefill.
- Or, if the sidecar cannot be persisted, the restore is a miss and the prefix is recomputed.

## Actual

- Ranks that restored the prefix from L3 produce different outputs from the rank that prefilled it, and their EAGLE acceptance collapses. They stay that way until `flush_cache`. The writer rank is unaffected.
- Indexer objects are 0 bytes, confirmed on the node after the runs: **168,007 of 168,007** `*_indexer` objects are 0 B, while all 171,454 KV objects hold 2,912,256 B (= 79 x 64 x 576).
- The kernel check reproduces: `dd ... bs=667392 oflag=direct` → `Invalid argument` and a 0-byte file; the same command with the 512-aligned size 667,648 succeeds.
- Boot and backup warnings were not captured: the affected pods were gone and no log collector was running.

## Evidence (12 pod-runs, 6 runs of 900 s, 2 engines x 4 DP ranks)

| Signal | Value |
|---|---|
| L3 restores of the 5,632-token prefix vs ranks with collapsed acceptance | 31 vs 31; per-engine match 12/12; never more than 3 of 4 ranks; writer rank always healthy |
| EAGLE accept length, healthy → restored rank | 2.24 → 1.24 (accept rate 0.41 → ~0.07); per-rank decode tok/s -50% |
| Target output | reasoning share of output tokens 0.52-0.65 → 0.21-0.38 per run (target changed, not only the draft) |
| `hicache_backup_bytes / tokens` = `load_back_bytes / tokens` | 55,932 B = 79 x (576 KV + 132 indexer), so the indexer is in host memory |
| Bytes written to the L3 device per run vs prediction | 390-415 GB measured; KV-only 390-427 GB; KV+indexer 479-525 GB. Indexer bytes never reach disk. |
| `prefetched_tokens_total` increments | always 5,632 (88 pages); 1,056- and 440-page prefixes are read (20-32 GB/run of device reads) and then discarded by the >128-page bounce limit |
| Control: same image, Qwen3.8 TP1 (all pools `zero_copy=True` under O_DIRECT) | L3 restores work, hit ratio 46.9% → 72.4% |

## Suspected code (v0.5.18; unchanged at the same points in v0.5.22 and main@1c2f42470c)

- `mem_cache/memory_pool_host.py:1110-1131`, `:1512-1521`: indexer page = (78 + 1 MTP) x 64 x 132 = 667,392 B, not 4096-aligned.
- `mem_cache/storage/nixl/hicache_nixl.py`:
  - `:453-471` (main `:471`): bounce fallback;
  - `:473-477` (main `:484`) and `:583-597`: slots `base + i*page_bytes`, with no padding;
  - `:227-236` (main `:240`): existence is `res is not None` and the returned size is ignored;
  - `:946-982`: bounce copy for every page marked ok;
  - `:555-562` (main `:564`): >128-page hybrid transfers are rejected rather than chunked;

items.title: [Bug]  Xid 13 "CTA Not Present" in HiCache kvcacheio transfer kernels on Blackwell (B20Z) — 7 crashes across 4 machines / 7 GPU instances under agentic load
items.author: elain
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug


**Summary**: Under sustained agentic (SWE-agent) load with HiCache hierarchical caching (`kernel` IO backend, `page_first` layout, Mooncake L3 storage backend), the GPU throws `Xid 13 Graphics SM Exception: CTA Not Present`, the NCCL watchdog fires `CUDA error: unspecified launch failure`, and the engine orderly-suicides (60s coredump wait → kill process tree). We have observed **7 crashes across 4 different machines and 7 distinct GPU instances** (two machines crashed on two *different* physical GPUs each), all with byte-identical signatures — ruling out GPU hardware failure.

**Crash signature** (identical across all 7 events):
```
NVRM: Xid (PCI:xx:xx.x): 13, Graphics SM Cga Exception on (GPC x, TPC x, SM x): CTA Not Present
NVRM: Xid (PCI:xx:xx.x): 13, pid=xxxxx, name=python3, Graphics Exception:
      channel 0x00000002, Class 0000cdc0, Offset 00000000, Data 00000000
```
Engine side:
```
[PG ID 2 PG GUID 3(tp:device) Rank N] Process group watchdog thread terminated with exception:
CUDA error: unspecified launch failure (cudaErrorLaunchFailure)
```

**Incident log** (all within 20 hours):

| # | Time | Machine | GPU (PCIe) | Concurrency | Cache state | Crash timing |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 10-23 13:50 | node-A | 63:00 | c192 | warm | KV usage 0.99, 205K pending, write_through churn |
| 2 | 10-23 20:26 | node-B | a3:00 | c160 | semi-warm | 2.6 min into run, fetch-heavy warmup |
| 3 | 10-23 20:50 | node-C | ab:00 | c160 | semi-warm | 4.0 min into run, fetch-heavy warmup |
| 4 | 10-24 07:27 | node-D | 67:00 | **c144** | **cold** (10h idle) | 2 min in; 5,720 HiCache prefetch ops in 5 min |
| 5 | 10-24 07:56 | node-A | **af:00** (2nd GPU!) | c150 | warm (ramped) | 5.8 min in, steady-state measurement |
| 6 | 10-24 08:22 | node-D | **63:00** (2nd GPU!) | c144 | fully warm | 4.2 min in, 3rd attempt of same level |
| 7 | 10-24 09:07 | node-B | **af:00** (2nd GPU!) | c144 + `reasoning_effort=low` | warm | 3.2 min in; **20+ Xid lines in one burst** on a single GPU |

Key observations:
1. **Not resource exhaustion**: crashes occur at KV token usage as low as 0.60, queue depth 0–3, GPU compute at ~11% of max running requests.
2. **Not hardware**: nodes A and B each crashed on two *different* physical GPUs with identical signatures; nodes C and D each crashed once. All 4 machines, 7 GPU instances, same `channel 0x2 / Class 0xcdc0 / CTA Not Present`.
3. **Trigger = HiCache transfer intensity**: every crash correlates with high volume of L1↔L2↔L3 KV transfers through the custom copy kernels (fetch bursts during warmup, write_through churn during eviction storms, or steady-state paging when working set exceeds L1). The fault is **probabilistic** — higher transfer intensity ⇒ earlier crash.
4. **`direct` IO backend is immune**: `--hicache-io-backend direct` (plain cudaMemcpyAsync) at the same c160 load ran **2/2 clean** — same data volume, same buses, same co-located Mooncake stores. This isolates the fault to the custom kernel path, not the data, the pinned host pool, or RDMA.
5. **Related known issues** (same Xid 13 CGA signature on Blackwell, different code paths):
   - #34340 (cutedsl TGV BF16 GEMM, B300, 2-CTA clusters)
   - #32855 (Kimi-K3 DSPARK, B300, ~218K context)
   - #34260 (Kimi-K3, clarifies Xid 13 CGA = thread-block cluster fault, not MMU)
   - #45989 (HiCache + Mooncake L3 scheduler admission bug — different failure mode, but same battlefront: HiCache+Mooncake under agentic load on GLM-5.3; their "device prefix shrank before admission" log also suggests lookup/admission races in the L3 interaction layer)

**Code localization** (v0.5.22, `python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/pool_host/dsa.py`):

The `kernel` IO backend dispatches both transfer directions to the `kvcacheio/hicache.cuh` CUDA kernel family:
- **Load (host→device, per-layer, page_first)**: `transfer_kv_per_layer_mla_pf_lf` (prebuilt `sgl_kernel.kvcacheio`)
- **Backup (device→host, all-layer, page_first)**: `transfer_hicache_all_layer_mla_staged_lf_pf` (JIT-compiled via `load_jit` from the same `hicache.cuh` header, staged through a device buffer) or prebuilt `transfer_kv_all_layer_mla_lf_pf`

All implicated ops share the `HiCacheKernel` template in `hicache.cuh` (with `block_quota` / `unroll` template parameters). GPU kernels directly read/write a single large pinned host tensor (up to 128 GB per rank, page_first layout) with device↔host transfers on two concurrent dedicated CUDA streams.

### Reproduction

**Workload**: SWE-agent session replay (Open-SWE-Traces via OpenHands framework), ~35K avg context per session, 98–99.8% prefix-cache hit rate, 128–160 concurrent sessions.

**Repro recipe**:
1. **High-yield (warm hierarchy, 2/2 for us)**: warm the cache with a lower-concurrency round (e.g., c128 for 5 min), then ramp to **c160** — crash within 2–5 min.
2. **Cold-start**: idle ≥ several hours (L1/L2 fully cold, L3 warm), start directly at **c144** — crash within ~2 min.
3. **Steady-state**: fully warm, run **c150+** sustained — crash within 3–6 min (probabilistic).

**Control experiments**:
- `--hicache-io-backend direct` at c160: **2/2 clean** (zero crashes, but ~33% lower throughput due to per-copy cudaMemcpy overhead)
- Staying at c128 or below (working set ≤ 75% of L1 pool, near-zero steady-state paging): **~10 runs over 2 days, zero crashes**

Happy to share full dmesg excerpts, engine scheduler logs (pre-crash HiCache prefetch bursts), NCCL watchdog traces, and the workload driver configuration.

### Additional context

- **Driver note*

items.title: [RFC]: Limit the use of envvars in vLLM
items.author: zhuohan123
items.body_excerpt:
### Motivation.

vLLM's envvars are on the edge of getting out of control. There are many envvars should instead be configs. Like the attention backend, all2all kernel backend, and even there is a flag to control KV cache layout. envvars are evil because:

1. It is equivalent of using global variables everywhere in the code, which is a bad programming practice.
2. envvars have no advanced structure like, hierarchy, typechecks, etc. 

In summary, I think envvars are the kind of thing that is very easy to add so people tend to add envvars as the shortest path to implement their feature, but this can quickly becomes unmanageable and makes the project very hard to use. 

### Proposed Change.

I think we should:

1. Spend some effort on reviewing the current envvars and move many of them to configs.
2. Have very strict bar on what can be an envvar and question every new envvars in vllm.

### Feedback Period.

_No response_

_No response_

_No response_

items.title: [Bug]: Inkling (InklingForConditionalGeneration) fails on SM120 — tml_fa4 attention lacks paged-KV support
items.author: Rawsejet
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

Serving `thinkingmachines/Inkling-Small-NVFP4` (`InklingForConditionalGeneration`) fails on **SM120** (RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell / GeForce Blackwell / DGX Spark) because the bundled Thinking Machines `tml_fa4` relative-attention kernel does not implement **paged KV** (or split-KV) on SM 12.0. vLLM's V1 engine always uses paged KV, so the forward pass aborts during startup profiling.

The NVFP4 **MoE/GEMM** path works fine on SM120 (`FLASHINFER_CUTLASS NvFp4` backend loads and weights load at ~78 GiB/GPU); only the **attention** kernel is gated off.

### Root cause

`vllm/third_party/tml_fa4/interface.py` (also mirrored at `vllm/vllm_flash_attn/cute/interface.py`), in the SM120 branch:

```python
elif arch // 10 == 12:
    # SM120 (Blackwell GeForce / DGX Spark): uses SM80 MMA with SM120 SMEM capacity
    assert not use_block_sparsity, "Block sparsity not supported on SM 12.0"
    assert page_table is None, "Paged KV not supported on SM 12.0 in this PR"
    assert not is_split_kv, "SplitKV not supported on SM 12.0 in this PR"
    fa_fwd = FlashAttentionForwardSm120(...)
```

Because vLLM serving passes a `page_table` (paged KV cache), the forward pass hits:

```
AssertionError: Paged KV not supported on SM 12.0 in this PR
RuntimeError: Worker failed with error 'Paged KV not supported on SM 12.0'
```

The cutedsl warmup also asserts `SM120 forward only supports num_splits=1` earlier (skippable via `--kernel-config.enable_cutedsl_warmup=False`), but the paged-KV assertion in the real forward is the hard blocker.

### Environment

- GPU: 2× NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Workstation Edition (SM120 / compute capability 12.0), 96 GiB each
- vLLM: `0.26.1rc1.dev376+g613411a90` (nightly, `wheels.vllm.ai/nightly`)
- torch `2.13.0+cu130`, flashinfer `0.6.15.post1`, CUDA 13.2 toolkit, driver 595.x
- TP=2

### Repro

```bash
vllm serve thinkingmachines/Inkling-Small-NVFP4 \
  --tensor-parallel-size 2 \
  --tokenizer-mode inkling \
  --reasoning-parser inkling --tool-call-parser inkling --enable-auto-tool-choice \
  --kernel-config.enable_flashinfer_autotune=False \
  --trust-remote-code
# env: VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=1
```

Startup: weights load, FP4 MoE backend selects, KV cache is sized, then the worker dies in the forward pass with the `Paged KV not supported on SM 12.0` assertion.

### Expected

Inkling attention (`FlashAttentionForwardSm120`) supports paged KV (and ideally split-KV) on SM120 so the model can be served, matching SM100/B200. Alternatively, a documented supported-hardware note that Inkling requires SM100+ (B200/GB200/H200/B300) would save others the investigation.

### Notes

Happy to test patches on SM120 hardware.

items.title: [L2][fs_native] Failed stores stay visible to lookups — later retrieves serve corrupted KV (gibberish output)
items.author: stefanskiasan
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

With the `fs_native` L2 adapter enabled, `Store task N to adapter 0 failed for
keys: [...]` warnings appear at a low but steady rate — and **every subsequent
retrieve that hits one of those keys returns corrupted KV**. The model answer
degenerates into gibberish, at temperature 0, reproducibly.

The failed store leaves the key visible to lookups. It is only a `WARNING`; no
exception is raised, and the key is not invalidated.

## Environment

- 8× MI355X (gfx950), ROCm 7.2.3, one server per 4-GPU replica
- vLLM with `glm_moe_dsa` (GLM-5.3, full model), TP4, MTP k=4,
  `--kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3`, `--block-size 16`, prefix caching on
- `LMCacheMPConnector`, `lmcache_driven` transfer mode, chunk-size 256
- Server: `--l1-size-gb 150 --separate-object-groups --eviction-policy LRU`
  `--l2-prefetch-policy retain`
  `--l2-adapter '{"type":"fs_native","base_path":"/l2","num_workers":8,"use_odirect":false}'`

## Reproduction

Two replicas, identical except for the L2 adapter:

| | replica A | replica B |
|---|---|---|
| `--l2-adapter fs_native` | yes | **no** |
| failed stores | 44 → 66 during eight requests | **0** in 25 049 stores |
| answers on a cache hit | **gibberish** | correct |

The cleanest probe is `cache_salt`, which changes only the cache key:

```
prompt without salt   (cache hit)   3.4 s   GARBAGE  '0.  district120 is0, the ...'
same prompt, new salt (cache miss)  5.0 s   CORRECT  '73605 The user has provided ...'
same prompt, new salt (cache miss)  5.0 s   CORRECT
prompt without salt   (cache hit)   3.4 s   GARBAGE  '1 district contains1.3,. ...'
```

Note the timing: the corrupted runs are **faster** than the correct ones —
they are served from the cache instead of being computed.

The corruption survives a full vLLM restart (the cache server outlives it) and
survives restarting the cache server itself, because new failures keep
occurring: 22 fresh failures during the eight requests above.

## Not the cause

- Disk: write test 4.9 GB/s into the L2 directory, inodes at 1 %, 459 GB free,
  ext4, no errors in the log and no traceback anywhere.
- vLLM side: with LMCache disabled entirely (prefix caching still on), all
  eight requests are correct.
- Recreating the same server **without** `--l2-adapter` makes the problem
  disappear completely: 0 failed stores, 8/8 correct, needle test 5/5 twice
  (the second run with a warm cache).

## Expected

A store that fails must not leave a lookup-visible key. Either the key is
rolled back on failure, or the retrieve path must validate that all object
groups for a key are actually present before serving it. Silently serving a
partially stored entry turns an I/O warning into a correctness bug that looks
like model failure — it cost us two and a half hours of debugging the model
before we suspected the cache.

Related: #4987 (IPC event churn on ROCm in the same connector).

items.title: [Bug] P2P load timeout can report terminal failure while the transfer is still active
items.author: 0andy
items.body_excerpt:
**Describe the bug**

`P2PL2Adapter.query_load_result()` returns a terminal all-zero `Bitmap` as soon as `load_timeout_s` expires, without querying or cancelling the underlying `TransferChannelClient` read ([p2p_l2_adapter.py#L333-L336](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/8d7d2c47e1edb8c107033ae709722b2c3a05dec4/lmcache/v1/distributed/l2_adapters/p2p_l2_adapter.py#L333-L336)). The read may still be in flight at that point, so the adapter reports "finished (failed)" for a load whose transfer has not reached a terminal state.

The existing test `test_load_deadline_expired_yields_failure` asserts exactly this behaviour, so I am raising it as a contract question rather than a regression: is a terminal load result allowed to precede the end of the transfer?

**To Reproduce**

On `dev` @ 8d7d2c47, add this test to `tests/v1/distributed/l2_adapters/test_p2p_l2_adapter.py`:

```python
def test_load_deadline_does_not_report_terminal_while_read_is_in_flight():
    keys = [_key(0)]
    now = [100.0]
    in_flight = TransferChannelReadResult(finished=False)
    with (
        _adapter(load_timeout_s=0.01) as (adapter, _mq, _tc_ctx, tc_client, _n),
        patch.object(p2p_mod.time, "monotonic", side_effect=lambda: now[0]),
    ):
        adapter._remote_addresses[keys[0]] = TransferChannelAddress(offset=100, size=10)
        tc_client.submit_read.return_value = 123
        tc_client.query_read_status.return_value = in_flight
        task_id = adapter.submit_load_task(
            keys, [MagicMock(shm_offset=0, shm_byte_length=10)]
        )
        now[0] = 100.02  # past the 0.01 s load deadline
        assert not in_flight.is_finished()
        assert adapter.query_load_result(task_id) is None
```

```
pytest -v tests/v1/distributed/l2_adapters/test_p2p_l2_adapter.py -k "deadline or not_finished"
```

Result (CPU-only build, transfer channel mocked):

```
>           assert adapter.query_load_result(task_id) is None
E           assert 0 is None
E            +  where 0 = query_load_result(0)

LMCache WARNING: P2P load task 0 timed out; treating as a failure (p2p_l2_adapter.py:335)

test_lookup_deadline_expired_yields_miss PASSED
test_load_not_finished_returns_none PASSED
test_load_deadline_expired_yields_failure PASSED
test_load_deadline_does_not_report_terminal_while_read_is_in_flight FAILED
1 failed, 3 passed
```

(`0` is the repr of a one-key, all-zero `Bitmap`, i.e. a terminal failure.)

This test only demonstrates the current behaviour; its assertion would need adjusting depending on which direction below is preferred.

**Expected behavior**

Either the adapter does not report a terminal load result while its transfer-channel read may still access the destination buffers, or the contract states explicitly that a terminal result does not imply the transfer has quiesced and callers handle that.

**Additional context**

To be clear about what is and is not shown:

*Reproduced (unit test above):* the read is modelled as unfinished, and after the deadline `query_load_result()` returns a terminal failure.

*Derived from reading the code, not reproduced:*
- On that result, `PrefetchController._poll_load_results()` calls `finish_write_and_delete()` for the failed keys and then `submit_unlock()` ([prefetch_controller.py#L1389-L1395](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/8d7d2c47e1edb8c107033ae709722b2c3a05dec4/lmcache/v1/distributed/storage_controllers/prefetch_controller.py#L1389-L1395)); for P2P, `submit_unlock()` sends `p2p_unlock_objects` to the peer ([#L277-L280](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/8d7d2c47e1edb8c107033ae709722b2c3a05dec4/lmcache/v1/distributed/l2_adapters/p2p_l2_adapter.py#L277-L280)). So both the destination staging buffer and the source-side lock are released.
- The NIXL transfer channel registers the whole L1 buffer once ([nixl_impl.py#L344](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/8d7d2c47e1edb8c107033ae709722b2c3a05dec4/lmcache/v1/distributed/transfer_channel/impl/nixl_impl.py#L344)). This creates a window in which a late read may write into memory that has since been reassigned to another key.
- After the timeout the adapter no longer queries the read, so the `NixlTransferChannelClient._tasks` entry and its xfer handle are only released on `close()` ([#L178-L181](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/8d7d2c47e1edb8c107033ae709722b2c3a05dec4/lmcache/v1/distributed/transfer_channel/impl/nixl_impl.py#L178-L181), [#L202-L206](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/8d7d2c47e1edb8c107033ae709722b2c3a05dec4/lmcache/v1/distributed/transfer_channel/impl/nixl_impl.py#L202-L206)).

*Not reproduced:* actual stale or corrupted KV data end to end. I have not run a two-instance NIXL test for this.

**Possible directions** (not proposing a specific fix yet)

- **A. Stay pending until the transfer is terminal.** After the deadline, keep polling `query_read_status()` and only report once it finishes. Simple ownership model; a hung transfer would hold its buffers and locks indefinitely.
- **B. Add per-task cancellation to `TransferChannelClient`** ([abstract.py#L52-L88](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/8d7d2c47e1edb8c107033ae709722b2c3a05dec4/lmcache/v1/distributed/transfer_channel/abstract.py#L52-L88) has only `submit_read`, `query_read_status`, `close`), and report terminal only once the cancel is confirmed. For NIXL this would map to `releaseXferReq`, which the BackendGuide says "can return error, meaning it was not successful in aborting the request", so it still needs A as a fallback. The Mooncake wrapper has no cancel today; I have not checked the engine itself.
- **C. Drop the adapter-level load deadline** and rely on the controller-level deadline from #5255, which already keeps late loads' buffers and locks until the load result arrives.

The P2P adapter is the runtime caller of `submit_read()`; the transfer-channel benchmark also calls it directly, so an API change in B would touch both.

**Related**

- #5263 — same ownership family, on the shutdown / TTL paths rat
items.author_work_intent: If maintainers agree this is a contract gap, I'm happy to work on the fix. I'd especially appreciate guidance on whether the preferred direction is to keep timed-out reads pending until terminal, add a TransferChannel cancell

items.title: [Bug] MP connector prometheus metrics crash vLLM startup under Ray Serve: histogram built without buckets
items.author: n-grieger
items.body_excerpt:
The Prometheus metrics of the MP connector added in 0.5.6 crash vLLM engine startup whenever the engine runs under Ray Serve LLM (`ray.serve.llm`). `LMCacheMPPromMetrics.__init__` builds `vllm:lmcache_mp_lookup_duration_seconds` without a `buckets` argument (`lmcache/integration/vllm/lmcache_mp_metrics.py:75`, added in PR #5024):

```python
histogram = self._histogram_cls(
    name="vllm:lmcache_mp_lookup_duration_seconds",
    documentation="LMCache MP lookup latency observed by vLLM.",
    labelnames=labelnames,
)   # no buckets
```

Under plain `vllm serve`, `_histogram_cls` is `prometheus_client.Histogram`, and a missing `buckets` means default buckets, so it works. Under Ray Serve, vLLM swaps in `vllm/v1/metrics/ray_wrappers.py`, whose `RayHistogramWrapper` runs `boundaries = buckets if buckets else []` and hands that to `ray.util.metrics.Histogram`. Ray rejects empty `boundaries` with `ValueError`, by design and since 2020. The engine replica dies inside the `AsyncLLM` constructor, after the engine core is already up:

```text
AsyncLLM.__init__ (StatLoggerManager)
  -> vllm loggers.py (kv_connector_prom)
  -> lmcache_mp_connector.py:1665 (build_prom_metrics)
  -> lmcache_mp_metrics.py:75 (LMCacheMPPromMetrics)
  -> vllm/v1/metrics/ray_wrappers.py:158 (RayHistogramWrapper)
  -> ray.util.metrics.Histogram -> ValueError: boundaries argument should be provided when using the Histogram class.
```

**To Reproduce**
Mirrors `tests/v1/test_mp_connector_metrics.py`, with vLLM's real Ray wrapper types instead of the `_Histogram` stub. Verified on `lmcache 0.5.6` + `vllm 0.31.0` + `ray 2.60.0`:

```python
from types import SimpleNamespace

from prometheus_client import Counter, Gauge, Histogram
from vllm.v1.metrics.ray_wrappers import (
    RayCounterWrapper,
    RayGaugeWrapper,
    RayHistogramWrapper,
)

from lmcache.integration.vllm.lmcache_mp_metrics import LMCacheMPPromMetrics

LMCacheMPPromMetrics(
    SimpleNamespace(kv_transfer_config=object()),
    {Counter: RayCounterWrapper, Gauge: RayGaugeWrapper, Histogram: RayHistogramWrapper},
    ["model_name", "engine"],
    {0: ["model", "0"]},
)
# ValueError: boundaries argument should be provided when using the Histogram class.
```

**Expected behavior**
`LMCacheMPPromMetrics` constructs successfully on every metrics backend. Passing explicit `buckets` fixes it independent of the backend and improves the metric itself: lookup latency ranges from sub-millisecond L1 host hits to seconds on remote backends, which the HTTP-oriented `prometheus_client` default buckets (top end 10s) fit poorly. Something like `buckets=(0.001, 0.005, 0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.5, 1.0, 5.0)` should match the real distribution.

Please tell me if this is something that should rather be fixed on VLLM's site. It seemed more robust to me to place it here but you will know better 😉

items.title: [Perf] MP server converts token ids to ints and back for every key
items.author: theminjunchoi
items.body_excerpt:
Hi! While profiling the MP server under a replayed vLLM trace, I noticed that a good share of the per-request CPU time goes into handling token ids.

Each key arrives with the token ids on the wire, and the server turns them into a tuple of Python ints, copies that into a list, and then packs every 256-token chunk back into big-endian uint32 bytes with `struct.pack` so blake3 can hash it (`token_hasher.py`). So we end up rebuilding the same bytes that could have been sent as-is.

For a single 2,048-token key, that path takes about 91 µs on my machine, while hashing slices of the packed bytes takes about 12 µs and gives the same chunk hashes.

Would it make sense to send the token ids in `IPCCacheServerKey` as packed bytes and hash them directly? The hashes would stay the same, so existing caches would keep hitting. The catch is that the key's wire format changes, so the client and server would need to be on the same LMCache version.

I have a change ready and will open a PR for it. Any feedback is very welcome.

items.title: Performance comparison for dense shared prefix + block-diagonal local mask: custom mask in BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheWrapper vs MultiLevelCascadeAttentionWrapper
items.author: catnanami
items.body_excerpt: I am trying to evaluate the best way to implement an attention pattern with a dense shared/global prefix plus a local block-diagonal suffix. The mask pattern is shown below: I am considering two implementations: BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheWrapper with a custom mask MultiLevelCascadeAttentionWrapper Questions: 1. For this pattern, is cascade attention expected to be faster than paged prefill with a custom mask? 2. Or is this pattern better handled by a custom kernel/backend? My use case is speculative decoding, where all verification tokens share the same prefix KV, but each local block should only attend to its own block.

comments.author: VectorPeak
comments.body:
For the mask in the image - a dense shared prefix on the left plus independent block-diagonal local regions on the right - `MultiLevelCascadeAttentionWrapper` is usually the better fit than `BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheWrapper` with one large custom mask.

The reason is that the custom-mask prefill path does not really exploit this structure as well: it still treats the problem like one masked attention problem over the full layout, so the block-diagonal sparsity mostly becomes masking overhead. Cascade attention lets you model this as:

- shared/global prefix KV: attended by all verification tokens
- local suffix KV: split into independent blocks/requests
- final result: merge prefix-attention state with each local block’s attention state

For speculative decoding, this is exactly the kind of case where cascade can help, especially when the shared prefix is large and the local verification blocks are relatively small. Each local block can be represented as a separate batch item sharing the same prefix. If the local part also needs causal masking inside each block, use the normal causal/local mask for that per-block suffix attention.

items.title: tool_choice "required" is advisory, not grammar-enforced (Qwen3, --jinja); a warm KV-cache prefix reliably flips the same near-tie
items.author: JesseWebDotCom
items.body_excerpt:
## What happens

`tool_choice: "required"` is not enforced by a grammar on this build: at `temperature: 0.7` with `cache_prompt: false` (so no cache is involved at all, `cached_tokens: 0` on every request), 2 of 10 otherwise-identical requests still answered in plain text with `tool_calls: []` instead of calling the tool, purely from sampling variance. A warm slot KV-cache prefix pushes that same near-tie the wrong way deterministically even at `temperature: 0`: llama-server returns the tool call on the first request, then answers in plain text with `tool_calls: []` on later requests whose prefix the slot's KV cache already holds. `cache_prompt: false` makes every request at `temperature: 0` honour the choice. `--cache-reuse 0` changes nothing.

## Build and model

- llama-server b10797, macOS arm64 (Apple M4 Pro, 24 GB, macOS 26.x)
- Qwen3-8B, Q4_K_M GGUF, the model's own chat template through `--jinja`
- Flags: `-c 32768 --parallel 1 -fa on -ngl all --reasoning off -ub 1024 --jinja --cache-reuse 256 -ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0 --metrics`

## Request (identical every time)

```json
{
  "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "who is the president of chile"}],
  "tools": [{"type": "function", "function": {"name": "websearch",
    "description": "Search the web.",
    "parameters": {"type": "object", "required": ["expression"],
      "properties": {"expression": {"type": "string"},
                     "category": {"type": "string", "enum": ["images"]},
                     "read_page": {"type": "boolean"}}}}}],
  "tool_choice": "required",
  "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": false},
  "max_tokens": 64, "temperature": 0, "cache_prompt": true
}
```

## Observed

| Set | Shape | Tool calls returned |
|---|---|---|
| A1 | identical request x5, `cache_prompt: false` | 5/5 (`usage.cached_tokens` 0) |
| A2 | identical request x5, `cache_prompt: true`, cache warm | 0/5 (`cached_tokens` 197 of 198; content "The current president of Chile is ...") |
| A3 | five requests differing only in the country, `cache_prompt: true` | 2/5 (peru, norway called the tool; chile, kenya, japan answered in text; all reused the prefix, 187 or 197 cached tokens) |
| A4 | fresh server with `--cache-reuse 0`, A2 again | 1/5 (the first request on the empty cache called the tool, the next four answered in text) |

Server log on every full-hit failure:

```
W slot   operator(): id  0 | task 185 | need to evaluate at least 1 token for each active slot (n_past = 198, task.n_tokens() = 198)
W slot   operator(): id  0 | task 185 | n_past was set to 197
```

The partial-reuse failures in A3 log no warning: ten or eleven new tokens are evaluated, then the reply is plain text.

## Expected

`tool_choice: "required"` returns a tool call on every request, whatever the slot's cache state; the OpenAI semantics do not depend on prompt caching.

## Open question for the maintainers

Is `required` enforced by a (non-lazy) grammar for the Qwen3 / Hermes-style template on this build, or only by the template's prompt? A grammar-enforced choice could not produce plain content in A2. If it is a grammar, the cache path appears to skip it; if it is not, the cache only changes which side of a near-tie the deterministic sampling lands on, and `required` is advisory. Happy to run either check.
