items.title: Misc. bug: Metal aborts on MUL_MAT with BF16 src1 at K >= 64, batch > 8 (no BF16 mul_mm kernel)
items.author: vieduy
items.body_excerpt:
### Name and Version

master @ 7170cad (after b11813), built with AppleClang 21.0.0 for Darwin arm64


### Operating systems

Mac

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

Other (Please specify in the next section)

### Command line

```shell
test-backend-ops test -b MTL0 -o MUL_MAT -p "type_a=bf16,type_b=bf16,m=64,n=17,k=64,"
```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

On Metal, a MUL_MAT whose src1 is BF16 aborts once K >= 64 and the batch (n) is above 8:

    kernel not found in any metal library: base = 'kernel_mul_mm_bf16_bf16'
    ggml_metal_encoder_set_pipeline: nil Metal pipeline (missing kernel; see compile_pipeline log above)

**Cause:**

- `ggml_metal_op_mul_mat_use_mm` (`ggml/src/ggml-metal/ggml-metal-common.cpp`) chooses `mul_mm` from the shape alone.
- `mul_mm` is only instantiated for F32 and F16 src1 (`kernel_mul_mm_<src0>_f32` / `_f16`), so a BF16 src1 gets a nil pipeline.
- `mul_mv` does have BF16 src1 kernels (`kernel_mul_mv_bf16_bf16`, `kernel_mul_mv_f32_bf16`), so smaller shapes work.

**Affected pairs:**

| src0 x src1 | K >= 64, n > 8 |
|---|---|
| BF16 x BF16 | abort (`kernel_mul_mm_bf16_bf16` not found) |
| F32 x BF16 | abort (`kernel_mul_mm_f32_bf16` not found) |
| F16 x BF16, Q4_0 x BF16 | not affected: Metal reports them unsupported, so they fall back to CPU |

**Why CI doesn't catch it:** every existing BF16 src1 case in `test-backend-ops` uses K < 64 or n <= 8, so none reaches `mul_mm`.

**Reach:** no model graph in `src/` produces a BF16 src1 for MUL_MAT. Even with a BF16 KV cache and flash attention off, the cache is src0 and the activations stay F32. It is reachable through the ggml API.

**Steps to reproduce:** stock master has no test that hits this. Add these two lines to `make_test_cases_eval()` in `tests/test-backend-ops.cpp`:

```cpp
test_cases.emplace_back(new test_mul_mat(GGML_TYPE_BF16, GGML_TYPE_BF16, 64, 17, 64, {1, 1}, {1, 1}));
test_cases.emplace_back(new test_mul_mat(GGML_TYPE_F32,  GGML_TYPE_BF16, 64, 17, 64, {1, 1}, {1, 1}));
```

Then build and run the command above. It exits with code 134 (abort). The same happens at K = 256.

**Hardware:** Apple M4 (10-core GPU), macOS 27.0.1.

**Proposed fix:** keep BF16 src1 off the `mul_mm` path, so it uses the existing `mul_mv` kernels. This is a one-line condition in `ggml_metal_op_mul_mat_use_mm`
### First Bad Commit

Unknown

### Relevant log output

<details>
<summary>Logs</summary>
<!-- Copy-pasted short logs go into the "console" area here -->

```console
ggml_metal_library_compile_pipeline: compiling pipeline: base = 'kernel_mul_mm_bf16_bf16', name = 'kernel_mul_mm_bf16_bf16_bci=0_bco=1_ne12=1_ne13=1_r2=1_r3=1'
ggml_metal_library_compile_pipeline: kernel not found in any metal library: base = 'kernel_mul_mm_bf16_bf16', name = 'kernel_mul_mm_bf16_bf16_bci=0_bco=1_ne12=1_ne13=1_r2=1_r3=1'
Testing 3 devices
Backend 1/3: MTL0

items.title: [Bug]: Ascend Direct 跨节点 put host 全局段 "Can't find remoteBuffer"（remote_accessible 未导出）
items.author: gygdh-001
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug
In a PD-disaggregated Ascend deployment, cross-node KV transfer via Ascend Direct fails on the host global segment. The ADXL one-sided `put` reports `Can't find remoteBuffer by key[<host-segment-addr>][8192]` — the buffer is not resolvable from the transferred key.

Environment: Atlas 800I A3, CANN 9.2.0, vLLM 0.30.0, SuperPod topology (inter-node HCCS, no RoCE switch).

Error chain:

    [hccl_one_sided_conn.cc:407] GetTransInfo: Can't find remoteBuffer by key[0x12e480060000][8192]
    [hccl_one_sided_service.cc:1242] InitAicpuTilingDataBuf: hcclRet -> 1
    [exception_handler.cc:24] HcclBatchPut: AICPU launch failed, code: 1
    [comm_channel.cc:469] operator(): ErrorNo: 103900 Failed to invoke DlHcclBatchPut, hccl_result = 1
    [adxl_engine_impl.cc:286] TransferSync: ErrorNo: 103900 Failed to TransferSync, operation:write, op_descs size:12, timeout:33064 ms

### Key observation / evidence
The failing keys are exactly the host-side 24GB global segment registered as `mem type:host`; none of the `mem type:device` KV buffers appears:

    register mem addr:0x12f0c0000000, length:25769803776, mem type:host    # prefill
    register mem addr:0x12e440000000, length:25769803776, mem type:host    # decode
    register mem addr:0x12e480000000, length:25769803776, mem type:host    # decode
    register mem addr:0x12dde3400000, length:1905917952,   mem type:device  # KV buffer

    key[0x12f0c0000000][8192/131072]
    key[0x12e440000000][8192/131072]
    key[0x12e480000000][8192/131072]

Even the prefill node's own host segment (`0x12f0c...`) fails the lookup. Since `remoteBuffer` here means the remote-accessible buffer table (not "buffer on the remote node"), a locally-owned segment also missing from that table is consistent with `remote_accessible` being dropped in `registerLocalMemory()` (the `(void)remote_accessible;` bug fixed by #4363), so the host segment is registered local-only and never exported.

### Suspected root cause
PR #4363 (commit 02bb6b1) — `AscendDirectTransport::registerLocalMemory()` did not propagate `remote_accessible` to the ADXL `MemDesc`, so buffers were registered local-only. Our build appears to run a Mooncake without that fix.

### Question
1. Which Mooncake release contains commit 02bb6b1 (#4363)? Is the host 24GB segment supposed to be registered `remote_accessible=true` for cross-node put?
2. `ASCEND_AUTO_CONNECT=1` did not change the error — does that rule out a connection-timing issue and confirm the buffer-registration flag?

- Enable self-contained requests with multiple images
- Simplify deployment in distributed environments

items.title: RFC: Plugin Extension Points Needed for MetaX GPU Support
items.author: yangxin-mx
items.body_excerpt:
# Proposal: Generalize SGLang Hardware Plugin Interfaces for MetaX GPU Support

> Discussion draft based on a SGLang 0.5.19-derived codebase. The names below are proposed API shapes, not claims that they already exist on the latest `main` branch. If an equivalent upstream seam already exists, we would prefer to use or extend it. This is an umbrella discussion that can be split into smaller PRs.

SGLang already has useful foundations: hardware-platform entry points, `SRTPlatform.init_backend()`, an explicit OOT forward registry for fused ops, and MoE runner/fused-function registration. See the [plugin documentation](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/main/docs/docs/hardware-platforms/plugin.mdx) and [expert-parallelism documentation](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/main/docs/docs/advanced_features/expert_parallelism.mdx). When adapting another CUDA-compatible GPU, however, we still encounter framework call sites that select a built-in class, import a vendor implementation, or call a kernel through a module-level symbol before a platform plugin can participate.

Our goal is to make required hardware behavior expressible through platform methods and explicit, typed registries. We do **not** propose replacing module globals or monkey-patching framework functions. A missing optional platform implementation should preserve the current built-in behavior; a selected but unsupported implementation should fail with a clear capability error rather than silently run an incompatible kernel. The plugin owns its vendor kernels and package dependencies. The framework owns common algorithms, selection rules, lifecycle, and validation.

The Python snippets below illustrate **proposed interfaces and call sites, not complete, runnable code already present in the repository**. `ExampleGpuPlatform` and `vendor_ops` stand for any vendor plugin. Exact parameters should be settled against existing types and call paths in the corresponding PRs. Each section shows both where the framework would connect the extension point and how a plugin would use it.

## 1. JIT toolchain and cache identity

### Adaptation problem

In the 0.5.19-derived tree, JIT compilation derives the device compiler, architecture and flags through CUDA/ROCm-oriented paths in `kernels/jit/utils/compile/toolchain.py`. The build path (`ninja.py`) and cache path (`cache.py`) must agree on these values. A plugin cannot safely supply a different device compiler by changing only one path: the cache may reuse a binary built for another SDK or architecture.

### Plugin-oriented proposal

- Add an optional `SRTPlatform.get_jit_toolchain() -> JitToolchainSpec | None`. The immutable spec should include the host/device compilers, toolkit root, target architecture, include/link paths and flags, plus an explicit SDK/ABI cache identity.
- Resolve the spec lazily when compilation starts, and pass the **same resolved spec** to command generation and cache-key generation. `None` keeps the existing built-in toolchain logic.
- Let the vendor plugin package its AOT extensions itself. The common AOT setup need not import or name each vendor SDK.

On the framework side, add the optional method in `srt/platforms/interface.py` and have `kernels/jit/utils/compile/{toolchain,ninja,cache}.py` consume the same spec:

```python
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class JitToolchainSpec:
    host_compiler: str
    device_compiler: str
    toolkit_root: str
    target_arch: str
    device_flags: tuple[str, ...] = ()
    include_dirs: tuple[str, ...] = ()
    link_flags: tuple[str, ...] = ()
    cache_identity: str = ""  # SDK/ABI version

class SRTPlatform(DeviceMixin):
    def get_jit_toolchain(self) -> JitToolchainSpec | None:
        return None

def compile_extension(source, **kwargs):
    spec = resolve_jit_toolchain(get_platform().get_jit_toolchain())
    cache_key = make_cache_key(source, spec=spec, **kwargs)
    return build_with_ninja(source, spec=spec, cache_key=cache_key, **kwargs)
```

The plugin only describes its own SDK; it does not modify global `CUDA_HOME` or framework compiler symbols:

```python
class ExampleGpuPlatform(SRTPlatform):
    def get_jit_toolchain(self) -> JitToolchainSpec:
        return JitToolchainSpec(
            host_compiler="/opt/example/bin/c++",
            device_compiler="/opt/example/bin/device-cc",
            toolkit_root="/opt/example",
            target_arch="example-arch",
            cache_identity="example-sdk-1:abi-1",
        )
```

## 2. Device properties and per-operator Triton tuning

### Adaptation problem

Several launch paths infer hardware behavior from CUDA properties or NVIDIA/AMD architecture names, while `num_stages`, warps, tile sizes and shared-memory limits are selected locally. A plugin may expose a CUDA-compatible device but still need different launch parameters; pretending to be a particular SM is not a sound capability contract.

### Plugin-oriented proposal

- Expose a read-only `DeviceKernelProfile` through the active platform, with architecture identifier, warp size, maximum shared-memory bytes and relevant device capabilities.
- Add an optional `tune_triton_launch(op, shape, dtype, default) -> TritonLaunchConfig`. Each caller first computes its present default, then asks the active platform for a per-operator override and validates it before launch. There should be no global change to Triton's defaults.
- Start with launch sites where hardware differences actually affect correctness or feasibility (MoE, quantization and attention), keeping other paths unchanged.

The framework could define device facts in `srt/platforms/device_mixin.py`/`interface.py` and consume the policy immediately before each Triton launch, keeping hardware facts separate from per-operator tuning:

```python

    arch: str
    warp_size: int

items.title: [RFC] diffusion: LTX-2 stage-1 distilled LoRA base restore is not exact
items.author: OnePunchMonk
items.body_excerpt:
## Problem

`LTX2Pipeline._unmerge_stage1_distilled_from_base` (`runtime/pipelines/ltx_2_pipeline.py`) restores the base by merging the stage-1 distilled LoRA again with strength `-s`, then calling `commit_merged_as_base()`.

That is not an exact inverse:
- the base is bf16, so `(W + s*dW) - s*dW` rounds twice;
- `_should_merge_in_fp32` returns False for any path containing `distilled-lora`, so both directions round in bf16, not just the final store.

The drift is small but permanent for the life of the server. It is hit when a request overrides the stage-1 distilled strength away from the value merged at init.

## Why not just fix it

An exact restore needs the pre-merge weights. `commit_merged_as_base()` overwrites each layer's `cpu_weight` snapshot with the merged weights, so the original base is gone. Keeping it means a second full host copy of the DiT, about 40 GB for the 20B/22B checkpoints.

## Options

1. Keep the pre-commit `cpu_weight` per layer and restore from it. Exact, but doubles host memory for the DiT snapshot.
2. Do the `-s` merge in fp32 (drop the `distilled-lora` fp32 exclusion for this path). Cheaper and closer, still not exact since the committed base is already bf16.
3. Do not restore: reload the transformer weights from disk when a request overrides the stage-1 strength. Exact, no extra memory, but the first such request is slow.
4. Accept the drift and document it.

Which trade-off do maintainers prefer? Happy to send the PR once there is a direction.

items.title: High VGPR usage after enabling true16 on gfx11/12 in Triton 3.9
items.author: woct0rdho
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the issue

I've proposed this in https://github.com/triton-lang/triton-windows/pull/57 with reproducers. This is a performance regression on gfx11 in Triton 3.9 compared to Triton 3.8 .

In Triton 3.9, true16 is enabled for gfx11, see https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/pull/11188 (and there had been a few back-and-forth changes on this). Basically true16 lets the compiler use one 32-bit register to store two 16-bit variables, so it should reduce VGPR usage in general if implemented properly.

However it's not implemented properly. When packing two 16-bit variables into one 32-bit register, the compiler may use two auxiliary 32-bit registers, see the FIXME comment in https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/blob/dba80dcdcd2c8648ec879880f364b141eebfc5b5/llvm/lib/Target/AMDGPU/AMDGPUISelDAGToDAG.cpp#L3948 . Therefore in the worst case it can use 3x VGPR compared to Triton 3.8 .

This issue also affects gfx12 before Triton 3.9 .

Currently this issue does not appear on Triton main branch. The LLVM pinned on Triton main branch has merged https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/pull/221960 and the unexpectedly high VGPR is no longer reproduced. (It's reproduced if we revert this commit.) However, the FIXME still exists in LLVM and it may bite us again in future.

Do you think the upstream Triton will accept a hot fix before the release of Triton 3.9 ? Also, do you know anyone working on this in LLVM?

cc @jammm @antiagainst 

### Environment details

Triton: commit 0a6e13e6e3 (release/3.9.x branch)
GPU: Radeon 8060S (gfx1151)

items.title: [RFC]: Support ViT Full CUDA Graph (Tracker)
items.author: shen-shanshan
items.body_excerpt:
### Motivation.

Multimodal large language models (e.g., Qwen3-VL, Qwen3.5, GLM-V, Kimi K2.5) rely on a Vision Transformer (ViT) encoder to process visual inputs before feeding them into the language model backbone. In production serving scenarios, the ViT forward pass involves launching a large number of small CUDA kernels — including patch embedding, layer normalization, multi-head self-attention, and MLP projections — each of which incurs non-trivial kernel launch overhead on the host side.

Currently, vLLM supports CUDA graph capture for the decoder (LLM) portion of the model, which has proven effective at reducing kernel launch costs and improving throughput. However, the ViT encoder is still executed eagerly, meaning every forward pass re-launches all kernels from scratch. Extending full CUDA graph support to the ViT encoder would allow the entire encoder forward pass to be captured and replayed as a single graph, eliminating per-kernel launch overhead and enabling more consistent, low-latency inference for multimodal models.

### Proposed Change.

items.title: [Feature]: Plan for enabling mypy in tests directory
items.author: hickeyma
items.body_excerpt:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

**Goal:** Enable MyPy static checking in the `/tests` directory.

**Implementation:** Move `tests/**` from `--follow-imports skip` to `--follow-imports silent` in [`tools/pre_commit/mypy.py`](../../tools/pre_commit/mypy.py), one directory at a time, **with each PR enforcing the directories it fixed**.

Partial: #26533

/cc @hmellor @yewentao256

---

### Plan

**Note on error counts:**

- Counts for **open** items (PR 6, 7, 8, 9, kv-C) were re-measured on **2026-10-21** against `main`
  with pre-commit's pinned toolchain:
  `mypy==1.20.2 --python-version 3.11 --follow-imports silent <dir>`, run from the repo root so the
  `pyproject.toml` overrides apply.
- Counts for **done** items are historical. They were measured before #59428 (2026-09-30), which turned
  off `arg-type` and `assignment` for `tests.*` in `pyproject.toml`. Those two codes no longer fire in
  tests, so the "Dominant codes" columns in the done sections overstate what's left to fix.

Current state on `main`: **1,680 errors in 170 files** across the 648 test files still checked at `skip`.

---

#### Blocker: removing a directory from `SEPARATE_GROUPS` enforces nothing

`group_files()` iterates `SEPARATE_GROUPS` in **list order** and `break`s on the
first prefix match. `"tests"` is the first entry, so every `tests/**` file is
claimed by it:

```python
>>> group_files(['tests/config/test_multimodal_config.py',
...              'tests/v1/shutdown/test_processor_error.py'])
{'tests': [both files]}     # never lands in 'tests/config' or 'tests/v1/shutdown'
```

A file only gets `follow_imports=silent` by matching **no** entry at all and
falling through to the `""` group. Since `"tests"` matches everything under
`tests/`, no per-directory removal can ever take effect before `"tests"` itself
is removed — which is the very last step.

**Sorting `SEPARATE_GROUPS` by longest prefix does not fix this** (verified):
with `tests/config` removed, its files still match `tests` and still run with
`skip`. Sorting only changes which *skip* group a file lands in, which is
cosmetic today.

Consequence if the plan is executed as originally written: every PR from 1
through kv-C fixes real errors but enforces none of them, and all of that work is
free to regress until the final PR. **PR 0 below fixes the mechanism so that
stops being true.**

---

#### PR 0 — Make per-directory enforcement possible (prerequisite) (#49570) **DONE**

<details><summary>read more...</summary>

Add an allowlist of verified-clean directories, matched **before**
`SEPARATE_GROUPS`, that routes files into the `""` group (no `--follow-imports`
flag → pyproject's `silent`):

```python
# Directories verified clean under follow_imports=silent. Checked before
# SEPARATE_GROUPS; these files join the "" group and are enforced at silent.
# Moving a directory from SEPARATE_GROUPS to here is what makes a fix stick.
SILENT_GROUPS: list[str] = []
```

In `group_files()`, before the `SEPARATE_GROUPS` loop:

```python
if any(re.match(f"^{d}.*", changed_file) for d in SILENT_GROUPS):
    file_groups[""].append(changed_file)
    continue
```

Also sort the `SEPARATE_GROUPS` loop by descending path length so sub-directory
groups stop being shadowed by their parents. This is cosmetic today (all those
groups run at `skip`) but keeps the per-group log labels honest as directories
drain.

Verified behaviour with `SILENT_GROUPS = ["tests/config", "tests/v1/shutdown"]`:

```python
{'':                    ['tests/config/a.py', 'tests/v1/shutdown/b.py', 'vllm/x.py'],
 'tests/compile/passes': ['tests/compile/passes/d.py'],
 'tests/v1/core':        ['tests/v1/core/c.py']}
```

Clean dirs are enforced at `silent`; everything unfixed keeps its `skip` group;
`"tests"` can stay in `SEPARATE_GROUPS` until the very end.

**Bundle PR 0 into PR 1** rather than shipping it alone — AGENTS.md discourages
standalone mechanical PRs, and PR 1 gives it substantive work to ride along with.

</details>

---

#### Per-PR recipe (applies to every open PR below)

Every PR in this plan follows the same four steps. A PR that stops after step 1
is preparatory only and must say so in its description.

1. **Fix** the errors in the directories the PR owns.
2. **Move** each fixed directory from `SEPARATE_GROUPS` (or from under the `tests` root group) to
   `SILENT_GROUPS` in the *same* PR. This is the step that makes the fix stick.
3. **Verify.** Both commands must pass:
   ```bash
   # use the same mypy version as the pre-commit hook; newer mypy releases can disagree
   uv pip install "mypy==1.20.2"

   # the directory is genuinely clean at the strictness you are about to enforce
   .venv/bin/mypy --python-version 3.11 --follow-imports silent \
       --warn-unused-ignores <dirs owned by this PR>

   # the hook as CI runs it, with the new grouping in effect
   pre-commit run -a mypy
   ```
   `--warn-unused-ignores` is not on in CI, but run it locally. It catches
   `# type: ignore` comments that were never needed. Because `arg-type` and `assignment` are
   disabled for `tests.*` (#59428), a `# type: ignore[arg-type]` or `# type: ignore[assignment]` is
   never needed in tests, and this flag will report it.
4. **Confirm the routing changed.** Cheap proof that step 2 took effect:
   ```bash
   .venv/bin/python -c "import sys; sys.path.insert(0,'tools/pre_commit'); \
     import mypy; print([k for k,v in mypy.group_files(['<a/file/in/the/dir.py>']).items() if v])"
   # must print [''] — not the directory name, and not 'tests'
   ```

**Leaf-before-parent ordering is still required**, now for scoping rather than
mechanism: fixing `tests/models/transformers` before `tests/models` means the parent
PR only deals with residual loose files in that directory, not the whole tree.

**Directories that aren't enforced regress.** For example, two kv-B files
(`unit/test_multi_connector.py`, `unit/utils.py`) picked up 11 new errors after kv-B merged, because
`tests/v1/kv_connector` stays at `skip` u

items.title: [Usage]: Recommended way to serve multiple models (e.g. embedding) on a single GPU
items.author: mfournioux
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment

**Description:**

### Context
We run vLLM to serve a small embedding model on a dedicated GPU. The model uses only a fraction of the GPU's memory and compute. We would like to co-locate several models on the same GPU to improve utilization.

### What we found
- A single vLLM process serves a single model.
- The docs say `gpu_memory_utilization` is a per-instance limit, so several instances can share a GPU (e.g. 0.5 each).
- Community answers say this works in online (server) mode, but not in offline mode with several `LLM` objects in one process (#6155).

### What we could not find
There is no official guidance on the recommended way to do this in production, in particular:
1. Is running several vLLM server instances on one GPU with split `--gpu-memory-utilization` values the officially recommended approach? Are there known limitations (e.g. memory profiling when instances start at the same time, CUDA graph memory, interference between workloads)?
2. Is there any plan for native multi-model serving in a single vLLM process or a built-in model router, or is this out of scope?
3. For small embedding models, are there recommended settings (e.g. `--gpu-memory-utilization`, `--max-model-len`, `--max-num-seqs`) to keep their footprint minimal?

### Request
Could you point us to the recommended approach ?

### How would you like to use vllm




### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

items.title: Eval bug: ubatch size leads to freezing of GPU+eGPU setup
items.author: Quas7
items.body_excerpt:
### Name and Version

llama-cli --version: 0.4.1-dev (but older ones as well)

First of all - great project... I love it! 

And I am not really sure, if this is a llama cpp issue or some Nvidia/TB3/whatever driver mess as well. 
But I wanted to share this in case someone else runs into this issue or if somebody can reproduce this for other setups.

Background...
I noticed during longer agent coding sessions that my GPU + eGPU setup (RTX3090 + external TB3 RTX3080Ti) freezes "randomly". Naturally, I started hunting a hardware bug at first (cables, connectors, powersupply,...) although the machine passes all GPU related benchmarks/stress-test for hours.
But recently I noticed that the freezes happen **only** during agent prompt decoding and that made me check the software side.

I can now reproduce this freeze issue 100% repeatable with an llama-bench run when setting high kv-prefill and larger prompt sizes (e.g. -p 5000 -d 100000) with standard ubatch size 512 (-ub 512).

Changing only ubatch to 256 (-ub 256) fixes this issue in 10/10 runs compared to 0/10 before.

It does not matter which quants I use for KV-cache or for the model - Q4, Q5, Q6 of a Qwen model all show the same ub-issue for the same pre-fill settings.
There is NO issue with ubatch using only the internal GPU.
I did not test with the TB-eGPU solo - if there is interest I would check that as well.
I have an oculink ordered as well out of frustration - will test with that for sure.

Freezes every time at the same point:
llama-bench.exe -m Qwen3.8-27B-TurbFCFus-735-882-Heret-Uncen-NEO-CODER-MA-Q4_K_M.gguf -p 5000 -n 0 -d 100000 -mg 0 -ts 24/12 -sm layer -ngl 999 -b 2048 -ub 512 -t 8 --load-mode none

Never freezes (only -ub 256 is changed):
llama-bench.exe -m Qwen3.8-27B-TurbFCFus-735-882-Heret-Uncen-NEO-CODER-MA-Q4_K_M.gguf -p 5000 -n 0 -d 100000 -mg 0 -ts 24/12 -sm layer -ngl 999 -b 2048 -ub 256 -t 8 --load-mode none


### Operating systems

Windows

### GGML backends

CUDA

### Hardware

i9 9900K
RTX 3090 (PCIe) + RTX 3080 Ti (eGPU, TB dock)

### Models

Qwen 3.8 27B gguf (happened for many of them)

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

llama-bench.exe -m Qwen3.8-27B-TurbFCFus-735-882-Heret-Uncen-NEO-CODER-MA-Q4_K_M.gguf -p 5000 -n 512 -d 100000 -mg 0 -ts 24/12 -sm layer -ngl 999 -b 2048 -ub 512 -t 8 --load-mode none

### First Bad Commit

not sure, if it is llama cpp related at all.

log freezes and shows nothing special before freezing

items.title: [RFC]: [Store] Shutdown handoff: index-preserving planned restart for a standalone master
items.author: Juhyun-Kim-Memphis
items.body_excerpt:
### Changes proposed

### Summary

A standalone (non-HA) Mooncake master loses its whole object index on every restart. In our deployment, almost every master restart is planned: an operator rolls a new image or changes a flag, and the process gets SIGTERM first.

This RFC proposes an opt-in **shutdown handoff** for that case. On SIGTERM, the old master stops serving, stops its background mutators, writes its final state to a local directory, and exits. The next master claims that state once, rebuilds the index and allocator state, and only then opens RPC.

The proposal rests on three properties:

1. **A standalone master keeps its index across a planned restart.**
2. **Zero steady-state cost.** There is no background work, no extra memory, and no new wait on the request path. The feature is off unless `--handoff_dir` is set.
3. **A failed or partial handoff can only lose entries (cache misses).** It never serves an entry whose memory may belong to something else.

It cannot be enabled together with HA and does not change the HA path. We run it in a fork and would like to upstream it in small PRs (Section 7), after hearing the maintainers' view on the direction and the failure policy (Section 5).

Related: #3774, #3808, #3167, #3771, #4406.

### 1. Problem

**After #4406, a standalone master has no restart path that keeps the index.** The remaining path is HA: batch OpLog in etcd plus standbys (#3808, #3167), which requires `enable_ha` with etcd. The removed legacy path did not keep the index in practice either: its default restore dropped objects whose lease had expired (#3761), and on `245e7106` it kept 0 of 25M keys.

In #3774 (an HA deployment), @Icedcoco explained that the batch OpLog design rebuilds the index from durable etcd history, and that recovery must fail closed. We agree with both points. This RFC is about deployments that do not run HA.

**What this costs us.** One production cell has 12 stores and up to about 25M keys. In the 30 days before early October 2026, its master was replaced 6 times. All 6 were operator rolls, with no crash. Each roll dropped the whole index, and after one of them the cell took about 8 minutes to refill 17.3M keys. Because a master roll empties the cache, we also postponed rolling a master image that carried upstream fixes.

The restart that hurts is the one the operator starts on purpose, which is also the easiest one to make safe.

### 2. Proposal

**Configuration.** `--handoff_dir=<path>` names a directory on the master node's local disk. It is empty by default, which disables the feature. Config validation rejects it together with `--enable_ha` before any worker or server starts. The first version supports only the OFFSET allocator; with any other allocator, the master logs the reason and starts empty.

**Shutdown (old master, on SIGTERM).**

1. Stop the RPC and admin servers, and wait for in-flight requests.
2. **Quiesce:** stop and join every background thread that changes metadata or allocator state. From here on nothing allocates or frees store memory, because the master is the only allocator.
3. **Admission:** check the cgroup memory budget for the write and for the later restore. If it does not fit, skip the snapshot; the next start is then empty, as today.
4. Write the objects with their COMPLETE replicas, the segment identities, and the quarantine ranges. The write uses the batch snapshot chunk codec (N03) with parallel workers, under a watchdog deadline shorter than the grace period.
5. Run fsync, publish `READY` by `rename`, and exit.

**Startup (new master).**

1. Take a `flock` on the directory. Refuse to restore if a `POISON` marker shows that two masters shared it.
2. Rename `READY` to `CLAIMED` before allocating anything, so each snapshot is restored at most once. Ignore snapshots older than `--handoff_max_age_sec`.
3. Run admission, restore the index, and rebuild the real allocator state. Any error resets the master to empty before RPC opens.
4. Mount the restored segments as neither readable nor allocatable, then open RPC.

**Remount by segment identity.** The memory tier needs no client or wire change. Stores call `ReMountSegment` after `NEED_REMOUNT`, and the `Segment` they send already carries a per-mount random id and the base address.

- If `client_id` (a random UUID per process), segment id, base, size, and endpoint all match, the segment opens. The check takes about 0.01 ms, whatever the key count.
- On any mismatch, for example a store that restarted during the gap, **all** restored entries of that segment are dropped.
- A store that never returns is removed by the normal client TTL path.

Today's `ValidateStandbyRemountSegment` compares only name, endpoint, and capacity. That is why A3 adds segment id and base to the persisted segment description.

**Not carried, so each becomes a miss:** in-flight puts (their ranges are quarantined), offload and promotion tasks, and Transfer Engine metadata. Stores re-publish their Transfer Engine metadata within 0.6–1.6 s.

### 3. Why this cannot serve wrong data

**Principle: a missing entry is a cache miss; a wrong entry is silent corruption.** Every failure path here ends in a missing entry.

#3771 was closed because a restored snapshot can point at memory that was reused after the snapshot, which was taken by a master that kept serving. The handoff rules this out by construction. Its snapshot is the final state of the only allocator. Nothing allocates while no master runs. The new master rebuilds the same allocator state before allocating anything, and restored entries open only after their store proves it has not changed.

| Mechanism | What it prevents |
| -- | -- |
| Serving and all background mutators stop before the snapshot | Allocation or free after the snapshot |
| In-flight puts are not exported; their ranges, and ranges the old master still held back, stay quarantined for the remaining hold time (up to `put_start_release_timeout`) | A late RDMA write landing on a new

items.title: [Bug]:  Gemma 4 fails to initialize with per-token-head KV cache quantization
items.author: lisp19
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment
The output of python collect_env.py ```text Use the builtin dockerfile to build & manually merge PR https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/39018 for turing devices base compatibility Main commit hash:726efe177bf22874743d11dfdfef9247dbfb5ff0 ```
### 🐛 Describe the bug Gemma 4 fails to initialize in vLLM V1 when `--kv_cache_dtype int8_per_token_head` is enabled. The same issue also affects `fp8_per_token_head`. The failure is caused by Gemma 4's hybrid attention layout using two different KV head dimensions: - sliding/local layers use `head_dim = 256` - global/full-attention layers use `head_dim = 512` With per-token-head KV quantization, each KV head also stores scale metadata per token. That extra scale payload breaks the exact 2:1 page-size ratio between the 512-dim and 256-dim layers, so V1 KV page-size unification fails during initialization. Minimal reproduction: ```bash vllm serve \ --kv_cache_dtype int8_per_token_head ``` Observed result: ```text (Worker_TP1 pid=248) ERROR 04-19 14:16:08 [multiproc_executor.py:971] File "/usr/local/lib/python3.12/dist-packages/vllm/v1/core/kv_cache_utils.py", line 942, in unify_kv_cache_spec_page_size (Worker_TP1 pid=248) ERROR 04-19 14:16:08 [multiproc_executor.py:971] raise NotImplementedError( (Worker_TP1 pid=248) ERROR 04-19 14:16:08 [multiproc_executor.py:971] NotImplementedError: The page size of the layer is not divisible by the maximum page size. Cannot unify by adjusting block_size. ``` Why this happens: - local layer page-size factor: `(256 * 1 byte * 2) + 8 = 520` - global layer page-size factor: `(512 * 1 byte * 2) + 8 = 1032` `1032` is not divisible by `520`, so the current page-size unification logic cannot reconcile the two layer types by changing `block_size` alone. Relevant code paths: - `vllm/model_executor/models/gemma4.py` - `vllm/model_executor/layers/attention/attention.py` - `vllm/v1/core/kv_cache_utils.py` - `vllm/v1/kv_cache_interface.py` - `vllm/v1/worker/gpu/attn_utils.py` - `vllm/v1/worker/gpu_model_runner.py` ## Environment | Item | Value | |---|---| | **Commit** | [`726efe177bf22874743d11dfdfef9247dbfb5ff0`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/commit/726efe177bf22874743d11dfdfef9247dbfb5ff0) | | **GPU** | 2× NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2080 Ti (22 GB, CC 7.5, Turing) | | **CUDA Driver** | 580.126.18, CUDA 13.0 | | **Python** | 3.12 (Docker) | | **Model** | Gemma4-31B AWQ 4-bit (`google/gemma-4-31b-it`), also reproduced with `cyankiwi/gemma-4-31B-it-AWQ-4bit` | I'm still new to this project, so if this report doesn't match the community's preferred format or I've misunderstood something basic, corrections are very welcome. Potential direction for a fix: I want to post a temporary workaround PR later for reference later, which as I tested, can solve this problem. But it certainly needs more review and discussion. ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

comments.author: noonghunna
comments.body:
Just posted a longer cross-rig validation finding on the PR thread: vllm-project/vllm#40391 (comment).

Short version: 2× RTX 3090 (Ampere consumer) + Gemma 4 31B + int8_per_token_head. We hit the same bug, explored two alternatives to lisp19's PR (generic spec-level unifier alone, and worker-runtime logic alone), and **both failure modes structurally confirm the PR's full-package design is correct**:

- Generic spec-level fix without the worker-side logical-shape view → boots but suffers severe decode-TPS decay (turn-1 33 → turn-5 10 TPS, 30% retention) — vLLM's generic strided-view path uses wrong dimension ordering for standard attention with `page_size_padded` set
- Worker-only overlay (no spec changes) → strict unifier still rejects → no boot
- Hybrid (generic unifier + worker view, no spec pre-padding) → boots but corrupts output

Adds Ampere consumer + INT8 per-token-head as a third cross-rig validation point alongside @cferra's earlier Blackwell consumer + FP8 validation. Worth surfacing for any reviewer eyeing the PR — the design is well-supported by the alternatives' failure modes. Full diagnostic at our [perheadkv-overlay-comparison.md](https://github.com/noonghunna/club-3090/blob/master/models/gemma-4-31b/vllm/patches/perheadkv-overlay-comparison.md).

comments.author: sergeykad
comments.body:
Still reproduces on **v0.26.0**, but the symptom has changed — it no longer fails to initialize, it silently costs KV capacity. Worth noting since the title no longer matches what users on current versions will see.

**Config:** `gemma-4-26B-A4B-it` FP8 (30 layers = 25 sliding `head_dim` 256 / 8 KV heads, 5 global `head_dim` 512 / 2 KV heads), single L40S (sm89), `TRITON_ATTN` (forced by the heterogeneous head dims), TP=1, `--max-model-len 32768`, prefix caching on.

**Measured, same 15.18 GiB KV budget, only `--kv-cache-dtype` changed:**

| dtype | KV pool | max concurrency @32k |
|---|---|---|
| `fp8` | 417,022 tokens | 12.73x |
| `fp8_per_token_head` | 325,335 tokens | 9.93x |

**−22% capacity.** The mechanism is the one in the original report: the inline fp32 scale pad makes the per-token page factors 520 (sliding) and 1032 (global). Without it they're 512 and 1024 — an exact 2:1 that unifies for free by doubling `block_size` on the sliding layers. With it, unification can't reconcile them that way and pads the sliding page up to the global one instead, so 25 of 30 layers pay ~2×. The scales themselves are only ~1.5% (`4/head_dim`); the cost is entirely in the unification fallback.

#40391 is still open. Flagging in case the init-failure path being resolved elsewhere makes this look fixed when the underlying page-size mismatch isn't.

comments.author: bluayer
comments.body:
Still reproduces on main (5fa7b7b0), and I'd like to work on a fix.

Cause: the inline fp32 scales make Gemma-4-26B pages 2064 B/token (full) vs 4160 B/token (sliding). That's not an integer ratio, so `unify_kv_cache_spec_page_size` pads the full page but keeps `block_size=16`, which leaves ~50% of each full-attention page empty.

Fix idea: grow the block to the largest multiple that fits before padding (16 → 32 here), guarded so the scheduler block LCM doesn't grow (#53007) and the padded page never needs to be split into kernel blocks.
  
Measured on 1× L40S with `RedHatAI/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-FP8-dynamic` (`max_model_len=32768`,`gpu_memory_utilization=0.9`), comparing the "GPU KV cache size" vLLM logs at startup, without vs. with the fix:
  - `fp8_per_token_head`: 163,599 → 189,526 tokens (+15.8% with fix)
  - `fp8`: unchanged (194,110)
  - GSM8K 5-shot (250 samples) stays within stderr for both

@heheda12345 @ivanium tagging you as owners of `v1/core`, and @ivanium since this builds on the padding behavior from #53007. Does this direction look OK? If so I'll open a PR with my fix.

items.title: [Bug] L2 serde (fp8 / turboquant) crashes on --separate-object-groups: MemoryObj.tensor views a multi-group buffer as one shape
items.author: dmmdea
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

With `--separate-object-groups`, the L2 serde processors (`fp8`, and `turboquant`) crash on any multi-group MemoryObj because they view the whole buffer as a single `meta.shape`, so a hybrid model that produces several groups per object cannot use an fp8/turboquant L2 tier at all — and it fails silently as far as serving is concerned (the seat looks healthy, the tier stores nothing).

### Environment

- LMCache 0.5.4 (MP server + `LMCacheMPConnector`); the file below is byte-identical on `main` (`ce08eea`).
- vLLM 0.28.0, torch 2.13.0+cu130, 2× RTX 5060 Ti (sm_120), model `RedHatAI/Qwen3.8-27B-INT4` (Qwen3.5-arch GDN hybrid: 48 linear-attention + 16 full-attention layers), `--mamba-cache-mode align`, chunk 784.

### Reproduce

`lmcache server … --separate-object-groups --l2-adapter '{"type":"fs_native","base_path":…,"serde":{"type":"fp8"}}'` (or `"turboquant"`), then drive any prefill that spills to L2.

### Actual

Every store to L2 fails:

```
Serde task (SERIALIZE) failed: RuntimeError: shape '[1, 16, 784, 2048]' is invalid for input of size 77070336
  (lmcache/v1/distributed/serde/fp8.py → lmcache/v1/memory_management.py)
```

`77070336 = 3 × (1·16·784·2048)` — three groups' worth of elements viewed as one group's shape. With `turboquant` one chunk (784 tokens) lands and the rest fail identically (cf. #4744).

### Why

`Fp8QuantizationSerializer.serialize` / `Deserializer.deserialize` read `src.tensor` / `dst.tensor`, and `MemoryObj.tensor` (`memory_management.py`, the MP object) returns `raw_data[:size].view(meta.dtype).view(meta.shape)` — one shape over the whole buffer. The per-group accessor `get_tensor(index)` and `meta.shapes`/`meta.dtypes` already exist, and `estimate_serialized_size` already sums over `layout_desc.shapes`; only the two data paths ignore them.

### Expected

Either the serde iterates the groups (`get_tensor(i)` for `i in range(len(meta.shapes))`, in the byte order the size estimator already assumes), in both directions, or the MP server rejects a serde on a separate-object-groups layout at config time with a clear message instead of failing per-store at runtime.

items.title: fs L2: per-rank group payloads collide on shared keys — half-size group-5 objects abort lookup promotion (hybrid groups, PP>1)
items.author: kaka86mm
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

On a PP>1 hybrid-KV-group model, the fs L2 tier never survives a server restart: lookups find the keys but abort promotion with `Incomplete read` size mismatches, so `lmcache_mp_lookup_hit_l2_*` stays 0 and everything recomputes. Evidence points to **per-rank group payloads colliding on shared keys** — one PP rank writes group-5 objects at exactly half the size the reader's spec-derived buffer expects.

## Environment

- 4× CMP 170HX (sm80), vLLM fork v0.13.0, PP=4 (`12,12,12,12`), MiMo-V2.6-Flash-RL — 6 hybrid groups, `group_tokens_per_block=[256,128,128,128,128,128]`
- `lmcache server --chunk-size 8192 --shm-name ... --max-gpu-workers 4 --supported-transfer-mode engine_driven --l1-size-gb 100 --no-l1-use-lazy --eviction-policy LRU --l2-adapter '{"type":"fs","base_path":"/lmcache-l2","relative_tmp_dir":"tmp"}'`
- lmcache 0.5.6.post4410 (PR #4410 head)

## Repro (deterministic)

1. Send a unique 200K-token prefix (same token ids both times) → prefill completes, objects written to L2.
2. Gracefully restart server and engine (`docker stop -t 60` both; no kills).
3. Resend the identical prefix.

Result: full recompute (~57 s), `lookup_hit_l2_tokens_total` / `lookup_hit_l2_keys_total` = **0**, and 27 warnings:

```
Incomplete read for -SEP-model@0x04000400@5@<hash>.data: expected 1310720, got 655360
```

## Evidence for per-rank payload collision

File-size census of the L2 dir after one 200K store:

| group | files × size |
|---|---|
| @0 | 243 × 41,943,040 + 81 × 62,914,560 |
| @1..@4 | 324 × 1,310,720 each |
| @5 | **243 × 1,310,720 + 81 × 655,360** |

- 324 = 4 ranks × 81 chunks; the 81 bad @5 files are exactly one rank's share. The PP ranks carry different layer compositions (rank 0 hosts the vision encoder, rank 3 the lm_head), so per-rank group payloads legitimately differ in size (see @0's 40 MB vs 60 MB classes).
- All 27 lookup-time mismatches are `@5` keys whose on-disk size (655,360) is exactly half of `expected = len(dst_buf)` (1,310,720) — the buffer comes from the engine-side group spec (`fs_l2_adapter.py`, standard async path: `expected = len(dst_buf)`), not from any per-object metadata.
- Atomic writes were enabled (`relative_tmp_dir=tmp`, `os.replace`), and these files were written by a fresh clean process with no interruption — truncation is ruled out; the writer wrote half.
- The reader `continue`s on mismatch, so the first bad object in a chain truncates the contiguous hit to zero → no promotion at all, not even partial.

This also retroactively explains the partial adoption we reported earlier (168/192 keys after a restart) and why `lookup_hit_l2` was 0 all day in production.

## Suggested directions

- Include the rank (or a payload-size discriminator) in the L2 object key, or assemble the full-group payload before writing under the shared key; or
- store the object's true byte length in a sidecar / the key name and size the read buffer from it, instead of deriving `expected` from the model group spec.

Happy to run instrumented builds or share the full server logs / file census on request.

(Prior context from the same rig: #5440 — the per-object cost thread; #4410 review.)

items.title: [Bug]: MiniMax-M3 (MXFP8) streaming: generation stops (empty delta, finish_reason=stop) right after reasoning closes, whenever a tool call should follow — non-streaming with identical payload succeeds
items.author: ZhandosSeitkaliyev
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment

`collect_env.py` could not be run on this host — no outbound internet access (air-gapped deployment). Manually collected equivalent below.

**Versions**
- vLLM: `0.27.0` (build `vllm-0.27.0-tp4-41db7380`)
- PyTorch: `2.13.0+cu129`
- Transformers: `5.15.0`
- GPU: 4x NVIDIA H200 (143771 MiB), driver `595.58.03`

**Model**
- `MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M3`
- Quantization: `mxfp8` (NVIDIA ModelOpt MXFP8 checkpoint, `weight_block_size=[1,32]`, MoE via `MarlinMxfp8LinearKernel`/`MARLIN` backend) — vLLM's own startup log flags this format as *"experimental and could change in future"*

**Launch command**
```bash
vllm serve /model --served-model-name MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M3 \
  --tensor-parallel-size 4 --block-size 128 --max-model-len 65536 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.93 --tool-call-parser minimax_m3 \
  --reasoning-parser minimax_m3 --enable-auto-tool-choice \
  --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000
```



### 🐛 Describe the bug

With `stream: true` and `tools` provided, for requests where the model's reasoning is longer / more hedging before deciding to call a tool, the SSE stream **stops immediately after the reasoning block closes**: the next chunk has an empty `delta` and `finish_reason: "stop"`. Nothing is generated after that — no content, no `tool_calls`. This is not a parsing failure; generation itself halts.

The byte-identical payload sent with `"stream": false` succeeds reliably (tested 6/6).

> **Note:** only reproduced so far on an MXFP8-quantized checkpoint (NVIDIA ModelOpt format). Untested whether an unquantized bf16 checkpoint is also affected.

**Minimal repro**

Flat 2-field tool schema — confirmed tool schema complexity/count is not the trigger (fails the same way with 1 tool or 5 tools):

```python
import requests

payload = {
    "model": "MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M3",
    "stream": True,
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "сделай docx с названием test и текстом привет"}],
    "tools": [{
        "type": "function",
        "function": {
            "name": "generate_docx_report",
            "description": "Generate a Word document from content.",
            "parameters": {
                "type": "object",
                "properties": {
                    "filename": {"type": "string"},
                    "content": {"type": "string"},
                },
                "required": ["filename", "content"],
            },
        },
    }],
    "tool_choice": "auto",
}

r = requests.post("http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions", json=payload, stream=True)
for line in r.iter_lines():
    if line:
        print(line.decode())
```

**Expected**

Reasoning closes, then either visible content or a populated `tool_calls` delta follows — same as the non-streaming response to the identical payload (`"stream": False` above).

**Observed**

After the last reasoning chunk, the stream emits one more chunk with an empty delta and `finish_reason: "stop"`, then ends. Nothing else is generated.

**Ruled out**
- Tool schema size — reproduces with both a minimal flat 2-field schema and a real ~2KB docstring-heavy schema
- Tool count — 1 tool vs 5 tools, same result
- Payload size in general — byte-identical payloads, only `stream` differs

**Correlation observed (not confirmed causal)**

Requests where the model's own reasoning is short/decisive stream through fine. Requests where reasoning is longer with self-correction (*"But I should check... Actually... Let me reconsider..."*) reliably hit the halt.

**Current workaround**

Routing tool-decision through a separate non-streaming call instead of native streaming tool-calling (application-level, not a real fix — costs 2x LLM calls per turn).



### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

items.author: aoshen02
items.body_excerpt:
> **Revision 2026-10-07.** This RFC was rewritten around a model of where the time and > memory of an RL `pause(mode="abort")` go, and the PR stacks that follow from it. The previous > text is preserved verbatim in a comment below and in > [`history-original-rfc.md`](https://github.com/aoshen02/vllm/blob/rfc57479/docs/rfc-57479/history-original-rfc.md); its GPU evidence is > summarised in §9. Long derivations, full tables and reproduction commands are on the fork > branch [`aoshen02/vllm@rfc57479/docs`](https://github.com/aoshen02/vllm/tree/rfc57479/docs/rfc-57479), together with the > measurement harness ([`harness/`](https://github.com/aoshen02/vllm/tree/rfc57479/docs/rfc-57479/harness)). # 0. TL;DR An RL trainer pauses generation with `POST /pause?mode=abort` before a weight update, and then needs every partial rollout back. With long outputs and top-k logprobs, the default `/inference/v1/generate` response is several GB per request. Both frontends spend most of the post-pause time building and serialising it. The Python frontend can also run out of memory before the pause. We model the cost per (position, top-k slot) entry, derive which terms dominate, and propose two independent PR stacks, one per frontend. Each stack has one default-format change (same bytes as today) and one opt-in compact format for RL. **Workload:** 32 non-streaming requests in flight, 16,384 input tokens, 245,760 output tokens each, top-128 logprobs, aborted together. DP8 with one mock engine per rank and the real `DPCoordinatorProc`; EP8 is engine-side and not modelled by the CPU mock. Times are seconds from the pause until the client has parsed every response. Memory is the frontend peak RSS: per process for Python (32 API servers on one node), total for Rust (one process). | n = 32, DP8 | Base `0fd2e8d503` | Python stack | Rust stack | |---|---|---|---| | **Default format** (bytes identical to base) | Python: **FAIL**, node memory floor after ~8 min at 36 GiB per process [S2]
Rust: **32.9–33.2 s**, **199–202 GiB** [S2][S3] | **21.3 s**, **9.5 GiB** per process (round-24 tip, two build threads [S27]); 21.6 s / 6.0 GiB with one thread [S7] | **20.73 s**, **14.47 GiB** [S4] | | **RL compact format** (opt-in) | not available | **1.80 s**, **2.0 GiB** per process [S7] | **1.85 s**, **11.86 GiB** [S5] | | Response size per request | Python 2,199.6 MB, Rust 3,408.7 MB [S7][S6] | default 2,199.6 MB; compact 337.0 MB | default 3,408.7 MB; compact 337.0 MB | At bs = 256, base Rust aborted on a failed 4 GiB allocation (measured at DP4 [S20]), and the base storage path fails at DP8 at the node memory floor [S8] (base Python itself was not run at bs = 256). Both stacks complete: RL compact 10.87 s (Python) and 10.91 [10.88–10.97] s (Rust, measured on the previous Rust tip; see §5 for why this carries over) with the official 8-core client, which is the limit there [S7][S3]. **Proposed PRs.** All are on base `0fd2e8d503`. They are drafts in the submitter's fork for review; nothing is opened against `vllm-project/vllm` yet. | # | Frontend | PR | Product LOC (+/−) | Tests | Depends on | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | P1 | Python | [Frontend-only sample-logprobs container hook](https://github.com/aoshen02/vllm/pull/109) | +301 / −13 | +715 | — | | P2 | Python | [Public APIs for generate endpoint plugins](https://github.com/aoshen02/vllm/pull/110): `start_generate`, `replace_route` | +261 / −20 | +434 | stacked on P1 for review order (no code dependency) | | P3 | Python | [generate: keep sample logprobs as engine rows, render without objects](https://github.com/aoshen02/vllm/pull/111) | +871 / −34 | +495 | P1 (code); stacked on P2 | | — | Python | [`vllm-rl-compact` endpoint plugin](https://github.com/aoshen02/vllm/pull/112) (out of tree, not proposed for merge) | 0 in `vllm/` (+1,443 under `plugins/`) | +2,682 | P1–P3 | | R-A | Rust | [server: stream the default generate body from the request runtime](https://github.com/aoshen02/vllm/pull/107) | +380 / −46 | +496 | — | | R-B | Rust | [server: opt-in compact logprobs format for raw generate](https://github.com/aoshen02/vllm/pull/108) | +241 / −13 | +400 / −1 | R-A | **Merge order:** Rust R-A → R-B. Python P1 → P2 → P3; the plugin is released separately once P1 and P2 are in. The two stacks are independent. Two Rust changes with mock-only gains are kept as backup branches and are not proposed (§4). # 1. Problem and scope **The operation.** In RL training the rollout manager calls `pause(mode="abort")` on every API server before each weight sync. Engines abort the running requests and the frontends return each partial completion with `finish_reason="abort"`. The trainer cannot start the update until it has all partials, so the time from the pause to the last parsed response is on the critical path of every training step. The pause/resume API is from RFC #32103. **The workload.** It is the shape of our production RL rollout: - 245,760 output tokens per request, top-128 logprobs, 16,384-token input, non-streaming; - DP8 EP8, n = 32 per frontend node in the main cells and bs = 256 in the cohort cells; - `ignore_eos`, no stop strings, no prompt logprobs. **What RL needs from each response:** the output `token_ids`, and for every position the top-k token ids and their float32 logprobs. It does not need text, decoded token strings, the sampled slot or ranks. **Out of scope:** - **R3 (routed experts):** deferred by the submitter. The default `routed_experts` path is unchanged. - **Streaming:** RL here uses non-streaming requests. Streaming default responses are unchanged; the compact format rejects `stream: true` with 400 in Rust. Python compact streaming lives only in the out-of-tree plugin. - Engine-side pause semantics and DP consensus are unchanged. # 2. items.title: [Bug][ROCm] `ROCM_ATTN` returns wrong attention (and can fault the GPU) on RDNA for head size ≥ 96 with KV block size ≠ 16, and for MHA with head size 192/256
items.author: nemanjaudovic
items.body_excerpt:
### Used environment

- GPU: AMD Radeon AI PRO R9700 (gfx1201, RDNA4), ROCm 10.2, torch 2.13.0+rocm10.2, triton 3.8.0
- vLLM: `main` @ dde9aca41c (2026-10-19); also seen on 426f3bd36 (2026-10-14)
- Backend: `ROCM_ATTN` (the default attention backend on RDNA)

### The bug

On RDNA, `ROCM_ATTN` decodes with its HIP paged-attention kernel only for head 128, block 16 and GQA 3–16. Everything else uses its Triton fallback: `kernel_paged_attention_2d` for decode, `context_attention_fwd` for prefill. For some layouts that path returns wrong attention outputs, and in some batches it crashes the process with a GPU memory-access fault inside `kernel_paged_attention_2d`.

**How it was found:** an A/B harness runs `ROCM_ATTN` as vLLM does:
- vLLM's KV-cache allocator;
- the backend's own `do_kv_cache_update()`, metadata builder and `forward()`;
- outputs compared to an fp32 PyTorch attention reference.

On correct layouts the error is ~0.001–0.01. On the failing ones it's 0.02–0.57; correct is within 0.02 + 0.02·|ref|. `TRITON_ATTN`, on identical inputs and the same cache shapes, matches the reference in all 14,608 batches.

**Results:** 12,389 batches where `ROCM_ATTN` is vLLM's default backend; 635 wrong outputs and 119 GPU faults.

| head size | KV block size | wrong | GPU fault | ok |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 96 | 528 | 175 | 57 | 120 |
| 128 | 32 | 0 | 24 | 66 |
| 128 | 64 | 24 | 0 | 66 |
| 128 | 528 | 42 | 12 | 500 |
| 192 | 16 (GQA 1 only) | 30 | 0 | 309 |
| 192 | 528 | 150 | 13 | 176 |
| 256 | 16 (GQA 1 only) | 33 | 0 | 1485 |
| 256 | 32 | 8 | 12 | 68 |
| 256 | 64 | 0 | 1 | 87 |
| 256 | 528 | 173 | 0 | 341 |

- **Never failed:** head 64 at any block size (16 / 32 / 64 / 528); head 96 at block 16; head 128 at block 16 (HIP kernel and Triton path).
- **Not specific to a dtype:** bf16 and fp16 both fail.
- **KV cache dtype:** all failures but one are with a 16-bit cache. An fp8 KV cache with the same shapes didn't fail.

Block 528 is a real configuration: hybrid models (e.g. Qwen3.5 / Qwen3-Next) use large KV blocks, and `ROCM_ATTN` declares `MultipleOf(16)` block sizes.

**There are two distinct patterns.**

**Pattern A: block size ≥ 32 (32, 64, 528) at padded head size ≥ 128 (head 96, 128, 192, 256).** Decode reads the cache wrongly.
- **Wrong:** decode batches, and the decode rows of mixed batches. These run `kernel_paged_attention_2d`, which also faults sometimes.
- **Correct:** prefill and short-query batches *on the same cached context*, e.g. a 1024-token chunk on 8192 cached tokens, read by `context_attention_fwd`. The repro also reads the cache back and finds it **exactly** equal to what was written. So the cache is correct, and the reader `kernel_paged_attention_2d` is wrong.
- **The error shrinks with context:** about 0.33 at 1k, 0.10 at 8k, 0.05 at 32k (head 96, block 528, 32 q / 8 KV heads). That suggests a bounded number of keys/values per request are read wrongly (e.g. one tile or one block), not every tile.
- In this kernel the tile is `TRITON_BLOCK_SIZE = min(block_size, 128)` for power-of-two blocks and 32 for other blocks. So every failing case has tiles of ≥ 32 tokens with `HEAD_SIZE_PADDED` ≥ 128; block 16 (16-token tiles) and head 64 never fail.

**Pattern B: block 16, MHA (GQA 1: 32 q / 32 KV heads), head 192 / 256.** Every batch that reads cached tokens is wrong:
- decode (`kernel_paged_attention_2d`);
- short queries;
- prefill chunks on cached context (`context_attention_fwd`).

Fresh prompts with no cached context (128–8192 tokens) are correct. **The repro confirms the KV cache is written wrongly:**
- reading the cache back through `ROCM_ATTN`'s own K/V views gives values up to 5.3 away from the keys and values written, while at GQA 4 (8 KV heads) it's exact;
- for block 16 with a native layout, `do_kv_cache_update()` uses the HIP `reshape_and_cache` (`PagedAttention.write_to_paged_cache`);
- so the writer is wrong for this shape, when `num_kv_heads × head_size` is large (6,144 / 8,192 elements per token).

Both readers are then fed bad data.

Example rows (bf16, error = max |out − ref|):

| layout | batch | `ROCM_ATTN` | `TRITON_ATTN` |
|---|---|---|---|
| 32/8 heads, head 96, block 528 | decode, 1 × 1k | wrong, 0.355 | ok |
| same | decode, 8 × 8k | wrong, 0.104 | ok |
| same | 1024-token chunk on 8k cached | ok | ok |
| 32/32 heads, head 256, block 16 | decode, 1 × 1k | wrong, 0.230 | ok |
| same | 1024-token chunk on 8k cached | wrong, 0.109 | ok |
| same | fresh 1024-token prompt | ok | ok |
| 32/8 heads, head 192, block 528 | decode, 1 × 8k | GPU fault in `kernel_paged_attention_2d` ("Page not present") | ok |

### Repro

`repro_rocm_attn.py` ([gist](https://gist.github.com/nemanjaudovic/d14acb71c4a21641dd791750225d4be5)) builds `ROCM_ATTN` exactly as vLLM does, with `TRITON_ATTN` as a control. For each case it prints three things:
- **write:** the cache, read back through `ROCM_ATTN`'s own K/V views, vs what was written (separates writer from reader);
- **output:** error vs fp32;
- **inputs:** whether query / keys / values were modified (stray writes).

```bash
HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 python3 repro_rocm_attn.py --case p1-d192-bs528   # pattern A
HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 python3 repro_rocm_attn.py --case p2-d256-bs16-gqa1 # pattern B
HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 python3 repro_rocm_attn.py                          # all cases
```

A GPU fault kills the process; run pattern A cases one at a time.

Output on gfx1201 (vLLM `ROCM_ATTN` code identical to `main` @ dde9aca41c):

```
### ok-d64-bs528 (exit 0)
# gfx1201 AMD Radeon AI Pro R9700S, vLLM 0.32.0rc1.dev443+g3b4de701f (/host/vllm/vllm/__init__.py), torch 2.13.0+rocm10.2.0a20261005
== ok-d64-bs528: q/kv heads 32/8, head 64, block 528, bfloat16, 1 request(s), q 1, context 1024
   layout KVCacheLayout.LHBNC, key_cache (3, 8, 8, 528, 8) strides (270336, 33792, 4224, 8, 1), value_cache (3, 8, 64, 528) strides (270336, 33792, 528, 1)
   ROCM_ATTN   output ok       max err 0.0006; write: k max diff 0, v max diff 0; inputs unchanged

items.title: [Discussion][MP] LMCache Interface and Protocol Compatibility
items.author: cage-goat
items.body_excerpt:
## Background

LMCache MP mode currently has several compatibility concerns:

1. **Older connectors may be incompatible with newer LMCache Servers.**  
   Changes to MP protocol fields, message formats, or field ordering may prevent an older connector from communicating correctly with a newer LMCache Server.

2. **LMCache interface changes require corresponding updates in vLLM and SGLang.**  
   When connector parameters, return values, or interface names change, vLLM and SGLang must update their integration code accordingly. Otherwise, they may no longer work correctly with LMCache.

3. **SGLang does not install LMCache by default.**  
   Users must select and install the `lmcache` package themselves. A successful installation does not necessarily mean that the connector is compatible with the installed SGLang version.

Based on these concerns, this issue seeks community input on the following two areas.

## 1. Connector Interface Stability and Compatibility Matrix

One topic for discussion is which LMCache connector interfaces should remain stable and how interface changes and deprecations should be managed. A stable interface boundary could reduce situations where LMCache, vLLM, and SGLang must all be upgraded at the same time.

A related question is whether the project should maintain a clear compatibility matrix covering:

- Compatible vLLM and LMCache/connector versions;
- Compatible SGLang and LMCache/connector versions.

## 2. MP Protocol Stability, Handshake, and Graceful Fallback

Another topic for discussion is how to define MP protocol compatibility rules so that future field and message-format changes remain backward-compatible whenever possible.

One possible direction is to introduce an MP protocol version handshake with behavior such as:

- The connector and LMCache Server exchange their supported protocol versions when establishing a connection;
- LMCache is enabled when both sides support a compatible version;
- If no compatible version is available, the connector automatically falls back to running without LMCache;
- After fallback, vLLM or SGLang continues normal inference and reports a clear reason for disabling LMCache.

The detailed protocol evolution rules, compatibility window, and handshake design should be determined through community discussion.

## Expected Outcome

This issue aims to help the community reach consensus on:

- The stable interface boundary for LMCache connectors;
- Whether and how to maintain a vLLM/SGLang compatibility matrix;
- Evolution rules for MP protocol fields and message formats;
- Protocol handshake and fallback behavior when versions are incompatible.

Once there is general agreement, the detailed design and implementation can be tracked in follow-up issues or pull requests.

items.title: MP mode: remaining unbounded request-state retention in vLLM client and sidecar prefetch bookkeeping
items.author: wuwanxu
items.body_excerpt:
## Deployment

We run a production **3P1D** deployment with vLLM and `LMCacheMPConnector`. Each serving node has a per-node LMCache sidecar; LMCache uses `fs_native` as the L2 adapter backed by local SSD. P2P, CacheBlend, and engine-driven transfer are not enabled.

The previous client-side MQ no-response leak is tracked separately in #5270. During a follow-up audit of upstream `dev` (checked at `05fc77a`, 2026-09-24), we found the two request-state retention paths below. This issue only reports the observed behavior and asks maintainers to determine the intended lifecycle and remediation.

## 1. vLLM client: `_returned_finished` grows for the worker lifetime

`LMCacheMPWorkerAdapter` creates:

```python
self._returned_finished: set[str] = set()
```

`_process_finished_stores()` uses this set to prevent a request ID from being reported repeatedly through `finished_sending`, then records returned IDs with:

```python
self._returned_finished.update(ret_stores)
```

We could not find a `discard`, `clear`, TTL, or capacity-based removal path. Therefore every request ID once returned as `finished_sending` remains resident until the vLLM worker exits. This path is exercised by normal successful requests as well as failure paths.

The set appears to be needed for async-scheduling deduplication after neighboring tracking sets are drained, but it also produces monotonic process-lifetime growth. With UUID-like Python request IDs, the retained footprint is roughly 150-200 bytes per request before allocator overhead; at sustained high QPS this can become material in a long-lived worker.

Relevant code:
- `lmcache/integration/vllm/vllm_multi_process_adapter.py` (`_returned_finished`, `_process_finished_stores`)

### Questions for maintainers

1. Is process-lifetime retention of every completed `finished_sending` request ID required by the vLLM connector contract?
2. What lifecycle or retention semantics should this deduplication state have in a long-running worker?

## 2. sidecar: abandoned prefetch jobs and completion Bitmaps are never reclaimed

`LookupModule` registers every lookup in:

```python
self._prefetch_jobs: dict[str, _PrefetchJob] = {}
```

The job is removed when `QUERY_PREFETCH_STATUS` or `WAIT_PREFETCH_STATUS` obtains a non-`None` completion result. If a client aborts or disconnects after LOOKUP, or stops polling after an RPC timeout/unhealthy transition, the job is not consumed by that path.

The corresponding `PrefetchController` completion state has the same consumer-driven ownership:

```python
self._completed_lookups: dict[PrefetchRequestId, int] = {}
self._completed_results: dict[PrefetchRequestId, Bitmap] = {}
```

`query_prefetch_result()` pops both the Bitmap and the lookup result. The source comment notes that failing to consume the prefetch result leaks memory. `Bitmap` is native/C++ memory, so its growth may not be visible in Python GC or tracemalloc. `END_SESSION` removes the session and touches L1 keys but does not remove the prefetch job or controller completion state.

In production we also see frequent `Session ... not found, skipping touch` warnings (roughly 378-953 over two hours), consistent with request-lifecycle skew and making normal client polling an unreliable sole ownership mechanism.

Relevant code:
- `lmcache/v1/multiprocess/modules/lookup.py` (`_prefetch_jobs`, `query_prefetch_status`, `end_session`)
- `lmcache/v1/distributed/storage_controllers/prefetch_controller.py` (`_completed_lookups`, `_completed_results`, `query_prefetch_result`)

### Questions for maintainers

1. What is the intended owner of a prefetch job and its completion result after the original client has abandoned the request?
2. Is there an existing cancellation or reclamation lifecycle that this MP path should use?
3. What cleanup ordering is required for an in-flight prefetch so that late completion cannot expose invalid L1 data or retain completion state?

## Expected behavior

For healthy-sidecar and abort/error paths alike, client and server request bookkeeping should have a defined bounded lifecycle. Abandoned request state should be reclaimable without requiring a vLLM worker or sidecar restart, while preserving correctness for normal in-flight requests.

## Reproduction direction

1. Run vLLM + `LMCacheMPConnector` + sidecar with an SSD-backed `fs_native` L2.
2. Send sustained requests and observe the vLLM worker: `_returned_finished` grows monotonically.
3. Submit LOOKUPs, then abort/disconnect before prefetch polling completes, or induce a prefetch-status timeout.
4. Observe `lmcache_mp.active_prefetch_jobs` and `PrefetchController.report_status()["completed_results_count"]`; entries can remain after the client has abandoned the request.

comments.author: neevmodh
comments.body:
Read through both paths in `upstream/dev` to check the analysis — can confirm both observations.

**Part 1 (`_returned_finished`):** Confirmed there's no eviction path on this set anywhere in `vllm_multi_process_adapter.py`. Looking at `_process_finished_stores`, the set's only real job is to stop the same `req_id` from being re-added to `ret_stores` if `finished_req_ids_from_engine` reports it again in a later call — but once vLLM's own engine stops mentioning a `req_id` (i.e. it's fully retired from the engine's tracking), `_returned_finished`'s entry for it can never be hit again by the loop that checks it, so it's dead weight from that point on. A conservative fix that doesn't touch the dedup semantics: at the end of `_process_finished_stores`, intersect `_returned_finished` with the union of `self.finished_stores` / `self.store_futures` / `finished_req_ids_from_engine`, so an ID is only retained while it's still reachable through one of the sets that could re-report it. Happy to send that as a small PR if a maintainer confirms there's no other call site relying on longer retention.

**Part 2 (prefetch jobs):** Confirmed `end_session` (`lookup.py:514`) is already the natural per-request teardown hook — it's called on `MP_REQUEST_END` and already knows the `request_id`. Adding `self._prefetch_jobs.pop(request_id, None)` there looks safe on the `LookupModule` side. The harder part is `PrefetchController`'s `_completed_lookups`/`_completed_results` (a *different* class, presumably reachable through session/controller wiring I didn't fully trace) — and your question #3 is the real blocker here: popping a `Bitmap` out from under a prefetch that completes *after* the client has already been torn down risks exactly the late-completion/invalid-L1-data race you flagged, since it's native memory. I don't think this half should be fixed without a maintainer confirming the intended ownership handoff at session end — happy to implement once that's settled, but I'd rather not guess at a fix that touches native memory lifecycle across processes.

comments.author: neevmodh
comments.body: Following up on my earlier analysis: opened #5363 for part 1 (the `_returned_finished` set). Rather than guess at exact removal timing (which depends on the vLLM engine-contract question I couldn't answer myself), it bounds the set with a small LRU cap instead — converts unbounded growth into bounded memory without needing that question resolved first. Part 2 (sidecar prefetch/completion state) is intentionally left alone, per my earlier comment on the native-memory ordering risk.

items.title: [MP] vLLM auto-start can't launch a gRPC server
items.author: theminjunchoi
items.body_excerpt:
With `lmcache.mp.autostart` on, the connector only accepts a `tcp://` endpoint and always starts a ZMQ server. A `grpc://` endpoint is rejected with "Expected a local TCP host:port endpoint", so anyone using the gRPC transport has to start the server by hand.

Passing `--transport grpc` through `lmcache.mp.autostart.server_args` with a `tcp://` endpoint doesn't work either. The server comes up as gRPC, but the launcher's health probe still speaks ZMQ, so startup waits until it times out.

The `grpc://` rejection was added on purpose in #3476, since the launcher could only start the endpoint it would actually probe. Now that the gRPC transport is planned as the default (#4877), I think auto-start should be able to launch it too. I have a fix ready and will open a PR shortly.

### Name and Version

llama-server, Windows releases b11577 (win-cuda-12.4-x64 and win-cuda-13.4-x64, "version: 0.6.0-dev (build 11577, commit cbe28bb3c), built with Clang 20.1.8 for Windows x86_64") and b10268 (win-cuda-12.4-x64, "version: 10268 (6b5224cfc)").

### GGML backends

CUDA

### Hardware

NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4080 SUPER (16 GB), driver 617.14. 62 GB RAM.

### Models

google/gemma-4-12B-it-qat-q4_0-gguf: `gemma-4-12b-it-qat-q4_0.gguf` with `mmproj-gemma-4-12b-it-qat-q4_0.gguf` (both from the HF repo, snapshot 29d0977).

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

Server command line:

```
llama-server.exe -m gemma-4-12b-it-qat-q4_0.gguf -ngl 999 -fa on -c 32768 -np 1 --no-context-shift --host 127.0.0.1 --port <port> -rea off --reasoning-format none -mm mmproj-gemma-4-12b-it-qat-q4_0.gguf
```

A chat completion over `/v1/chat/completions` with one image (1024x1024 PNG, base64 data URL) plus about 4.5k tokens of text (system prompt and conversation) kills the server with a CUDA illegal memory access. Sometimes the first request with the image dies, sometimes the first succeeds and the second (same slot, prompt cache hit, ~100 new tokens) dies. Text-only requests of the same size die much more rarely (1 of 4 runs).

The same model, the same flags and the same requests run fine on the Linux Docker image (build b10257, CUDA 13.3) on the same card.

Windows Event Log for each crash: `llama-server.exe`, exception 0xc0000409 in ucrtbase.dll (fail fast / abort).

Unknown; b10268 (August) already shows it, less often than b11577.

items.title: [Bug]: HA snapshot recovery does not update applied sequence metric
items.author: Icedcoco
items.body_excerpt:
### Bug Report

### Summary

When an HA standby starts from a batch OpLog snapshot, the snapshot state and recovery cursor are restored successfully, but the exported `ha_oplog_applied_sequence_id` metric remains at its initial value. This makes the metric disagree with the standby's actual recovery position.

### Reproduction

The issue is reproducible with a snapshot whose recovered sequence is `117` and which has no incremental OpLog entries to apply after the snapshot:

1. Create and publish a valid batch OpLog snapshot covering sequence `117`.
2. Start an HA standby with snapshot bootstrap enabled.
3. Allow snapshot recovery to complete and the standby to enter `WATCHING`.
4. Read the standby metrics and synchronization status.

Observed result:

```text
recovery log:          snapshot/applied = 117
OpLogApplier expected:  118
snapshot applied batch: 51
standby state:          WATCHING
sync status applied:    117
ha_oplog_applied_sequence_id: 0
```

The standby's internal cursor and synchronization status show that sequence `117` has been recovered, while the exported applied-sequence gauge still reports `0`.

### Root cause

`OpLogApplier::Recover(last_applied_sequence_id)` updates only `expected_sequence_id` to `last_applied_sequence_id + 1`. It does not update the HA applied-sequence gauge.

The gauge is currently updated when an individual `ApplyOpLogEntry` succeeds. The snapshot bootstrap path installs the recovered baseline through `HotStandbyService::LoadBatchOpLogSnapshotBaselineLocked` and updates the standby's internal `applied_seq_id_`, but does not update `ha_oplog_applied_sequence_id`. Therefore, a snapshot with an empty incremental tail leaves the exported gauge at its initial value.

### Impact

- Monitoring reports an incorrect applied sequence immediately after snapshot recovery.
- Any alert, readiness check, or recovery validation based on `ha_oplog_applied_sequence_id` or derived lag can report a false failure or an incorrect recovery state.
- Operators cannot distinguish a metric reporting error from an actual OpLog replay failure using the exported metrics alone.

This is an observability and recovery-validation defect. The current evidence does not indicate data loss or incorrect recovered object metadata; the internal recovery cursor is correct.

### Expected behavior

After a successful snapshot recovery, `ha_oplog_applied_sequence_id` must equal the latest sequence represented by the recovered baseline, even when no incremental OpLog entries follow it:

```text
snapshot_applied_sequence = 117
ha_oplog_applied_sequence_id = 117
expected_sequence_id = 118
```

When incremental entries are subsequently applied, the metric must continue advancing to the latest successfully applied sequence.

### Scope of the fix

Synchronize the applied-sequence gauge with the recovered baseline during snapshot/bootstrap installation. Check all recovery paths that establish a baseline, including batch snapshot recovery, ordinary snapshot recovery, and local warm restart, so that the metric does not depend on at least one later OpLog entry being replayed.

Do not change the recovered cursor or treat the metric as the source of truth; the metric should reflect the already recovered cursor.

### Acceptance criteria

Add regression coverage for:

1. Snapshot recovery with no incremental OpLog tail.
2. Snapshot recovery followed by incremental entries.
3. A baseline at sequence `0`.
4. Consistency between the applied sequence, expected sequence, snapshot batch, and lag metrics.

The tests should verify both the internal synchronization status and the exported `ha_oplog_applied_sequence_id` metric.

### Additional context

The metric is defined as the "Latest OpLog sequence ID applied by Standby". A successful snapshot recovery already reports the recovered sequence in recovery logs and synchronization status, so the exported metric should expose the same value rather than remain at its process-start default.
