comments.author: bryand410
comments.body:
Verified against `main` — @Icedcoco's diagnosis holds at every line it names, and it reaches
further than the report suggests. Four findings, in order of how much they change the fix.

**1. This is not specific to batch snapshots — it hits four start paths.**

`OpLogApplier::Recover` (`mooncake-store/src/ha/oplog/oplog_applier.cpp:153-158`) writes exactly
one thing:

```cpp
void OpLogApplier::Recover(uint64_t last_applied_sequence_id) {
    expected_sequence_id_.store(last_applied_sequence_id + 1);
    LOG(INFO) << "OpLogApplier: recovered from sequence_id=" ...
}
```

The gauge is only advanced from inside `ApplyOpLogEntry` (`oplog_applier.cpp:129-134`), i.e. once
per *replayed entry*. So any path that establishes a baseline without replaying an entry leaves the
exported gauge at its process-start value. There are four, not one:

| Path | Source | Baseline set | Gauge after |
|---|---|---|---|
| Batch OpLog snapshot | `LoadBatchOpLogSnapshotBaselineLocked` (`hot_standby_service.cpp:240-271`, baseline from `:260`) | yes | **stale** |
| Warm restart, recoverable local state | `Recover(local_last_seq_id)` (`hot_standby_service.cpp:218`) | yes | **stale** |
| Ordinary snapshot baseline | `LoadSnapshotBaselineLocked` (`hot_standby_service.cpp:232-238`) | 0 | **never leaves 0** |
| Empty cluster start | same function | 0 | 0 — correct |

Row 3 is the one I'd flag hardest, because it is not a staleness bug but a permanent silence: that
path calls `Recover(0)`, so the gauge stays `0` for the whole life of the process **unless** an
OpLog entry is later replayed. A standby that recovers from an empty baseline and then only serves
reads will export `ha_oplog_applied_sequence_id: 0` forever while its cursor is correct.

Row 2 matters for a different reason: it means this is not a snapshot-bootstrap problem at all. Any
standby process that restarts with local state but no new entries to apply reports `0`.

**2. The two callers of `Recover` do not agree on the contract.** In `LoadSnapshotBaselineLocked`,
`Recover(0)` is followed by `baseline_seq_id` staying `0` — consistent. In
`LoadBatchOpLogSnapshotBaselineLocked`, the baseline is derived *back out* from the applier:

```cpp
baseline_seq_id = oplog_applier_->GetExpectedSequenceId() - 1;   // hot_standby_service.cpp:260
```

That is the applier's state being read as the source of truth for the service's cursor. So the
inconsistency is structural: `Recover` owns `expected_sequence_id_` but not the gauge, while the
caller reconstructs the baseline from the applier. Any fix that only patches the batch-snapshot
path will leave row 2 and row 3 wrong.

**3. The correct value is already computed five lines above, and the gauge ignores it.**

```cpp
batch_snapshot_baseline_ = DurablePrefix{.batch_id = restored->last_applied_batch_id,
                                         .last_seq  = restored->last_applied_seq};   // :261-263
```

So no new plumbing is needed to know the correct number on this path — the value the gauge should
carry is set five lines earlier. Note also that `Recover` sets `expected_sequence_id_` to
`baseline + 1`, and `:260` inverts that back. The two agree today, but they are two independent
expressions of the same quantity, which is worth collapsing while this is being fixed.

**4. On the metric's own tests.** `TestSetOpLogAppliedSequenceId`
(`mooncake-store/tests/ha/standby/ha_metric_manager_test.cpp:154-157`) verifies the setter:
`set_oplog_applied_sequence_id(456)` → `get_oplog_applied_sequence_id() == 456`. So the gauge
plumbing works; what has no coverage is **the replayed-entry coupling** — that the value is only
ever written from `ApplyOpLogEntry`. For the regression tests proposed in the issue,
`rebootstrap_test.cpp:306,346-348` is the closest existing harness: it already asserts
`service_->GetLatestAppliedSequenceId()` **and** `GetSyncStatus().applied_seq_id` together, which is
the internal/external pair the acceptance criteria ask for.

items.title: [Bug]: MemFabric TENT registers adjacent buffers individually, potentially causing overlapping memory registrations
items.author: jamesjxliu
items.body_excerpt:
### Bug Report

The vector overload of MemFabricTransport::addMemoryBuffer() currently loops over the buffers and calls the single-buffer registration method for each one.
MemFabric aligns memory ranges to NPU page boundaries before registering them. Two adjacent, non-overlapping buffers can therefore produce overlapping aligned ranges when registered separately. With device_urma, the subsequent memory registration may fail with an “overlaps existing MR” error.

items.title: [RFC] pd: Prefill short requests on the decode worker that caches their prefix (PPD)
items.author: alphabetc1
items.body_excerpt:
## TL;DR

In agentic and multi-turn traffic, the decode worker that served the previous turn already holds almost all of the next prompt in its radix cache: the previous prompt plus the tokens it decoded. Today the next turn still goes prefill -> KV transfer -> decode, even when only a few hundred tokens are new. This RFC lets the router send such a request **only to the decode worker**, which prefills the uncached suffix itself (chunked prefill), then decodes it. We call this **PPD** (prefill on the decode worker, for short prefills). Requests the router does not mark keep the normal PD path, so one decode worker serves both.

## Why

- **The prefill worker's cache is the wrong one.** It caches turn N's prompt but not turn N's output, which was generated on the decode worker. So turn N+1 misses on prefill at the first output token, while the decode worker's radix cache (`--disaggregation-decode-enable-radix-cache`) holds prompt N plus output N.
- **The PD path has a fixed cost that a short prefill cannot hide:** a bootstrap handshake, the prefill worker's queue, the KV transfer, and the decode worker's preallocation and polling. With HiCache, cache hit rates of 90%+ are common for agentic sessions, so the computed part is often a few hundred tokens, and the fixed cost dominates TTFT.
- The prefill worker spends compute and network bandwidth on work the decode worker can do in one or two short extend steps.

## Flow

Red blocks are new; everything else exists today.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Client
    participant R as sgl-router
    participant P as Prefill worker
    participant D as Decode worker

    C->>R: request (turn N+1)
    R->>R: prefix lookup in the KV-event index (prefill and decode workers)

    rect rgb(255, 224, 224)
        Note over R,D: NEW: decode worker holds the prefix, uncached suffix is short
        R->>D: request + disagg_local_prefill=true (no bootstrap fields)
        D->>D: match decode radix tree, chunked prefill of the suffix
        D->>D: decode in the same running batch as PD requests
        D-->>R: stream tokens
    end

    Note over R,D: otherwise, unchanged PD path
    R->>P: request + bootstrap fields
    R->>D: request + bootstrap fields
    P->>D: KV transfer
    D-->>R: stream tokens
    R-->>C: response
```

## Who does what

| | Today | New |
|---|---|---|
| **sgl-router** (`experimental/sgl-router`) | `select_workers` (`src/server/routes/chat.rs`) looks up prefix matches, picks a prefill worker, then a decode peer with `DecodePolicyKind::{PowerOfTwo, LegacyHostAffinity}`; `dispatch` (`routes/chat/forward.rs`) sends both legs with one bootstrap room | Before picking a prefill worker, look up the decode workers' cached prefix in the same KV-event index. If a decode worker's uncached suffix is at most a threshold and its load allows, dispatch to that decode worker only, with `disagg_local_prefill: true`. Credit the decode worker, not a prefill worker, with the prefix (`record_prefill_route`). Pick decode workers with session or prefix affinity, so a conversation returns to the decode worker that holds it. |
| **Decode worker** | Admits only transferred requests: prealloc queue -> transfer queue -> waiting queue -> prebuilt batch | `--disaggregation-decode-enable-local-prefill`: a marked request enters `waiting_queue` and runs through the aggregated scheduler (radix match, chunked prefill, optional mixed chunk). Transferred requests move to a separate `disagg_decode_prebuilt_queue`. |
| **Prefill worker** | Prefills and transfers every PD request | No change; it just sees fewer short requests. |
| **Request API** | `bootstrap_host/port/room`, `disagg_prefill_dp_rank` | `disagg_local_prefill: bool` on `/generate`, `/v1/chat/completions`, `/v1/completions`, `/v1/responses`. A decode worker without the flag rejects it with 400. |

## Engine design (phase 1)

The decode worker becomes "an aggregated scheduler with a second source of requests that skip prefill":

1. **Queues.** With the flag on, `waiting_queue` holds only requests prefilled on this worker, so the aggregated code paths (prefill admission, priority, abort, timeouts, load reporting) keep their meaning. Transferred requests wait in `disagg_decode_prebuilt_queue`. With the flag off, nothing moves.
2. **Scheduling.** Each step first merges newly transferred requests into the running batch, as today, then calls the aggregated `get_next_batch_to_run`, which merges the last prefill batch, runs the next prefill chunk if any, and otherwise decodes. `--chunked-prefill-size` bounds a local prefill step and so the decode stall it causes; `--enable-mixed-chunk` lets running requests decode in the same step.
3. **Memory.** Preallocation for transferred requests reserves the remaining chunks of the in-flight local prefill, so remote admissions cannot starve it. Local admission uses the aggregated `PrefillAdder` budget, and decode retraction covers over-commit, as in aggregated serving.
4. **Retraction and pause.** A locally prefilled request has no prefill peer, so it is never rebootstrapped. When it is retracted, the worker skips the host backup and prefills it again locally, as an aggregated server does.
5. **Cache.** Phase 1 builds on the decode radix tree, not decode HiCache. Decode-side L2/L3 will come through the linker, so a local prefill can later hit KV that the decode worker offloaded.

Phase 1 rejects pipeline parallelism, DP attention, MoE all-to-all backends (their buffers are sized for decode batches), HiSparse, and decode host KV buffering.

## Phases

1. **Engine** (#45423): the flag, the request field, the scheduling and memory changes above, docs, unit tests, and an e2e test.
2. **sgl-router**: the decode-side prefix lookup and the local-prefill decision, `--pd-local-prefill-max-uncached-tokens`, decode affinity, and metrics for local versus PD routes.
3. **Engine**: DP attention and DeepEP decode. All-to-all buffers must fit a prefill chunk, and

items.title: A kernel that calls two `@triton.jit` helpers differing only in a captured value silently runs the first helper for both calls instead of each its own
items.author: Hughshine
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug


**TL;DR.** A kernel that calls two `@triton.jit` helpers with the same module, qualname and argument types silently runs the first helper's body for both calls, even when the helpers differ in what they capture. Root cause: a captured value (a `tl.constexpr` or another `@triton.jit` function) acts as an indirect parameter of the helper, but it is not part of the helper's generated name. `CodeGenerator.call_JitFunction` names the private function it generates for a helper `module.qualname__<argument types>`, where constexpr arguments contribute their values, and calls the existing function when one with that name is already in the module. Helpers made by one factory (`def make(c): C = tl.constexpr(c); @triton.jit def h(x): return x + C`) are one way to get such helpers. Possible fix: remember which `JITFunction` owns each generated name and give another function that wants the same name a numbered suffix; names of helpers that do not collide stay as they are.

Since [#7105](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/pull/7105) ("This allows building Zig-style generics in Triton") closure variables can be used inside kernels, so a factory can return helpers that differ only in a captured `tl.constexpr`. A kernel that calls two of them hits this bug. The control in the fold below calls only the second helper and is correct.

```python
import sys

import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl


def make_add(c):
    C = tl.constexpr(c)

    @triton.jit
    def add_c(x):
        return x + C

    return add_c


add_one = make_add(1.0)
add_hundred = make_add(100.0)


@triton.jit
def kernel(O):
    tl.store(O, add_one(tl.load(O)))
    tl.store(O + 1, add_hundred(tl.load(O + 1)))


o = torch.zeros(2, device="cuda")
kernel[(1, )](o)
print(o.tolist(), "expected [1.0, 100.0]")
sys.exit(1 if o.tolist() != [1.0, 100.0] else 0)
```

Observed on main @6fe3348e6 (exit code 1):
```
[1.0, 1.0] expected [1.0, 100.0]
```
Expected: `[1.0, 100.0]`, each helper's own result. The kernel's cache key is right (the two helpers have different `cache_key`s, because the captured `tl.constexpr` is part of them); the wrong function is in the IR the frontend generates. Before inlining, the module has one `tt.func private @"__main__.make_add.<locals>.add_c__fp32"` whose body has `arith.constant 1.0`, and both call sites call it.

<details>
<summary>The same with a control that calls only the second helper, 16-element blocks and a fresh cache directory</summary>

```python
import os
import sys
import tempfile

os.environ["TRITON_CACHE_DIR"] = tempfile.mkdtemp()  # fresh on-disk cache
import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl


def make_add(c):
    C = tl.constexpr(c)

    @triton.jit
    def add_c(x):
        return x + C

    return add_c


add_one = make_add(1.0)
add_hundred = make_add(100.0)
print("triton", triton.__version__, triton.__file__)
print("same qualname:", add_one.__qualname__ == add_hundred.__qualname__, add_one.__qualname__)


@triton.jit
def kernel(X, O, BLOCK: tl.constexpr):
    offs = tl.arange(0, BLOCK)
    x = tl.load(X + offs)
    tl.store(O + offs, add_one(x))
    tl.store(O + BLOCK + offs, add_hundred(x))


@triton.jit
def control(X, O, BLOCK: tl.constexpr):  # only the second helper
    offs = tl.arange(0, BLOCK)
    tl.store(O + offs, add_hundred(tl.load(X + offs)))


x = torch.zeros(16, device="cuda")
o = torch.zeros(32, device="cuda")
control[(1, )](x, o, 16)
print("control, add_hundred alone:", o[0].item(), "(expected 100.0)")
o.zero_()
kernel[(1, )](x, o, 16)
print("kernel, add_one / add_hundred:", o[0].item(), o[16].item(), "(expected 1.0 100.0)")
bad = o[0].item() != 1.0 or o[16].item() != 100.0
print("BUG REPRODUCED" if bad else "no bug")
sys.exit(1 if bad else 0)
```

Observed on main @6fe3348e6 (exit code 1):
```
triton 3.9.0 .../python/triton/__init__.py
same qualname: True make_add.<locals>.add_c
control, add_hundred alone: 100.0 (expected 100.0)
kernel, add_one / add_hundred: 1.0 1.0 (expected 1.0 100.0)
BUG REPRODUCED
```
Expected: `1.0 100.0` for the kernel; the control prints 100.0 on main and with the change, and with the change the kernel prints `1.0 100.0` and `no bug` (exit code 0).
</details>

**Where the name is reused.** `mangle_fn` builds the name from `get_full_name(fn)`, which is `f"{fn.__module__}.{fn.__qualname__}"` ([code_generator.py#L32-L41](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/6fe3348e6e907584e07e593ab19a35caee95c37a/python/triton/compiler/code_generator.py#L32-L41), [jit.py#L468-L469](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/6fe3348e6e907584e07e593ab19a35caee95c37a/python/triton/runtime/jit.py#L468-L469)), plus the mangled argument types. `call_JitFunction` then generates the body only `if not self.module.has_function(fn_name)` and otherwise takes the return type from `self.function_ret_types[fn_name]` ([code_generator.py#L1446-L1484](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/6fe3348e6e907584e07e593ab19a35caee95c37a/python/triton/compiler/code_generator.py#L1446-L1484)). Nothing in that path looks at which `JITFunction` the name was first generated for. A constexpr argument that is a `JITFunction` is mangled by its `repr`, `JITFunction(module:qualname)` ([core.py#L207-L212](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/6fe3348e6e907584e07e593ab19a35caee95c37a/python/triton/language/core.py#L207-L212)), which is the same string for every factory product.

**When it triggers.** One kernel compilation calls two or more distinct `JITFunction` objects with the same `__module__` and `__qualname__` and the same argument types. Measured on an L40S, one fresh cache directory per row, with `x = arange(16)`; each cell is the output at index 1 of the calls in order, so helpers that add 1 and 100 should give `[2.0, 101.0]`:

| the kernel calls | main @6fe3348e6 |
|---|---|
| `add_one(x)` and `add_hundred(x)` from one factory (as in the reproducer) | `[2.0, 2.0]` instead of `[2.0, 101.0]` |
| two helpers whose closures hold differen

items.title: [TritonGPU] fuse-nested-loops computes the fused trip count as ceildivsi(ub - lb, step) in the i32 IV type; `ub - lb` overflows and the flattened loop runs 0
items.author: wildoranges
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

With `tl.range(..., flatten=True)`, `tritongpu-fuse-nested-loops` computes the outer trip count as `ceildivsi(ub - lb, step)` in the loop's IV type:
https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/2122e24efc1886bfa36337c1f5b07c47d827b1d4/lib/Dialect/TritonGPU/Transforms/FuseNestedLoops.cpp#L285-L293

The pass's own comment promises a wider type: "Use an integer bitwidth twice the size of the largest integer, up to 64 bits, to avoid overflow". The code only takes the maximum of the IV widths, though:
https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/2122e24efc1886bfa36337c1f5b07c47d827b1d4/lib/Dialect/TritonGPU/Transforms/FuseNestedLoops.cpp#L558-L569

For a valid i32 loop whose `ub - lb` exceeds `INT32_MAX`, the subtraction wraps, the computed trip count is negative or zero, and the fused loop does not run at all.

`fuse_tripcount.py`:
```python
# tritongpu-fuse-nested-loops computes the outer trip count as ceildivsi(ub - lb, step) in the i32
# induction-variable type; ub - lb overflows although the loop itself never overflows.
import torch, triton, triton.language as tl

@triton.jit
def kernel(out_ptr, LB, UB, STEP, N_INNER, FLATTEN: tl.constexpr):
    acc = 0
    for i in tl.range(LB, UB, STEP, flatten=FLATTEN):
        for j in range(0, N_INNER):
            acc += 1
    tl.store(out_ptr, acc)

LB, UB, STEP, N_INNER = -2**31 + 5, 2**30, 2**29, 3    # iv: -2147483643, ..., 5, 536870917 (6 iterations)
for flatten in [False, True]:
    out = torch.zeros(1, dtype=torch.int32, device="cuda")
    kernel[(1,)](out, LB, UB, STEP, N_INNER, flatten)
    print(f"flatten={flatten}: acc={out.item()} expected={len(range(LB, UB, STEP)) * N_INNER}")
```

```console
$ python fuse_tripcount.py
flatten=False: acc=18 expected=18
flatten=True: acc=0 expected=18
$ TRITON_INTERPRET=1 python fuse_tripcount.py
flatten=False: acc=18 expected=18
flatten=True: acc=18 expected=18
```

The outer loop runs 6 times, over IVs -2147483643 … 536870917, and none of them overflows. `ub - lb = 2^30 - (-2^31 + 5)` does not fit in i32.

A possible fix: compute the lengths in a type twice as wide as the IV, as the comment says (i64 for i32 IVs), or use `(ub - lb)` with overflow-aware unsigned arithmetic when `step > 0`.

### Environment details

- Triton: main @ 2122e24efc1886bfa36337c1f5b07c47d827b1d4 (2026-10-16), built from source (`pip install -e .`), Python 3.12
- PyTorch 2.11.0+cu128
- GPU: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090 (sm_86), driver 595.80, Linux x86_64
score_reasons: 匹配 Kernel 与正确性

items.title: [RFC]: A Reusable KV Compression Layer for Transfer and Storage
items.author: Zedong-Liu
items.body_excerpt:
### Motivation.

**Reference baseline:** vLLM v0.32.0

We propose an optional, reusable KV compression capability in vLLM for KV transfer and storage. KVServe (SIGCOMM 2026) manages the compression workflow, including pluggable algorithm composition, profile selection, and encoding/decoding. Mooncake P/D transfer is the first integration. The initial upstream implementation uses fixed compression profiles; adaptive selection and optimized backends follow through the same abstraction. 

## 1. Why This Capability Is Needed

Disaggregated serving makes KV cache a payload that moves between workers and can be stored remotely for reuse. Longer contexts increase the amount of state to move, while faster prefill can generate KV faster than a deployment's network can drain it. Transfer and restore costs can therefore limit the benefits of separating compute or reusing cached prefixes.

The KVServe paper measures communication at **16%–60% of job completion time** in its Llama-3.1/Qasper P/D experiments over 10–50 Gb/s links. [KVServe, §2.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2605.13734v1#S2.SS1) *Prefill-as-a-Service* reports KV production rates of **59.93 Gb/s for MiniMax-M2.5** and **8.25 Gb/s for Qwen3.5-397B** at 32K tokens on 8×H200. Hybrid attention reduces bandwidth demand, but KV movement remains a systems concern. [Prefill-as-a-Service, Table 3](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.15039v2#S2.T3)

Compression can reduce the cost of these boundaries, but its benefit depends on encoding overhead, bandwidth, and quality requirements. A reusable capability lets backends consume suitable representations while algorithms and selection policies evolve independently.

### Proposed Change.

## 2. Proposed Abstraction and Initial Scope

The **target architecture** has three parts:

- **Algorithm library:** KVServe manages a library that already supports KIVI, CacheGen, MixHQ, and further combinations of transformation, quantization, and lossless coding. Different providers can supply algorithm implementations through this framework.
- **Runtime policy:** select an algorithm or profile according to KV volume, effective bandwidth, compression overhead, and latency/quality budgets, with raw transfer available when compression is not beneficial. Static profiles are currently the primary mode; dynamic selection is a beta option.
- **Representation contract:** encode KV into payloads with codec-owned reconstruction metadata, and decode them into a destination KV view. Metadata is opaque to the transport. The connector retains cache mapping, request coordination, and lifecycle responsibilities.

vLLM owns the reusable integration contract. **KVServe manages the compression workflow and runtime policy, while pluggable providers supply algorithm-specific implementations behind the common interface.**  Mooncake continues to supply the transport, preserving vLLM's scheduling and cache ownership. This boundary avoids coupling the connector to one algorithm or requiring users of the original path to install compression dependencies.

The **initial upstream implementation** is deliberately bounded: the reusable contract, minimal workspace support, and fixed-profile Mooncake P/D integration. Adaptive selection and optimized backends are the second stage. The capability could later extend to Mooncake Store, encoding KV before storage and decoding it on retrieval; storage policy and persistence requirements would be addressed separately.

## 3. Evidence from Mooncake Integration

We have implemented a Mooncake P/D prototype based on vLLM v0.30.0. KV is compressed before Mooncake transfers it and restored into the decode worker's cache before generation proceeds. The integration code and tests are in the [`kvsfuse-vllm0.30.0` directory](https://github.com/hpdps-group/KVServe/tree/ead92f4abd196543207bc0bd8586a44bc97067b4/kvsfuse-vllm0.30.0).

Cross-host tests use **200 Gb/s inter-node links**, LongBench HotpotQA, 200 requests per configuration, and `max_tokens=32`. Two full-attention models demonstrate performance benefits:

- **Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, TP2:** mean TTFT decreases from 1.85 s to 1.32 s at concurrency 1, with **1.40× faster batch completion**. At concurrency 8, mean TTFT decreases from 7.27 s to 6.18 s.
- **Qwen3-30B-A3B, TP4:** mean TTFT decreases by **19.2%–19.7%** at concurrency 1/8/16, averaged over three repeats.

**Qwen3.8-27B** demonstrates hybrid-model support: tested raw and compressed configurations complete 200/200 requests at TP2 and TP4. We use this result as compatibility evidence, without claiming acceleration for the hybrid model.

Separate Llama-3.1 quality measurements show a **2.36 percentage-point** HotpotQA score reduction, with higher compressed scores on GSM8K and Qasper. These results establish feasibility and illustrate profile-dependent tradeoffs. They evaluate fixed profiles and do not validate beta dynamic selection in Mooncake. Full measurements and implementation-specific validation belong in the accompanying design note and subsequent PR review.



### Feedback Period.

1–2 weeks

### CC List.

@dtcccc @LCAIZJ @ivanium @NickLucche @ApostaC @stmatengss 
This proposal is related to the Mooncake P/D roadmap (#36948) and Mooncake Store roadmap (#45036); feedback from KV Connector and Mooncake maintainers would be especially helpful.

### Any Other Things.

## 4. Requested Maintainer Decisions

We seek agreement on the integration boundary and initial scope before submitting implementation PRs. Our plan has two stages: **PR 1** introduces the reusable interface, minimal workspace support, and Mooncake fixed-profile integration; **PR 2** adds adaptive selection and optimized backends. Detailed APIs, protocol changes, and validation will be reviewed with those patches.

The first stage will preserve the original disabled-compression path and include its regression tests. Additional connectors, persistent storage, and offline profiling tooling are outside that stage. The intended outcome is a small c

items.title: Eval bug: SYCL F16: NaN output on dense Qwen3.8-27B Q4_K_M since #29107 (IQ3 code reorder); fused GEMM off fixes it (Arc Pro B70)
items.author: killercatfish
items.body_excerpt:
### Name and Version
llama.cpp b11755 (704366d), built with IntelLLVM 2026.1.0, `-DGGML_SYCL=ON -DGGML_SYCL_F16=ON -DGGML_SYCL_DNN=OFF`

### Operating systems
Linux (Ubuntu 26.04, kernel 7.0.0-38, xe driver)

### GGML backends
SYCL

### Hardware
Intel Arc Pro B70 (BMG-G31, 32 GB), Ryzen 5 7600X. Compute runtime 26.22.38646.6, IGC 2.36.3, Level Zero 1.28.6.

### Models
unsloth Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q4_K_M.gguf (dense, hybrid Gated DeltaNet; weights Q4_K/Q5_K/Q6_K)

### Problem description & steps to reproduce
With `GGML_SYCL_F16=ON` (or `GGML_SYCL_DYNAMIC_PRECISION=F16/BF16`), every answer is one odd token followed by
`!!!!...` (token 0, i.e. NaN logits), at any prompt length, even 124 tokens. Turning off only the XMX fused
dequant-GEMM (`GGML_SYCL_XMX_GATHER_TYPES=0`) gives correct output. Bisected to #29107 (see Regression).

```
ONEAPI_DEVICE_SELECTOR=level_zero:0 ./llama-server -m Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q4_K_M.gguf -ngl 99 -fa on -sm none -c 32768 --jinja
# greedy, thinking off: ask it to repeat a code planted in the prompt
```

| Build / env | Output | Prompt tok/s (2K) |
|---|---|---|
| `GGML_SYCL_F16=OFF` (default) | correct to 14K tokens | ~270 |
| `GGML_SYCL_F16=ON` | `!!!!` garbage, every length | ~640 |
| F16=OFF + `GGML_SYCL_DYNAMIC_PRECISION=F16` | garbage | ~290 |
| F16=OFF + `GGML_SYCL_DYNAMIC_PRECISION=BF16` | garbage (so not f16 overflow) | ~290 |
| F16=ON + `GGML_SYCL_XMX_GATHER_TYPES=0` | **correct** | ~540-700 |
| F16=ON + `GGML_SYCL_DYNAMIC_PRECISION=F32` | correct | ~257 |

Also tried, no change: compute runtime 26.18.38308.1 + IGC 2.34.4 (the `.devops/intel.Dockerfile` pin), flash
attention off. `test-backend-ops -o MUL_MAT` passes 2273/2273 on the same build, so the test shapes don't reach this
path (they're small; the failing GEMMs here are K=5120, M up to 248320).

**Regression:** same model, same flags, `-DGGML_SYCL_F16=ON`, each tag built fresh:
| tag | result |
|---|---|
| b11491, b11493 (#29245 adds `fused-gemm.cpp`), b11497, b11540, b11565 | correct |
| **b11635** (parent of 529ac893) | **correct** |
| **b11636** (= 529ac893, #29107 "sycl: IQ3 code reorder") | **`!!!!` garbage** |
| b11684, b11685, b11755 | garbage |

#29107 adds "reorder-aware dequantization for subsequent prefill operations" and touches the mul_mat dispatch in
`ggml-sycl.cpp`. Our guess, not verified in the code: after it, the fused GEMM (#29245) reads Q4_K weights in the
reordered layout as if they were plain (or the reverse). Masking out only Q5_K or only Q6_K
(`GGML_SYCL_XMX_GATHER_TYPES`) still gave garbage; masking out only Q4_K was inconclusive (one run, which hit an
unrelated GPU fault on our chipset-slot card before answering).
Workaround until fixed: `GGML_SYCL_XMX_GATHER_TYPES=0`, or `GGML_SYCL_ENABLE_OPT=0` (untested by us).

### First Bad Commit
529ac893 (#29107)

### Relevant log output
No error is printed; the server returns 200 with the garbage text.

_Measured on our own hardware; the investigation and this write-up were done with Claude Code (Anthropic)._

items.author: FaizJamal06
items.body_excerpt:
### Name and Version

.\llama-cli.exe --version
version: 0.7.0-dev (build 11809, commit 0b1281aee)
built with Clang 20.1.8 for Windows x86_64

Prebuilt Vulkan release: llama-b11809-bin-win-vulkan-x64.zip

### Operating systems

Windows

### GGML backends

Vulkan

### Hardware

Intel Core i7-11390H (4C/8T) + Intel Iris Xe Graphics (integrated, uma: 1; Vulkan reports 8061 MiB total / 7402 MiB free), 16 GB DDR4-3200
GPU driver: Intel 32.0.101.7077
OS: Windows 11 Home 26H2 (OS build 26300.9711)

### Models

Flint UD-IQ2_XXS (11.04 GiB): https://huggingface.co/unsloth/flint-GGUF/blob/main/flint-UD-IQ2_XXS.gguf
Control model that works on Vulkan: https://huggingface.co/ggml-org/gemma-3-1b-it-GGUF (Q4_K_M)

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

I tried running the Flint 2-bit version UD-IQ2_XXS on my laptop that's got 16GB RAM and integrated graphics. I tried adding compute using the GPU via Vulkan (integrated), but it kept crashing with ErrorOutOfDeviceMemory. I expected the model to load, since the same model loads on the CPU and works fine in the CPU build. The GPU showed it had 7.4 GB free, yet it couldn't handle a few hundred MB (failed allocations: 333,310,976 / 580,712,448 / 830,476,288 bytes). Next I tried using 0 layers on the GPU, it crashed. Then I reduced the batch to -ub 128, it crashed. I noticed #30888 had some fix, tried that setting (`GGML_VK_DISABLE_HOST_VISIBLE_VIDMEM=1`), it did not work. Used llama-completion, that crashed too. Then I tried a tiny model, Gemma 1B (ggml-org/gemma-3-1b-it-GGUF Q4_K_M), using Vulkan: it works, even fully on the GPU (-ngl 99). It fails with Flint, so there's a problem with Vulkan and Flint. I kept getting the "failed to allocate pinned memory" message in the terminal (only in the llama-completion runs). The model runs on the CPU at 8.5 t/s (llama-bench, 8 threads). I can't figure out why Flint is not working with Vulkan on the GPU. It might be the new Flint architecture, or an 11GB model on 16GB RAM might be too much.

I rebooted and tried it, yet it failed the same way (580,712,448 byte allocation).

Related: #30251 – same failure with the log "failed to allocate compute pp buffers", also "failed to allocate pinned memory", but theirs was AMD integrated and mine is Intel Iris Xe. A restart fixes the issue for them but not for me, but Gemma 1B works well.
#30888 – had the same ErrorOutOfDeviceMemory, but they had a dedicated AMD graphics card, and changing the setting to GGML_VK_DISABLE_HOST_VISIBLE_VIDMEM=1 was given as the fix. The fix did not work for me.

Steps to reproduce (Vulkan build b11809, Windows, fresh boot, no env vars set):

```
llama-completion.exe -m flint-UD-IQ2_XXS.gguf -ngl 0 -fit off -c 4096 -p "Hello" -n 16

items.title: Eval bug: minimax-m3: build_moe_ffn() drops the per-expert NVFP4 scale → garbled output (M3.1 Flash)
items.author: MOUNTAIN0724
items.body_excerpt:
### Name and Version

$ ./llama-server --version
version: 0.7.0-dev (build 1, commit f64a498)
built with GNU 15.2.0 for Linux x86_64

Built from master commit f64a498 (2026-10-23):
  cmake -B build-cuda -DGGML_CUDA=ON -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=120a
  cmake --build build-cuda -j16
The offending build_moe_ffn() call is unchanged in 9145ddb (current master).

### Operating systems

Linux

### GGML backends

CUDA

### Hardware

AMD Ryzen 7 9700X (16 threads, AVX-512 / AVX512_BF16 / AVX512_VNNI) +
NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090 32 GB (sm_120a, driver 595.99.02, CUDA 13.3), 128 GB RAM

### Models

MiniMax M3.1 Flash (MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M3.1-Flash) — 428B total / 23B active MoE.

No public GGUF exists yet (model released 4 days ago), so it was converted locally with this
repo's convert_hf_to_gguf.py into a mixed bf16/NVFP4 GGUF (242 GiB) and then requantized to
Q2_K (146 GiB, 2.93 BPW) with llama-imatrix + llama-quantize. Both variants show the same bug.

Architecture: 60 layers (3 leading dense), 128 routed experts top-4 + 1 shared,
NVFP4 routed experts + MXFP8 dense, sigmoid gating + e_score_correction_bias, swigluoai,
partial rotary (64 of 128 dims), MSA on all layers.

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

The model loads completely cleanly — check_tensor_dims passes, done_getting_tensors passes
(1359 tensors), no NaN warnings — but produces pure token soup on every prompt. Same garbage for:

- mixed bf16/NVFP4 GGUF and Q2_K requantized GGUF
- MSA attention (-fa on) and dense fallback (-fa off)
- -cmoe and full CPU

Reproduce:

```bash
./llama-server -m m31f-q2_k.gguf -cmoe -c 4096 \
    --cache-type-k q8_0 --cache-type-v q8_0 -t 16 --jinja

curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8090/v1/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"prompt":"The capital of France is","max_tokens":16,"temperature":0}'
```

Output: 'TBhyd saturation Licensed估 PRESSYCAVAicator必须要PCMpledPRAbeen LamLEEsx barrCLRiq'

Root cause: src/models/minimax-m3.cpp calls build_moe_ffn() without the three per-expert
scale arguments:

```cpp
    ggml_tensor * moe_out = build_moe_ffn(cur,
            model.layers[il].ffn_gate_inp,
            model.layers[il].ffn_up_exps,
            model.layers[il].ffn_gate_exps,
            model.layers[il].ffn_down_exps,
            model.layers[il].ffn_exp_probs_b,
            n_expert, n_expert_used,
            LLM_FFN_SWIGLU_OAI_MOE, hparams.expert_weights_norm,
            hparams.expert_weights_scale,
            (llama_expert_gating_func_type) hparams.expert_gating_func,
            il);                  // <-- stops here
```

build_moe_ffn() declares them with defaults (src/llama-graph.h:1177):

```cpp
    ggml_tensor * up_exps_s   = nullptr,
    ggml_tensor * gate_exps_s = nullptr,
    ggml_tensor * down_exps_s = nullptr,
```

so build_lora_mm_id() never enters its `if (w_s)` branch and
`blk.N.ffn_{gate,up,down}_exps.scale` (the per-expert NVFP4 scale2) is never applied. The
tensors *are* loaded — llama-model.cpp's generic scale pass creates
layer.ffn_{gate,down,up}_exps_s with TENSOR_NOT_REQUIRED — they are simply never forwarded
to the graph. With NVFP4 the GGUF payload is `q * block_scale` while the converter keeps
`1/global_scale` in .scale, so the expert weights come out global_scale times too large
(measured G ≈ 15123 for M3.1) and the MoE branch swamps the residual.

How I narrowed it down:

1. Verified every converted tensor against the official safetensors (token_embd, lm_head,
   MXFP8 attn_q/attn_output, NVFP4 routed experts after applying .scale, Gemma norms, dense
   FFN, shared experts) — all cos = 1.000000, so conversion/quantization is not at fault.
2. Built a 3-layer dense-only model with
   `llama-quantize --prune-layers 3,4,...,59 --allow-requantize`; its top-8 logits match a
   straight Python re-implementation of
   transformers/models/minimax_m3_vl/modeling_minimax_m3_vl.py exactly (identical token
   order, logprob offset is just the log-softmax constant). Dense layers, attention, rope,
   Gemma-norm and swigluoai are correct.
3. A 4-layer model (3 dense + 1 MoE) diverges completely: llama.cpp
   'unique','arts','roach',' fis' vs reference 'ウ','£','ย','ก','ふ'.
4. Zeroing only layer 3's FFN output with a temporary ggml_scale(cur, 0.0f) hook restores the
   3-layer logits; zeroing its attention output does not. The fault is in the MoE branch, not
   in attention/MSA/rope.

Fix:

```cpp
                    il,
                    /* probs_in     */ nullptr,
                    /* gate_up_exps */ nullptr,
                    /* up_exps_s    */ model.layers[il].ffn_up_exps_s,
                    /* gate_exps_s  */ model.layers[il].ffn_gate_exps_s,
                    /* down_exps_s  */ model.layers[il].ffn_down_exps_s);
```

After this the 4-layer model matches the Python reference exactly and the full 60-layer Q2_K
model answers coherently (traditional-Chinese explanation of quantum entanglement; Python
Fibonacci function with complexity notes), prefill 3.59 / decode 5.12 t/s.

Non-NVFP4 minimax-m3 models are unaffected: ffn_*_exps_s is nullptr there, so if (w_s) is
skipped exactly as before.

Happy to send a PR for this.

---

Separately, same model: M3.1's checkpoint carries indexer.{q,k}_proj + indexer.{q,k}_norm
on every layer including the three leading dense ones, but load_arch_tensors() only
creates them inside the i >= n_layer_dense_lead branch, so a GGUF from the official
checkpoint aborts at load with:

```text
done_getting_tensors: wrong number of tensors; expected 1359, got 1347
```

(difference = 3 dense layers × 4 tensors). Either create the indexer tensors for all layers
(dense layers never read them in the graph) or drop them in the converter for dense layers —
whichever you prefer, and I'll send that as a separate PR.

### First Bad Commit

Not a regression — there is no first bad commit to bisect. M3 support landed in #24908 and build_moe_ffn() was called without the per-expert scale arguments from the start. It becomes visible only for models w

items.title: Eval bug: SYCL: XMX-ESIMD path makes MoE prompt processing ~35% slower on Arc Pro B70
items.author: thomasmcrowe
items.body_excerpt:
# SYCL: XMX-ESIMD path is ~35% slower for MoE prompt processing on Arc Pro B70 (regression in `d81d0d8fb`)

## Summary

On an Intel Arc Pro B70 (Battlemage), the SYCL backend regressed prompt processing by
**28–35%** between `339f3242c` (build 11783) and `edc353842` (build 11851) for a `qwen35moe`
MoE model (Ornith-1.5-35B-A3B Q5_K_M, 256K ctx). Decode is unchanged.

The regression is fully attributable to the XMX-ESIMD path: running the **same** `edc353842`
binary with `GGML_SYCL_ENABLE_XMX_ESIMD=0` restores the old numbers exactly (1,749 vs 1,131
t/s at 32K prompt, 1,597 vs 1,053 at 64K). The suspected commit is
`d81d0d8fb95e52a66992bcfc212b1891b4d2f94a` ("Multi-column on Intel XMX matrix engines
refactored", #29864), which is the only commit in the range that changes these kernels.

MoE inference is hit hard because expert routing leaves only a handful of tokens per expert
even during prefill, so the multi-column (2–80 columns) path that was written for
speculative-decoding verification also handles most of prompt processing.

## Environment

| | |
|---|---|
| GPU | Intel(R) Arc(TM) Pro B70 Graphics, 32 GB (Xe2 / Battlemage), Level-Zero 1.17.39758, driver 26.35.39758 |
| CPU / OS | i7-14700K, Arch Linux, kernel 7.2.11-arch1-1 |
| oneAPI | 2026.0 (IntelLLVM 2026.0.0), oneDNN 3.11, MKL 2026.0, TBB 2023.0 |
| Build | `-DGGML_SYCL=ON -DGGML_SYCL_F16=ON -DMKL_LINK=dynamic -DMKL_SYCL_LINK=dynamic`, `icx`/`icpx` |
| Old build | `0.7.0-dev (build 11783, commit 339f3242c)` |
| New build | `0.7.0-dev (build 11851, commit edc353842)` |

Both binaries link `libdnnl.so.3` and `libmkl_sycl_blas.so.6` (verified with `ldd`); the local
tree only carries a dormant patch that replaces two `GGML_ABORT`s in the device-memory query
with a 30 GiB fallback, and it never fires on this box (the real query succeeds).

## Model and flags

`Ornith-1.5-35B-A3B Q5_K_M` (`qwen35moe`, 24 GB, 256 experts, ~3B active/token), served by
`llama-server` with:

```
--gpu-layers 999 --fit off --ctx-size 262144
--flash-attn on --batch-size 2048 --ubatch-size 2048
--cache-type-k q8_0 --cache-type-v q8_0
--parallel 1 --cont-batching --metrics
--spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-n-max 3
--cache-ram 24576
```

Single slot, one request at a time, nothing else on the GPU. Env:
`UR_L0_ENABLE_RELAXED_ALLOCATION_LIMITS=0`, `SYCL_PI_LEVEL_ZERO_USE_IMMEDIATE_COMMANDLISTS=1`,
`ZES_ENABLE_SYSMAN=1`.

## Measurements

Method: `POST /completion` with `"cache_prompt": false` and `"n_predict": 64`, one prompt per
size, reading `timings.prompt_per_second` and `timings.predicted_per_second`. Prompt sizes are
the tokenized lengths. The 32K point is measured twice; within-run repeatability is ~0.3% on
prefill and ~2% on decode.

### Cross-build curve (same box, same flags, same day)

| prompt tokens | prefill b11783 | prefill b11851 | delta | decode b11783 | decode b11851 |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1,055 | 558.5 | 564.3 | +1.0% | 55.77 | 69.94 |
| 8,223 | 1,666.0 | 1,116.7 | **-33.0%** | 66.41 | 63.40 |
| 32,799 | 1,752.0 | 1,130.6 | **-35.5%** | 52.37 | 53.45 |
| 65,567 | 1,597.0 | 1,050.6 | **-34.2%** | 46.85 | 47.19 |
| 131,103 | 1,375.7 | 950.0 | **-30.9%** | 36.29 | 36.45 |
| 193,567 | 1,218.6 | 871.8 | **-28.4%** | 36.46 | 32.91 |
| 32,799 (repeat) | 1,746.5 | 1,129.9 | **-35.3%** | 51.25 | 60.99 |

A rollback control (same b11783 binary, new process) reproduced 1,749.2 / 1,596.8 t/s at
32K / 64K, so the gap is not drift between runs.

### Same-binary isolation (`edc353842`, only the env var differs)

| flag | 32K prefill | 64K prefill | 32K decode |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `GGML_SYCL_ENABLE_XMX_ESIMD=1` (default) | 1,131.3 | 1,052.6 | 56.9 |
| `GGML_SYCL_ENABLE_XMX_ESIMD=0` | **1,748.9** | **1,597.3** | 58.1 |

Both runs report `0.7.0-dev (build 11851, commit edc353842)`; the flag was confirmed in
`/proc/<pid>/environ` at run time. The `=0` numbers are within 0.1% of the b11783 build.

## Reproduction

```bash
GGML_SYCL_ENABLE_XMX_ESIMD=1 llama-server -m model.gguf --gpu-layers 999 \
  --ctx-size 262144 --batch-size 2048 --ubatch-size 2048 \
  --flash-attn on --cache-type-k q8_0 --cache-type-v q8_0 --parallel 1 --metrics
# prompt 32799 tokens, cache_prompt=false  -> ~1,130 t/s

GGML_SYCL_ENABLE_XMX_ESIMD=0 llama-server ...   # same everything else
# prompt 32799 tokens, cache_prompt=false  -> ~1,749 t/s
```

## Analysis / hypothesis

`GGML_SYCL_ENABLE_XMX_ESIMD` gates `ggml_sycl_xmx_enabled()`, which is consumed by:

- `mmvq.cpp` — `ggml_sycl_mul_mat_vec_q_xmx_type()` (multi-column mmvq, 2..`GGML_SYCL_XMX_MAX_COLS`=80
  columns, plus the single-column Q2_K/Q3_K/Q8_0 case) and `ggml_sycl_mul_mat_vec_q_glu_xmx()`;
- `ggml-sycl.cpp` — `can_use_xmx_batch()`, which extends `can_use_mul_mat_vec_q()` past
  `MMVQ_MAX_BATCH_SIZE`.

None of those obviously matches a 2,048-token prefill batch, which is why I suspect the MoE
expert dispatch: after routing, each expert sees only a few tokens (roughly 2048/256 ≈ 8 on
average), which lands squarely in the 2–80 column range these kernels target. If that is the
case, the multi-column kernels are not just a spec-decode optimization for MoE models — they
sit on the prompt-processing hot path.

I have not profiled the kernels, so I cannot say whether the loss is occupancy, the reorder
layout, the 64-byte-alignment fallbacks, or the short-row variant; the numbers are stable and
reproducible either way.

## What I am asking

1. Is prompt processing on MoE models expected to route through the multi-column XMX path?
   If yes, this is a real regression for MoE prefill, not just a spec-decode trade-off.
2. Is there a supported way to keep the decode gain while avoiding the prefill loss — e.g. a
   shape/column-range gate (`GGML_SYCL_XMX_MAX_COLS`, `GGML_SYCL_XMX_GATHER_SHAPES`), or should
   the dispatch avoid this path for large `src1->ne[1]`?
3. Happy to test patches or run `GGML_SYCL_DEBUG=1` with per-op timing if that helps.

For now the machine stays on `339f3242c`; `edc353842` is parked and the worka

items.title: [RFC]: TENT-Native UB/URMA Transport
items.author: zchuango
items.body_excerpt:
### Changes proposed

## Summary

This RFC proposes adding a **TENT-native UB transport** backed by the openEuler UMDK URMA APIs.

The goal is to make UB a first-class TENT transport whose runtime-facing interfaces and architectural responsibilities are aligned with the existing TENT RDMA transport.

The intended data path is:

```text
TENT Request
    → UbTask / UbSlice
    → TENT UB Workers
    → UbContext / UbEndpoint / UbJfc
    → URMA Adapter
    → liburma
```

TENT owns task scheduling, slicing, endpoint lifecycle, telemetry, cancellation, and failure recovery. The URMA adapter is limited to native resource management and URMA API translation.

The initial hardware scope is **host DRAM-to-DRAM transfer**. Additional memory types should be enabled only after their registration, topology, and access semantics have been validated.

---

## Related Work

UB/URMA support was previously introduced for the classic Mooncake Transfer Engine in #1773, #1805, and #1855. That work established the underlying URMA device, memory-registration, endpoint, build, mock, and testing capabilities.

This RFC builds on that foundation but focuses on a different architectural scope: implementing UB as a TENT-native transport with TENT-owned tasks, slices, workers, endpoint lifecycle, scheduling signals, cancellation, and failure recovery.

---

## Motivation

TENT provides transport-independent runtime capabilities such as:

- transport selection;
  
- task and slice lifecycle management;
  
- admission control and priority scheduling;
  
- cancellation;
  
- receiver-side credits;
  
- runtime bandwidth estimation;
  
- path failover and health monitoring.
  

To participate fully in this model, UB should expose the same logical capabilities as TENT RDMA.

A native implementation allows the TENT scheduler to observe UB runtime information such as:

- UB device availability;
  
- Jetty and remote-path health;
  
- JFC completion pressure;
  
- outstanding requests and inflight bytes;
  
- estimated bandwidth;
  
- endpoint generations;
  
- timeout and error statistics.
  

---

## Proposed Architecture

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    APP[Application / Store] --> RT[TENT Runtime]

    RT --> AQ[Admission Queue]
    AQ --> TS[Transport Selector]
    TS --> RC[Receiver Credit Gate]

    RC --> UB[UbTransport]
    UB --> WK[UbTask / UbSlice / Workers]

    WK --> PS[Device and Path Selection]
    PS --> CTX[UbContext]
    PS --> ES[EndpointStore]

    ES --> EP[UbEndpoint]
    CTX --> JFC[UbJfc]

    CTX --> UA[URMA Adapter]
    EP --> UA
    JFC --> UA
    UA --> LIB[liburma / UMDK]

    JFC --> TM[Telemetry and Health]
    TM --> WK
    TM --> AQ
```

The main architectural boundary is:

> TENT owns scheduling and policy. The URMA adapter owns only native URMA operations and resource lifetime.

---

## Alignment with TENT RDMA

The UB implementation should follow the same logical decomposition and public semantics as TENT RDMA.

| TENT RDMA | Proposed TENT UB |
| --- | --- |
| `RdmaTransport` | `UbTransport` |
| `RdmaSubBatch` | `UbSubBatch` |
| `RdmaTask` | `UbTask` |
| `RdmaSlice` | `UbSlice` |
| `RdmaContext` | `UbContext` |
| `RdmaCQ` | `UbJfc` |
| `RdmaEndPoint` | `UbEndpoint` |
| QP  | Jetty |
| CQ  | JFC |
| MR  | URMA target segment |
| GID | EID |
| `ibv_post_send()` | `urma_post_jetty_send_wr()` |
| `ibv_poll_cq()` | `urma_poll_jfc()` |

The TENT-facing interfaces and state semantics should remain consistent, while native URMA terminology should be preserved inside the transport.

---

## TENT Transport Interface

`UbTransport` should directly implement the common TENT transport operations:

```text
install()
uninstall()

allocateSubBatch()
freeSubBatch()

submitTransferTasks()
getTransferStatus()

addMemoryBuffer()
removeMemoryBuffer()

getEstimatedBandwidth()

supportsCancellation()
cancelTransferTask()
```

Notification support may remain disabled initially until a native UB notification path is implemented.

TENT runtime code should not directly depend on URMA handles such as:

```text
urma_jetty_t
urma_jfc_t
urma_target_seg_t
```

---

## Proposed File Layout

```text
mooncake-transfer-engine/tent/
├── include/tent/transport/ub/
│   ├── ub_transport.h
│   ├── context.h
│   ├── jfc.h
│   ├── endpoint.h
│   ├── endpoint_store.h
│   ├── slice.h
│   ├── workers.h
│   ├── buffers.h
│   ├── rail_monitor.h
│   ├── quota.h
│   ├── params.h
│   └── urma_adapter.h
│
└── src/transport/ub/
    ├── CMakeLists.txt
    ├── ub_transport.cpp
    ├── context.cpp
    ├── jfc.cpp
    ├── endpoint.cpp
    ├── endpoint_store.cpp
    ├── workers.cpp
    ├── buffers.cpp
    ├── rail_monitor.cpp
    ├── quota.cpp
    └── urma_adapter.cpp
```

The first implementation does not need to complete every optional scheduling feature, but the module boundaries should support later extensions without redesigning the data path.

---

## URMA Adapter Boundary

The URMA adapter should only expose low-level operations:

- URMA initialization and shutdown;
  
- device and EID discovery;
  
- context creation and destruction;
  
- asynchronous event FD exposure;
  
- local segment registration;
  
- remote segment import;
  
- JFC/JFCE creation and polling;
  
- Jetty creation, import, bind, reset, quiesce, and destruction;
  
- READ/WRITE work-request submission.
  

It should not contain:

- TENT task scheduling;
  
- slice spraying;
  
- receiver-credit policy;
  
- transport selection;
  
- retry policy;
  
- admission control;
  
- rail-health decisions.
  

Full URMA asynchronous-event consumption and acknowledgement may be added later if required by the provider and recovery model.

---

## Endpoint Lifecycle

At the conceptual level, UB endpoints should follow the same forward-only lifecycle semantics as TENT RDMA:

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> UNINIT
    UNINIT --> HANDSHAKING
    HANDSHAKING --> READY
    HANDSHAKING --> DESTROYING
    READY --> DESTROYING
    DESTROYING --> DESTROYED
    DESTROYED --> [*]
```

items.title: [RFC]: Unify Mooncake's Python package, build, and release architecture
items.author: Aionw
items.body_excerpt:
### Changes proposed

## Summary

Establish `python/mooncake` as the single source of truth for all tracked Python code distributed as the `mooncake` import package.

Use `scikit-build-core` as the single PEP 517 build backend. It will combine tracked Python sources with native artifacts supplied through explicit CMake install rules, without copying generated files into the source tree.

Use `cibuildwheel` as the standard release-wheel execution layer for supported manylinux variants. Hardware-specific builders may retain specialized runners and toolchains, but must consume the same PEP 517 backend and produce the same validated artifact contract.

This RFC also defines:

- subsystem-oriented Python module boundaries;
- private native extension modules behind stable public Python facades;
- explicit core, optional, development, and hardware dependency groups;
- isolated installed-wheel validation;
- a checked invariant between Git tags, package metadata, and wheel metadata;
- centralized publication to PyPI and GitHub Releases;
- independently retryable hardware-specific release variants.

Distribution names such as `mooncake-transfer-engine` and its hardware variants remain unchanged. The installed import package remains `mooncake`.

Background and a detailed walkthrough are available in [Mooncake Python Packaging Refactor](https://aionw.github.io/posts/mooncake-python-package-refactoring/).

## Relationship to existing RFCs

This proposal overlaps with two existing RFCs:

- #3425, **Refactor the `mooncake-wheel` package layout**, identifies the same fragmented Python source layout and build-time copying problems. Its target architecture keeps `mooncake-wheel/mooncake` as the source root and retains public native module names. This proposal goes further by introducing `python/mooncake` as a source-only package root, private native extensions, `scikit-build-core`, explicit dependency groups, and installed-wheel validation. If accepted, this RFC should supersede the narrower target architecture in #3425.

- #3130, **Release Branch Workflow for Stable Releases**, overlaps with the release-validation part of this proposal. It focuses on release branches and TestPyPI validation, while this RFC defines the package build contract, artifact identity, wheel validation, and centralized publication. The two proposals are complementary: #3130 may define how a release commit is selected and stabilized, while this RFC defines how that commit becomes validated and published Python distributions.

## Motivation

### Python has no single source root

Tracked Python code currently lives under several component directories, including:

- `mooncake-wheel/mooncake`;
- `mooncake-integration`;
- `mooncake-reshard/python/mooncake`;
- EP and PG component directories.

Whether a Python file enters the wheel can depend on imperative copy logic in `scripts/build_wheel.sh`. Development and tests may consequently import a different file from the one installed from a wheel.

### The source package is also used as a staging directory

Wheel construction copies shared libraries, executables, metadata, and Python files into the tracked package directory. Interrupted or consecutive variant builds can leave stale or variant-specific artifacts in the source tree.

A source directory should not also be a mutable wheel assembly workspace.

### Module boundaries no longer match subsystem boundaries

The package root currently contains Store utilities, structured object storage, EP helpers, services, SSD administration, command-line entry points, and framework integrations.

Large modules such as `structured_object_store.py` combine models, manifests, serialization, buffer management, transport behavior, and optional codecs. The flat layout obscures ownership and allows optional dependencies to leak into core imports.

### Dependencies are implicit

Different modules use NumPy, PyTorch, Pillow, msgspec, ZeroMQ, FastAPI, httpx, Paramiko, vLLM, and hardware runtimes.

Making all of them mandatory would produce an unnecessarily large core installation. Leaving them undeclared produces incomplete environments and late `ModuleNotFoundError` failures.

### Release artifacts need one checked identity

Actions artifacts, PyPI distributions, and GitHub Release assets serve different purposes, but they must refer to the same immutable source and package version.

The build and publication workflows should check this explicitly rather than derive similar version strings independently.

## Design principles

1. All tracked Python package code lives under `python/mooncake`.
2. PEP 517 is the only public Python build interface.
3. Generated files never enter tracked Python source directories.
4. Public API modules are stable Python facades; native filenames are private implementation details.
5. Core imports do not load unrelated integrations or hardware runtimes.
6. Release gates test an installed wheel outside the source tree.
7. Git tags, `pyproject.toml`, and wheel metadata must agree.
8. Builders build and validate; only a centralized publisher may publish.
9. Obsolete source locations, namespace extensions, staging scripts, and internal import paths are removed rather than retained as compatibility layers.

## Proposed repository layout

```text
Mooncake/
  pyproject.toml

  python/
    pyrightconfig.json

    mooncake/
      __init__.py

      engine/
        __init__.py
        shared_segment.py

      store/
        __init__.py
        async_client.py
        buffer_pool.py
        config.py
        structured/
          __init__.py
          api.py
          models.py
          manifest.py
          transport.py
          buffer.py
          codecs/

      ep/
        __init__.py
        buffer.py
        elastic_buffer.py

      pg/
        __init__.py

      reshard/
        __init__.py
        contracts/
        weight/

      allocators/
      integrations/
        dataproto/
        vllm/
      services/
      ssd/
      cli/

items.title: [RFC]: [Store] Add object storage as a first-class replica tier
items.author: particle128
items.body_excerpt:
### Changes proposed # [RFC]: [Store] Add object storage as a first-class replica tier This proposal introduces object storage as a first-class replica tier, reusing the [existing OSS adapter](https://kvcache-ai.github.io/Mooncake/design/store/oss-backend.html). The new types, configuration options, and protocol extensions below are proposed changes. ## 1. Goals and scope The current object storage integration follows the FileStorage / LOCAL_DISK path: the MEMORY owner performs uploads, and reads also depend on that owner. This proposal introduces an `OBJECT_STORAGE` replica alongside MEMORY, LOCAL_DISK, DFS, and NOF_SSD: - The Master manages object locations, replica states, and lifecycle; Clients access shared object storage directly using descriptors. - The Master configures one of three write modes: synchronous writes, asynchronous replication after a memory write, or direct offload on memory eviction. - Object replicas support deletion and background reclamation. - Once an object replica is committed, other Clients can read it even after the original writer/owner goes offline. The initial implementation reuses the OSS adapter while keeping the interface provider-neutral. Each Mooncake object maps to one backend object. Object aggregation, cascading MEMORY → SSD → object storage, a unified redesign of all external storage tiers, and general idempotency enhancements to the shared Start/End/Revoke protocol are out of scope. ## 2. Architecture ```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph MP["Master process"] M["Object directory, write mode, lease / pin"] M --> D["Existing MEMORY / LOCAL_DISK / DFS / NOF_SSD"] M --> O["New OBJECT_STORAGE
object_key + object_size"] M --> G["Pending deletions / retries
Existing background maintenance"] G -->|"DELETE after protection ends"| GA["ObjectStorageAdapter
Master-side instance"] end C["Requesting Client / SDK"] <-->|"PutStart / PutEnd / Query"| M C -->|"Synchronous writes / direct reads"| B["ObjectStorageBackend"] W["MEMORY owner
Offload executor"] -. "Fetch tasks / report completion" .-> M W -->|"Background upload from MEMORY"| B B --> A["ObjectStorageAdapter
Client-side GetBatch / PutBatch"] A --> S["Shared object storage"] GA --> S classDef added fill:#fff0d6,stroke:#d97706,stroke-width:2px; class O,B,G added; ``` - Backends and adapters are in-process modules, with separate instances in each participating process. The Master does not carry object GET/PUT data traffic, but uses its own adapter for background DELETE operations. - Deletion and retries reuse the Master's existing background maintenance mechanism, without requiring a dedicated GC thread or service. Only known pending deletions are processed; the entire bucket is not scanned. - Both background modes reuse the owner's offload queue, heartbeat, and source-replica protection, extending them with an object-storage target and completion reporting. Reads no longer depend on the owner after the object replica is committed. - As with DFS, the Master manages replicas while Clients access shared storage directly. Objects are addressed by key, without file-offset allocation or inheritance from the DFS allocator interface. ## 3. Metadata and configuration ### 3.1 Replica descriptor ```cpp struct ObjectStorageDescriptor { std::string object_key; uint64_t object_size; }; // Added to ReplicateConfig size_t os_replica_num{0}; ``` `ObjectStorageDescriptor` is added to the existing `Replica::Descriptor::descriptor_variant`. Replica `id` and `status` remain in the shared outer descriptor rather than being duplicated in the object descriptor. Enabling object replicas requires support in the Master and all participating Clients. The initial implementation does not promise mixed-version operation with older releases. - `os_replica_num` initially supports 0 or 1, defaulting to 0. A value of 1 requests one object replica according to the Master's policy. It is neither the object service's internal replication factor nor an indication that the replica is already complete. - The initial write requires at least one MEMORY replica. After the object replica is committed, MEMORY replicas may be evicted under the normal protection rules. - `object_key` is a backend object name allocated by the Master, separate from the application's key. The adapter handles prefixes and encoding. - Upsert, Put after Remove, and reallocation after abandoning an old task use new object names, so late uploads or old deletion tasks cannot affect new data. Ordinary retries of the same task reuse its `object_key`. This does not introduce a user-facing multi-version KV API. - Existing shared object-checksum metadata is reused; provider ETags are not treated as a generic content checksum. Using a separate object name isolates successive values of the same application key. For example, if `Put(K)` follows `Remove(K)` before the old background DELETE finishes, using K for both backend objects would let the delayed DELETE remove the new data. The Master maps the application key to an `object_key`, so old tasks operate only on the old object. The same isolation applies to Upsert and late uploads. ### 3.2 Cluster-wide backend configuration Initially, each cluster uses a single object storage backend. The Master publishes non-secret configuration to Clients: provider, endpoint, bucket/namespace, and prefix. Clients fetch and cache it during initialization. The Master uses the same storage target for reclamation; descriptors do not duplicate this configuration. An object's full location is **the cluster-wide endpoint / bucket / prefix plus `object_key`**. Client-side and Master-side adapters use credentials configured in their respective processes, reusing the existing OSS environment variables without introducing a credential service: ```text MOONCAKE_OSS_ACCESS_KEY_ID MOONCAKE_OSS_ACCESS_KEY_SECRET MOONCAKE_OSS_SECURITY_TOK

items.title: [RFC]: [Store] HA: Protect in-flight PutStart allocations across failover with a segment-owner ledger
items.author: SongOf
items.body_excerpt:
### Changes proposed

## Summary

In HA mode, memory allocations (`PutStart`, `UpsertStart`, `CopyStart`, `MoveStart`, `PromotionAllocStart` and their variants) are not written to the OpLog. After a failover, the promoted leader therefore cannot see ranges that are still being written. It may give such a range to another key, or serve an object as `COMPLETE` while an in-place upsert is still overwriting it. Either way a reader can get wrong bytes, with no error.

The HA roadmap (#3808, RL02, from RFC #2979) fixes this by making `REPLICA_CREATE` durable before `PutStart` returns. That adds at least one etcd commit to every write.

This RFC proposes a lighter protection for memory replicas, with no quorum write on the write path. The process that owns a segment keeps a small **ledger** of the ranges being written in it, fenced by the leader's term. At failover, the promoted leader learns those ranges from the owners and keeps them reserved.

It is a proposal for review. Nothing here is implemented.

## Motivation

- **Unlogged ranges look free after failover.** The promoted leader rebuilds its index from the snapshot and the durable OpLog, which do not include ranges handed out but not yet completed.
- **In-place upserts are not logged.** When the size is unchanged, `UpsertStart` rewrites the existing buffers in place. A promoted leader still sees the old object as `COMPLETE`.
- **Writers can be arbitrarily late.** #4491 shows timed-out slices landing long after a put was revoked. A fix that waits for writers to finish cannot rely on a time bound.
- **RL02 puts etcd latency on every write.** Its tail latency follows etcd.

## Goals and non-goals

Goals:

- After a failover, no reader gets wrong bytes from a memory replica because a range was reused while still being written, or because an object was served while being overwritten in place.
- No etcd commit, or other quorum write, on the write path.
- No reliance on how long a writer can take.
- Safe rolling upgrades in any order, and no behavior change until the mode is raised to `takeover` or `enforce`.

Non-goals:

- Losing a recent `PUT_END` on failover. Per #3885, that is part of the cache contract.
- Readers that hold descriptors from a former leader.
- Non-HA masters, and NoF, DFS and CXL replicas (see "Scope").

## Proposal

### Overview

1. **Ledger on the segment owner.** Each client that mounts a memory segment keeps an in-process ledger of the ranges that may still be written in it. A segment's memory and its RDMA registration live and die with that process, so no quorum store is needed.
2. **Register before writing.** A writer registers each range with the segment's owner before its first transfer to it, under the term of the leader that allocated the range. The owner returns a unique ledger token for that write attempt. The writer writes only after the registration is acknowledged.
3. **Fencing by term.** A term is the pair (`view_version`, leader session token). The owner accepts registrations only under its current term.
4. **Takeover on mount and remount.** When the owner mounts or remounts a segment, it moves to the current leader's term and reports its entries before the remount. From then on it rejects registrations under any other term. The leader accepts a report only under its own term, and applies it before the segment can be allocated from.
5. **Reconciliation.** For each reported entry, the leader does one of three things:
   - if the entry is the same allocation as a restored replica that is already complete, it keeps that replica;
   - if the entry overlaps any other restored replica, it hides that replica and later removes it, never serving it again (this covers in-place upserts);
   - if the entry overlaps nothing it restored, it reserves the range.
6. **Completion identity.** Completion RPCs (`PutEnd`, `PutRevoke` and the others) carry the term of their allocation. A leader rejects completions from another term, so a write that started before a failover cannot complete or free a write started after it.
7. **Safe clearing.** A writer clears its entry by token, and only after both of these:
   - its completion RPC has returned;
   - its transfers have fully drained.

   The owner tells the leader when reported entries are cleared, so the leader can release them.

### Why this is safe

Within the scope below, every writer of a segment registers. The owner processes a registration and a takeover in some order. If the registration comes first, the takeover reports it, and the new leader protects the range. If the takeover comes first, the registration carries an older term and is rejected, so the writer never writes. A stale leader that keeps allocating is fenced the same way.

The argument rests on six rules, none of which involves a timeout or a clock:

1. No two leaders share a term, and the owner never moves to an older term.
2. A writer writes a range only after its registration is acknowledged.
3. A leader allocates on a segment only after applying that segment's report, made under its own term.
4. A leader accepts a completion only if it was issued under its own term.
5. An entry is removed only by its own token.
6. An entry is cleared only after its completion has returned and its transfers have drained.

Terms are safe on all three HA backends (etcd, Redis, k8s), because session tokens are unique per leadership. If a backend's `view_version` ever goes backwards, the affected segments stop accepting remounts until an operator intervenes. That loses capacity, not data.

### Scope

- **Covered:** memory replicas (host, GPU and EGM memory) on segments whose owner and leader run ledger-enabled builds, with the mode at `enforce`. The guarantee is per segment, because an unregistered writer could corrupt a registered one. So in `enforce` the leader refuses memory allocations to clients that have not declared ledger support.
- **Not covered:**
  - **NoF:** it has no long-lived owner process, and NoF failover has a

items.title: [Bug]: Direct NVMe-oF requests past segment end can report partial I/O as COMPLETED
items.author: RuiqingFeng
items.body_excerpt:
## Environment and affected path

Mooncake upstream main c67a88f381f69e869045f353539e90c76e738830
(2026-10-23). This concerns the classic Transfer Engine's direct
NVMeoFTransport::submitTransfer(batch_id, entries) path, not Store's SPDK
NoF path or NVMe KV backend. The MultiTransport task-batch path is a
separate, explicitly unsupported interface for this transport.

## Reproduction

Create an NVMe-oF segment with two 4096-byte buffers. Allocate a direct
transport batch and submit a WRITE with target_offset=4096 and length=8192.
The segment is only 8192 bytes long, so half the request lies outside it.

Observed with the real transport and descriptor-pool sources linked to fake
cuFile entry points on Linux (GCC 13.3, C++20):

- submitTransfer returns OK and submits one 4096-byte cuFile operation.
- Once that submitted slice completes, getTransferStatus reports COMPLETED
  with transferred_bytes=4096, although requested_bytes=8192.
- A submission containing a valid request followed by an invalid request
  also mutates the batch and submits I/O instead of rejecting the call.

The fake backend records submitted cuFile parameters and completes exactly
those operations; no real GPU, NVMe device, or storage DMA was exercised.
Two legal single-/cross-buffer control cases pass on the same baseline.

## Expected behavior

Reject a request that is not fully covered by the segment with
InvalidArgument before creating any tasks, slices, file handles, or I/O
parameters for that submission. Check every request before mutating the
batch, retain any existing tasks, and permit a subsequent valid submission.
Use overflow-safe arithmetic for the segment length and request range.
This is validation atomicity, not transactional I/O after successful submit.

## Cause

submitTransfer intersects each request with nvmeof_buffers and only submits
those intersections. It never verifies that the requested interval is fully
covered. aggregateTransferStatus only aggregates submitted slices, so it
cannot detect bytes that were omitted before submission. The request-end
addition and cumulative buffer lengths are also unchecked.

## Related work and proposed fix

I searched upstream issues and PRs using the authenticated GitHub API.
#2893 and #2939 address task submission/completion correlation and terminal
failure propagation. Open PR #2917 changes cancellation/draining and
submission-error rollback; its submitTransfer diff still uses the existing
intersection-only slicing without full request-range validation. This report
covers pre-submission range validation, not that lifecycle work.

I have prepared a focused fix and regression tests for full-range
prevalidation, integer overflow, mixed-validity submissions, retry and
existing-task preservation. I would like to contribute the fix.

## AI assistance

Codex assisted with investigation, implementation and test preparation.

items.title: [Bug]: transfer_check_status only checks the first task of a batch_transfer_async_* batch
items.author: arun-elr
items.body_excerpt:
### Bug Report

`transfer_check_status(batch_id)` only looks at task 0. Batches from `batch_transfer_async_write/read` have one task per buffer, so if task 0 completes and a later task fails, it returns 1 and frees the batch as if everything landed. Hit this in M*, an inference engine that polls async reads w/ `transfer_check_status`.

Env:
- `mooncake-transfer-engine-non-cuda==0.3.13.post1` wheel, and main `dd1217b6` built from source
- Ubuntu 24.04 x86_64, CPU only, TCP (`MC_FORCE_TCP=1`, `P2PHANDSHAKE`)
- same result on main w/ `MC_USE_TENT=1`

Repro (one process, two engines; the second write goes 1 byte past the target's registered buffer, so the target rejects it):

```python
import ctypes
import time

from mooncake.engine import TransferEngine

SIZE, CHUNK = 1 << 20, 4096
target, initiator = TransferEngine(), TransferEngine()
for te in (target, initiator):
    assert te.initialize("127.0.0.1", "P2PHANDSHAKE", "tcp", "") == 0
seg = f"127.0.0.1:{target.get_rpc_port()}"

dst = ctypes.create_string_buffer(SIZE)
src = ctypes.create_string_buffer(2 * CHUNK)
dst_addr, src_addr = ctypes.addressof(dst), ctypes.addressof(src)
assert target.register_memory(dst_addr, SIZE) == 0
assert initiator.register_memory(src_addr, 2 * CHUNK) == 0

past_end = dst_addr + SIZE  # not registered on the target
for name, peers in (
    ("good, past_end", [dst_addr, past_end]),
    ("past_end, good", [past_end, dst_addr]),
):
    bid = initiator.batch_transfer_async_write(
        seg, [src_addr, src_addr + CHUNK], peers, [CHUNK, CHUNK]
    )
    rc = 0
    while rc == 0:
        rc = initiator.transfer_check_status(bid)
        time.sleep(0.005)
    print(f"{name}: {rc}")
```

Expected: `-1` for both orders.

Actual (3/3 runs, both versions), even though the target logs `WRITE rejected by server` both times:

```
good, past_end: 1
past_end, good: -1
```

Cause: `TransferEnginePy::transferCheckStatus` calls `engine_->getTransferStatus(batch_id, 0, status)` (`mooncake-integration/transfer_engine/transfer_engine_py.cpp:1377` on main), while `batchTransferAsync` (`:1207`) submits one task per buffer. The Python API docs suggest using `transfer_check_status()` with `batch_transfer_async_*()`, so this isn't just a `transfer_submit_write` thing.

`TransferEngine::getBatchTransferStatus` already checks every task on classic TE and TENT. I have a small fix + test and will open a PR.

### Before submitting...

- [x] Ensure you searched for relevant issues and read the [documentation]

items.title: [Testing] _concurrent may report success when a child process is terminated by a signal
items.author: zh301
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

`_concurrent()` in `python/triton/_test_runner.py` can return a successful status even when one of its child processes is terminated by a signal.

The function currently aggregates child return codes using `max()`:

```python
def _concurrent(commands):
    processes = [subprocess.Popen(command, cwd=cwd, env=environment) for command, cwd, environment in commands]
    return max(process.wait() for process in processes)
```

On POSIX systems, `subprocess.Popen.wait()` returns a negative value when a process is terminated by a signal. For example, a process terminated by `SIGTERM` returns `-15`.

Therefore, if one child exits successfully with `0` and another is terminated by `SIGTERM` with `-15`, the aggregate result is:

```python
max(0, -15) == 0
```

The caller consequently treats the concurrent test run as successful, even though one of the test processes was terminated.

## Minimal reproducer

Save the following as `repro_concurrent_signal.py` in the root of a Triton source checkout:

```python
import os
import signal
import sys

from triton._test_runner import _concurrent


cwd = os.getcwd()
environment = os.environ.copy()

commands = [
    (
        [sys.executable, "-c", "pass"],
        cwd,
        environment,
    ),
    (
        [
            sys.executable,
            "-c",
            "import os, signal; os.kill(os.getpid(), signal.SIGTERM)",
        ],
        cwd,
        environment,
    ),
]

status = _concurrent(commands)

print(f"_concurrent status: {status}")
assert status != 0, (
    "_concurrent returned success even though one child "
    "was terminated by SIGTERM"
)
```

Run it from the Triton checkout root:

```bash
PYTHONPATH=python python3 repro_concurrent_signal.py
```

No GPU is required.

## Actual result

The source-level pytest regression test reports:

```text
bug_repros/test_concurrent_signal_status.py:36: in test_signal_terminated_child_makes_concurrent_run_fail
    assert status != 0, (
E   AssertionError: _concurrent returned success even though one child was terminated by SIGTERM
E   assert 0 != 0
```

## Expected result

`_concurrent()` should return a nonzero status whenever any child process exits with a nonzero status, including negative return codes representing signal termination.

The aggregation should not allow a successful child return code (`0`) to hide a signal-terminated child return code (`-N`).

Python documents negative subprocess return codes on POSIX as meaning that the process was terminated by signal `N`:

https://docs.python.org/3/library/subprocess.html#subprocess.Popen.returncode

### Environment details

Triton: source checkout from main, commit 2122e24efc1886bfa36337c1f5b07c47d827b1d4
Python: 3.12.3
OS: Linux, AutoDL container
GPU: Not required
Platform requirement: POSIX signal return-code semantics
