items.title: Starting a localization (l10n) effort for LMCache
items.author: quaid
items.body_excerpt:
I'd like to propose we start building a localization community around LMCache, beginning with blog posts and expanding to documentation and other parts of the website over time.

tl;dr – 
- localizing content and software is valuable to all of us;
- we can automate the toil of translation but we need human editors who can review the translations and make sure they are properly localized;
- localization means words and phrases are fixed so the final product makes more sense to a native reader;
- we can use RHLF to improve this process and reduce toil over time.

## What is the problem

We already receive blog posts written natively in Mandarin and English. This is a good thing.

But we also need to localize this content without putting a burden on people. Fortunately this content has completed a technical review before being translated, so the focus can be on fixing idioms and grammar for better understanding by the widest audience.

## Why this matters

Ultimately this is about attracting more users to LMCache, some of whom will become intentional contributors over time.

Twenty-five years ago, localization (l10n) projects were one of the main ways Linux distributions and communities like the Fedora Project made headway into new parts of the world. It usually wasn't a corporate initiative. It was people who were enthusiastic about bringing free and open source software to their fellow country members, and who put in the effort to translate strings and make the software make sense locally. That work produced translations AND collaborations. It grew contributors, built regional communities, and carried the free software and open source ethos into places it hadn't reached before.

LMCache has users and watchers all over the world, and there are almost certainly people already adjacent to this project who could help bring information and education about the software to their local communities.

## What I'm proposing

We form loosely as `l10n-sig` out of anyone who wants to be an editor and approver for one or more languages. Languages get added when someone steps forward to take one. Rather than announcing a target list and hoping it fills in, we start with whoever volunteers.

I'm volunteering to be an editor and reviewer for anything translated to English, and I'd love more help with that role. I'm confident we can get Mandarin covered right away. But what else and how?

Japanese and Korean are the obvious early candidates given where our users are, but the principle is that a language becomes active when a person is willing to own it.

It only takes one person to get things started and be the gravity to bring another language.

As I said above, this isn't only English needing localizing. I currently have an original blog post written in Mandarin that I want to bring into English through this same process. I'd like to stop doing one at a time reviews by asking around in Slack to see who might need a break from creating features or fixing bugs. I'd rather offer the opportunity to people who aren't or can't create features or fix bugs.

Therefore, posts written originally in any language are welcome, and translation should flow in whatever direction it needs to.

## This is not a request for volunteer translation labor

LLM translation is pretty good now, and we should lean on it for the first pass. What we need is a human review step, and there are two kinds of people who can do that well.

The first is someone capable in both the source and target language, who can read the machine translation and confirm the meaning carried over and the tone is right. Not necessarily final-polish copy editing — a human or AI copy edit can always be applied later — just confirmation that it makes sense and reads naturally.

The second, and possibly just as valuable, is someone technical who knows their own language well and doesn't necessarily read the source language at all. Because the models are good enough now, a domain expert can look at a translated technical passage and say "ah, I see what this was trying to say" and correct the terminology so it's actually right in their language. Technical accuracy matters as much as idiomatic flow, and that person is well placed to catch it.

So the ask is much closer to "read this and tell us if it sounds right" than "translate three thousand words."

## How the workflow might look

Initially all of this can be manual, while we work out which models produce the best tone for technical writing in each language and we develop any necessary skills.

Longer term this could be automated — a GitHub Action that sends a published post to a translation model, then loads the result into WordPress as a draft where a translation editor reviews and approves it. It could also live partly outside the repo, with approval happening after the fact rather than as a gate. The goal is to distribute this work rather than make it dependent on a paid staffer, and to remove the need to ask permission before contributing.

If anyone already knows of a toolchain or process for this, please say so. I'd much rather adopt something that works than stand up and maintain our own infrastructure.

## What I'm looking for

Ideas or helping hands for:

- Thoughts on the approach
- Pointers to existing tooling
- Anyone in

items.title: llama : integer type consistency in `llama.h`
items.author: MarcusDunn
items.body_excerpt:
# Feature Description

llama.h should prefer to use `sized` (always) + `signed` (mostly) integers.

# Motivation

The integer types in `llama.h` right now are.

| Count | Type            |
|---------|------------------|
| 33      | `int`              |
| 10      | `int32_t`       |
| 24      | `uint32_t`     |
| 2        | `int64_t`       |
| 2        | `uint64_t`    | 

In #4540 there was a discussion around preferences for integer types on new methods. 

Avoiding `int` makes cross platform code simpler at essentially no cost.
Signed makes arithmetic simpler at the cost of some bits if you need something large.

# Possible Implementation

1. Change all `int`'s to `int32_t`
2. As code changes try to prefer signed integers.

We could also do some higher-impact things, but I'd take the lower-impact slower changes over a large find-and-replace.

items.title: [Feature Request] Add a shared end-to-end benchmark driver for C++ Store and Store-RS
items.author: Ziy1-Tan
items.body_excerpt:
## Problem

The C++ Store and Store-RS ship separate end-to-end benchmarks with different workloads, CLI options, and metric definitions. Comparing the two tools mixes tool differences with implementation differences.

Store-RS has incomplete NoF and registered-buffer support. NoF copy reads and writes work; NoF promotion and NoF zero-copy reads do not. Without a capability model, those cases either disappear from comparisons or surface as performance failures.

## Proposal

Make `store_kv_bench.py` the shared end-to-end driver for both implementations:

```text
--store-backend cpp
--store-backend rs
```

Both paths use the same workload settings and report the same phase names and metrics. The driver owns the argument surface. Each backend supplies a small setup adapter, because the two `setup()` signatures differ: Store-RS takes `transport_metadata_url` as its second positional argument where the C++ facade takes `metadata_server`, and the Store-RS facade does not export `ReplicateConfig`.

The work is split into four stages. Stages 1 and 2 run on a single node over TCP with no RDMA, NoF, or GPU. Stage 3 is code-only. Stage 4 needs an NVMe-oF target.

## Capability states

Each reserved scenario reports two values: the capability of the implementation, and the result of running the scenario.

Capability values:

```text
supported
not_configured
not_implemented
```

Result values:

```text
PASS
FAIL
SKIP_NOT_CONFIGURED
SKIP_NOT_IMPLEMENTED
```

Partially covered scenarios take `supported` or `not_implemented` for the scenario as a whole, and the notes column records which sub-operations exist. The tables keep to these three capability values.

## Stages

### Stage 1: shared driver and memory workloads

| Scenario | C++ Store | Store-RS | Behavior | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Memory put/get | supported | supported | run | |
| Batch memory put/get | supported | supported | run | |

Benchmark phases exercised: `verify_write`, `fill`, `write_perf`, `read_perf`, `mixed_rw`.

### Stage 2: registered-buffer I/O

| Scenario | C++ Store | Store-RS | Behavior | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Registered-buffer write/read, single | supported | supported | run | `put_from` / `get_into` |
| Registered-buffer write/read, batch | supported | supported | run | `batch_put_from` / `batch_get_into` |

Phase names and metric fields match Stage 1. Only the I/O API changes. Over TCP the data path still copies, so the scenario measures the registered-buffer API, not wire-level zero copy.

### Stage 3: capability reporting for NoF

This stage runs on any build, with or without NoF support. The driver probes backend capability and configuration, then reports a skip instead of zero throughput or an error.

| Scenario | C++ Store | Store-RS | Behavior | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| NoF replica count | supported | not_configured | skip until wired | The Rust builder accepts a replica count; the Python benchmark path does not expose it |
| NoF promotion | supported | not_implemented | report and skip on Store-RS | C++ covers configured replicas only |
| NoF zero-copy read | supported | not_implemented | report and skip on Store-RS | C++ registers through SPDK |
| NoF zero-copy write | not_implemented | not_implemented | report and skip on both | C++ has no dedicated zero-copy write workload |

NoF target failure stays out of scope. C++ health behavior is implementation-specific and Store-RS health behavior is partial; comparing them needs a follow-up issue.

### Stage 4: NoF copy comparison

| Scenario | C++ Store | Store-RS | Behavior | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| NoF copy write/read | supported | supported | run when configured | Requires an SPDK NVMe-oF target with a registered namespace |

## Alternatives

Keep the existing tools and compare `mooncake-store-rs-bench` with `store_kv_bench.py`. Their workloads and metrics differ, so the results would not isolate Store behavior.

Put the C++ microbenchmarks behind the same interface. Out of scope: allocator, Master, OpLog, and storage-backend benchmarks depend on C++ internals.

## Use cases

- Compare both implementations on the same workload and hardware.
- Establish repeatable baselines and detect performance regressions.
- Separate routing, transport, placement, and storage effects.
- Track NoF and zero-copy support without reporting missing work as a regression.

## Acceptance criteria

Stage 1:

- One `store_kv_bench.py` invocation selects either backend.
- Shared scenarios use the same phase names and metric fields.
- Request, key, byte, success, miss, and verification counts mean the same thing on both backends.
- A parity run covers `verify_write`, `fill`, `write_perf`, `read_perf`, and `mixed_rw`.
- The summary records the backend, transport, routing mode, hardware, and workload settings.

Stage 2:

- Registered-buffer single and batch I/O reuse the Stage 1 phase names and metric fields.
- A backend without registered-buffer support reports its capability state instead of a misleading error.

Stage 3:

- Missing NoF or zero-copy support reports `SKIP_NOT_IMPLEMENTED`, not zero throughput.
- Scenarios that exist but are not configured report `SKIP_NOT_CONFIGURED`.
- A skip result names the capability state and the reason.

Stage 4:

- Configured NoF copy scenarios run on both backends and produce comparable results.

## Scope

This is post-upstream benchmark work, not a blocker for RFC #3504. C++ microbenchmarks stay separate. `mooncake-store-rs-bench` remains the Store-RS tool for soak tests, multi-tenant checks, cold-tier diagnostics, and NoF validation the shared workload cannot express. Stages 1 and 2 need one node and TCP. Stage 3 needs no hardware. Stage 4 needs an NVMe-oF target.

## Related work

- RFC #3504: masterless Store-RS scope and validation
- `mooncake-store-rs-bench`: Store-RS benchmark, verification, and soak tool
- `mooncake-store/benchmarks/store_kv_bench.py`: current C++ end-to-end benchmark

items.author: peastman
items.body_excerpt:
I'm just getting started with Triton.  I can't find any documentation on some very basic concepts.  If you can point me to something I missed I'd be grateful.  If not, perhaps someone could answer these questions?

What types of values can be passed to a kernel?  PyTorch tensors obviously, as well as ints, floats, and bools.  Anything else?

The grid is defined by a lambda that takes a single argument called `meta`.  What is `meta`?

How do I access a single element of a tensor?  Say `a` and `b` are tensors and `i` is an int.  I want to write `c = a[i]*b` to multiply `b` by an element of `a`.  That produces an error.  What's the correct way of doing it?

What is the difference between a `tensor_descriptor` and a `TensorDescriptor`?  What is each used for and how do I use them?

What is the exact significance of annotating an argument with `tl.constexpr`?  Does it mean the kernel will get recompiled every time a new value of that argument is encountered?  What can be done with a constexpr value that can't be done with other ones?

How about `tl.const`?  Is it just for error checking, to avoid accidentally modifying something that shouldn't be modified, or does it have other effects?

Thanks for your help!

items.title: KernelLens: Deploying Triton Kernels to C++ Inference Engines (TensorRT & ONNX)
items.author: Just1truc
items.body_excerpt:
# Deploying OpenAI Triton Kernels to C++ Inference Runtimes (ONNX Runtime & TensorRT) with KernelLens

Hey Triton Community!

If you write custom `@triton.jit` kernels in Python for LLM operators (FlashAttention, Fused RMSNorm, SwiGLU, Selective Scans), you’ve probably hit the deployment bottleneck: How do you run your Python Triton kernels inside production C++ inference engines like NVIDIA TensorRT or Microsoft ONNX Runtime?

Traditionally, developers had two frustrating choices:
1. **Stay in Python PyTorch Eager/Dynamo**: Forfeiting TensorRT/ORT global graph optimizations across standard model layers.
2. **Manual C++/CUDA Rewrites**: Throw away Python Triton code and manually rewrite kernels in CUDA C++ (`__global__`) while authoring hundreds of lines of `OrtCustomOp` / `nvinfer1::IPluginV2DynamicExt` boilerplate.

To solve this, we created [**KernelLens**](https://github.com/Just1truc/kernel_lens), an open-source compiler framework from [Galiad Research](https://galiad-research.com) that automatically compiles PyTorch models containing Python `@triton.jit` kernels into native C++ plugins for ONNX Runtime and TensorRT in **1 line of Python**.

---

## Step-by-Step Guide to Run the Working Example

Follow these 3 simple steps to test KernelLens on any CUDA-enabled GPU machine:

### Step 1: Install Dependencies
```bash
pip install torch triton kernel-lens
```

### Step 2: Save the Python Script (`example.py`)
Save the following code into a file named `example.py`:

```python
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import triton
import triton.language as tl
import kernel_lens as kl

# 1. Define a standard OpenAI Triton Kernel
@triton.jit
def add_kernel(x_ptr, y_ptr, out_ptr, n_elements, BLOCK_SIZE: tl.constexpr):
    pid = tl.program_id(axis=0)
    block_start = pid * BLOCK_SIZE
    offsets = block_start + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE)
    mask = offsets < n_elements
    x = tl.load(x_ptr + offsets, mask=mask)
    y = tl.load(y_ptr + offsets, mask=mask)
    output = x + y
    tl.store(out_ptr + offsets, output, mask=mask)

# 2. Wrap the Triton Kernel inside a PyTorch Module
class VectorAddModule(nn.Module):
    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor, y: torch.Tensor):
        out = torch.empty_like(x)
        n_elements = x.numel()
        grid = lambda meta: (triton.cdiv(n_elements, meta['BLOCK_SIZE']),)
        add_kernel[grid](<x, y, out, n_elements, BLOCK_SIZE=1024>)
        return out

if __name__ == '__main__':
    device = 'cuda' if torch.cuda.is_available() else 'cpu'
    x = torch.randn(4096, device=device, dtype=torch.float32)
    y = torch.randn(4096, device=device, dtype=torch.float32)
    model = VectorAddModule().to(device)

    print("Compiling PyTorch + Triton Model with KernelLens...")
    
    # 3. Compile Model to C++ Plugins in 1 Line
    compiled_model = kl.compile(
        model, 
        (x, y), 
        name="simple_vector_add", 
        backends=["onnx", "tensorrt"]
    )
    
    print("Executing Zero-Copy Inference in ONNX Runtime...")
    ort_output = compiled_model.run((x, y), backend="onnx")
    
    print("Executing Zero-Copy Inference in TensorRT...")
    trt_output = compiled_model.run((x, y), backend="tensorrt")

    # 4. Verify Numerical Parity against PyTorch Result
    torch_expected = x + y
    max_diff_ort = (ort_output - torch_expected).abs().max().item()
    max_diff_trt = (trt_output - torch_expected).abs().max().item()

    print("Verification Complete!")
    print(f"ORT Max Floating-Point Difference: {max_diff_ort:.6e}")
    print(f"TRT Max Floating-Point Difference: {max_diff_trt:.6e}")
    print(f"Exact Numerical Match (ORT): {torch.allclose(ort_output, torch_expected)}")
    print(f"Exact Numerical Match (TRT): {torch.allclose(trt_output, torch_expected)}")
```

### Step 3: Execute the Test
```bash
python3 example.py
```

### Expected Terminal Output
```text
Compiling PyTorch + Triton Model with KernelLens...
Executing Zero-Copy Inference in ONNX Runtime...
Executing Zero-Copy Inference in TensorRT...
Verification Complete!
ORT Max Floating-Point Difference: 0.000000e+00
TRT Max Floating-Point Difference: 0.000000e+00
Exact Numerical Match (ORT): True
Exact Numerical Match (TRT): True
```

---

## How it Works Under the Hood 🛠️

1. **PTX & Metadata Extraction**: KernelLens intercepts `@triton.jit` launches, extracting compiled PTX assembly strings, dynamic shared memory bytes, and parameter bitwidths directly from Triton’s compiler cache.
2. **SymPy Grid Transpilation**: Triton grid functions (e.g., `grid = lambda META: (triton.cdiv(M, BLOCK_SIZE),)`) are parsed via AST inspection into pure C++ integer arithmetic, evaluated dynamically at inference time with $< 0.5 \ \mu\text{s}$ CPU overhead.
3. **C++/CUDA Plugin Synthesis**: Synthesizes production-ready C++ source files implementing `Ort::CustomOp` and `nvinfer1::IPluginV2DynamicExt`, executing the PTX assembly via CUDA Driver API (`cuModuleLoadData` & `cuLaunchKernel`).
4. **Zero-Copy VRAM Binding**: Directly maps PyTorch VRAM pointers (`data_ptr()`) to ONNX Runtime `IOBinding` and TensorRT `setTensorAddress()`.
5. **Hardware Hardening**: Automatically injects dynamic 16-byte address checks to prevent misaligned vector load crashes (`ld.global.v4.b32`), and applies PTX ISA version clamping (`.version 9.0`) for NVIDIA Blackwell (`sm_120a`) GPU driver compatibility.

---

## Benchmarks & Numerical Parity

Across LLaMA 3, Mistral, Qwen 2.5, and Liger-Kernel operators, KernelLens achieves **$3.4\times$ to $7.0\times$ speedups** over eager PyTorch execution while maintaining exact floating-point numerical parity ($\text{MaxDiff} = 0.00\text{e}+00$).

---

## Links & Resources

* 💻 **GitHub**: [Just1truc/kernel_lens](https://github.com/Just1truc/kernel_lens)
* 📦 **PyPI**: `pip install kernel-lens`
* 📄 **Technical Report (DOI)**: [10.5281/zenodo.23194523](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo

items.title: Anthropic /v1/messages: inline system messages are merged into the leading system prompt, so every Claude Code turn misses the prefix cache after that point
items.author: Mearman
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment

vLLM v0.32.0 (the `vllm/vllm-openai` image, linux/arm64), NVIDIA GB10 (sm_121), CUDA 13, driver 580.178.04. I have not attached `collect_env.py` output; the report concerns the Anthropic endpoint's handling of system messages and the model's chat template.

### 🐛 Describe the bug

When the chat template requires system-first ordering (Qwen3.5/3.8 here), `_should_merge_inline_system` is true and `_convert_system_message` appends every inline `system` message to the leading system prompt (vllm/entrypoints/anthropic/serving.py, v0.32.0). Claude Code sends inline system messages whose text changes from turn to turn (skill listings, reminders, deferred tool additions). Because they are merged to the top of the prompt, a change in one changes tokens near the start and nothing after it can be reused.

Request shape from Claude Code 2.1.309 (contents omitted): `system` with three text blocks, then `messages` of user (large), system (text plus `tool_addition` blocks), assistant, user (tool_result), system (text). Between consecutive turns the first system message changes by a few dozen characters.

On Qwen3.8-27B NVFP4 (hybrid), v0.32.0, prefix caching on, replaying consecutive turns of one real session of about 52K to 65K tokens, in order, on a fresh server:

- as sent: prefix hits stay at about 19,000 tokens for every turn, first token 30 to 43 s each;
- the same turns with each inline system message rewritten as user-role content in the same position: hits of 51,200, 54,400, 59,200 and 60,800 tokens, first token 1.9 to 5.9 s.

The server logs a warning that this merge happens and suggests a template that accepts non-leading system messages. That works around it, but it leaves Claude Code users with a hybrid model on a prefix cache that never helps past the system prompt, and the merge is silent apart from the one warning.

Related, not the same: #52978 (trailing system messages), #59172 (repeated warnings for merged system messages).

### Before submitting a new issue...

I searched for existing issues; #52978 and #59172 are related but cover trailing system messages and repeated warnings.

items.title: [Bug] Hybrid Mamba/GDN persistence silently stores 1 of N kernel pages on vLLM >= 0.26 (0.5.3, 0.5.4, dev)
items.author: dl4rce
items.body_excerpt:
**Label**

bug, mp

**Describe the bug**

Persistent (disk-tier) KV-cache restore for hybrid Mamba/GDN + full-attention
models in MP mode silently stores and restores only **1 of N kernel pages per
chunk** on vLLM >= 0.26. Restores complete "successfully" with high reported
hit rates but return wrong answers.

Root cause: commit `65c2ae81` ("[Core][MP] Support Mamba/GDN hybrid models
(Qwen3.5) (#3613)") added `_SubpagedAttentionViewEdit` in
`lmcache/integration/vllm/kv_cache_group_edits.py` to re-view subpaged
full-attention (FA) KV at registration time — but the edit only pattern-matches
vLLM < 0.26's **5-dim** KV layout. vLLM >= 0.26 registers full-attention KV as
**4-dim K/V-packed** (FlashInfer in our runs), so no edit rule matches, the raw
subpaged geometry flows into the `kv_layer_groups` compression math, and the FA
group is misclassified as slot-compressed:

- the reserved host object is sized for **one** kernel page instead of
  N = tokens_per_block // slots_per_block pages (25 and 17 in our two configs);
- only the **first** kernel page of each chunk is copied on store and requested
  on retrieve;
- the L2 (disk) tier faithfully persists ~4% of the attention KV with **no error
  raised**. After an engine restart, restores report high external hit rates
  (the Mamba group restores fine) but produce wrong continuations.

`kv_cache_group_edits.py` is **byte-identical** on v0.5.3, v0.5.4 and dev @
`1a430626`, so every version is affected under vLLM >= 0.26. The intended fix
from `65c2ae81` ships in all of them — it just never activates.

On 0.5.3 a second, independent bug compounds this: paging a multi-page FA object
through the single-page GPU staging buffer mutates the shared
`MemoryObj.meta.address` between in-flight async copies, corrupting the host
buffer (~96% zeros, no exception). dev has since hardened that path
(size-mismatch ValueError, immutable staging descriptors), so dev fails loudly
rather than corrupting — but the feature stays broken until layout matching is
fixed.

Refs #4247 (adjacent symptoms, same code path) — this is an independent
confirmation with a root cause and a verified fix.

**To Reproduce**

No special hardware needed — any hybrid Mamba/GDN + full-attention model where
vLLM picks a unified block size larger than the attention kernel page size
(vLLM logs "Setting attention block size … to ensure that attention page size is
>= mamba page size"):

1. Serve a hybrid Mamba/GDN model on vLLM >= 0.26 with LMCache 0.5.3 in MP mode
   (`LMCacheMPConnector`) and an L2 disk tier. Our primary repro: vLLM
   `--mamba-cache-mode align --enable-prefix-caching --max-model-len 131072
   --max-num-batched-tokens 3199 -tp 2` with MTP speculative decoding (3 tokens);
   LMCache server with separate object groups, L1 CPU + L2 local-disk tier.
2. Send a prompt longer than one chunk with a unique fact (e.g. a random 24-hex
   key) buried mid-context.
3. Confirm it stored — the server logs the store, and an immediate re-ask of the
   identical prompt hits cache and answers correctly.
4. Kill vLLM **and** the LMCache server completely, so the next restore can only
   come from the L2 disk tier.
5. Restart both, re-send the identical prompt, ask for the buried fact.
6. Observe: high reported hit rate (95–99%) and a fast "restore", but a
   wrong/garbage answer. Per-chunk md5 of the FA host objects differs between
   store and restore; stored FA objects show zero_frac ≈ 0.96.

Verified on LMCache 0.5.3 + vLLM 0.27.1, hybrid GDN-class model (Qwen3.8, 27B),
TP=2, tokens_per_block=1600 / slots_per_block=64 → 25:1 subpaging. Cross-checked
at TP=1 with a smaller hybrid, 544/32 → 17:1 — same bug, so it is geometry-driven
(tokens_per_block > slots_per_block on an uncompressed `kv_size==2` group), not
TP-, model- or quant-driven.

**Expected behavior**

Step 6 returns the exact buried fact, identical to a cold run with no cache.
Concretely: `_SubpagedAttentionViewEdit` matches the registered KV layout on
vLLM >= 0.26, the registration-time re-view activates, all N kernel pages per
chunk are stored and restored, and a post-restart disk-tier restore returns the
same answers as a cold prefill.

**Screenshots**

N/A (server-side). Evidence available instead: per-chunk/per-rank md5 comparisons
of FA host objects on store vs restore, zero-fraction stats of stored objects,
and the restart-based verification suite below.

**Desktop (please complete the following information):**

 - OS: Linux (server)
 - LMCache: 0.5.3 wheel (also affects 0.5.4 and dev @ `1a430626` — file
   byte-identical), MP mode, LMCache server with separate object groups,
   L1 CPU + L2 local-disk tier
 - vLLM: 0.27.1 (`--mamba-cache-mode align`), TP=2 primary / TP=1 cross-check
 - Browser/Version: N/A

The verification environment was a pristine `lmcache==0.5.3` install plus our
4-file patch only. A local backport of #4600 (`error_block_ids` on retrieve
failure in `vllm_multi_process_adapter.py`) that the box previously carried was
reverted to stock before the run.

**Smartphone (please complete the following information):**

N/A

**Additional context**

We have a working, verified fix as a 4-file patch against the 0.5.3 wheel — no
vLLM changes needed, vLLM's block tables were correct throughout:
https://github.com/dl4rce/lmcache-hybrid-gdn-restore-fix (Apache-2.0;
`patches/lmcache-053-hybrid-fa.patch`, EXPLAINER.md walks the root cause).

Verification (12/12, 2026-08-22): full engine kill + restart, restore from the
L2 disk tier only, exact buried-key answer required. Measured on patch rev 2
(sha256 `ec14d5012…`) applied to a pristine `lmcache==0.5.3` install.

| Context | Restore E2E | Cold E2E | Speedup | Restore TTFT | Cold TTFT | Speedup | Hit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 5k tok  | 2.13 s | 5.62 s  | 2.6x | 1.00 s | 4.95 s  | 5.0x | 97.0% |
| 13k tok | 2.31 s | 13.08 s | 5.7x | 1.58 s | 12.62 s | 8.0x | 98.8% |
| 26k tok | 3.60 s | 27.41 s | 7.6x | 2.72 s | 26.97 s | 9.9x | 98.7% |

Cold-namespace control: 0

items.title: Eval bug: CUDA Q4_1/Q5_1 mat-vec kernels overflow fp16 when multiplying the block offset by the Q8_1 block sum (gpt-oss emits "G", NaN logits)
items.author: denizyuret
items.body_excerpt:
### Name and Version

```
version: 11800 (d454a204e)
built with GNU 13.2.0 for Linux x86_64 (CUDA 12.8, CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=90)
```

Also reproduced on b11538 (79e2e74eb). The affected code is unchanged on current master (b11803).

### Operating systems

Linux

### GGML backends

CUDA

### Hardware

NVIDIA H100 64 GB (MareNostrum 5 ACC), 1 to 2 GPUs

### Models

`openai/gpt-oss-120b` and `openai/gpt-oss-20b`, converted with `convert_hf_to_gguf.py --outtype bf16` (MXFP4 experts kept), expert tensors requantized with `llama-quantize` to Q4_1 (with an imatrix; the fault does not depend on it). Q5_1 uses the same kernel code and should be affected the same way (not tested).

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

gpt-oss with expert tensors quantized to Q4_1 intermittently writes the letter "G" into its replies, typically right after a control token (`<|channel|>Ganalysis`, `<|start|>Gassistant`), which breaks the Harmony parsing in llama-server (HTTP 500, "The model produced output that does not match the expected peg-native format"). Prompt processing is fine; the fault is in decoding, and with `-ub 8` (prompts through the mat-vec kernels too) 26 of 30 replies fail.

**Cause.** `vec_dot_q4_1_q8_1_impl` (and the `vec_dot_q5_1_q8_1_impl` and `vec_dot_q8_1_q8_1_impl` variants) in `ggml/src/ggml-cuda/vecdotq.cuh` compute `dm4 * ds8` with one fp16 `__hmul2` under `FAST_FP16_AVAILABLE`, i.e. `d4*d8` and `m4*s8` in fp16. `s8` is the sum of 32 activation values; gpt-oss has Q4_1 blocks whose offset `m4` reaches -512 (`blk.12.ffn_down_exps.weight`), so at tokens with large activations the product exceeds 65504 and becomes inf; the token's logits are NaN. The MMQ kernels multiply the same scales in fp32, which is why only decoding (and `-ub <= 8`) is affected. The non-fast-fp16 branch of the same function already multiplies in fp32.

**Reproduction.**

- `llama-server -ngl 999`, H100, GSM8K 5-shot chat prompts (`/v1/chat/completions`, about 800 tokens each), greedy: at default batching about 30 % of the 120B replies contain "G" and fail to parse (20B: 2 to 7 %); with `-ub 8`, 26 of 30. Q4_0 experts on the same prompts: none.
- The "G" is deterministic per prompt and position; it carries over within a slot because the NaN position stays in the KV cache.

**Fix (verified).** Multiply the scales in fp32 in the three functions:

```diff
-#ifdef FAST_FP16_AVAILABLE
-    const float2 tmp = __half22float2(__hmul2(dm4, ds8));
-    const float d4d8 = tmp.x;
-    const float m4s8 = tmp.y;
-#else
     const float2 dm4f = __half22float2(dm4);
     const float2 ds8f = __half22float2(ds8);
     const float d4d8 = dm4f.x * ds8f.x;
     const float m4s8 = dm4f.y * ds8f.y;
-#endif // FAST_FP16_AVAILABLE
```

and the same for `vec_dot_q5_1_q8_1_impl` (dm5) and `vec_dot_q8_1_q8_1_impl` (dm8).

Verified on H100 (b11800 + this change): 120B Q4_1, first 30 GSM8K and 30 ARC questions, 0 malformed replies, GSM8K 28/30 (default batching) and 29/30 (`-ub 8`), ARC 30/30 and 30/30; before the fix at `-ub 8`: 3/30 and 3/30 with 26 malformed each. No measurable decode slowdown. I am not opening a PR; the diff is here for whoever maintains the CUDA kernels (there may be a cheaper fix, e.g. keeping fp16 for `d4*d8` only).

A second, independent fp16 overflow affects gpt-oss with IQ1_M/TQ1_0/TQ2_0 experts (the dequantize + cuBLAS fallback), reported separately.

### First Bad Commit

Not bisected; present in b11538 and b11800. The fp16 `__hmul2` scale product is old code.

### Relevant log output

```
W common_chat_peg_parse: unparsed peg-native output: <|channel|>Ganalysis<|message|>We need to compute 17*23. 17*20 = 340, 17*3 = 51, sum = 391. So answer: 391. The user wants "the number only after thinking it through." So just output "391".<|end|><|start|>assistant<|channel|>final<|message|>391
W srv          stop: cancel task, id_task = 0
W srv    operator(): got exception: {"error":{"code":500,"message":"The model produced output that does not match the expected peg-native format","type":"server_error"}}
```

items.title: sglang:cache_hit_rate gauge drops to 0.0 on prefill reports with zero tokens
items.author: cshintov
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] 1. I have searched related issues but cannot get the expected help.
- [x] 2. The bug has not been fixed in the latest version.
- [x] 3. I have provided environment info and a reproduction.
- [x] 4. This is a bug report, not a question.
- [x] 5. Written in English.

### Describe the bug

`sglang:cache_hit_rate` oscillates between the true value and `0.0` under normal serving load.

In `SchedulerMetricsReporter.report_prefill_stats`, the hit rate is computed as:

```python
total_tokens = effective_input_tokens + effective_hit_tokens
cache_hit_rate = effective_hit_tokens / total_tokens if total_tokens > 0 else 0.0
...
self.stats.cache_hit_rate = cache_hit_rate
```

When `total_tokens == 0` the expression yields `0.0`, and that `0.0` is **assigned to `self.stats.cache_hit_rate`
and published** by the `self.metrics_collector.log_stats(self.stats)` call a few lines later. It is not a
"no data" signal — it is a real, exported zero.

So any Prometheus query over the gauge (`avg_over_time`, `rate`, Grafana panels, alert rules) is dragged
down by samples that carry no information. On a server with a genuine ~96% prefix-cache hit rate the
gauge alternates between ~0.96 and 0.0, which reads as a broken cache.

This is distinct from #12459 / PR #24427, which fixed the **decode** path overwriting the gauge
(the `# cache_hit_rate is prefill-owned (per-report semantics); decode ticks must not reset it`
comment at `report_decode_stats`). The decode path is fine. The remaining leak is the prefill path
publishing a fabricated `0.0` computed from a zero-denominator **prefill report**, not from zero hits.

### Measured evidence

Sampling `sglang:cache_hit_rate` every 4 s on a live server under normal load:

```
12:43:19 gauge=0.9915966386554622
12:43:23 gauge=0.0
12:43:27 gauge=0.0
12:43:32 gauge=0.9333333333333333
12:43:36 gauge=0.0
12:43:40 gauge=0.9583333333333334
12:43:44 gauge=0.9583333333333334
12:43:48 gauge=0.9583333333333334
```

The same server's cumulative counters show the cache is healthy:

```
sglang:prompt_tokens_total  = 44,012,237
sglang:cached_tokens_total  = 36,287,744   -> 82.4% overall hit rate
```

and `usage.prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens` returns 7,424 of 7,625 prompt tokens (97.4%) on a warm
repeat. The gauge is the only place the cache looks broken.

### Reproduction

1. Start a server with `--enable-metrics` and prefix caching (default).
2. Generate load with a mix of short and long prompts, e.g. `bench_serving` or a looping client.
3. `watch -n1 "curl -s localhost:30000/metrics | grep ^sglang:cache_hit_rate"`
4. The value will intermittently drop to `0.0` while the counters continue to show a high hit rate.

### Expected behaviour

A report that carries no cache information should not overwrite the gauge. Either:

- skip the assignment and leave the previous value in place (matching the decode-path fix in #24427), or
- publish `NaN` so Prometheus/`avg_over_time` ignores the sample.

### Environment

- SGLang built from source, `0.0.0.dev0`, upstream `main` @ `f86a04a` (2026-10-19)
- 3× NVIDIA DGX Spark, TP=3, `--enable-metrics`
- Model: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash
- Also observed with `--enable-priority-scheduling`

### Proposed fix

I have a patch ready and will open a PR against `main` that skips the gauge write when
`total_tokens == 0`, keeping the last known-good value, plus a unit test. Happy to adjust if
maintainers prefer the `NaN` variant.

items.title: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 on two 16 GB RTX 5070 Ti with the routed experts on the CPU (SGLang + KTransformers, 1M context)
items.author: 05yuki
items.body_excerpt:
https://github.com/05yuki/deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017-ktransformers runs DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 on one machine with ordinary GPUs:

- **CPU:** the 384 routed experts a layer run on the CPU in MXFP4, through KTransformers' kt-kernel.
- **GPU:** attention, the most-used experts and the prefill run on the GPUs, through SGLang.
- **Disk:** the engram tables (~200 GB) are read straight from the checkpoint.

The repository holds patches against SGLang main `9c0f6d6a` and KTransformers `95009ea`, plus a `setup.sh` that builds them and a `serve.sh` that sizes the launch to the machine.

## Results

Hardware: 2 × EPYC 7452 (Zen 2, AVX2), 512 GB DDR4, 2 × RTX 5070 Ti 16 GB (SM120), TP2.

Every row was measured with the repository's `tools/bench.py` at tag `2026-10-23-0135`. Each table comes from a single launch.

Decode, 1,024 tokens a reply:

| Text | tok/s |
|---|---|
| Japanese prose | 47.1 |
| Chinese prose | 40.6 |
| Math | 40.0 |
| English prose | 38.5 |
| JSON | 37.2 |
| English technical prose | 35.4 |
| Python code | 35.3 |

Prefill, one prompt of random token ids:

| Prompt (tokens) | tok/s | Time |
|---|---|---|
| 35,000 | 1,301 | 27 s |
| 131,072 | 1,515 | 1.4 min |
| 524,288 | 1,209 | 7.2 min |
| 1,000,000 | 943 | 18 min |

One card (TP1) also runs, at 32.0 tok/s decode on Japanese prose.

## Accuracy

The served model is scored against the checkpoint's own `inference/model.py`. The reference runs one layer at a time on one 16 GB card. Both score the same 24 pieces of 480 tokens from two public-domain texts, one Japanese and one English, teacher-forced. Results at tag `2026-10-23-1702`:

| Run | Mean NLL | Minus the reference (SE over the pieces) |
|---|---|---|
| Reference | 0.7185 | |
| Served, two GPUs | 0.7181 | -0.0004 (0.0040) |
| Served, one GPU | 0.7194 | +0.0008 (0.0050) |

The scripts are in the repo, `tools/ref-nll.py` and `tools/nll.py`, so anyone can rerun this; the reference takes about 4 minutes and needs no server.

## Upstream

Fixes we found along the way, sent as PRs:

- #45810: the KT path applied the routed scaling factor twice after #44993. NLL drops from 2.878 to 2.596.
- #45851: the V4.1 KV cache layouts on SM120 / SM121, through FlashInfer's SM120 sparse MLA.
- #45745: the torch indexer scores its chunk in place (3 → 1 GiB).
- #45183, #45185, #45188: the KT expert mask, the FP8 qdq of the attention output that V4.1-Flash-1017 needs, and zero GPU experts.
- #45184: a configurable load barrier timeout.
- #45931: the pool configurator costs a ratio-1/2 compressed KV entry at 584 bytes, but V41_FP4 entries are 288. On one card this takes the pool from 98,560 to 180,480 tokens.

Earlier PRs from the same setup:

- #39605: a host-staged all-reduce for two GPUs without peer access (the repository's tier 2).
- #41350: kt reads num_hidden_layers from text_config for multimodal checkpoints.
- On kvcache-ai/sglang:
  - kvcache-ai/sglang#83 (merged): the compressed-attention pool honours --max-total-tokens.
  - kvcache-ai/sglang#84: partial-expert Marlin MoE.
  - kvcache-ai/sglang#97: the KT GPU-expert remap without expert-location metadata.
  - kvcache-ai/sglang#98: VRAM for the full-GPU prefill slot.
  - kvcache-ai/sglang#103: shard loaders that skip the CPU experts.

GGUF work for the same CPU/GPU hybrid on other models: #43427, #43430, #43445, #43626, #43636, #43650, #43677.

The rest of the repository is specific to running experts on the CPU. It covers:

- streaming the experts for prefill;
- lending free KV pages to the most-used experts;
- an all-reduce through host memory for GPUs without peer access.

The tiers and the effect of each patch are in [docs/patches.md](https://github.com/05yuki/deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017-ktransformers/blob/main/docs/patches.md).

If any of these would be useful upstream, we are glad to split them into PRs.

items.body_excerpt:
Working on a kernel I got a CompilationError when trying to launch it, and while the CompilationError message points to the "problem" it doesn't specify what the problem is.  I eventually figured out that it doesn't like when you call `load` with `other` set but `mask` set to None.  I don't mind that restriction, but it would be nice if the CompilationError message said something to that effect.  I didn't see any specifics in the error message.  Perhaps it's buried in the traceback, but the trackback gets truncated in Jupyter notebooks because it's so exceedingly long.

Triton version 2.0.0.dev20221202

The kernel:

```
@triton.jit
def _clip_embed_fused(
	A,         # *Pointer* to first input vector (257xN).
	Out,       # *Pointer* to output vector (257xN).
	Position,  # *Pointer* position vector (257xN).
	Weight,    # *Pointer* weight vector (N).
	Bias,      # *Pointer* bias vector (N).
	eps: tl.constexpr,
):
	# position of elements processed by this program
	row = tl.program_id(0)
	Out += row * 1024
	A += row * 1024
	Position += row * 1024

	# loads
	cols = tl.arange(0, 1024)
	mask = cols < 1024
	a = tl.load(A + cols, other=0.).to(tl.float32)
	weight = tl.load(Weight + cols)
	bias = tl.load(Bias + cols)
	position = tl.load(Position + cols, other=0.).to(tl.float32)

	# position embedding
	a += position

	# compute mean
	mean = tl.sum(a, axis=0) / 1024

	# compute variance
	var = tl.sum((a - mean) * (a - mean), axis=0) / 1024
	rstd = 1 / tl.sqrt(var + eps)

	# multiply by weight and add bias
	a_hat = (a - mean) * rstd
	out = a_hat * weight + bias

	# write-back

items.title: SIGSEGV in torch::jit::invokeOperatorFromPython (transpose) with NVFP4 + DFlash + torch.compile on Blackwell SM120
items.author: windboat01
items.body_excerpt:
## Bug Description

vLLM (v0.24.0) crashes with SIGSEGV in `torch::jit::invokeOperatorFromPython` during `THPVariable_transpose` when serving a **NVFP4-quantized** Qwen3.6-27B model with **DFlash speculative decoding + torch.compile (inductor) + CUDA graph PIECEWISE** mode on **NVIDIA Blackwell (SM 12.0)** hardware.

The crash is deterministic under continuous load, occurring after 20–36 minutes of serving 8 concurrent requests. Disabling torch.compile (`--enforce-eager`) avoids the crash but incurs ~50% generation throughput loss.

## Crash Signature

```
Signal: SIGSEGV
C++ stack trace:
  #0  signal_handler(int)
  #1  handler(int, siginfo_t*, void*)
  #3  torch::jit::invokeOperatorFromPython(...)
      at /workspace/torch/csrc/jit/python/script_class_alias_analysis.cpp:12
  #4  THPVariable_transpose
      at /workspace/torch/csrc/autograd/python_variable.cpp:0
  #5  PythonArgParser::raw_parse(...)
      at /workspace/torch/csrc/utils/python_arg_parser.cpp:117
```

The crash manifests as an `EngineDeadError` propagated to the API server:

```
vllm.v1.engine.exceptions.EngineDeadError: EngineCore encountered an issue.
```

`TORCH_SHOW_CPP_STACKTRACES=1` output shows the crash always occurs in the `transpose` call path, originating from Python argument parsing code reading corrupted memory.

## Environment

| Component | Version |
|-----------|---------|
| vLLM | 0.24.0 |
| PyTorch | 2.11.0+cu130 (GCC 13.3) |
| CUDA (torch) | 13.0 |
| cuDNN | 91900 |
| Driver | NVIDIA 595.71.05 |
| GPU | NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Max-Q (SM 12.0, 96 GiB) |
| Python | 3.12.3 |
| FlashInfer | 0.6.14 |
| DeepGEMM | vendored (vllm.third_party.deep_gemm) |
| OS | Ubuntu 24.04 LTS (Noble) |

## Model & Quantization

- **Target model**: Huihui-Qwen3.6-27B-abliterated-NVFP4-MTP (ModelOpt NVFP4 quantization)
- **Draft model**: Qwen3.6-27B-DFlash (DFlash head, 5 speculative tokens)
- **GEMM kernel**: FlashInferB12xNvFp4LinearKernel (autotuned fp4_gemm)

## Reproduction (vLLM launch args)

```bash
python -m vllm.entrypoints.openai.api_server \
  --model /path/to/Huihui-Qwen3.6-27B-abliterated-NVFP4-MTP \
  --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 \
  --dtype auto \
  --trust-remote-code \
  --max-model-len 262144 \
  --max-num-seqs 8 \
  --enable-prefix-caching \
  --max-num-batched-tokens 16384 \
  --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \
  --reasoning-parser qwen3 \
  --log-error-stack \
  --aggregate-engine-logging \
  --speculative-config '{"method":"dflash","model":"/path/to/Qwen3.6-27B-DFlash","num_speculative_tokens":5,"draft_sample_method":"probabilistic"}'
```

## Logs (selected, 17:14–18:50 startup)

```
(EngineCore pid=40033) INFO 07-10 17:14:34 [__init__.py:939] Using FlashInferB12xNvFp4LinearKernel for NVFP4 GEMM
(EngineCore pid=40033) INFO 07-10 17:14:37 [llm_base_proposer.py:1350] Detected EAGLE model without its own embed_tokens...
(EngineCore pid=40033) INFO 07-10 17:14:49 [compilation.py:1405] CUDAGraphMode.FULL_AND_PIECEWISE is not supported with spec-decode for attention backend FlashInferBackend; setting cudagraph_mode=PIECEWISE
(EngineCore pid=40033) INFO 07-10 17:14:54 [deep_gemm.py:202] DeepGEMM PDL enabled on vllm.third_party.deep_gemm.
(EngineCore pid=40033) [AutoTuner]: Autotuning fp4_gemm... (22 profiles)
(EngineCore pid=40033) Capturing CUDA graphs (mixed prefill-decode, PIECEWISE): 15/15
(EngineCore pid=40033) INFO 07-10 17:15:20 [jit_monitor.py:60] Kernel JIT monitor activated
(APIServer pid=39942) INFO 07-10 17:15:50 [metrics.py:120] Acceptance rate: 62.7%, Accepted: 627.45 tok/s
(APIServer pid=39942) INFO 07-10 17:15:50 [loggers.py:273] Generation throughput: 829.6 tok/s
```

The server starts successfully, serves requests with high throughput (~800 tok/s generation, ~2600 tok/s prompt), then crashes after 20–36 minutes under continuous 8-concurrent-request load. No error log before the SIGSEGV — it leaves no recoverable stack in the vLLM log file because the C++ signal handler writes to stderr while Python-level logging is already failing.

The crash is non-deterministic in exact timing but is guaranteed under sustained load. Multiple restart cycles show the same pattern: 1–5 successful minutes → crash → restart. Memory corruption accumulates over time.

## Analysis & Suspected Root Cause

The crash in `torch::jit::invokeOperatorFromPython` → `THPVariable_transpose` → `PythonArgParser::raw_parse` (SIGSEGV) indicates that the C++ `PythonArgParser` is reading corrupted memory when parsing arguments for the `transpose` operation. This is a classical delayed-manifestation pattern:

1. **Primary suspect**: The cuBLASLt heuristic (used indirectly via FlashInfer's NVFP4 GEMM autotuner) corrupts memory during autotuning or execution on Blackwell SM 12.0 silicon. This is a known stability vector:
   - vLLM issue [#35566](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/35566): "NVFP4 on SM120 CUDA illegal memory access" (resolved via `--moe-backend marlin` for MoE models)
   - flashinfer issue [#3085](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/issues/3085): "cuBLAS bmm_fp8 autotune segfault in Blackwell" (driver/RTX PRO 6000 specific)

2. **Secondary factor**: The PIECEWISE CUDA graph mode may entangle corrupted state across graph segments, as the corruption is already present in the graph-captured buffer state.

3. **Why torch.compile is hit hardest**: When torch.compile is active, the `transpose` operation lands in a JIT-compiled graph fragment. The JIT interpreter (`invokeOperatorFromPython`) reads tensor metadata that was written by the CUDA graph replay — if the underlying tensor data/metadata was corrupted earlier by NVFP4 GEMM kernel, the `PythonArgParser` dereferences an invalid pointer and segfaults.

## Additional Observations

- Setting `--enforce-eager` (disabling both torch.compile and CUDA graphs) avoids the crash completely but reduces generation throughput from ~800 tok/s to ~400 tok/s.
- Setting `VLLM_CUTLASS_PREFER_DISABLE_CUBLASLT=1` does NOT avoid the crash (the NVFP4 GE

items.title: [Feature]: SM8x (Ampere A100/A800) support for DeepSeek-V4-Flash / DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 DSpark
items.author: thomaslwang
items.body_excerpt:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

DeepSeek released [DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731](https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731) today (same `DeepseekV4ForCausalLM` architecture as DeepSeek-V4-Flash). Neither checkpoint currently runs on SM8x (Ampere: A100/A800, RTX 30xx) — #40851 tracks the (substantial) user demand; this issue proposes and tracks a concrete contribution.

I have a working prototype on 8x A800 80GB (vLLM main @ `a074fd564` + a rebased community kernel set + fixes below): **40.6 tok/s single-stream decode** with cudagraphs, batch-8 at ~115 tok/s aggregate, boots at `max_model_len=1,048,576`, and retrieves a needle exactly from a 200k-token context. Quality validated (multi-step arithmetic, code generation, needle retrieval). So SM8x support is feasible with Triton/PyTorch fallbacks at usable speeds — no new CUDA required.

**Verified blocker chain on SM8x (main, empirical):**
1. Triton on SM80 cannot emit `fp8e4nv`: hits `_fused_inv_rope_fp8_quant_per_head` (o_proj path) and every fp8 KV-cache write kernel; fp8 KV is mandatory for DSv4. (Workaround exists: manual e4m3 bit manipulation, proven in the community fork.)
2. `flash_mla_sparse_fwd` is SM90a/SM100f-only; DSv4 decode additionally needs the dual-cache (`extra_k_cache`) + `attn_sink` + per-token-topk variant. A portable Triton bf16 sparse-MLA path works (community fork).
3. DeepGEMM `fp8_einsum` (o_proj) and MegaMoE are Hopper+; bf16 reference path (`rocm_inv_rope_einsum`, already in-tree for ROCm/XPU) works.
4. `wo_a` (`is_bmm` layer) gets Marlin-repacked to int32 while the DSv4 o_proj consumes the raw block-fp8 weight — needs a repack exclusion.

Already working on SM8x with no changes: the indexer Triton fallbacks (`fp8_mqa_logits_triton` / `fp8_paged_mqa_logits_triton`), MXFP4 experts via MarlinExperts, fp8 linear via Marlin.

**Bugs found while prototyping (arch-independent, will send as a separate small PR):**
- **int32 pointer-arithmetic overflow in `_fp8_paged_mqa_logits_kernel`** (`vllm/v1/attention/ops/mqa_logits_triton.py`): `block_idx` (int32, from the block table) is multiplied by the KV-pool block stride without an int64 cast. With the unified KV pool the per-layer view stride is ~1e6 elements, so the product wraps for `block_idx ≥ ~2065` → illegal memory access, or **silent corruption** when the wrapped address lands in mapped memory. Every other pool-accessing Triton kernel in-tree already casts (`.to(tl.int64)`). This affects **any model using the SM80/SM121 indexer fallback** (DSv4 and GLM DSA alike) once the pool exceeds ~2k blocks — i.e. exactly under long-context or concurrent load.
- Same kernel's tail store is masked only by `mask_n`, not `k_offset < context_len` (writes past the row for tail blocks).
- `mhc_pre_broadcast_tilelang` calls DeepGEMM `tf32_hc_prenorm_gemm` unconditionally — its siblings guard on `is_deep_gemm_supported()` and fall back to `_tilelang_hc_prenorm_gemm`; the broadcast variant missed the guard. This is the `hyperconnection.hpp:56 Unsupported architecture` error reported in #40851.
- `fused_inv_rope_fp8_quant`: `launch_pdl` is a declared kernel parameter but the non-PDL branch omits it → `TypeError` on every pre-Hopper arch.

**Proposed contribution plan:**
1. **PR A (small, immediate):** the arch-independent fixes above (int64 cast + tail-store mask; DeepGEMM guard; `launch_pdl`). These fix real crashes/corruption independent of any new backend.
2. **PR B:** SM8x enablement for DeepSeek-V4 — an `ampere/` hardware backend under `vllm/models/deepseek_v4/` mirroring the existing `xpu/` layout (portable Triton bf16 sparse-MLA decode/prefill, manual-e4m3 cache writes, bf16 o_proj, Marlin repack exclusion for `is_bmm`, fused Triton MHC gates+sinkhorn for the hyperconnection layers), gated on `capability.major == 8`. This builds on the kernels from the community fork [Lasimeri/vllm-dsv4-ampere](https://github.com/Lasimeri/vllm-dsv4-ampere) (with credit), rebased onto current main, plus the fixes and the MHC fusion.

I'm aware of the sentiment that SM<90 for DSv4 "better lives in a fork" (PR #40906 discussion). Given the fleet sizes reported in #40851 and that this is all Python/Triton behind an arch gate (no new build targets, no impact on SM90+ paths), I'd like to ask maintainers whether a gated `ampere/` backend PR would be considered. If the answer is fork-only, PR A still stands on its own.

### Alternatives

- Keep SM8x support in out-of-tree forks (status quo): fragments quickly against main; the corruption-class bug above still needs an in-tree fix either way.
- llama.cpp `dsv4` branch: works but lacks vLLM's serving stack (continuous batching, prefix caching, OpenAI API parity).

### Additional context

Hardware: 8x NVIDIA A800 80GB PCIe (SM80), single node. All findings verified empirically on this machine against main @ `a074fd564`; happy to share full logs/repros. Analysis and prototyping were AI-assisted; I have validated every change and result end-to-end on the target hardware and will own the PRs.

Related: #40851 (user demand thread), PR #38476 / #47629 (GLM DSA SM8x sparse-MLA, same indexer fallback infrastructure).

items.title: [Bug]: Cross-request context contamination via shared-prefix KV reuse in PD disaggregation with automatic prefix caching — clean with `--no-enable-prefix-caching`
items.author: Siquan-Li
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

With automatic prefix caching enabled (the default) in a NIXL prefill/decode disaggregated deployment serving DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, responses intermittently contain **content from other requests** — cross-request context contamination ("crosstalk"). We have a scriptable reproducer on `/v1/chat/completions` (details below): with a long **identical shared prefix** across requests, 46/48 *sequential* requests returned another request's canary code; at concurrency 128 it was 122/128. Disabling prefix caching on the prefill node **and** all decode nodes (`--no-enable-prefix-caching`) eliminated the contamination.

## Deployment topology (at reproduction time)

```
Clients (multi-turn agent sessions; every request starts with the same large system prompt)
        |
        v
vllm-router 0.1.15  --policy round_robin --kv-connector nixl   (port 30000)
        |
   +----+------------------+
   v                       v
Prefill node              2x Decode nodes
1x node, 8x H100, TP=8    1x node each, 8x H100, TP=8
kv_producer  :8001        kv_consumer  :8002
        \____ NIXL KV transfer ____/
```

(Since 2026-10-12 we run 2P1D; all reproduction data below was collected on the 1P2D topology above.)

## Environment

- vLLM 0.31.0, built from main @ `db9527a46` (2026-10-02), local build tagged `+cu129`; torch 2.13.0+cu129, transformers 5.17.0, nixl 1.4.1
- Driver 550.54.15, nodes of 8× H100 80GB (sm90)
- Model: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (1M context), `FLASHMLA_SPARSE_DSV41` attention backend, block size 64
- Speculative decoding: `{"method":"dspark","num_speculative_tokens":5,"draft_sample_method":"probabilistic","rejection_sample_method":"block","enable_adaptive_verification":true}`
- `--max-num-batched-tokens 4096 --max-num-seqs 32 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.92`
- Note: PR #57662 (fix for #57661) was **not merged** at the time of writing, so this build cannot contain it.

## Symptom

Every request shares a long common prefix — in the wild this was Claude Code on the Anthropic-compatible `/v1/messages` endpoint, whose fixed large system prompt is identical across all sessions. With automatic prefix caching on, users in **different, unrelated sessions** intermittently received responses containing content from *another* session (the model "remembered" details, file names, or instructions belonging to someone else's conversation). Affected requests completed with HTTP 200; no errors or warnings in server logs.

## Reproducer (scriptable, `/v1/chat/completions`)

Design: N requests, each consisting of a **long identical shared prefix** plus a per-request distinct tail that embeds a unique canary code. After all responses complete, each output is scanned for canary codes belonging to *other* requests ("foreign" hits).

Results with automatic prefix caching **enabled** (default):

| Scenario | Requests | Outputs containing a foreign canary code |
|---|---|---|
| Sequential (C=1) | 48 | **46/48** |
| Concurrent (C=128) | 128 | **122/128** |

Key observations:

- Concurrency is **not** required — sequential single-stream requests contaminate at ~96%. Sharing a long identical prefix is the trigger.
- Canaries that varied the prefix, or shared only long *suffixes*, did **not** reproduce; earlier negative canary results were a design gap, not evidence against the bug.
- With `--no-enable-prefix-caching` on P **and** both D nodes: 0 foreign hits, and the Claude Code symptom disappeared entirely (verified by the same users plus a 16-way concurrent keepalive, ~3,000 rounds over 17 h).

The canary script is available on request.

## What we have *not* isolated

- We disabled prefix caching on all three nodes at once, so we cannot attribute the reuse to the prefill-side cache, the decode-side cache, or the P↔D KV-transfer interplay (e.g. a consumer trusting producer block IDs for freed/reused blocks, or refcount/eviction asymmetry between P and D).
- No root-cause analysis on the vLLM side yet; happy to invest in narrowing this down with maintainer guidance.

## Hypothesis (unverified)

Under PD disaggregation, prefix-cache blocks belonging to a completed request are re-served to a later request that hashes to the same shared prefix, but the physical KV content behind those blocks has been freed/reassigned — so the later request decodes against another request's KV. The serial (C=1) repro suggests the race is between request completion/reuse bookkeeping rather than simultaneous scheduling.

## Why this is not #57661

#57661 (and fix PR #57662 — still unmerged) describes NIXL transfer regions deduplicated by `base_addr` alone, truncating the compressor `state_cache` transfer for hybrid-attention layers, producing **garbled/empty output**. Our failure mode is different:

1. Symptom: our outputs are coherent but contain **another request's content**; we never observed garbling or empty content/reasoning fields.
2. Toggle sensitivity: our contamination disappears completely with `--no-enable-prefix-caching`; the region-geometry bug in #57661 is independent of the prefix-caching toggle.
3. Mechanism: truncated/misaligned compressor state cannot inject well-formed content from a different request.

We plan to validate our repro against #57662's branch as well, to rule out any interaction; both issues affect the same model + NIXL PD combination with silent HTTP-200 failures.

## Related issues

- #57661 — NIXL P/D silent output corruption (hybrid-attention region dedup), fix PR #57662 (unmerged at writing)
- #56009 — request/response cross-talk symptom, no root cause identified
- #52627 — silent output corruption in 1P1D NIXL PD, different connector combination
- #47930 — DSpark draft acceptance collapse with automatic prefix caching (another prefix-caching × disaggregation interaction)

## Offer

We keep a H100 1P2D/2P1D testbed with this exact model and can: share the canary script, run targeted repro attempts on candidate patches (including #57662), or provide `collect_env.py` output on request.

items.title: [Bug][DSv4.1][SM120] enable_adaptive_verification is rejected on SM120 — device-query-lens support is gated to SM90/SM100 only
items.author: Lei-010
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment

```
vLLM             : 0.31.1rc1.dev253+g7d0b4e57a
PyTorch          : 2.13.0+cu130
GPU              : 8 × NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell (SM120), PCIe, no NVLink
Model            : DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (published DSpark config)
Driver / CUDA    : 570.x / 13.0
```

Relevant serve flags:

```bash
--tensor-parallel-size 8 --block-size 64 --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \
--attention-config '{"indexer_kv_dtype":"fp8"}' \
--speculative-config '{"method":"dspark","num_speculative_tokens":3,"enable_adaptive_verification":true}' \
--max-cudagraph-capture-size 512 --max-model-len 1048576 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.93
```

### 🐛 Describe the bug

Adding `enable_adaptive_verification: true` to the DSpark speculative config makes engine startup fail
deterministically on SM120, in `profile_cudagraph_memory` (i.e. before the engine is ever up):

```
ValueError: Adaptive verification trims verification requests on device, which the
DeepseekV41IndexerBackend attention backend does not support. Pass
enable_adaptive_verification=false in the speculative config, or use a backend that does.
```

Stack (trimmed):

```
gpu_worker.py:671   in determine_available_memory
    cudagraph_memory_estimate = self.model_runner.profile_cudagraph_memory()
...
adaptive_verification.py:465-470  maybe_create_adaptive_verification_manager
    # The selector rejects unsupported backends, but models that
    # hard-wire theirs (e.g. DeepSeek-V4) never go through it.
    backend = get_query_lens_mismatch_unsupported_backend(...)
    if backend is not None: raise ValueError(...)
```

The same config with `enable_adaptive_verification: false` (or omitted) serves fine, so this is a
capability gate, not a runtime failure.

### Root cause

`DeepseekV41IndexerBackend` is hard-wired for DeepSeek-V4.1
(`vllm/models/deepseek_v4_1/attention.py:get_attn_backend`), so it bypasses the backend selector and
reaches `supports_device_cpu_query_lens_mismatch()` directly:

```python
# vllm/v1/attention/backends/mla/indexer.py
class DeepseekV32IndexerBackend(AttentionBackend):
    @classmethod
    def supports_device_cpu_query_lens_mismatch(cls) -> bool:
        # Only the varlen paged MQA logits kernel takes per-request query
        # lengths from device tensors natively. Hopper can instead flatten each
        # query into a single-token row using device-built metadata.
        return _supports_varlen_paged_mqa_logits() or _supports_flattened_device_query_lens()

def _supports_varlen_paged_mqa_logits() -> bool:
    return current_platform.is_cuda() and current_platform.is_device_capability_family(100) and has_deep_gemm()

def _supports_flattened_device_query_lens() -> bool:
    return current_platform.is_cuda() and current_platform.is_device_capability_family(90) and has_deep_gemm()

class DeepseekV4IndexerBackend(DeepseekV32IndexerBackend):
    @classmethod
    def supports_device_cpu_query_lens_mismatch(cls) -> bool:
        return current_platform.is_rocm() or super().supports_device_cpu_query_lens_mismatch()
```

SM120 is in neither capability family, and there is no SM120 branch — so adaptive verification is
unreachable on this hardware regardless of the rest of the config. ROCm got an explicit path
(`_rocm_supports_flattened_device_query_lens()`, from #56620), and #62515 is doing the analogous
thing for `FlashInferMLASparseSM90Backend`. SM120 (and presumably SM121/GB10) has no equivalent.

### Why this matters (measured motivation for a fixed draft length being wrong)

We ran a same-machine A/B on this box (same image, cold start per arm, only
`num_speculative_tokens` / `enable_adaptive_verification` differ; engine counters sampled from
`/metrics`; `k_effective` equals the configured k in every fixed arm, so the arms behaved as configured):

| load | k=3 tok/s | accept | k=7 tok/s | accept | Δ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| single stream | 168.0 | – | 152.6 | – | −9.2% |
| c=8 greedy | 624.9 | 47.3% | 467.0 | 25.1% | −25.3% |
| c=8 sampled (T=0.7) | 520.2 | 44.7% | 392.7 | 23.4% | −24.5% |
| c=32 greedy | 1216.1 | 60.4% | 1297.5 | 35.5% | **+6.7%** |
| c=64 greedy | 2020.9 | 59.7% | 1480.7 | 35.6% | −26.7% |
| c=128 greedy | 2818.2 | 59.8% | 1729.6 | 35.2% | −38.6% |

Acceptance moves from 47% at c=8 to ~60% at c≥32 on the *same* k=3 config, i.e. the optimal draft
depth is a function of the running batch — exactly the regime adaptive verification is designed for,
and here no fixed k is good: k=7 wins only at c=32 and loses up to 38.6% at c=128. This is the
strongest argument we can produce that the SM120 gap is worth closing rather than "use k=3".

### Question / ask

1. Is SM120 excluded from `_supports_*_device_query_lens()` deliberately (missing kernel on
   SM120), or just not covered yet?
2. If the flattened path (`#62515` style, `get_varlen_cudagraph_max_query_len`) is reachable on
   SM120, would extending the capability check be enough? We are happy to test a patch and report
   numbers on 8×RTX PRO 6000.
3. Related: on SM120 our FlashInfer runtime page sizes are `[None, 1, 4, 128]` — block size 64 is
   absent (we run `--block-size 64` via #60762). If the varlen paged MQA logits kernel is what gates
   SM120, that missing page size may be the real blocker; if so this issue is downstream of #60762
   and can be closed against it.

Happy to attach the full logs, per-arm `docker inspect` JSON, and the bench harness if useful.

items.title: What is the first practical limit of persistent KV across Agent steps?
items.author: RyanX0198
items.body_excerpt:
Hi maintainers — I’m Rui from Psync.labs. Recent sampling and decode-interface work led me to a question about long-running local Agent workloads.

Persistent KV could reduce repeated prefill, but only if cache identity, layout, eviction and framework boundaries stay correct as models, adapters and stages change. Which condition is most likely to invalidate the idea in practice: layout incompatibility, model or tokenizer changes, fragmentation, eviction quality loss, scheduler interference, or missing cross-framework contracts?

One counterexample or minimum test would be especially useful. @yzh119

— Rui, Psync.labs

comments.author: eprogressing
comments.body:
For an agent that changes adapters or rewrites its prompt between steps, I would check **cache identity/correctness before fragmentation or scheduling**. That is a conditional priority, not a measured ranking of workloads.

A concrete counterexample is switching from adapter A to adapter B while retaining A's KV. If B changes the value projection (or earlier hidden states), identical token IDs and identical tensor shapes do not make those cached values valid for B. Similarly, editing earlier tool results breaks reuse past the unchanged token prefix in an ordinary causal transformer. Rendering the same conversation differently can also change that prefix.

I would start with this small integration test:

1. Under A, prefill a short token prefix P, then process suffix S using the cached prefix. Compare the next-token logits with a fresh A forward pass on P+S, within an appropriate numerical tolerance.
2. Use a distinct, nonzero B adapter that affects `v_proj`. Repeat with a fresh B prefill as the reference. Your cache manager should reject A's cache; forcibly reusing it is the negative control, which can expose a discrepancy.
3. Edit one early token in P and verify that cache lookup stops at the unchanged prefix. Check logits, rather than just generated text: argmax can hide a difference.

This is consistent with [vLLM's prefix-cache design](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/design/prefix_caching/), which keys blocks using the parent hash, block tokens and extra hashes such as LoRA IDs. Adapter IDs also need versioning/invalidation if their weights can change in place.

After that, check the storage contract separately: [FlashInfer's KV layout documentation](https://docs.flashinfer.ai/tutorials/kv_layout.html) specifies NHD/HND layouts and page metadata. Matching semantics alone does not make a buffer portable between frameworks.

Prepared with Codex assistance from the linked documentation. The integration test above was initially a proposal; the execution update below now supplies an actual mechanism test. Is your agent retaining one model/adapter with append-only history, or switching adapters and rewriting history?


---
**GPU experiment update (2026-10-11):** I ran the actual Transformers/PEFT forward path on an A100-SXM4-40GB, plus CPU controls: Torch 2.14.1+cu130, Transformers 5.19.0, PEFT 0.21.2. This is a random three-layer Llama (hidden 64, four attention heads/two KV heads), with rank-four v_proj LoRA; it does not exercise FlashInfer's attention kernel or a production agent cache manager.

Across seeds 0/1/2, CPU/CUDA and float32/float64, all 72 comparison expectations held. Correct same-adapter reuse, an adapter-name change with exactly zero update, and reuse limited to the two tokens preceding a prefix edit agreed with fresh forwarding (maximum absolute logit error <=1.49e-7; predeclared tolerances float32 1e-5 / float64 1e-10). Forcibly reusing A's KV with nonzero B produced max-absolute differences 0.2205–0.2727; retaining the old full prefix after the edit produced 0.1082–0.2622. Each stale-cache case changed argmax in only 4/12 trials, so comparing all logits matters. Each path used a newly created cache with asserted sequence lengths.

This supports the specific correctness counterexample, not a universal ranking against fragmentation/scheduling. It does not measure answer quality, throughput, cross-framework layout compatibility, or automatic rejection by a cache manager. [Reproduction scripts, full inputs/logits, versions and results](https://gist.github.com/eprogressing/84db3e068aabbe449f8629a3f362a6e5). Prepared with Codex assistance; these runs were actually executed.

items.title: Qwen3-Embedding-8B-Q8_0 on Metal returns all-null embeddings for any `import { X } from "` input and poisons the slot afterwards
items.author: neomatrixyzy
items.body_excerpt:
**Environment**: macOS 27 (Darwin 27.0.0), Apple Silicon (Mac Studio), llama.cpp **b10534** and **b11052** (both reproduce), model `Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-8B-GGUF` Q8_0 (file_type 7, `qwen3.pooling_type = 3`), server args `--embeddings --parallel 1 --ubatch-size 2048 --batch-size 2048` (also reproduces with defaults, `-fa off`, `-ctk/-ctv f32`, `--ubatch-size 512`).

**Repro** (deterministic, 9 tokens):
```bash
llama-server --embeddings --model Qwen3-Embedding-8B-Q8_0.gguf --port 8080
curl -s localhost:8080/v1/embeddings -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model":"x","input":"import { useState } from \"react\";"}' | head -c 200
# -> {"object":"list","data":[{"object":"embedding","embedding":[null,null,null,... (4096 nulls)
```
Tokens: `import`, ` {`, ` use`…, ` }`, ` from`, ` "`, … — `import { X }` alone and `const x = f();` are fine; the ` from "` continuation triggers it. After one such request **every subsequent embedding on the same server is also all-null** (e.g. plain lorem ipsum, 273 tokens) until restart.

**Isolation**
- `-ngl 0` (CPU only): finite, correct-looking vector for the same input.
- `-ngl 34` (of 36 layers): finite; `-ngl 35` and `-ngl 36`: null → the NaN originates in the last two transformer layers on the Metal backend.
- `Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B-Q8_0` on Metal: finite for the same inputs.
- HTTP status is 200 and the JSON is otherwise well-formed, so clients that validate coordinates classify it as a malformed response; clients that don't will silently store NaN vectors.

**Expected**: finite embeddings, and no cross-request state carry-over between independent embedding requests.

**Workaround**: `--n-gpu-layers 34` (speed impact ~+30% on a 273-token input in our setup).

items.title: Misc. bug: jinja: Functionary v3.2 template errors with HTTP 500 (`selectattr: unknown test 'type'`) on `oneOf` params
items.author: JoeyPatricio
items.body_excerpt:
### Name and Version

version: 0.7.0-dev (build 11829, commit 18f65360)
built with GNU 16.2.1 for linux x86_64

### Operating systems

Linux

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

libllama (core library), llama-server

### Command line

```shell
llama-server -m stories260K.gguf --jinja --chat-template-file models/templates/meetkai-functionary-medium-v3.2.jinja --port 8099
```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

With the Functionary v3.2 template, a request whose tool has a parameter using `oneOf` fails with HTTP 500 before generation starts. Although a tool without `oneOf` renders fine.

**Steps to reproduce**

Start the server with the command line above, then run:

```
curl -s localhost:8099/apply-template -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
  "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "hi"}],
  "tools": [{"type": "function", "function": {"name": "f", "description": "d",
    "parameters": {"type": "object", "properties": {
      "x": {"oneOf": [{"type": "string"}, {"type": "integer"}]}}}}}]}'
```

Expected: the prompt renders with `x?: string | integer`, which is what Jinja2 produces for the same input.
Actual: HTTP 500 with `selectattr: unknown test 'type'` (full error in the logs below).

Changing `x` to `{"type": "string"}` renders `x?: string`, so `oneOf` is the trigger.

**Cause**

Line 38 of the template calls `param["oneOf"]|selectattr("type", "defined")`.

`select`, `reject`, `selectattr` and `rejectattr` are all registered to one function in `common/jinja/value.cpp`, which picks the argument layout from the argument count. With 3 arguments it treats position 1 as a test name, so `type` gets looked up as a test and the lookup fails. That is right for `select` but wrong for `selectattr`, where position 1 is the attribute. The 2-argument case has the opposite problem: `select('odd')` is treated as an attribute lookup, so it returns nothing.


I have a fix with regression tests and will open a PR shortly.

### First Bad Commit

c15395f73 (#18462). The bug has been present since the engine was added. Later commits (#18955 and #29574) look like they only changed how the attribute value is read.

### Relevant log output

{"error":{"code":500,"message":"...While executing FilterExpression at line 38, column 46 ...
{%- set one_of_types = param[\"oneOf\"]|selectattr(\"type\", \"defined\")|list -%}
...Error: selectattr: unknown test 'type'","type":"server_error"}}
