items.title: [Bug]: TRITON_MLA is not batch invariant under chunked prefill with `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1` (DeepSeek-V2-Lite, DeepSeek-V3.1)
items.author: yifanFengg
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment

- vLLM `main` at `f590eb2448a51028f6044c6f60104ce0ef3189e9`, torch 2.13.0+cu130
- NVIDIA GB300 (SM 10.3), driver 580.167.08, CUDA toolkit 13.1
- Models: `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V2-Lite-Chat` (TP=1) and `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V3.1` (TP=4)
- Attention backend: `TRITON_MLA`, `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1`

### 🐛 Describe the bug


With `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1`, the output of an MLA model changes when its prefill is split into chunks. Both DeepSeek models above fail the chunked-prefill test of the batch-invariance suite, while their needle tests and `bs1_vs_bsN` bitwise tests pass. Both are on the tested-models list in `docs/features/batch_invariance.md`.

**Repro**

```bash
VLLM_TEST_MODEL=deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V2-Lite-Chat \
  pytest -v -s "tests/v1/determinism/test_batch_invariance.py::test_logprobs_bitwise_batch_invariance_ragged_chunked_prefill[TRITON_MLA]"
```

```text
AssertionError: Batch invariance violated under chunked prefill (max_num_batched_tokens=131):
prompt 1 (263 tokens): logprobs differ, max|delta|=8.945e-02; prompt 8 (248 tokens): tokens differ;
prompt 10 (97 tokens): tokens differ; ...
```

Three runs in fresh processes give the same failure and the same delta. `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V3.1` fails the same test the same way.

**Isolation**

The difference does not need other requests in the batch. One prompt run alone, with only the token budget changed:

| `max_num_batched_tokens` | Prefill | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 4096 | one chunk | reference |
| 131 | several chunks | selected-token logprobs differ from the first step (about 1e-3), sampled tokens differ from decode step 9 |

Other observations:

- With `max_num_batched_tokens=4096` the batched test input shows no mismatch. With 512 one prompt still mismatches.
- `enforce_eager=True` still fails, so CUDA graphs and `torch.compile` are not needed to trigger it.
- Prefix caching is off (the test disables it, and it is disabled for `TRITON_MLA` in batch-invariant mode).

Since chunk boundaries depend on the scheduler's token budget, and so on the other requests in the step, this makes the output depend on batch composition.

**Suspected area (not proven)**

The MLA prefill path for a chunk that has cached context (`_compute_prefill_context` in `mla_attention.py`): cached context is gathered and up-projected per context chunk, attended separately, and combined with `merge_attn_states`. A single-chunk prefill does not go through that merge, and merging LSE-rescaled partial results is not bitwise associative. I have not instrumented it at layer level. #46592 discusses canonical chunk boundaries for a related reason (prefix caching).

**CI coverage**

The Batch Invariance jobs run the full `test_batch_invariance.py` only with the default model. For `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V2-Lite-Chat` they run only the needle test with `-k TRITON_MLA`, so the chunked-prefill test (added in #55612) is not exercised for `TRITON_MLA`.

I only ran this on GB300, but nothing in this path looks Blackwell-specific. Happy to run more experiments on this hardware.



### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

items.title: [Roadmap]Fast Engine Recovery: Weight Cache Daemon
items.author: liusy58
items.body_excerpt:
# [Roadmap] Fast Engine Recovery: Weight Cache Daemon 
@liusy58 @QiuMike @alexnails 
Phase 1 landed in #27139 — a per-rank daemon holds post-quantized weights and serves them over CUDA IPC; weight load drops from ~306–327s to <1s on Qwen3-235B FP8 ([blog](https://www.lmsys.org/blog/2026-08-21-sglang-fast-recovery)). This issue tracks the next steps. Contributions and feedback are welcome.

Related: #27052 (Fast Recovery framework), #27310 (GPU Memory Service / VMM)

Goals: <10s cold restart and <1s warm standby switch; broaden model & quant coverage; make the cache outlive the daemon; make resident weights usable beyond the one GPU they sit on.

Where Phase 1 stands: TP + PP, single-node and multi-node launch (each node spawns its share of ranks and joins one dist group), zero-copy IPC per GPU, unquantized + block-wise FP8. Not yet: cross-node daemon coordination / failover, DP & EP shard keying, spec-decoding draft models, weight update / sleep-wake, cache surviving daemon death.

## Model & quantization coverage

- [ ] parity harness — disk-load vs daemon-load `state_dict` diff (names / shape / dtype / stride / byte hash) + short GSM8K gate; required evidence for every new allowlist entry
- [ ] carry post-processing metadata in the manifest (final shape/stride, layout tag, whitelisted module attrs) instead of reproducing `process_weights_after_loading` on a meta-init model — this is what blocks most quant methods today
- [ ] quant methods: per-tensor fp8 / w8a8 int8 / mxfp8 / nvfp4 / compressed-tensors / awq / gptq-marlin #32398 
- [ ] archs: MoE (DeepSeek V3/V4, Ling, Kimi K3) / hybrid linear attention / multimodal (vision tower + projector) / LoRA base weights https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/33684
- [ ] MTP & EAGLE draft models (per-rank draft daemon), removing the `--speculative-algorithm` rejection in `server_args.py` #32744
- [ ] generic post-map rebuild hook to replace the hardcoded `_rebuild_stale_views`; make tied storages, param→buffer flips and non-persistent buffers explicit in the manifest
- [ ] publish the support matrix in docs; unsupported combinations keep hard-erroring (no silent wrong numerics)

## Transport: CUDA VMM shareable handles (#27310 §4.2)



- [ ] `vmm_fd` backend (skeleton already in `weight_cache/transport.py`): `cuMemCreate` + FD handles over `SCM_RIGHTS`, VA reservation on import, `torch_ipc` stays the fallback, `--weight-cache-transport {auto,torch_ipc,vmm_fd}` #33279
- [ ] `mooncake` backend https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/36293


## Weight update without reload

- [ ] epoch handoff on stable VAs: readers unmap → writer commits → readers remap at the same VAs, so captured CUDA graphs stay valid
- [ ] daemon as the weight delivery agent for trainer pushes (NCCL/RDMA); un-gate the `update_weights_*` rejections in `weight_updater.py`
- [ ] colocated RL: engine itself takes the writer role, same protocol, no daemon in the loop

## Multi-instance & cross-GPU sharing

- [ ] key the cache by physical GPU UUID + config fingerprint (plus optional `--weight-cache-namespace`) under a configurable runtime dir. Today the socket is `/tmp/sglang_weight_cache_rank{global_rank}.sock`, so 2× tp=4 on one 8-GPU node collide and rank 0 of the second instance attaches to the GPU 0 daemon
- [ ] discovery: replace static socket paths with a lightweight registry (file-based dir, optionally etcd) so an engine rank selects a daemon by `CacheConfig` match rather than by process rank, and locates daemons across nodes without a manual `--weight-cache-socket`
- [ ] `--weight-cache-peer-copy` — when no daemon holds the shard on the local GPU, `cudaMemcpyPeerAsync` it from a peer-GPU daemon (NVLink-domain check, chunked on a low-priority stream, bandwidth cap so a serving neighbour is not disturbed). 1× memory per instance, sub-second over NVLink vs ~300s from disk
- [ ] preference order local zero-copy > peer copy > disk, reported per rank
- [ ] fleet fill: a daemon fills itself from a peer daemon instead of disk (P2P on-node, NCCL/RDMA cross-node), so a fleet cold start pays one disk read per shard group — the real bottleneck for 1T+ models on shared FS; align with the checkpoint-engine broadcast path
- [ ] out of scope for now: resharding across TP/EP topologies (tp=4 daemon → tp=8 engine)

## Multi-node, DP & EP

- [ ] primary–secondary daemon coordination for multi-node TP (e.g. TP=16 = 2 nodes × 8 GPUs): primary orchestrates daemon startup, cross-node NCCL process-group formation and readiness signalling; secondaries load their local shards in parallel and serve IPC handles to engines on their own node. Basic multi-node launch already works via `--nnodes/--node-rank/--dist-init-method`; what is missing is the cluster state machine
- [ ] cross-node daemon lifecycle: primary tracks which secondaries are alive, triggers coordinated restarts, signals engines on a dead secondary's node to fall back to disk; promote a secondary when the primary dies
- [ ] DP support: every DP rank on a GPU maps the same daemon's handles, so a model is read from disk and quantized exactly once per GPU regardless of DP degree (today each DP rank disk-loads independently). This is about supporting SGLang's DP deployment model, not cross-GPU sharing
- [ ] EP support: expert shards differ per EP rank, so cache and key them by `ep_rank`; handle partial expert loading when a rank owns a subset of experts
- [ ] `CacheConfig`: add `ep_rank`, `dp_rank` and `node_rank` for correct shard identification under EP and multi-node (`dp_size`/`ep_size` are already there)

## Ops & reliability

- [ ] `daemon status` command + Prometheus metrics (resident bytes, attached clients, load time, hit / mismatch / fallback), and an engine endpoint reporting how each rank got its weights
- [ ] runtime dir with owner-only permissions + `SO_PEERCRED` check before handing out handles (no world-writable `/tmp` sockets)
- [ ] `protocol_version` in the handshake with a documented skew policy (the env stamp alrea

items.title: [CI] Add label-controlled CI for external contributors
items.author: googs1025
items.body_excerpt:
Related to #3135.

This issue tracks the label-controlled CI workflow for external contributors as a separate follow-up to the broader CI runner usage reduction work in #3135.

## Summary

Add a CI approval label for pull requests opened by external contributors. Expensive CI jobs should wait until a maintainer reviews the PR and applies the label.

Repository members and trusted contributors should keep the current automatic CI behavior. The exact label name can be decided during implementation.

## Motivation

As more contributors use AI tools, we may receive more PRs and more frequent updates to each PR. Every update can start image builds, integration tests, and E2E tests, even when the PR is still under review or has basic issues.

AIBrix uses the GitHub-hosted runner pool shared by the vllm-project organization. Repeated CI runs from unfinished external PRs can use a large part of this pool.

Most AIBrix checks can also run locally because they do not require a GPU. External contributors should run local checks and address review comments before requesting the expensive CI jobs.

## Proposed behavior

- Repository members and trusted contributors continue to run CI automatically.
- External contributors can still receive lightweight checks and review feedback without starting the expensive CI jobs.
- Image builds, integration tests, and E2E tests wait for a dedicated CI approval label.
- Only maintainers with the required repository permission can approve the CI run.
- The approval is tied to the current PR HEAD SHA.
- When an external contributor pushes a new commit, the previous approval becomes invalid and the label is removed or ignored.
- A maintainer reviews the new changes and applies the label again when the PR is ready.
- Nightly and release workflows are not affected.

The implementation may use a label such as `ci-approved`, `ready-for-ci`, or another name agreed by the maintainers.

## Contributor experience

When an external PR is waiting for approval, the bot or status check should explain:

- which CI jobs are waiting;
- that the contributor should run the available checks locally;
- that a maintainer will start CI after the PR is ready;
- that pushing a new commit will require a new approval.

There should be one lightweight gate check that always reports the current state. This avoids required checks staying in an unclear Pending state because an entire workflow was skipped.

## Security requirements

A trusted workflow may check permissions, manage the label, and record the approved HEAD SHA. It must not checkout or execute code from the pull request when running with a write token or repository secrets.

The actual build and test jobs should continue to run in an unprivileged `pull_request` context without write permissions or secrets.

The workflow must also verify the PR HEAD SHA before starting CI. A label left from an older commit must not authorize a newer commit.

## Acceptance criteria

- An external PR without the CI approval label does not start expensive CI jobs.
- A maintainer can apply the label and start CI for the current HEAD SHA.
- A new commit invalidates the previous approval.
- A contributor without the required permission cannot authorize CI.
- Repository members and trusted contributors keep the current automatic behavior.
- Nightly and release CI continue to run normally.
- The PR page clearly shows whether CI is waiting for approval, running, or completed.
- No workflow with elevated permissions executes code from an external PR.

## Out of scope

This issue does not define path-based E2E selection. Component-aware test selection should be handled in a separate issue.

items.title: [RFC]: Hybrid-model KV offloading with incremental state/span records
items.author: mynotwo
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

I would like feedback on an experimental external KV connector for hybrid
models that combine recurrent state and full-attention KV blocks. It stores
an aligned recurrent-state boundary together with incremental attention spans
and uses AIBrix backends to restore an evicted prefix.

Source and limitations:
https://github.com/mynotwo/aibrix-hybrid-kvcache

Technical explanation:
https://github.com/mynotwo/aibrix-hybrid-kvcache/blob/main/python/aibrix_kvcache/tools/qwen_next_hybrid/TECHNICAL_NOTE.md

This is a downstream experiment, not a claim of production readiness or
validated model support. I am proposing small upstream foundations first,
with the connector remaining downstream until correctness and interface
questions are resolved.

### Motivation

A hybrid prefix needs recurrent state at a valid boundary as well as attention
blocks. An attention-only record cannot by itself express those resume
requirements. Incremental attention spans also avoid writing the same long
prefix at every turn.

The intended contribution is a representation and external-connector path
that reuses AIBrix storage abstractions, with explicit failure fallback and
profiling of actual raw, encoded, transferred and stored byte domains.

### Proposed Change

The downstream code has three layers:

1. A bounded process-local MEMORY byte backend with LRU eviction, reader
   leases, capacity accounting, duplicate-key conflict handling and a
   variable-payload capability. This is a small, independently testable
   first contribution; it does not enable hybrid serving on its own.
2. Hybrid boundary/span planning and a per-rank index. A record becomes
   eligible only after all required rank/part reports and a complete
   ancestor-span chain are available.
3. A vLLM external connector with IDENTITY records, optional framed GPU ANS,
   chunked H2D transfer, record/layout checks, asynchronous bounded saves
   and recompute-on-load-failure behavior. Traces connect save, local miss,
   external load and import across processes.

The code targets the external connector APIs in vLLM 0.30.0. Importing the
connector in that runtime succeeds. Compatibility with other versions or
model layouts has not been established.

**Evidence and unresolved correctness:** 63 constructed-tensor layout,
scheduler, store and codec tests pass on H800 with Torch 2.13.0+cu130/CUDA
13.0, including ANS bytewise round trips and corruption rejection. Related
compression/profiler/L2/acceptance unit suites pass locally. These are not
whole-model acceptance results: a historical development run reports FAIL
because per-rank verification was incomplete and externally resumed tokens
differed from local-prefix-hit tokens. The cause is unresolved. The strict
acceptance gate remains in place, and I am not proposing performance or
model-support guarantees based on that run.

Verification scope and commands:
https://github.com/mynotwo/aibrix-hybrid-kvcache/blob/main/python/aibrix_kvcache/tools/qwen_next_hybrid/VERIFICATION.md

Questions for maintainers:

- Is `aibrix_kvcache/integration/vllm/hybrid` an appropriate ownership boundary?
- Is an optional variable-payload byte capability plus a bounded MEMORY
  backend a useful first PR, independently of the connector?
- Which backend and model/runtime combination should define upstream
  end-to-end acceptance?
- Would you prefer profiler/record utilities before hybrid integration, or
  to keep the profiler downstream until the connector contract is settled?

### Alternatives Considered

- Keep the full integration downstream: reasonable while model-level
  correctness remains unresolved; it leaves duplicated integration work.
- Store the whole prefix at every turn: simpler dependencies but repeats
  attention data and still needs recurrent-boundary semantics.
- Patch model/engine hot paths: a stronger runtime coupling than using the
  external connector API; this proposal does not require that direction.

### Area

KV Cache

items.title: `trtllm_batch_decode_with_kv_cache_mla`: FP8 64-head persistent KeepsAb corrupts random 16-head tiles (NaN LSE)
items.author: kpham-sgl
items.body_excerpt:
`trtllm_batch_decode_with_kv_cache_mla(..., sparse_mla_top_k=2048, return_lse=True)` with FP8 Q/KV and **64 query heads** returns wrong output and NaN or wrong LSE on a handful of (row, 16-head tile) units once the batch has a few hundred rows and KV is short. The same inputs through two 32-head calls, through 128 heads, or in BF16 are correct.

Hits any sparse MLA decode/extend with 64 query heads per KV head in FP8: DeepSeek-V3.2 / GLM-5 at a TP that lands 64 heads on one rank, and context-parallel decode that gathers heads (sglang DSA DCP8 on GLM-5.3, sgl-project/sglang#43735). Extend batches of a few thousand rows fail on nearly every launch.

## Env

- NVIDIA B300 (SM103), 148 SMs. flashinfer-python / cubin / jit-cache **0.7.0.post1**, torch 2.14.1+cu130
- `0.7.1` and `main` use the same trtllm-gen artifact `2d6a5a029eefcc388ec0ceb87efb55d8bcce5c3c/fmha/trtllm-gen/` and the same `selectSparseMlaGenerationKernel`, so this is expected there too.

## Kernel

`FLASHINFER_LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG`, 64 heads, FP8, KV length 64:

```
fmhaSm100fKernel_QkvE4m3OBfloat16HQk576HV512HVPerCta256PagedKvDenseStaticTokenSparseP1VarSeqQ64Kv128PersistentKeepsAbForGen
numCtasX = 1, numCtasY = 2, numCtasZ = <rows>
```

Clean controls select a different kernel: 32 heads → `...Q32Kv128PersistentSwapsAbForGen`; 128 heads → `...Q64Kv128Persistent2CtaKeepsAbForGen` (`clusterDimX=2`); BF16 → the `QkvBfloat16` build of this same Q64 KeepsAb kernel. KV length 2048 at small batch selects the non-persistent `...MultiCtasKvGmemSep...StaticKeepsAbForGen`.

Selection is `selectSparseMlaGenerationKernel` in `include/flashinfer/trtllm/fmha/fmhaKernels.cuh` (`numHeadsQ > 32` → KeepsMmaAb, tileSizeQ 64; 128 heads with batch > ~9 → 2CTA). Unchanged on main as of 2026-10-12.

## Repro

FP8, counter buffer passed, PDL off. One 64-head call against two 32-head calls on the same inputs.

```python
import math, torch, flashinfer, flashinfer.decode, flashinfer.utils
ROWS, LENGTH, HEADS, TOPK = 16384, 64, 64, 2048
SCALE = 1 / math.sqrt(192)
torch.manual_seed(981)
q = (torch.randn((ROWS, 1, HEADS, 576), device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16) * 0.1).to(torch.float8_e4m3fn)
kv = (torch.randn((math.ceil(LENGTH / 64), 1, 64, 576), device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16) * 0.1).to(torch.float8_e4m3fn)
indices = torch.full((ROWS, 1, TOPK), -1, dtype=torch.int32, device="cuda")
indices[:, :, :LENGTH] = torch.arange(LENGTH, dtype=torch.int32, device="cuda")
lengths = torch.full((ROWS,), LENGTH, dtype=torch.int32, device="cuda")
workspace = torch.zeros(8 * HEADS * ROWS * 256 + (1 << 20) + (1536 << 20), dtype=torch.uint8, device="cuda")
counter = torch.zeros(flashinfer.utils.get_trtllm_gen_multi_ctas_kv_counter_bytes(
    ROWS, HEADS, flashinfer.utils.get_device_sm_count(torch.device("cuda"))), dtype=torch.uint8, device="cuda")

def invoke(query):
    return flashinfer.decode.trtllm_batch_decode_with_kv_cache_mla(
        query=query, kv_cache=kv, workspace_buffer=workspace,
        qk_nope_head_dim=128, kv_lora_rank=512, qk_rope_head_dim=64,
        block_tables=indices, seq_lens=lengths, max_seq_len=LENGTH,
        sparse_mla_top_k=TOPK, bmm1_scale=SCALE, backend="trtllm-gen",
        return_lse=True, multi_ctas_kv_counter_buffer=counter, enable_pdl=False)

left, right = invoke(q[:, :, :32].contiguous()), invoke(q[:, :, 32:].contiguous())
ref = torch.cat((left[0], right[0]), dim=2).reshape(ROWS, HEADS, 512)
out, lse = invoke(q)
err = (out.reshape(ROWS, HEADS, 512).float() - ref.float()).abs()
print(float(err.nan_to_num(nan=math.inf).max()), int((err.amax(-1) > 0.02).sum()), float(lse.isnan().sum()))
```

```
16,384 rows: 10/10 launches fail
4,096: 3/5    1,024: 2/5    256: 0/5
KV length 2048 (16,384 rows): 0/5
```

The 32-head split matches a float32 PyTorch reference (max abs error ~1e-3 on sampled rows).

## Sweep

5–10 launches each, full float32 reference on every row.

| Variable | Clean | Fails |
|---|---|---|
| Heads (16k rows, KV 64) | 16, 32 (also 32 at 32k and 65,535 rows), 128 | 64 |
| Rows (64 heads, KV 64) | 256 | 384 (1/10), then 512 … 16,384 (10/10) |
| KV length (64 heads, 16k rows) | 128, 256, 512, 1024, 2047, 2048 | 1, 63, 64, 65 (5/5), 129, 130 (9–10/10) |
| Dtype | BF16 Q/KV | FP8 Q/KV |
| Sparse vs dense | `sparse_mla_top_k=0` | sparse |
| PDL, `max_seq_len=2048`, fresh workspace + counter, no counter buffer | no effect | |

Each failing launch has 1–7 bad rows. In a bad row exactly one aligned 16-head tile (heads 0–15, 16–31, 32–47, or 48–63) is wrong across all 512 V dims, and that tile's LSE is NaN or off by several units. Which rows and tiles change per launch. The bad output is not another row's result. The multi-CTA KV counter stays all-zero, so this is the single-CTA path.

KV lengths that are an exact multiple of 128 (one or two full tiles) are clean. A partial last tile with at most two tiles fails; a longer partial last tile (2047) is clean. Persistent scheduler + FP8 + a partially filled KV tile + a grid larger than the resident CTAs points at a pipeline or shared-memory reuse race in the persistent Q64 KeepsAb kernel.
score_reasons: 匹配 KV 与存储、Serving 与评测、Kernel 与正确性

items.title: [Perf][GB300] CUTLASS mm_fp4 autotuning has 12.59% latency spread and often loses to the default path
items.author: yufeiwu-nv
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

On one NVIDIA GB300, fresh-process autotuning of CUTLASS `mm_fp4` at M=1024, N=896, K=1024 produces a **12.59% spread in per-process median latency**. Five of six tuned measurements are slower than their paired untuned controls, by up to **9.52%**.

This is a performance-stability report, not a numerical correctness failure or a bisected commit regression. The evidence does not isolate tactic selection as the only cause: tuned t0 is also slower than the untuned default, which resolves to t0.

## Environment and method

- GB300 (SM103, 152 SMs), same physical GPU for all 24 benchmark invocations.
- Driver 580.173.10; PyTorch 2.14.0+cu130; CUDA 13.0.
- FlashInfer 0.7.2 at `af71dd7c8a841122838daacc949a4da735c92e82`, `b2b6500abd75f9fb33e58bf28ab96c0cb17f7e85`, and `12199dba2ffdfe00c8e9b624df31c634eabee0f4`.
- CUTLASS submodule `b46b16d003484063bca4ed365e44095c4c6ed633`; nvidia-cutlass-dsl 4.7.0.
- cupti-python 13.4.0; nvidia-cuda-cupti 13.4.92; cuda-bindings 13.0.3.
- cuDNN 9.24.0.43; cudnn-frontend 1.31.0.
- NVFP4 inputs, 128x4 scale layout, BF16 output, seed 42, PDL disabled.
- Final measurements: CUPTI + CUDA Graph + cold L2, 5 dry runs and 30 measured iterations.
- Three commits × two shapes × tuned/untuned × two rounds = 24 fresh processes, all completed successfully with `--refcheck` enabled.
- Round 0 visits commits in the order listed above; round 1 reverses that order. At each commit, tuned cases run before untuned cases.
- No persistent tuning winner is loaded (`autotune_cache=None`). JIT workspace is reused per commit.
- Recorded SHA256 hashes of `flashinfer/gemm/gemm_base.py`, `flashinfer/autotuner/autotuner.py`, and `benchmarks/routines/gemm.py` are identical across the three commits.

## Results

DeepSeek-R1-tagged shape: **M=1024, N=896, K=1024**. Times are microseconds; round numbering is zero-based.

| Commit | Round | Tuned tactic | Tuned median | Untuned median | Tuned vs. untuned |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| af71dd7 | 0 | 3 | 4.576 | 4.7355 | -3.37% |
| af71dd7 | 1 | 0 | 4.992 | 4.688 | +6.48% |
| b2b6500 | 0 | 23 | 5.152 | 4.704 | +9.52% |
| b2b6500 | 1 | 0 | 4.992 | 4.688 | +6.48% |
| 12199db | 0 | 23 | 5.152 | 4.704 | +9.52% |
| 12199db | 1 | 10 | 4.848 | 4.672 | +3.77% |

Spread is `(max / min - 1) * 100`: **12.59% tuned**, **1.36% untuned**. Within-process latency standard deviations are 0.055–0.129 us for tuned runs and 0.086–0.104 us for untuned runs.

The Llama-3 control shape, **M=512, N=5120, K=8192**, selects t50/t51. Its six tuned medians are 13.7925–13.856 us (**0.46% spread**), versus 18.768–18.848 us untuned. Tactic identity changes there without a material performance change.

## Reproduction

Install one of the commits above with its dependencies and run from `benchmarks/`, selecting one GB300:

```bash
export CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0
for round in 0 1; do
  python3 flashinfer_benchmark.py \
    --routine mm_fp4 --m 1024 --n 896 --k 1024 \
    --out_dtype bfloat16 --backends cudnn cutlass cute-dsl trtllm b12x \
    --use_128x4_sf_layout --use_nvfp4 --autotune --refcheck \
    --random_seed 42 --num_iters 30 --dry_run_iters 5 --use_cupti \
    -vv --generate_repro_command --case_tag DeepSeek-R1 \
    --output_path "deepseek-tuned-${round}.csv"
  python3 flashinfer_benchmark.py \
    --routine mm_fp4 --m 1024 --n 896 --k 1024 \
    --out_dtype bfloat16 --backends cudnn cutlass cute-dsl trtllm b12x \
    --use_128x4_sf_layout --use_nvfp4 --refcheck \
    --random_seed 42 --num_iters 30 --dry_run_iters 5 --use_cupti \
    -vv --generate_repro_command --case_tag DeepSeek-R1 \
    --output_path "deepseek-untuned-${round}.csv"
done
```

This is the per-shape reproduction; the original matrix also ran the Llama-3 shape in each arm. `b12x` is skipped as unsupported on SM103. Selected tactics were recorded from the return value of `AutoTuner.choose_one`; the target CSV row is `cutlass_autotune` or `cutlass`.

## Investigation notes and expected behavior

- In [the SM103 launcher](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/blob/12199db/csrc/fp4_gemm_cutlass_sm103.cu#L136), untuned `tactic=-1` maps to **t0**. Both tuned-t0 runs are 4.992 us versus 4.688 us for their untuned-t0 controls. Thus the full latency difference cannot be attributed only to changing kernel configurations.
- This FP4 path profiles candidates with CUDA Events and cold-L2 graph replay (default 3 warmups, 10 samples), then selects the minimum without an independent finalist recheck. Final benchmark measurements use CUPTI. This measurement difference is a candidate explanation, not a proven root cause.
- The artifacts do not contain per-candidate profiling scores or per-sample clock/power telemetry. A fixed-tactic comparison before/after tuning, matched measurement policy, and interleaved finalist/default rescoring would help distinguish selection noise from tuning-induced runtime-state differences.

Autotuning should avoid material run-to-run performance degradation and repeated losses to the default path under equivalent conditions. Exact tactic identity need not be deterministic for equivalent candidates.

Temporary CI mitigation: retain the existing untuned CUTLASS row for the DeepSeek-R1 shape and omit only its GB300 CUTLASS autotuned measurement. Other backends and the Llama-3 autotuned case remain enabled. This is not an upstream fix or evidence that t3 is universally optimal.

Related: #6112 reports a different CuTe-DSL shape/backend; this report does not establish a shared root cause. No retest of current main or newer commits is claimed.

items.author: cuihangbin
items.body_excerpt:
Owner: @cuihangbin
Related PR: #6342
Review target: 2026-11-20 (four weeks); this is a review target, not a stable-graduation commitment.

Propose an explicit experimental `backend="sm120_cute"` for GDN prefill on RTX 6000D (SM120/156 SMs). It replaces the old pipeline32 stable-path opt-in. Stable default dispatch remains unchanged.

Use case: inference with Qwen-style TP1/TP2 head shapes, D=128, BF16/FP16 QKV, native finite FP32 log gates, FP32 beta/state and matching immutable CPU sequence metadata. The CuTe implementation uses segmented boundary generation and V64/V128 consumers. It does not require FlashQLA, TileLang or FLA at runtime; MIT provenance notices are retained.

Unsupported calls, including checkpoints, state pools, low-precision state and linear/raw gates, use the official FlashInfer implementation. The old aggregate checkpoint capacity bound is removed with the old pipeline32 path. Public-API tests cover remainder lengths [100], [64,32] and [200,200] at interval64, and BF16/FP16/FP8 state fallback.

Why experimental: the current pipeline32 PR does not demonstrate broad gains against official default dispatch. The subsequent CuTe rework is materially different and needs commit-specific public-call evidence and production qualification. It must not enter stable automatic selection on the strength of internal-kernel measurements.

Validation: 69 GPU tests pass on RTX6000D, including independent FP64 recurrence, full/tail and index-dtype cache switching, public checkpoint/state fallback and CUDA graph replay. Public-API memcheck reports zero kernel memory errors. Scoped CI and maintainer review remain required. Public-call evidence on code commit 3cd6473fd4 is now attached to PR #6342: 46 cases, 24 faster, 18 slower, 4 within 2%, including official gate materialization and experimental preallocated-buffer copies. Complete rows and raw samples are committed. The configured pre-commit bootstrap encountered a remote GitHub timeout; direct Ruff/format/mypy checks pass. Maintainer CI remains required.

Graduation criteria:
- Reproducible public-call gains against the then-current official default route on representative supported workloads, with all timing boundaries stated.
- Correctness/CI approval, production usage evidence and a maintainable support/specialization policy.
- Agreement on supported contracts and maintenance burden before stable admission.

At the review target, graduate only if these criteria and maintainers' requirements are met; otherwise request a documented extension with meaningful progress, or remove the backend under the experimental policy.

items.title: Misc. bug: OpenVINO NPU: SIGSEGV/WeightlessCacheAttribute on Intel Core Ultra 7 255H (Linux)
items.author: Chipy1
items.body_excerpt:
## Name and Version
```
$ ./build/bin/llama-cli --version
version: b10068-571d0d540
built with cc (GCC) 16.1.1 20250618 for x86_64-linux-gnu
```

OpenVINO 2026.2.1-2 (chaotic-aur), onetbb 2023.0.0-1
NPU driver 1.33.0, Intel AI Boost (arch 3720)
OS: Arch Linux, kernel 7.1.3

## Command line
```
GGML_OPENVINO_DEVICE=NPU ./build/bin/llama-cli \
  -m Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct-Q4_K_M.gguf \
  -p "Hello" -n 10
```

## Problem description
Running llama.cpp with OpenVINO NPU backend on Intel Core Ultra 7 255H (Arrow Lake-P) results in two failure modes depending on NPUW configuration:

**Mode 1: Without NPUW** — SIGSEGV in `pthread_once` inside `libopenvino_intel_npu_plugin.so`. Appears to be a TBB race condition during NPU plugin initialization.

Backtrace:
```
#0  std::once_flag::_Prepare_execution (libllama-server-impl.so)
#1  pthread_once (libc.so.6)
#2  libopenvino_intel_npu_plugin.so
```

Minimal C++ test (`ov::Core` + `get_available_devices()`) works fine. Python bindings work fine. Crash only occurs during model compilation within llama.cpp context.

**Mode 2: With NPUW** (`NPU_USE_NPUW=YES`, `NPUW_WEIGHTS_BANK=shared`, etc.) — avoids SIGSEGV but fails with:
```
No "WeightlessCacheAttribute" has been found in any of the model's Constant nodes.
This attribute is required for running the "weights separation" flow.
```

The `ov::WeightlessCacheAttribute` class exists in `libopenvino.so` but its header is not installed in the distro package, so it cannot be added to weight `Constant` nodes from the OpenVINO backend.

Without `NPUW_WEIGHTS_BANK=shared`, falls back to Mode 1 (SIGSEGV).

## Related issues
Similar NPU-related issues exist, but our case is distinct:
- #25809 — first-run RoPE shape mismatch on Windows; second run succeeds via NPUW cache. Our crash is a SIGSEGV in driver init, not a shape error, and no second-run workaround.
- #25324 — same CPU (255H) on Windows, but crashes with `GGML_ASSERT` in CPU ops, not in NPU plugin.
- #23984 — f32/f16 type mismatch on NPU compilation, not a driver-level crash.

## Steps to reproduce
1. Build with `cmake -DGGML_OPENVINO=ON ..`
2. Download any small Llama GGUF (e.g., Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct-Q4_K_M)
3. Run:
   ```
   GGML_OPENVINO_DEVICE=NPU ./build/bin/llama-simple -m model.gguf -p "Hello" -n 10
   ```
   Result: SIGSEGV
4. Run with NPUW config (current code sets `NPUW_WEIGHTS_BANK=shared`):
   Result: `WeightlessCacheAttribute` error

## Expected behavior
NPU inference works, similar to CPU-only build which produces 39 t/s on 1B model.

items.title: [Bug]: ModelClaim engine crashes with IndexError in kvcached get_new_blocks after the controller raises its KV limit above the engine's initial block pool
items.author: Jeffwan
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

A vLLM engine started by the ModelClaim runtime (kvcached-patched) crashes with `IndexError` after the controller raises its KV limit above the KV block pool the engine allocated at startup. EngineCore exits, the runtime restarts the engine (`restart_count` +1), and every request to that model fails until it is back (about 40 s for an 8B model).

```
File ".../vllm/v1/core/single_type_kv_cache_manager.py", line 399, in allocate_new_blocks
    new_blocks = self.block_pool.get_new_blocks(num_new_blocks)
File ".../kvcached/integration/vllm/patches.py", line 1003, in get_new_blocks
    block = self.kv_block_pool[bid]
IndexError: list index out of range
EngineCore encountered a fatal error.
```

What we observed:

1. vLLM sizes the block table once, at engine start: `self.kv_block_pool = [KVCacheBlockClass(i) for i in range(num_gpu_blocks)]`. For a single Qwen3-8B-FP8 engine on an A100-40GB this is 26.2 GiB of blocks (kvcached log: `Using kvcached process-local KV capacity: ... available=28173858448 bytes`).
2. When that engine is alone on the card, `planKVLimits` gives it the engine's held KV plus the whole remaining card, 29.0 GiB. Nothing caps the limit at the engine's initial pool ([kvplan.go#L114-L127](https://github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/blob/main/pkg/controller/modelclaim/kvplan.go#L114-L127)). The event reads `KV limit set to 29.0 GiB, from 26.2 GiB`.
3. kvcached then hands out block ids up to the new limit. An id at or above `num_gpu_blocks` indexes past `kv_block_pool`.

We hit the crash 4 times in one benchmark run:

- **History captured:** in the two crashes whose limit history we captured, the engine had been raised above its initial pool. One of them crashed 4 minutes after its limit had been lowered from 29.0 GiB back to 9.2 GiB, when a second engine was placed. Lowering the limit afterwards did not prevent the crash.
- **History not captured:** the other two engines ran in the same setup, alone on the card first.
- **Never above the pool:** engines whose limit never exceeded their initial pool never crashed, across dozens of KV-saturating runs. These include engines placed next to an existing engine and engines started in pairs or groups.
- **Above the pool, no crash:** two engines were raised above their pool briefly and did not crash: a 0.6B engine at concurrency 1 (36.7 vs 34.9 GiB), and an 8B engine under load for 90 s. Exceeding the pool is necessary but not sufficient; the crash depends on how many blocks get allocated afterwards.
- **Prefix caching and reset:** prefix caching makes it trigger sooner, but it is not required: one crash happened with `--no-enable-prefix-caching`. `/reset_prefix_cache` is not required either.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Deploy a warm pool with one GPU (`samples/modelclaim/warm-runtime-pool.yaml`, 1× A100-40GB) and no pool policy annotation.
2. Apply one ModelClaim alone on that pod:
   ```yaml
   spec:
     modelName: qwen3-8b-z
     artifactURL: huggingface://Qwen/Qwen3-8B-FP8
     engine: vllm
     perGPU:
       maximumFootprint: 10752Mi
       kvFloor: 2Gi
     engineConfig:
       args:
         --max-model-len: "8192"
         --max-num-seqs: "32"
         --max-num-batched-tokens: "2048"
   ```
3. Check the event `KV limit set to 29.0 GiB, from 26.2 GiB` (runtime snapshot `kv_capacity_bytes: 31132614656`).
4. Send RAG-shaped load directly to the engine port. Repeat with `--seed 1`, `2`, `3`:
   ```bash
   vllm bench serve --backend openai-chat --base-url http://<pod-ip>:<engine-port> \
     --endpoint /v1/chat/completions --model qwen3-8b-z --tokenizer Qwen/Qwen3-8B-FP8 \
     --dataset-name random --random-input-len 1024 --random-output-len 128 \
     --num-prompts 300 --request-rate 32 --max-concurrency 16 --ignore-eos --seed 1
   ```
   Runs 1 and 2 complete 300/300. Run 3 crashed after 144 requests, and the snapshot showed `restart_count: 1`.

### Expected behavior

- The controller never sets an engine's KV limit above the KV capacity the engine sized its block table for at startup. Room on the card beyond that stays unassigned, or goes to other engines.
- Suggested fix: the runtime reports each engine's initial KV capacity in the snapshot (the kvcached segment's `total_size` when the engine came up, or `num_gpu_blocks` × block bytes). `planKVLimits` caps `kvLimitBytes` at it. Add a regression test where a single engine on a card gets a capped limit.
- kvcached should also clamp or reject a limit beyond `num_gpu_blocks` instead of handing out out-of-range block ids. We will report that side to ovg-project/kvcached.

### Environment

- Image `ghcr.io/ovg-project/kvcached-vllm:kvcached-v0.1.6-vllm-v0.30.0` (vLLM 0.30.0, kvcached 0.1.6), runtime built with `make docker-build-kvcached-runtime`.
- 1× NVIDIA A100-SXM4-40GB, driver 570.148.08, single-node minikube.
- Models: Qwen/Qwen3-8B-FP8 (all 4 crashes) and Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B.

### Area

Orchestration (controllers, CRDs)

items.title: [Tracking] KV event correctness and compatibility
items.author: andakai
items.body_excerpt:
Track the work needed to make KV events reliable across model architectures and speculative-decoding modes, including Dynamo, llm-d, and vLLM Router compatibility.

## Goal

Downstream consumers should be able to determine which cache entries are resident and how much of a request can actually be reused. This requires correct events for attention blocks, recurrent checkpoints, partial hits, and speculative rollback, together with reliable publication and recovery.

Architecture support and speculative-decoding support are core deliverables. The checklist below combines known defects with the remaining support and validation work; an unchecked architecture or mode does not mean every configuration is broken. Priorities describe the proposed order of work for this tracker.

## P1 — Architecture support and cache semantics

- [ ] **Establish coverage across cache layouts:** dense attention, MLA, SWA, pure Mamba, linear/recurrent attention including GDN, Mamba/GDN hybrids, and sparse/compressed layouts. Verify event content and actual reusable prefixes for full and partial hits, including configurations where hash and physical block sizes differ.
- [ ] **Fix sparse/partial full reporting.** `kv_cache_report_mode="full"` raises `IndexError` on hybrid partial hits — [#57358](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/57358).
- [ ] **Fix sparse token/hash alignment.** Null or masked blocks are omitted from hashes but retained in the token span; one emitted hash can describe multiple blocks — [#44488](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/44488).
- [ ] **Preserve partial-block ancestry.** Events can reference a parent that was never published — [#58119](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/58119); related fixes [#62195](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/62195), [#58121](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/58121). Also cover promotion that removes the new entry's parent — [#58394](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/58394).
- [ ] **Describe recurrent checkpoints in events.** Recurrent offload events currently use insufficient placeholders — [#62510](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/62510), [#62613](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/62613).
- [ ] **Match hybrid prefixes using both attention coverage and recurrent checkpoints.** Downstream matches can overestimate reusable prefixes — [Dynamo #16794](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/issues/16794); [#16876](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/pull/16876), [#16875](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/pull/16875).
- [ ] **Complete partial-entry support in consumers.** [llm-d-router #3255](https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d-router/pull/3255) skips unresolved sub-canonical stores rather than indexing them; this does not complete partial-hit support.
- [ ] **Use effective block sizes for DCP full reporting.** The physical/effective size mismatch triggers an assertion — [#50118](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/50118). DCP GPU validation remains outstanding.

- [ ] **Align vLLM Router group and event-source handling.** Its event-backed `kv_aware` path is another consumer to validate. Track hybrid/linear-attention group support in [vLLM Router #436](https://github.com/vllm-project/router/issues/436), and live/replay source validation in [#401](https://github.com/vllm-project/router/pull/401). Existing event ingestion does not establish hybrid checkpoint correctness.

## P1 — Speculative-decoding support

- [ ] **Cover MTP, EAGLE, DFlash, and DSpark on applicable architectures.** Validate accepted and rejected tokens, partial hits, rollback, and draft-side cache groups. Events must agree with committed cache state and usable checkpoints.
- [ ] **Handle rollback without requiring a nonexistent partial endpoint.** With the tested [#57358](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/57358) candidate, ordinary partial-hit full reporting completes, but speculative rollback still raises `AssertionError` when the allowed reuse boundary differs from the registered endpoint. Preserve this regression alongside the full-report fix.

## P1 — Cache lifecycle and downstream indexes

- [ ] **Align store, full-report, and removal semantics.** In an llm-d Go filter replay, `store → full report → final remove` leaves a stale reference. Separately, vLLM can emit a removal while another copy remains cached. Agree on presence versus per-copy semantics so both cases produce the correct index — related to [#58508](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/58508).
- [ ] **Publish idle resets immediately.** `AllBlocksCleared` remains queued until another request arrives. The tested [#58881](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/58881) candidate fixes this case.
- [ ] **Preserve child stores when parent mappings arrive later** — [llm-d-router #3588](https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d-router/pull/3588).
- [ ] **Add end-to-end consumer regressions.** Compare event-derived indexes with actual cache lookup through repeated full reports, duplicate stores, eviction, reset, and reconnect in Dynamo, llm-d, and vLLM Router. Include concurrent requests and preemption in lifecycle coverage.

## P1 — Connectors and inference reliability

- [ ] **Avoid native LMCache hook failures.** The native adapter lacks `get_kv_events`, but the connector calls it — [#62216](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/62216), [#62223](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/62223). Guarding the missing hook does not itself provide native event support.
- [ ] **Preserve delayed offload metadata across key reuse.** Four targeted regressions fail on the baseline and pass with [#63129](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/63129), addressing [#63037](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/63037). The tested candidate also fails two existing failed-promotion tests with stale `store_pending`; resolve that regression before treating the fix as complete.
- [ ] **Report only retrievable offload checkpoints.** Manager lookup misses an advertised interi

items.title: Should LMCacheMPConnector honor kv_transfer_config.kv_role — or is MP mode intentionally always-kv_both?
items.author: kezboard233
items.body_excerpt:
## Context

We run a production-shaped POC on 8×V100 (two vLLM TP4 instances of Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 sharing one LMCache MP server with a CPU L1 tier) and filed #5143 with a runtime-verified repro: an engine launched with `kv_role="kv_consumer"` still stores every request's KV into the shared L1 — a single 32K-token cold request produced `168 × "Stored 784"` lines (= full prefix × 4 TP ranks), and the only engine that received any request in that window was the `kv_consumer` one.

We later found #4665 (closed by its author without maintainer response) reporting the same mechanism from the CacheBlend angle: the single-process connector honors `kv_role` / `skip_save`, the MP connector honors neither. As of today's `dev`, `lmcache_mp_connector.py` still contains no occurrence of `kv_role` / `kv_consumer` / `kv_producer` / `force_skip_save`.

## The design question

Before we contribute a patch, we want to check intent: **is MP mode intentionally "every connected engine writes"?** Two readings:

1. **Contract gap** — vLLM makes `kv_role` mandatory, documents it as "Whether this vLLM instance produces, consumes KV cache, or both", and exposes `is_kv_producer` / `is_kv_consumer` for connectors to branch on; LMCache's own single-process adapter honors it (`force_skip_save` in `vllm_v1_adapter.py`). Under this reading we'd gladly contribute a small PR that skips store-metadata generation when `is_kv_consumer` (mirroring the single-process gate), so warm-then-read-only fleets and PD-style topologies become possible on the MP path.

2. **Intentional always-kv_both** — the MP tier is a shared scratch space where every connected engine contributes. Under this reading we'd instead ask for the intent to be documented, plus ideally a one-line warning at connector init when `kv_role != "kv_both"`, so users aren't misled (we only noticed via instrumented counter evidence ourselves).

Happy to do either — a steer from maintainers decides which.

(Impact context: no correctness issue — stored content is identical — but a consumer-role engine burns D2H bandwidth and shared-L1 capacity; a 32K prefix on our model is ≈8.6 GB across 4 ranks.)

items.title: [Bug]: Grouped MLA generation cubins are registered as Dense in kernelMetaInfo.h but named and selected as Causal
items.author: lucifer1004
items.body_excerpt:
### System Info

TensorRT-LLM main, `cpp/tensorrt_llm/kernels/trtllmGenKernels/fmha/cubin/kernelMetaInfo.h` (artifacts from #19591). On release/1.3 the table is split per architecture since #20022; the same rows are in `kernelMetaInfoSm100f.h` and `kernelMetaInfoSm107.h` (see the location list below). Seen on SM107; the SM100f rows have the same pattern.

### Who can help?

@pengbowang-nv @farazkh80 (#15009)

### Information

- [ ] The official example scripts
- [x] My own modified scripts

### Reproduction

All 36 grouped MLA generation cubins (`fmhaSm100fKernel_...` and `fmhaSm107aKernel_Qkv{Bfloat16,E4m3}OBfloat16HQk576HV512{,HVPerCta128,HVPerCta256}PagedKvCausalP32...VarSeqQ64Kv128{Static,Persistent}GroupedKeepsAbForGen`; per architecture 9 with BF16 and 9 with E4M3 Q/KV, 18 for `kSM_100f`, 18 for `kSM_107`) have `Causal` in the function name, but their `mMaskType` field is `0` (`TrtllmGenAttentionMaskType::Dense`). Locations:

- main @ 13e19d6cf3, `kernelMetaInfo.h`: SM100f BF16 lines 19057-19110, SM100f E4M3 19347-19400, SM107 BF16 20903-21019, SM107 E4M3 21907-22023.
- release/1.3 @ c9d1169641 (after #20022): `kernelMetaInfoSm100f.h` lines 243-296 (BF16) and 533-586 (E4M3); `kernelMetaInfoSm107.h` lines 887-1003 (BF16) and 1835-1951 (E4M3). The values are unchanged by the split. The grouped P128 E4M3 H128 cubins added there for SM107 are registered with `mMaskType = 1` (Causal), so only the HQk576 grouped MLA rows are affected.

`mMaskType` is part of the hash that the cubin path looks up (`hashFromFmhaOptions` -> `hashID`). With `FmhaOptions::mSelectsGroupedMla = true`, the autotuner selects the grouped kernel with a causal mask for MLA generation with multiple query tokens, so the lookup fails (`Trtllm-gen kernels not found`), and the only remaining route is NVRTC. On SM107, NVRTC currently fails for these configurations (separate issue). We had to map Causal back to Dense for grouped MLA kernels in `algoFilterForCubinPath` before the cubins could be used.

With that mapping, the cubins give the expected causal result: compared with the non-grouped kernel on SM107, outputs are bit-identical for KV lengths 16 and 64, and at most 2 bf16 ulp apart from 256 up to 128K. So the kernels behave as their names say, and only the metadata is off. #15009 also mentions that its re-exported rows were changed to `maskType=Causal` "to match the shipped lib's grouped mask rewrite".

### Expected behavior

The registered mask type matches what the kernel implements and what the selector asks for, so that grouped MLA generation cubins can be found without a remapping.

### actual behavior

`mMaskType = Dense` for kernels named `...Causal...`; the cubin lookup misses them when grouped MLA selection is enabled.

### additional notes

This does not affect main today because `mSelectsGroupedMla` is never set in TensorRT-LLM. It blocks enabling it (#15009), together with the missing `cumSeqLensQ/Kv` in the MLA generation path (#20375). If the right fix is on the export side, a regenerated `kernelMetaInfo.h` (`kernelMetaInfoSm100f.h` / `kernelMetaInfoSm107.h` after #20022) would be enough; otherwise I can send the remapping as a small PR.

Related: #20375, #20377, #20382 (FP8-KV grouped MLA hang for head counts that do not divide 64).

items.title: [Bug]: fill_template.py fails with ValueError when a substitution value contains a colon
items.author: ShryukGrandhi
items.body_excerpt:
### System Info

- CPU architecture: arm64 (also reproducible on x86_64; the script is pure Python)
- TensorRT-LLM branch: main (commit c6350002f)
- Python 3.12
- No GPU needed to reproduce

### Who can help?

_No response_

### Information

- [x] The official example scripts

### Reproduction

`triton_backend/tools/fill_template.py` says substitutions support escaping, but a value that contains a colon (escaped or not) crashes the script:

```bash
printf 'url: "${url}"\n' > config.pbtxt
python3 triton_backend/tools/fill_template.py config.pbtxt 'url:http\://localhost\:8000'
```

```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "triton_backend/tools/fill_template.py", line 70, in <module>
    main(**vars(args))
  File "triton_backend/tools/fill_template.py", line 43, in main
    key, value = split(sub, ":")
ValueError: too many values to unpack (expected 2)
```

`main()` first runs `split(substitutions, ",")`, which already removes every backslash, and then runs `split(sub, ":")` on the result. By the time the second split runs, `\:` has turned into a plain `:`. So the value gets split again. The same double unescaping means a literal backslash in a value has to be written as four backslashes.

### Expected behavior

`url:http\://localhost\:8000` should produce `url: "http://localhost:8000"`. Only the first colon should separate the key from the value, so values such as URLs, `host:port` or Windows paths can be passed.

### actual behavior

The script exits with `ValueError: too many values to unpack (expected 2)` and the template is left unfilled.

### additional notes

Splitting each `key:value` pair on its first colon only (`sub.split(":", 1)`) fixes it.

items.title: [Bug]: etcd watch callback cancels discovery watch under asyncio debug mode
items.author: codebreaker77
items.body_excerpt:
On main `46d9966b54d9d11998b712e732fb20f64d4d35c0`, a real etcd notification can
cancel a live watch and leave its asyncio reader blocked when debug mode is
enabled. Re-requesting the same prefix returns the cached dead handle.

## Reproduction

With a dedicated etcd 3.5 server and a matching TensorRT-LLM Python environment:

```python
import asyncio
import uuid
from tensorrt_llm.serve.cluster_storage import Etcd3ClusterStorage

async def main():
    storage = Etcd3ClusterStorage("etcd://127.0.0.1:2379", "repro")
    prefix = "watch-repro/" + uuid.uuid4().hex + "/"
    watch = await storage.watch(prefix)
    pending = asyncio.create_task(watch.drain())
    await asyncio.sleep(0)  # reader waits before the SDK thread delivers
    assert await storage.set(prefix + "worker", "registered")
    print("key:", await storage.get(prefix + "worker"), flush=True)
    print(await pending, flush=True)

asyncio.run(main(), debug=True)
```

Run under an external process timeout: the failed wakeup can leave an orphaned
reader, so an asyncio timeout is not a sufficient whole-process safety bound.
Setting `debug=False` is the successful control.

## Observed

Three independent runs against real etcd all produced:

- Debug off: event delivered; SDK watch stays active.
- Debug on: logs `Non-thread-safe operation invoked on an event loop other than
  the current one`; no event delivered; key still readable; SDK watch removed.
- After recording failure and repairing the orphaned wakeup for test cleanup,
  disabling debug and calling `watch(prefix)` returns the same cached handle;
  a second etcd write produces no notification.

This could make a discovery consumer stop receiving worker changes. No router
state, model-serving traffic or GPU effects were measured. Production-mode
controls passed; the established runtime failure is under asyncio debug.

## Cause / proposed scope

`Etcd3WatchEventQueue.add_events_from_resp` mutates an asyncio queue directly on
the etcd SDK callback thread. Its later `call_soon_threadsafe(lambda: None)` is
too late to make that queue operation safe. The exception handler then cancels
the watch, while storage keeps its cached handle.

Capture the owning event loop and enqueue events on that loop using
`call_soon_threadsafe`, with focused threaded-delivery and pending-reader tests.
The unsafe pattern was already flagged in an old review:
https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM/pull/8210#discussion_r2415560025
I found no dedicated issue or current fix through searches for etcd/thread,
debug, watch/reconnect and the queue class name. This report adds runtime
evidence rather than claiming the pattern was previously unknown.

## Validation boundary

Real etcd-sdk-python 0.0.7 with Docker etcd 3.5.21. Full unchanged storage/logger
source modules loaded while bypassing TensorRT/native package initialization.
Windows Python 3.10 client with real-server I/O; supplementary actual-thread and
SDK-event checks also reproduce on Linux Python 3.12. The normal-package snippet
above and model serving were not executed locally. This is separate from the
expired-lease failure in #20529.

## Proposed patch and follow-up validation

A focused fix is available on [my fork](https://github.com/codebreaker77/TensorRT-LLM/tree/fix/20684-etcd-watch-threading),
commit [819f5c8f](https://github.com/codebreaker77/TensorRT-LLM/commit/819f5c8f).
It captures the owning event loop and schedules queue insertion onto that loop,
removing the private queue-loop wakeup. It does not include the separate lease
recovery work from #20529.

The nine new CPU cases produce 5 failures / 4 passes on unchanged source and
9 passes with the fix. The full existing storage suite plus these cases passes
62 tests on Linux Python 3.12. Six real-etcd runs with the fix (three each with
debug on/off) deliver two successive notifications and keep the watch active.
The same native-bootstrap isolation described above applies; no full-package,
model-serving or GPU validation is claimed. Applicable formatting/lint checks
pass. The branch is prepared for issue triage; no upstream PR has been opened.

items.title: CUTLASS 4.8.1
items.author: Junkai-Wu
items.body_excerpt:
### CuTe DSL * Bug fixes and improvements: - Fixed an issue with `cute.extern` where functions with zero arguments would generate invalid type signatures. Compiling such functions a second time would fail. - Clear error/warning are now emitted for `CopyUniversalOp` with memory attributes specified ([!3711](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/issues/3711)). - CUTLASS Primitives' `tensormap_replace` now keeps device-side TMA descriptor updates safe when a descriptor is shrunk below its original extent (e.g. grouped GEMM) and fixes a possible illegal memory access on Blackwell/Rubin. This behavior can be opted out by specifying `keep_oob_fetch_window=True`. See https://docs.nvidia.com/datacenter/tesla/tesla-release-notes-595-91-07/index.html#known-issues for more details on the known `cuTensorMapEncodeTiled` bug. - Fixed unintended `sys.path` modification that could break imports in some environments where Torch was not installed e.g. JAX. * Known issues - Due to a bug in CTK, the use of some packed instructions result in invalid code generation. Given the nature of the instructions and how they are explicitly used, we have chosen to not silently rewrite these, but rather are flagging until the upstream compiler fixes are available. - Avoid packed higher-throughput FP8 (MMA_K=128) subtraction via inline PTX `sub.rn.e4m3x4.e4m3x4` or `sub.rn.e5m2x4.e5m2x4`, as incorrect code generation can produce wrong results. - Some CUTLASS Primitives packed mixed-input ops compile incorrectly on Rubin (sm107a/sm107f), resulting in wrong code generation. The specific patterns include: - Packed mul, sub, and add ops with bf16x2 or fp16x2 result type and f32x2 input type when result is converted to fp32 later. APIs affected: `add_packed_f16x2_f32x2_f32x2`, `add_packed_bf16x2_f32x2_f32x2`, `mul_packed_f16x2_f32x2_f32x2`, `mul_packed_bf16x2_f32x2_f32x2`, `sub_packed_f16x2_f32x2_f32x2`, `sub_packed_bf16x2_f32x2_f32x2` - For example: ``` x = prims.mul_packed_bf16x2_f32x2_f32x2(a, b) out[0], out[1] = f32(x[0]), f32(x[1]) # out[0], out[1] are wrong ``` - Packed mul op with bf16x2 or fp16x2 result type and mixed bf16x2 and fp16x2 input types when the first operand is a compilation-time constant. APIs affected: `mul_packed_bf16x2_bf16x2_f16x2`, `mul_packed_f16x2_f16x2_bf16x2` - For example: ``` x = prims.mul_packed_bf16x2_bf16x2_f16x2(2.0, b) # x is wrong x = prims.mul_packed_f16x2_f16x2_bf16x2(2.0, b) # x is wrong ``` * This release has been tested against the following packages: - FlashAttention: [main (1fc0221)](https://github.com/Dao-AILab/flash-attention/commit/1fc0221183e799363001394a12dd9e78e15f5dda) - Quack: [main (35266c32)](https://github.com/Dao-AILab/quack/commit/35266c3298f0e9bf6d5f46c30aace2eaeae517e3) - FlashInfer: [main (399b6c1)](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/commit/399b6c1d31a13f38dd827018f89c6a04c8487acb) - cuDNN-Frontend: [deveop (986ef4d)](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cudnn-frontend/commit/986ef4d9078089ae9f0656dd65f15011309e4347) - Pytorch: [main (ca883d5)](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/commit/ca883d596dd5c0ce182976ed979d69d167ad706c) - TensorRT-LLM: [main (cc63e66)](https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM/commit/cc63e66daf52644f1441e117bb7ba67d20566016)
This discussion was created from the release CUTLASS 4.8.1.

items.title: [RFC] [Feature] Intra-Device Heterogeneous Memory Allocation Support
items.author: jackbondpreston-arm
items.body_excerpt:
# 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

### Terminology: Inter- vs Intra-Device Heterogeneous Memory
We define **intra**-device heterogeneous memory as memory which is heterogeneous (has different properties), *within the same device*.
PyTorch currently supports **inter**-device heterogeneous memory by enabling applications to allocate Tensors on different devices, ie. through the `device` parameter on `Tensor` constructors:

```python^Q
torch.zeros(..., device="cuda") # allocate Tensor in CUDA memory, using CUDA allocator
```

but not for intra-device heterogeneous memory.

### Motivation
Heterogeneous host-side memory is becoming more common. Some example implementations that existed previously, are available today, or are coming soon include:

- Intel's [Sapphire Rapids HBM/Xeon Max](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sapphire_Rapids#Sapphire_Rapids-HBM_(High_Bandwidth_Memory/Xeon_Max_Series)): 64GB on-chip HBM, with "flat mode" supporting putting HBM and DRAM on different NUMA nodes.
- SiPearl's [Rhea](https://sipearl.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/PR_SiPearl_Rhea1_EN.pdf) and [Rhea-2](https://www.anandtech.com/show/21295/sipearls-rhea2-cpu-added-to-roadmap-second-gen-european-cpu-for-hpc): On-chip HBM and off-chip DDR.
- In the future, expected increasing prevalence of CXL.mem - adding another tier of heterogeneous memory to systems utilising it.
- A future trend towards more DDR + [Non-volatile Memory (NVM)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-volatile_memory) platforms.

Making the most of these platforms with multiple types of host-memory will likely include application programmers making choices about which memory type they want certain allocations to be on. In PyTorch, this means allowing applications to specify which memory backing a Tensor will use - as this is the main unit of storage within PyTorch. An application may wish to place Tensors on HBM in order to maximise bandwidth when performing ML operations, or to place on DRAM to make use of capacity in cases of oversubscription. 
Currently PyTorch has no way to allow applications to place tensors on specific memory types within a device, so application programmers can't maximise performance and usage on these heterogeneous systems.

### Feature: Support for intra-device heterogeneous memory support
The proposal is to implement support for another layer of memory heterogeneity - *intra-device* heterogeneity on top of *inter-device* heterogeneity. 
For example, in a case where a CPU has multiple types of memory, a PyTorch application can choose which of these their Tensor will be backed by, when using the CPU device. 
The same could also be applicable to other devices (e.g. CUDA, XPU, etc.) - if they have multiple types of memory, some application programmers in the future may want finer-grained control of the Tensors' backing.

## Design

### Extra (Default) Parameter for `Device`s
An extra optional parameter will be added to the `torch.device`/`c10::Device` constructors, allowing the specification of a memory type within that device. This can then be provided to Tensor constructors, to specify that the Tensor should be allocated on this device, *and* on a specific memory type within this device:

```python
cpu_hbm = torch.device("cpu", 0, memory_type="hbm")

x = torch.zeros(1000, device=cpu_hbm)
```

Also supported will be the string representation of devices:

```python
# type[:[index][:[memory_type]]]

torch.device('cpu:0:hbm') == torch.device(type='cpu', index=0, memory_type='hbm')
torch.device('cpu::hbm') == torch.device(type='cpu', memory_type='hbm')
torch.device('cuda:1:') == torch.device('cuda:1') = torch.device(type='cuda', index=1)
```

The parameter will be of an enum type, containing all the memory types supported by any devices in PyTorch. For example:

```cpp
/* New enum - MemoryType */
enum class MemoryType {
    DEFAULT,
    DDR,
    HBM,
    CXL,
    PMEM,
    DISK,
    // ...
}
```

The default value for MemoryType, if not specified, is `DEFAULT`. This will use the default memory type, which must be whichever memory type PyTorch used before this change, for backwards compatibility.

The heterogeneous allocation support will be implemented *by the device allocator*. The MemoryType from the `torch.device` used for the Tensor allocation will be passed through to the allocator's `allocate` method:

```
/* c10/core/Allocator.h                           */
/* Example change for demonstration purposes only */

struct C10_API Allocator {
  virtual ~Allocator() = default;

  virtual DataPtr allocate(size_t n) = 0;

  virtual DataPtr allocate(size_t n, MemoryType memType = MemoryType::DEFAULT) {
    // default is to ignore memType, devices can provide implementations using this parameter where necessary
    return allocate(n);
  }

  // ...
```

Currently the `StorageImpl` constructors do not take any information about the `device` argument provided to the Tensor constructor functions, only a pointer to the dispatched Allocator. Thus, the `MemoryType` (or the whole `Device`) will have to be passed down through e.g. `empty_generic` as an extra argument, through `StorageImpl` and down to the `Allocator::allocate()` function.

The `DataPtr`'s `device_` member will record the `MemoryType` *actually used* for the allocation, in cases where it differs from the user's request.


### API to query supported heterogeneous memory devices
Additionally, we propose adding an API to allow users to check the heterogeneous memory currently available for use on each device. This would have different implementations per-device, but would return an enumeration of the types of memory.

```python
# Equivalent - can accept a device or string, like Tensor constructors
>>> torch.get_device_memory_types("cpu")
>>> torch.get_device_memory_types(torch.device("cpu")) 
[ "ddr", "hbm", "cxl" ]

# Example implementation for CUDA, if it did not support heterogeneous memory types
>>> torch.get_device_memory_types("cuda:1")
[ ]
```

A device can return nothi

items.title: [dynamo] Meta-issue: torch.compile gaps found via the CPython test suite
items.author: guilhermeleobas
items.body_excerpt:
I asked an agent to look at the graph break messages from the CPython test suite and
summarize the missing features in Dynamo. This is not an exhaustive list of all missing
features, but it contains some of the gaps that we want to close in the near term.

Some items are harder than they look (`functools.lru_cache` is the usual example).

## Disclaimer

I really appreciate anyone who tries to contribute to the project, but please avoid creating LLM generated code without really understand what the AI is doing. This just burns resources and human review time.

## How to run

```bash
# one module
PYTORCH_TEST_WITH_DYNAMO=1 python test/cpython/v3_13/test_iter.py -v

# one test
PYTORCH_TEST_WITH_DYNAMO=1 python test/cpython/v3_13/test_iter.py -v -k test_countOf
```

PyTorch must be built against Python 3.13. A known-failing test reports as `skipped` with
the graph-break reason attached, because it has a file under
`test/dynamo_expected_failures/CPython313-<module>-<Class>.<test>`. **Deleting that file is
part of your fix** - CI fails the test as an unexpected success otherwise.

---

## Shared root causes

The six items below each account for several failures across unrelated modules. Fixing one
unlocks every test listed under it, which makes these the highest-leverage work in this
issue.

### 1. `type.__new__` on a C-implemented type

`Unsupported method call: type.__new__`. This is the general "constructing any
non-allowlisted C-implemented type" gap, confirmed at four unrelated call sites. Probably
the single highest-leverage fix here.

- [ ] `test_functools.py::TestLRUPy::test_lru_no_args` and `TestLRUC::test_lru_no_args` - `@lru_cache` decoration
- [x] `test_set.py::TestSetSubclass::test_keywords_in_subclass` - `set`/`frozenset` subclassing (#196425)
- [ ] `test_sys.py::ExceptHookTest::test_excepthook` - `io.StringIO()` construction
- [ ] `test_contextlib.py::TestRedirectStdout::test_enter_result_is_target` - `io.StringIO()` construction

### 2. `Read uninitialized cell` (gb0091)

One root cause, eight tests, four unrelated modules - containers, exceptions, iterators.

- [ ] `test_list.py::ListTest::test_repr_mutate`
- [ ] `test_dict.py::DictTest::test_getitem`
- [ ] `test_dict.py::DictTest::test_reentrant_insertion`
- [ ] `test_dict.py::DictTest::test_str_nonstr`
- [ ] `test_set.py::_TestJointOps::test_deepcopy`
- [ ] `test_exceptions.py::NameErrorTests::test_gh_111654`
- [ ] `test_iter.py::TestCase::test_3720`
- [ ] `test_iter.py::TestCase::test_free_after_iterating`

### 3. Detected user errors don't surface as the real exception

Dynamo already knows the call is invalid, but instead of raising the `TypeError` CPython
would raise, it produces a generic wrapper, an internal crash, or an
`InternalTorchDynamoError`. Three severities, same underlying gap: user errors detected
during tracing need a path to "raise the real exception."

Generic `Unsupported: invalid call to builtin op handler` instead of a real `TypeError`
(`variables/builtin.py`, builtin-call argument binding):

- [x] `test_builtin.py::BuiltinTest::test_filter` (#196432)
- [x] `test_builtin.py::BuiltinTest::test_isinstance` (#196432)
- [x] `test_builtin.py::BuiltinTest::test_issubclass` (#196432)
- [x] `test_builtin.py::BuiltinTest::test_map` (#196432)
- [x] `test_builtin.py::TestSorted::test_bad_arguments` (#196432)
- [x] `test_builtin.py::TestSorted::test_baddecorator` (#196432)
- [x] `test_builtin.py::TestType::test_bad_args` (#196432)
- [x] `except 42:` - graph-breaks with `Exception with bad expected type`, CPython raises `TypeError` (#196432)
- [x] `except (ValueError, 42):` - tuple with a bad member (#196432)
- [x] `except <instance>:` - an instance, not a class (#196432)
- [x] `except "string":` (#196432)

Dynamo's own argument validation crashes:

- [x] `test_builtin.py::BuiltinTest::test_hasattr` - `hasattr(sys, 1)` crashes Dynamo's arg validation (#196432)

items.title: [RFC] Rerun code skips in rerun-disabled-tests
items.author: amdfaa
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

`rerun-disabled-tests` (`PYTORCH_TEST_RERUN_DISABLED_TESTS=1`) reruns tests that are still skipped by a DISABLED GitHub issue, so a run of greens can justify closing that issue. This RFC adds the same kind of signal for a code skip: a skip for a known failure on a machine that can run the test. A capability skip stays skipped. That is a missing library, `onlyCUDA`, `skipIf` / `skipUnless`, `requires_*`, or a version floor.

Two drafts start this work:

- PyTorch, which publishes the signal and does not delete decorators: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/199916
- test-infra, which would later open one daily draft proposing deletions and does not merge them: https://github.com/pytorch/test-infra/pull/9026

## Motivation

| Who | Need |
| --- | --- |
| Test authors | A skip for a known failure can outlive the failure. With no GitHub issue to close, nothing prompts deleting the decorator. |
| CI | The nightly job already reruns DISABLED-issue skips. A code skip never produces a pass or a fail. |

## Background

A DISABLED issue skip already has a loop. While the issue is open, the nightly job runs the test. 150 greens in 7 days and 0 reds, plus 14 quiet days, are the bar for closing the issue. Closing it removes the skip.

A code skip has no issue. The decorator is the only record, and it stays in force during `rerun-disabled-tests`. The nightly job cannot tell a fixed code skip from one that still fails.

This RFC leaves the issue path and the `rerun_disabled_tests` upload unchanged. Code-skip reruns go to a separate prefix, `rerun_disabled_code_skips`.

```
Python skip decorator
        ↓
mark safe-to-rerun skips
        ↓
pytest collection temporarily removes those skips
        ↓
test body passes, fails, or remains skipped
        ↓
JUnit XML retains the original skip reason
        ↓
results upload to rerun_disabled_code_skips
        ↓
test-infra can eventually propose deleting fixed decorators
```

Only code skips are marked safe to rerun. Capability skips are not marked.

Collection drops those marks for that job only. The decorator stays in the source file.

The body then passes, fails, or remains skipped. It remains skipped when a capability skip still applies. A pass or a fail does not edit the file.

The JUnit row keeps the original skip reason, so a pass or a fail can still be matched to the decorator that was lifted.

Those rows upload to `rerun_disabled_code_skips` and are not added to `rerun_disabled_tests`.

test-infra can later propose deleting decorators that clear the same bar as closing a DISABLED issue: 150 greens in 7 days and 0 reds. There is no 14-day quiet period, because a code skip has no issue. https://github.com/pytorch/test-infra/pull/9026 is that last step. It would open one daily draft pull request. That draft does not merge.

## Goals

- Run code skips in `rerun-disabled-tests`.
- Leave capability skips skipped, on every platform.
- Keep the original skip reason on the result when the body passes or fails.
- Upload code-skip reruns only to `rerun_disabled_code_skips`.
- Leave `rerun_disabled_tests` unchanged.
- Propose decorator deletions in a later human-reviewed draft. Do not delete them here.

## Non-goals

- Deleting decorators in https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/199916.
- Merging a deletion from https://github.com/pytorch/test-infra/pull/9026.
- Rerunning capability skips.
- Changing the DISABLED-issue path, its upload, or its 14 quiet days.
- Limiting the split to one platform.

## Alternatives

- Leave code skips until someone deletes them by hand. A fixed test stays skipped, with no green-run count behind a deletion.
- Upload code-skip reruns into `rerun_disabled_tests`. This RFC uses a separate prefix so the existing collection stays as it is.
- Rerun every skip. Failures on a machine that cannot run the test would be mixed in with real regressions.

## Additional context

- PyTorch: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/199916
- test-infra: https://github.com/pytorch/test-infra/pull/9026
- Deletion bar: 150 greens in 7 days and 0 reds. No 14-day quiet period.

items.title: [symm_mem] Local CUDA allocation leaks acquired resources when VMM setup fails
items.author: jackLei0901
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

I identified an ownership management flaw in the local allocation path of CUDA SymmetricMemory: resources are acquired prior to the construction of the `AllocationRef` object, yet there is no rollback mechanism in place should subsequent setup steps fail. CUDA documentation indicates that failures can occur during address reservation and mapping. I verified this lack of cleanup by using deterministic fault injection during the reservation, mapping, and access setup phases; however, I have not yet reproduced the issue naturally in actual workloads, nor have I confirmed its specific impact on production environments.

#### AI-assisted technical report

Codex assisted with the source analysis, candidate fix and regression test. The results below are from a source-built comparison on one RTX 4090.

`CUDASymmetricMemoryAllocator::alloc` constructs `AllocationRef` only after `map_block`, `cudaMemsetAsync` and `cudaStreamSynchronize`. If reserve, map or access setup throws, resources acquired earlier in the call are not unwound. The source also leaves an unowned-resource window if memset or synchronization throws; those two failures were not injected.

Source: [allocation and ownership handoff](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/215856938cfe9347ea2d0a20a766577e45fa5bb8/torch/csrc/distributed/c10d/symm_mem/CUDASymmetricMemory.cu#L450-L503), [map_block](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/215856938cfe9347ea2d0a20a766577e45fa5bb8/torch/csrc/distributed/c10d/symm_mem/CUDASymmetricMemoryUtils.cpp#L336-L356).

[CUDA documents out-of-memory errors for address reservation and mapping](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/archive/13.0.0/cuda-driver-api/group__CUDA__VA.html), both called here after handle creation. The tests use deterministic failure injection to check cleanup; no natural workload reproduction or production impact is claimed.

The standalone C++ gtest calls the allocator's public C++ `alloc`/`free` interface and temporarily intercepts `DriverAPI` to inject reserve/map/access errors, checking resources and event traces before fixture cleanup.

| Case | Base | Local fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Reserve fails | Handle remains; `release` missing | Pass |
| Map fails | Reservation and handle remain; `address_free` and `release` missing | Pass |
| Access setup fails | Mapping, reservation and handle remain; `unmap`, `address_free` and `release` missing | Pass |
| Normal allocation, data round-trip and free | Pass | Pass |

The fix also passed an unfiltered run: 4 tests, 0 failures, 0 skips.

Executed test source, target patch and instructions: https://gist.github.com/jackLei0901/18d5fad87b52119cee5d329b32da16c0.

The candidate guards acquisition in the CUDA `alloc` path until `AllocationRef` construction succeeds, then runs memset/synchronize under that owner and its existing destructor/cleanup gate. The four cases do not inject memset/synchronize failures.

Shared `map_block`, received descriptors, peer/multicast rollback, normal-path address-reservation release and ROCm are unchanged.

Owner-construction failure, memset/synchronize failure, secondary cleanup failure, Fabric, peer/multicast and ROCm behaviour were not runtime-tested. No upstream CI execution of the new binary is claimed.

#### Reporter conclusion and questions

I would like to submit a local-only CUDA fix that guards acquired resources until `AllocationRef` takes ownership, while leaving `map_block` and its peer/multicast callers unchanged. Do you support this scope? Would you accept a standalone C++ gtest that includes temporary DriverAPI interception? If so, which existing CI task should it be integrated into? I examined the CI entry points for SymmetricMemory and noticed they run Python test suites; would you prefer a Python-level regression test instead?

### Versions

> ```text
> PyTorch: 2.16.0a0+git2158569
> Source commit: 215856938cfe9347ea2d0a20a766577e45fa5bb8
> CUDA build version: 13.0
> CUDA toolkit: 13.0.88
> GPU: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090, capability 8.9
> OS: Linux
> SymmetricMemory backend: CUDA
> Caching allocator: native
> ```
