items.title: [dynamo] current_stream(<device index>) under torch.compile silently returns the tracked device's stream (wrong device)
items.author: AAYESLY
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

Surfaced while reviewing #192970 (the reproducer used torch_openreg;
filed as a follow-up).

## Bug

Under `torch.compile`, querying the current stream of an explicit device
index that is not the traced device silently returns the **tracked
(traced-device) stream** - the wrong device's stream - instead of erroring:

```python
import torch, torch_npu  # 2 NPU devices visible; reproduces identically
                          # with torch_openreg per the original finding

torch.zeros(1, device="npu:1")  # initialize device 1's default stream

def fn(x):
    return torch.npu.current_stream(1), x + 1

x = torch.ones(2, device="npu")
eager = fn(x)[0]
compiled = torch.compile(fn, backend="eager", fullgraph=True)(x)[0]
assert eager.device_index == compiled.device_index, "wrong stream returned"
# AssertionError: eager device_index=1, compiled device_index=0
```

## Root cause

`handle_current_stream` resolves the request through
`SymbolicStreamState.cur_stream(device)`, which scans the tracked stream
stack for a matching device and **falls back to the top entry** when none
matches. The stack only ever holds the traced device's current stream, so
`current_stream(1)` while tracing device 0 falls back to device 0's stream.
The type-level mismatch check from #192970 does not catch this (same device
type, different index). The behavior is pre-existing for cuda/xpu through
the same handler; #192970's registration loop extends it to out-of-tree
backends, which makes it observable.


### Versions

PyTorch version: 2.15.0.dev20260928+cpu
Is debug build: False
CUDA used to build PyTorch: None
ROCm SDK used to build PyTorch: N/A
HIP used to build PyTorch: N/A

items.title: CUDA training loop runs ~50x slower while a DataLoader iterates in a background thread, since 2.10.0
items.author: Y-T-G
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

PyTorch appears to be slower in newer versions. From my testing, slowdown starts at 2.10.0. It slows down when dataloader is involved. I have attached repro steps.

#### AI-generated report

> The section below was written by Claude Code (Anthropic) from measurements it ran on our machine. The numbers and logs are copied from those runs.

Since torch 2.10.0, a launch-bound CUDA training loop slows from about 8.4 ms to about 400 ms per step while a `DataLoader` with workers delivers large batches in a background thread of the same process. On 2.9.1 the same loader adds under 0.5 ms per step. The loop alone runs at the same speed on every version.

Repro below. The main thread trains a small conv net with AMP and calls `.item()` once per step. With `loader`, a daemon thread iterates a `DataLoader` (8 workers, batch 64, `uint8` 3x640x640 images, about 79 MB per batch) and drops each batch.

```python
import os
import sys
import threading
import time

import torch
import torch.nn as nn


class Images(torch.utils.data.Dataset):
    def __len__(self):
        return 1 << 20

    def __getitem__(self, i):
        return torch.full((3, 640, 640), i % 255, dtype=torch.uint8)


def drain(loader):
    for _ in loader:  # receive each ~79 MB shared-memory batch and drop it
        pass


def main():
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    model = nn.Sequential(
        *[nn.Sequential(nn.Conv2d(32, 32, 3, padding=1), nn.BatchNorm2d(32), nn.SiLU()) for _ in range(40)]
    ).cuda()
    opt = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
    x = torch.randn(16, 32, 64, 64, device="cuda")

    if sys.argv[1] == "loader":
        loader = torch.utils.data.DataLoader(Images(), batch_size=64, num_workers=8)
        threading.Thread(target=drain, args=(loader,), daemon=True).start()
        time.sleep(5)  # let the workers start

    def step():
        with torch.autocast("cuda", dtype=torch.float16):
            loss = model(x).float().mean()
        loss.backward()
        opt.step()
        opt.zero_grad()
        return loss.item()

    for _ in range(30):
        step()
    times = []
    for _ in range(5):
        torch.cuda.synchronize()
        t = time.perf_counter()
        for _ in range(50):
            step()
        torch.cuda.synchronize()
        times.append((time.perf_counter() - t) / 50 * 1e3)
    print(f"torch {torch.__version__}  background={sys.argv[1]:6s}  ms/step median {sorted(times)[2]:.2f}  all {[round(t, 2) for t in times]}", flush=True)
    os._exit(0)  # skip tearing down the daemon thread's workers


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

items.title: [Data] Converting multi-chunk variable-shaped tensor columns to pandas skips the dense fast path
items.author: rayo5o
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

#66122 made `TensorDtype.__from_arrow__` return one dense view when a variable-shaped tensor column has uniformly shaped rows. That only happens for a single chunk ([pandas.py#L436-L452](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/f4f37d399886529c69c201cca9a714ace9c7c06e/python/ray/data/_internal/tensor_extensions/pandas.py#L436-L452)). With two or more chunks, each chunk still goes through `to_numpy()`, which returns one ndarray per row, and the rows are then stacked one by one. The PR left this out of scope ([description](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/pull/66122), [review](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/pull/66122#pullrequestreview-5242470499)).

`iter_batches` runs into this whenever a batch spans two blocks. `Batcher` joins blocks with the same schema through `pa.concat_tables`, so the column reaches `__from_arrow__` with one chunk per block.

Proposed change: in the multi-chunk branch, convert each chunk with `tensor_array_to_numpy()`. If every chunk comes back dense with the same row shape, join them with one `np.concatenate`. Otherwise keep the current path, which also covers the dense-plus-ragged case that #66122 mentions. Chunks sit in different buffers, so this still copies once and is not zero-copy like the single-chunk case. It replaces the per-row stacking with one contiguous copy.

Measured with `iter_batches(batch_size=..., batch_format="pandas")` over a materialized dataset whose blocks hold uniformly shaped `ArrowVariableShapedTensorArray` rows. In "aligned", each block is one batch, so every batch column has 1 chunk. In "crossing", each block is half a batch, so every batch column has 2 chunks. "crossing + prototype" applies the change above inside the benchmark process only. Median of 5 runs, each in a fresh process.

| rows | batch size | layout | total | inside `__from_arrow__` |
|---|---:|---|---:|---:|
| 65,536 × (128,) float32 | 1024 | aligned | 144 ms | 9.6 ms |
| | | crossing | 346 ms | 156 ms |
| | | crossing + prototype | 209 ms | 27 ms |
| 2,048 × (224, 224, 3) uint8 | 64 | aligned | 120 ms | 8.0 ms |
| | | crossing | 172 ms | 82 ms |
| | | crossing + prototype | 160 ms | 62 ms |

Most of the gain is with small rows, where per-row work dominates: the conversion goes from 156 ms to 27 ms and the whole loop from 346 ms to 209 ms. With image-sized rows both paths are mostly the copy itself, so the change helps less (82 ms to 62 ms). Output was checked to be the same in all three layouts.

I couldn't find an open issue or PR for this. #67236 also edits `__from_arrow__`, but only adds null-row checks around this branch.

I'll open a PR for this. cc @marwan116 @rayhhome since it follows up on #66122.

<details>
<summary>Benchmark script</summary>

Run each layout in a fresh process, e.g. `python bench.py --layout crossing --prototype --shape 224x224x3 --dtype uint8 --batch-size 64 --rows 2048`.

```python
"""iter_batches(batch_format="pandas") on a uniformly shaped variable-shaped
tensor column, with batches that come from one block vs. span two blocks.

One run per process. Prints one JSON line.

  python multichunk_iter_batches_bench.py --layout aligned|crossing \
      [--prototype] [--shape 128] [--dtype float32] [--batch-size 1024] [--rows 65536]

aligned:   rows_per_block == batch_size, so every batch column has 1 chunk.
crossing:  rows_per_block == batch_size // 2, so every batch column has 2 chunks.
--prototype replaces the multi-chunk branch of TensorDtype.__from_arrow__ inside
this process only (per-chunk tensor_array_to_numpy + one np.concatenate), to
estimate what a fix would buy. Ray source is not modified.
"""

import argparse
import json
import time

import numpy as np
import pyarrow as pa

import ray
from ray.data._internal.tensor_extensions import pandas as tpd
from ray.data._internal.tensor_extensions.arrow import (
    ArrowVariableShapedTensorArray,
    tensor_array_to_numpy,
)

p = argparse.ArgumentParser()
p.add_argument("--layout", choices=["aligned", "crossing"], required=True)
p.add_argument("--prototype", action="store_true")
p.add_argument("--shape", default="128")
p.add_argument("--dtype", default="float32")
p.add_argument("--batch-size", type=int, default=1024)
p.add_argument("--rows", type=int, default=65536)
args = p.parse_args()

shape = tuple(int(s) for s in args.shape.split("x"))
rows_per_block = args.batch_size if args.layout == "aligned" else args.batch_size // 2
num_blocks = args.rows // rows_per_block

# Instrument __from_arrow__: chunk counts and time spent inside it.
stats = {"calls": 0, "chunks": {}, "seconds": 0.0}
orig_from_arrow = tpd.TensorDtype.__from_arrow__


def prototype_from_arrow(self, array):
    if isinstance(array, pa.ChunkedArray) and array.num_chunks > 1:
        parts = [tensor_array_to_numpy(c) for c in array.iterchunks()]
        if all(p.dtype != object for p in parts) and len(
            {p.shape[1:] for p in parts}
        ) == 1:
            return tpd.TensorArray(np.concatenate(parts))
    return orig_from_arrow(self, array)


inner = prototype_from_arrow if args.prototype else orig_from_arrow


def timed_from_arrow(self, array):
    n = array.num_chunks if isinstance(array, pa.ChunkedArray) else 1
    stats["chunks"][n] = stats["chunks"].get(n, 0) + 1
    stats["calls"] += 1
    s = time.perf_counter()
    out = inner(self, array)
    stats["seconds"] += time.perf_counter() - s
    return out


tpd.TensorDtype.__from_arrow__ = timed_from_arrow

ray.init(num_cpus=4, include_dashboard=False, log_to_driver=False)

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
tables = []
for b in range(num_blocks):
    rows = [
        rng.random(shape).astype(args.dtype) if args.dtype.startswith("float")
        else rng.integers(0, 255, shape).astype(args.dtype)
        for _ in range(rows_per_block)
    ]
    tables.append(pa.table({"x": ArrowVariableShapedTensorArray.from_numpy(rows)}))
ds = ray.data.from_arrow(tables).materialize()
assert ds.num_blocks() == num_blocks

checksum = 0.0
s = time.perf_counter()

items.title: [RLlib] MultiAgentEnvRunner can downgrade WEIGHTS_SEQ_NO after rejecting stale module state
items.author: lindicaphxag-tech
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

`MultiAgentEnvRunner.set_state` uses `WEIGHTS_SEQ_NO` to reject stale positive-version module states, but **unconditionally assigns the incoming positive version to `self._weights_seq_no` even when the module weights were not applied**. A delayed older state therefore makes a runner's advertised version regress, despite its parameters remaining newer.

This is a separate, remaining EnvRunner-side version invariant from the learner-side correction in #67131; I have not mixed the two production patches.

## Deterministic counterexample using the current production method

Checked against the current `ray-project/ray` `master` implementation in `python/ray/rllib/env/multi_agent_env_runner.py`:

1. Runner is at `_weights_seq_no=8`, with policy parameters for version 8.
2. `set_state({COMPONENT_RL_MODULE: stale_v7_weights, WEIGHTS_SEQ_NO: 7})` is called (e.g. an explicit out-of-order state delivery).
3. The existing guard correctly **skips applying stale_v7_weights** (`8 < 7` is false).
4. However, the later `if weights_seq_no > 0: self._weights_seq_no = weights_seq_no` **downgrades the reported version from 8 to 7**.
5. Another version-8 delivery is now incorrectly considered new, triggering a redundant module update. External consumers observing the runner version see a version inconsistent with the current parameters.

A [source-extracted CPU regression with real production `Learner.set_state` and `MultiAgentEnvRunner.set_state` methods](https://github.com/lindicaphxag-tech/ray/blob/ci/rllib-learner-version-contract-20261022/ci/rllib_learner_weight_version_contract.py) reproduces the runner downgrade independently of #67131. The [passing GitHub Actions run](https://github.com/lindicaphxag-tech/ray/actions/runs/39810724497) records:

```
CONFIRMED SEPARATE DOWNSTREAM GAP: EnvRunner rejected stale parameters but downgraded its seq 8 -> 7
```

That fixture uses simple deterministic module objects (no live Ray actors); it proves the reachable method-level state transition, **not** that live Ray actor message reordering has been observed in a deployed workload. Stale explicit `set_state` and checkpoint ordering semantics should be discussed before changing behavior.

## Proposed narrowly scoped contract

For a positive `WEIGHTS_SEQ_NO`, `set_state` must never decrease a runner's version when it skips applying older parameters. A missing or zero version retains its documented force-apply behavior and must not advance the sequence without an agreed publication contract.

Potential minimal correction: only update `_weights_seq_no` when `weights_seq_no > self._weights_seq_no`, with a native `MultiAgentEnvRunner.set_state` test asserting weights and version remain coherent for stale / equal / newer values; include a forced module-only update case as a compatibility guard. A separate test should validate the exported `get_state` version.

## Scope and maintainer question

This is a focused state-provenance correctness case, not an assertion of RL training quality improvement, distributed linearizability, or a measured production incident. It is related to but separate from #67131 (which addresses `Learner.set_state`); the best separation is probably to finish #67131 without expanding its diff, then patch `MultiAgentEnvRunner` in a small independent PR.

Would maintainers prefer this as a separate narrow PR, or combined with the existing weight-sequence discussion? I can prepare a native test and minimal implementation once the intended semantics are confirmed.

AI assistance was used for the source audit and deterministic harness. All claims above are limited to the actual code and observed Actions logs.


### Minimal candidate and completed red/green validation — 2026-10-22

A targeted **two-file** solution is now ready on my fork, based directly on current official `master@a82c56e`: [compare only the candidate implementation and native tests](https://github.com/lindicaphxag-tech/ray/compare/a82c56ee769fc02b1e4442d2ade57c9713263443...fix/rllib-envrunner-monotonic-seq-20261022). Production diff: **2 lines inserted / 2 deleted** in `multi_agent_env_runner.py`; native test: 42 lines. It preserves the existing force-update behavior for missing/zero `WEIGHTS_SEQ_NO` and the newer-version path. No broader API or learner changes.

The independent [CPU source-extracted red/green GitHub Actions run **completed successfully**](https://github.com/lindicaphxag-tech/ray/actions/runs/39811945539). It executes the actual `MultiAgentEnvRunner.set_state` body from both the patch and pinned unchanged official source. It confirms:
- Original: stale v7 payload rejected by runner at v8, yet version **8 → 7**; subsequent already-resident v8 is unnecessarily applied again.
- Proposed: stale v7 is rejected **without** downgrade; equal v8 is a no-op; newer v9 updates module/version together; unversioned module-only state still force-applies without incrementing the global version.
- Candidate production/native-test source compilation and focused static checks pass. Full native Ray runtime and multi-actor CI **not yet run**; this is not a claim of deployed message reordering.

[Scoped fork CI PR #5](https://github.com/lindicaphxag-tech/ray/pull/5) contains independent verification scripts/workflow **only**, excluded from the proposed upstream diff. To keep existing [Learner-side PR #67131](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/pull/67131) reviewable, I propose handling this EnvRunner-side guarantee in a separate minimal PR once a maintainer agrees with the intended version semantics.

items.title: [RLlib] Rejected Learner snapshots can still overwrite optimizer and training-selector state
items.author: lindicaphxag-tech
items.body_excerpt:
## Problem: a rejected Learner snapshot can still change what gets trained

A Learner checkpoint may contain **RLModule weights**, **optimizer state**, and the **should_module_be_updated** selector, together with WEIGHTS_SEQ_NO. Today the weight component is rejected for an old/equal positive version, but the optimizer state and trainability selector can still be applied. In addition, an optimizer-only packet carrying a higher version can publish a weight version **without installing weights**.

These are three related causal-admission requirements:

1. If a versioned **module+optimizer** bundle is refused, its attached optimizer must not be installed.
2. If a versioned **module+trainability-selector** bundle is refused, its attached selector must not change which modules are trained next.
3. A **model weight version** may advance only after a model-state install or a local training update. Optimizer-only and selector-only packets remain independently supported.

### Concrete evidence (all tests execute the real production method)

- **Real PyTorch Adam:** delayed paired v9->v10 state corruption changes the next Adam parameter update by L2=0.000322280417; equal-sequence different-source state changes it by L2=0.05105971. The guarded candidate preserves the consistent reference update.
- **Actual Ray 2.59.0 native Learner:** 4 native TestLearner methods, including its real should_module_be_updated(DEFAULT_MODULE_ID) routing decision. The *prior two-component candidate* passes the first 3 tests but fails the new selector test; the refined candidate passes all 4. [Native red/green CI](https://github.com/lindicaphxag-tech/ray/actions/runs/39915547493)
- **Source-driven bounded sequence check:** 52 packet kinds (full, paired, module-only, module+selector, optimizer-only, selector-only, metadata-only; versions 0..3 and two sources). Across 143,364 ordered traces of 1..3 calls, the prior candidate violates the selector-coherence rule in 43,784 traces; the new candidate has no violations of the specified finite-model properties. [Bounded validation CI](https://github.com/lindicaphxag-tech/ray/actions/runs/39914974923)
- **Unmodified official Ray master** also reproduces the same-version foreign-Adam state mismatch and optimizer-only false weight publication: [official-master negative control](https://github.com/lindicaphxag-tech/ray/actions/runs/39905764492).

### Small candidate for maintainers

[Two-file diff relative to existing PR #67131](https://github.com/lindicaphxag-tech/ray/compare/fix/rllib-version-unversioned-set-state-20261018...review/rllib-three-component-causal-state-20261023)

Production uses one module_update_accepted predicate, evaluated **before changing the version**, and applies it to model weights, accompanying optimizer state, accompanying trainability selection, and version publication. This preserves optimizer-only and selector-only state transfers, forced unversioned installs and strictly newer versioned installs. The review branch changes only learner.py and its native tests; research/CI scripts remain separate.

[Research note, exact transition rules, proof scope and counterexamples](https://github.com/lindicaphxag-tech/ray/blob/research/rllib-trainable-policy-state-coherence-20261023/research/RLLIB_THREE_COMPONENT_ADMISSION_20261023.md)

### Maintainer question

For a **complete checkpoint with version equal to the current Learner**, should we retain the current strict-newer module rule (reject the *entire* equal-version bundle), or introduce an explicit authoritative force-restore behavior that applies all three components together? Either choice should avoid silently combining different source states.

**Scope:** These runs verify successful-call admission coherence under finite sequential schedules. They do **not** prove ACID rollback if a component setter throws, live multi-actor interleaving safety, real RL-return improvements, or full latest-master integration. Existing [#67131](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/pull/67131) remains Open with Buildkite Microcheck failures; I have **not** expanded or superseded that PR without maintainer agreement.


### End-to-end training-step consequence and a protocol boundary (2026-10-23)

The earlier two-component guard could still import `should_module_be_updated`
from a rejected equal-version snapshot, excluding the default policy from
the next training batch. I extended the validation from state mocks to a
**real Ray 2.59.0 Learner updating a native CartPole batch of 200 rows**,
keeping the same installed runtime and test method for both variants.

- **Previous two-component candidate:** the injected rejected snapshot changes
  the trainable selector to `{"stale_opponent"}`; the live default policy is
  excluded. The actual update path on this Ray wheel raises
  `UnboundLocalError` with no parameter change (`max |Δθ|=0`).
- **Current three-component candidate:** the rejected selector is ignored;
  the default policy remains eligible and the real Learner completes the
  same training-batch update (`max |Δθ|=0.001000002027`).
- All four checked-out native TestLearner methods pass under the candidate;
  the previous candidate fails only the newly introduced selector-provenance
  test. Ruff and Black are green.

[Actual gradient-step red/green GitHub Actions](https://github.com/lindicaphxag-tech/ray/actions/runs/39923421681)
· [review-only two-file diff](https://github.com/lindicaphxag-tech/ray/compare/fix/rllib-version-unversioned-set-state-20261018...review/rllib-three-component-causal-state-20261023).

**Important boundary:** the actual `get_state(components=COMPONENT_OPTIMIZER)`
response still includes `should_module_be_updated` and `WEIGHTS_SEQ_NO`,
even though the caller selected only optimizer state. An intentional joint
optimizer+selector update and an optimizer-only request with incidental
selector metadata can yield the **same wire packet**. Thus the receiver

items.title: [Data] Terminal-only waits are counted as task output backpressure
items.author: Yin-1022
items.body_excerpt:
## Problem / Description

While reviewing #67180, I noticed a separate, pre-existing issue in DataOpTask's output-backpressure accounting.

`DataOpTask._track_task_`output_backpressure() currently starts the output-backpressure timer whenever `max_bytes_to_read == 0`. 
However, a zero read budget does not necessarily mean that the task has unread output.

For example, an empty streaming task can already have its stream fully exhausted, with no block or metadata output left to consume, while the driver is only waiting to observe terminal completion. 
If on_data_ready() is called with a zero output-read budget during this period, the task still accumulates task_output_backpressure_s.

This means time spent waiting only for terminal confirmation can be reported as output backpressure even though no output is waiting to be read.

This issue is separate from #67180 and reproduces on the unmodified current implementation.

## Minimal Reproduction
A minimal internal-API regression case is:

```
streaming_gen = create_stub_streaming_gen(block_nbytes=[])

task = DataOpTask(
    0,
    streaming_gen,
    BlockRefCounter(),
    "test_op",
)

ray.get(streaming_gen.completed(), timeout=20)
assert streaming_gen._stream_exhausted()

clock = [100.0]
monkeypatch.setattr(
    "ray.data._internal.execution.interfaces.physical_operator.time.perf_counter",
    lambda: clock[0],
)

fetcher = InlineMetadataFetcher()

# No output exists; only terminal completion remains.
assert task.on_data_ready(0, fetcher) == 0

clock[0] += 10

# Allow the current implementation to observe EOF and finish.
assert task.on_data_ready(1, fetcher) == 0

assert task.has_finished
assert task._total_output_backpressure_s == 0
```

### Actual behavior (unmodified Ray):
```
task._total_output_backpressure_s == 10.0
```

The task reports 10 seconds of output backpressure even though the streaming generator produced no output.

### Expected behavior:
```
task._total_output_backpressure_s == 0
```

Waiting only for terminal completion should not count as output backpressure when there is no unread block or metadata output.

Actual unread output should continue to count normally, including the case where the generator stream is already exhausted but a block/metadata pair has already been pulled and remains pending inside DataOpTask.

## Proposal

Track output backpressure only when both conditions are true:

1. max_bytes_to_read == 0
2. the task still has unread output.

A task still has unread output when at least one of the following holds:

1. _pending_block_ref is non-ni;
2. _pending_meta_ref is non-nil
3. the streaming generator has not yet been exhausted.

If a backpressure interval is already open and these conditions stop being true, close the interval even if the output-read budget remains zero. 
This prevents terminal-only waiting time from being included in the metric while preserving accounting for actual pending output.

items.author: lindicaphxag-tech
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

On the new RLlib stack, `Algorithm.restore_env_runners` correctly reconstructs modules and copies RLModule weights/version/connector state from the healthy local EnvRunner into a restored remote EnvRunner. **It does not restore the local EnvRunner's runtime-modified `policy_mapping_fn` or `policies_to_train`.** Those values are not serialized in `MultiAgentEnvRunner.get_state()`, so recovery can yield the *new correct weights with the old policy routing/training selection*.

This is especially relevant for dynamic multi-agent leagues, which update `env_runner.config.multi_agent(policy_mapping_fn=..., policies_to_train=...)` after adding/cloning policies. This is a **distinct recovery-consistency issue** from #67103's intra-runner weight-installation-before-mapping guarantee and from #67284's version monotonicity issue.

### Production mechanism

- `MultiAgentEnvRunner.get_state()` returns RLModule weights, `WEIGHTS_SEQ_NO`, connector state and sampled-step counters, but no runtime multi-agent mapping or trainability selectors.
- `Algorithm.restore_env_runners()` reconstructs modules from `MultiRLModuleSpec.from_module(from_env_runner.module)`, then invokes `er.set_state(ray.get(state_ref))` on restored actors. It does not copy `from_env_runner.config.policy_mapping_fn` or `policies_to_train`.
- `Algorithm.add_module()` changes the AlgorithmConfig only when passed `new_agent_to_module_mapping_fn` / `new_should_module_be_updated`; callbacks that update EnvRunner config directly can leave the original construction config behind. Restored workers cannot rely solely on default constructor configuration to recover dynamic mapping.

### Exact deterministic counterexample, with actual Ray Actor RPC

1. Local source EnvRunner now has modules `main=42` and `league_1=17`, weight sequence v5, mapping `league_1`, trainable set `{main,league_1}`.
2. A freshly constructed remote Ray Actor has only `main=-7`, seq v0, original mapping `main`, trainable set `{main}`.
3. Run the **actual extracted production** `Algorithm.restore_env_runners`, `MultiAgentEnvRunner.get_state`, `set_state` methods through a real `FaultTolerantActorManager` and `EnvRunnerGroup.foreach_env_runner`. The "restored" Actor is explicitly recreated in the test; no process crash is claimed.
4. **Official unchanged source**: remote Actor has correct modules/weights `42,17` and seq `5`, **but still routes to `main`** and trains only `main`.
5. **Minimal candidate**: capture the local source's mapping and trainable set alongside the weight state, and install them on the *same restored actor after* its weights: final mapping `league_1`, trainable set `{main,league_1}`.

[Real Ray Actor red/green GitHub Actions — **success**](https://github.com/lindicaphxag-tech/ray/actions/runs/39904779455); [source-method red/green — **success**](https://github.com/lindicaphxag-tech/ray/actions/runs/39904518727).

The complete fork-only test and workflow are on [fork PR #8](https://github.com/lindicaphxag-tech/ray/pull/8). The separate [production-only candidate](https://github.com/lindicaphxag-tech/ray/compare/7795d644673b4a4ed4d407fd9e7b0ca981e9606b...fix/rllib-restored-runner-dynamic-policy-config-20261023) changes only `python/ray/rllib/algorithms/algorithm.py`, without changing the existing upstream #67103 head.

### Proposed recovery contract and boundaries

When restoring with a **local source EnvRunner**, replicate the coherent tuple `(module specification, module weights, weight version, policy_mapping_fn, policies_to_train)`. Install the module and state *before* enabling its matching routing selector on that same actor.

This is **not** a linearizable cross-cluster activation protocol, does not yet address recovery when no local source EnvRunner exists, and is **not** a full native same-commit Ray 3.0 integration test. Actual actor-RPC tests used the released compiled Ray 2.59.0 wheel plus the current production method bodies; policy modules are small deterministic scalar state objects.

**Maintainer question:** Is a recovery-specific copy of the current local EnvRunner policy mapping and training selector desirable in the generic `Algorithm.restore_env_runners` path, or should this information be formalized as part of a dedicated (versioned) multi-agent runtime configuration checkpoint? I can prepare a targeted native Ray test for whichever contract is intended, keeping #67103 focused.

AI tooling assisted the audit and deterministic harness; the scope/limitations above are based on the actual code and successful Actions logs.

### Native regression candidate and repeated complete CI (2026-10-23)

Added a focused native `TestAlgorithm.test_restore_env_runner_reinstates_runtime_multi_agent_routing` case in the *fork-only candidate* `python/ray/rllib/algorithms/tests/test_algorithm.py`. It calls the production `Algorithm.restore_env_runners` method, checks the missing module is reconstructed, confirms module state installation precedes updated `policy_mapping_fn` and `policies_to_train`, and checks the restoration counter.

Current candidate consists of just [**two upstream files**](https://github.com/lindicaphxag-tech/ray/compare/7795d644673b4a4ed4d407fd9e7b0ca981e9606b...fix/rllib-restored-runner-dynamic-policy-config-20261023): the Algorithm restoration method and that native test. The new test is compiled and passes focused Ruff static analysis; full same-commit Ray pytest is **not yet executed**. The legacy test file has two pre-existing Ruff formatting differences outside the changed unit, intentionally not rewritten.

[**Actual Ray Actor RPC official-vs-candidate CI: Success**](https://github.com/lindicaphxag-tech/ray/actions/runs/39905808096). items.title: [Data] DownstreamCapacityBackpressurePolicy applies no backpressure when the downstream operator has 0 bytes in flight, so an operator's output queue can fill the whole object-store budget
items.author: praateekmahajan
items.body_excerpt:
**Impact, in short:** because of this, when the downstream operator has nothing in flight (actors starting up, or a starved or backpressured downstream), an upstream operator keeps being admitted. Its output queue grows until it takes the whole Ray Data object-store budget. After that, every downstream operator is blocked on `pending_output_exceeds_object_store_budget`, the actor autoscaler sees no runnable work and scales the pools down, and throughput collapses until the queue drains.

It is a throughput collapse, not a hard deadlock: `OutputBackpressureGuard` still lets one block through, so the pipeline crawls and then recovers. We hit it on Ray 2.57.0 in a 6-operator single-node pipeline (fanout reader → repartition → 3 actor stages → writer): throughput went ~1,340 → ~540 rows/s and GPU utilization 100% → 14–37% for ~15 min, twice in one run. A minimal CPU-only repro is below; it also reproduces on today's nightly.


### What happened + What you expected to happen

`DownstreamCapacityBackpressurePolicy` compares an operator's queued output with its downstream "capacity" (the bytes of inputs held by the downstream operator's running tasks). When that capacity is exactly 0, the policy treats it as "no backpressure":

```python
# python/ray/data/_internal/execution/backpressure_policy/downstream_capacity_backpressure_policy.py
# Ray 2.57.0: _get_queue_ratio, L174-181
# master @ 7023d11 (2026-10-23): _get_output_pressure, L183-186
downstream_capacity_size_bytes = self._get_downstream_capacity_size_bytes(op)
if downstream_capacity_size_bytes == 0:
    # No downstream capacity to backpressure against, so no backpressure.
    return 0
```

Downstream capacity is 0 whenever the downstream operator has no tasks running. That happens often, for example:
- an actor pool is still starting (the actors load a model in `__init__`);
- the downstream operator is CPU-starved, or is itself backpressured by its own downstream, so it is between tasks.

In those moments the upstream operator is admitted and its outputs are read with no limit from this policy. That holds even when its output queue is hundreds of times larger than anything downstream is processing, and when its object-store budget is already 97-100% used. The `OBJECT_STORE_BUDGET_UTIL_THRESHOLD` gate does not help here, because it can only turn backpressure off, never on. The only thing that stops the growth is the shared object-store budget (`ResourceBudgetBackpressurePolicy`), so one operator ends up taking the whole shared pool.

**Expected:** if downstream has nothing in flight and the operator already has output queued (and is above the utilization threshold), the queue/capacity ratio is effectively infinite, so the operator should be backpressured. It should not get a free pass. The queued output is already available to the downstream operator, so holding the producer back costs no throughput.

#### Minimal repro (below), Ray 2.57.0 and nightly (master 7023d11), 16 CPUs, Ray Data object-store limit 1 GiB

`fanout map_batches (TaskPool size 2) -> repartition(target_num_rows_per_block=1) -> actor pool (20 s __init__, 0.2 s/row)`. While the actors start, `StreamingRepartition` has `downstream_capacity_bytes=0` and keeps getting `False` (no backpressure) until its queue is 609 MB and its budget is 100% used:

```
DEBUG downstream_capacity_backpressure_policy.py:209 -- Backpressure change StreamingRepartition[...]: None -> False (queue_ratio=0.00, queue_size_bytes=0, downstream_capacity_bytes=0, utilized_budget_fraction=None)
DEBUG downstream_capacity_backpressure_policy.py:209 -- Backpressure change StreamingRepartition[...]: False -> True (queue_ratio=581.00, queue_size_bytes=609241248, downstream_capacity_bytes=1048608, utilized_budget_fraction=1.0)
DEBUG downstream_capacity_backpressure_policy.py:209 -- Backpressure change StreamingRepartition[...]: True -> False (queue_ratio=0.00, queue_size_bytes=552616416, downstream_capacity_bytes=0, utilized_budget_fraction=0.965...)
```

The output of an instrumented version of the repro (1 s samples taken inside the executor loop) shows the same pattern on both versions:

| run (one run each) | peak Ray Data object-store use | peak StreamingRepartition usage | "allowed" with util > 0.5, capacity = 0, queue > 0 | rows | wall |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2.57.0 stock | **83.5 %** | **608 MB** | 181 | 3200/3200 | 192 s |
| 2.57.0 + fix below | 45 % | 248 MB | 0 | 3200/3200 | 193 s |
| nightly 7023d11 stock | **83.7 %** | **578 MB** | 183 | 3200/3200 | 160 s (repeat: 174 s) |
| nightly + fix below | 46 % | 244 MB | 0 | 3200/3200 | 174 s (repeat: 173 s) |

Stock 2.57.0 timeline (consumer actors not ready until ~33 s):
```
t_s  repartition_MB  consumer_actors  consumer_inflight_MB  global_used_frac
17.2      22               0                 0                 0.29
22.6     270               0                 0                 0.55
27.9     520               0                 0                 0.80
30.0     608               0                 0                 0.84
```
With the fix, `StreamingRepartition` stops at ~159 MB (global 0.44) at t=22 s, with a log line `False -> True (queue_ratio=inf, queue_size_bytes=156244976, downstream_capacity_bytes=0, utilized_budget_fraction=0.528)`. It resumes normal ratio-based pacing once the consumer has inputs in flight (`True -> False (queue_ratio=139.50, ..., downstream_capacity_bytes=1048624, utilized_budget_fraction=0.4998)`). In both versions every row arrives, with no deadlock and no change in throughput.

#### Production impact (same code path, different trigger)

The pipeline is a 6-operator pipeline on Ray 2.57.0: `fanout reader map_batches (generator UDF, TaskPool size 2, one ~3.8 GB input file -> ~23k rows) -> repartition(target_num_rows_per_block=1) -> 3 actor-pool stages -> writer`. `StreamingRepartition` was CPU-starved and/or backpressured by its downstream, and showed `Tasks: 0` in 302 of 542 executor debug dumps. Each time, the reader was let

items.title: [RFC]: Support Encode/Prefill/Decode (EPD) Disaggregation in AIBrix Gateway
items.author: varungup90
items.body_excerpt: ### Summary This RFC proposes adding Encode/Prefill/Decode (EPD) disaggregation support to AIBrix Gateway. Today, AIBrix supports Prefill/Decode (PD) disaggregation. With growing multimodal workloads, the encoding stage can also become a significant and independently scalable part of inference. EPD disaggregation separates inference into three stages: * Encode (E): Process multimodal inputs such as image, video, or audio and generate intermediate representations. * Prefill (P): Process prompt tokens and encoder outputs and generate KV cache. * Decode (D): Perform autoregressive token generation. The Gateway should become aware of these worker roles and route requests to the appropriate Encode, Prefill, and Decode worker pools. ### Motivation Encode, Prefill, and Decode have different compute and memory characteristics. Running all stages on the same workers can lead to resource contention and makes it difficult to scale each stage independently. EPD disaggregation enables: * Independent scaling of Encode, Prefill, and Decode workers. * Better resource utilization for multimodal workloads. * Different hardware or parallelism configurations for each stage. * Isolation of expensive multimodal encoding from Prefill/Decode workloads. * Reuse of the existing AIBrix PD routing architecture for multimodal serving. vLLM has started supporting disaggregated encoder architectures, including EPD-style deployments: * https://docs.vllm.ai/projects/ascend/en/latest/user_guide/feature_guide/epd_disaggregation.html * https://docs.vllm.ai/en/stable/features/disagg_encoder/ ### Proposed Change Extend AIBrix Gateway’s existing PD disaggregation support to understand an additional Encode worker role. Conceptually: For multimodal requests, the Gateway should: 1. Identify compatible Encode, Prefill, and Decode workers. 2. Select workers using the existing AIBrix load-balancing framework. 3. Pass the required routing/transfer metadata to the inference engine. 4. Allow the inference engine and its connectors to handle encoder-output and KV-cache transfers. For text-only requests, the Encode stage can be bypassed and existing PD routing can continue to be used. The implementation should reuse the existing PD routing infrastructure as much as possible rather than introducing a separate routing architecture. Initial Scope * Add encode as a supported worker role alongside prefill and decode. * Discover and maintain Encode/Prefill/Decode worker pools. * Extend PD routing to select a compatible E/P/D execution path. * Support multimodal requests requiring an Encode stage. * Keep encoder-output and KV-cache transfer outside of the Gateway. * Add basic stage-level routing metrics and failure handling. Future work can explore encoder-cache-aware routing, heterogeneous hardware selection, and independent autoscaling of E/P/D worker pools. Open Questions * Should Encode workers be shared across multiple Prefill/Decode pools? * What metadata should the Gateway provide to coordinate encoder-output transfer? * Should worker selection happen in E → P → D order, or should Decode/Prefill capacity drive the selection first? * How much of the existing PD router can be generalized into an EPD stage-aware router? ### Alternatives Considered _No response_ ### Area Not sure

items.title: [RFC]: Support asynchronous video generation in the Batch API
items.author: scarlet25151
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

Add `/v1/videos` as a Batch endpoint. Clients submit OpenAI-style Batch JSONL, and the Batch worker creates each video job, waits for its terminal status, and saves the generated content to AIBrix file storage before reporting the row as completed.

The first backend protocol is vLLM-Omni's Videos API. MiniMax-H3 reference-conditioned generation is a motivating workload; model-specific parameters remain request data. The implementation reuses Batch dispatch, concurrency, progress tracking, and storage, together with the gateway's existing asynchronous-job routing.

### Motivation

AIBrix already supports individual asynchronous video jobs, but its Batch execution path expects a single JSON request followed by a final JSON response. A video job has a different lifecycle: creation returns an ID, generation continues in the backend, and the content is downloaded separately. Treating the create response as the completed Batch result would finish rows before generation succeeds and release concurrency slots while work is still queued.

Users running offline video datasets need the existing Batch capabilities: JSONL input, bounded concurrency, per-row results and errors, interruption recovery, and output retrieval after worker resources have been released. A backend-local video ID alone is insufficient when the Batch runtime owns and later removes the generating Pod.

This proposal follows [RFC #2674](https://github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/issues/2674) and its merged implementation, [PR #2740](https://github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/pull/2740). That work supplies public job identity, ownership, persistence, and Pod routing. This RFC adds a Batch consumer of that API. The backend remains authoritative for video status and content; the gateway registry remains a routing catalog.

[RFC #1595](https://github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/issues/1595) discusses an xDiT generation API, and [RFC #1966](https://github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/issues/1966) discusses broader multimodal serving. This proposal is limited to executing Videos API requests through Batch.

### Proposed Change

Extend the existing Batch request lifecycle so one video row includes creation, polling, content persistence, and result writing. Keep protocol handling in the Batch client and bind Batch storage and progress operations from the job driver.

#### 1. Input contract

Accept `endpoint: "/v1/videos"` when creating a Batch. Each input line retains the existing `custom_id`, `method`, `url`, and `body` envelope. Require `POST`, a model, and a string prompt for this endpoint.

Example input line, expanded for readability:

```json
{
  "custom_id": "video-001",
  "method": "POST",
  "url": "/v1/videos",
  "body": {
    "model": "minimax-h3",
    "prompt": "Continue the motion shown in the reference clip.",
    "video_reference": {
      "video_url": "https://media.example.com/reference.mp4"
    },
    "num_inference_steps": 50,
    "flow_shift": 12.0,
    "extra_params": {
      "task": "ref2va",
      "duration": 4.0,
      "audio_flow_shift": 3.0
    }
  }
}
```

The URL above is illustrative. Actual inputs may use backend-accessible URLs or supported data URLs. Images use `image_reference.image_url`. Reference objects or lists retain the shape supported by the selected backend version.

The Batch client converts the JSON body into `multipart/form-data`, as required by vLLM-Omni:

| JSONL value | Wire representation |
| --- | --- |
| Scalar parameters, such as `prompt`, `model`, or `num_inference_steps` | Corresponding text form field |
| `image_reference`, `video_reference`, and `audio_reference` | JSON-encoded form field |
| `extra_params` and other supported JSON-valued parameters | JSON-encoded form field |

The compatibility target is the Batch envelope and Videos endpoint lifecycle. The reference fields and `extra_params` are vLLM-Omni extensions, not a promise that every body is accepted by OpenAI or another backend. The first implementation supports JSON-representable inputs; resolving uploaded file IDs or worker-local file paths into multipart uploads is outside its scope.

Existing chat JSONL is not reinterpreted by model name. A user migrating a dataset must explicitly convert its text and media fields into a Videos body. The worker does not infer `task`, generation parameters, or media semantics from `minimax-h3`.

#### 2. Execution and completion

The normal, validated Batch path already counts input rows and dispatches them concurrently:

```text
MDS validation -> job driver -> runtime connection -> DispatchEngine
-> Channel.send -> output/error JSONL -> request counts
```

Add the following Videos execution branch:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Read a validated Batch row"] --> B["Acquire a dispatch slot and select a channel"]
    B --> C{"Saved execution handle?"}
    C -->|No| D["Convert JSON to multipart and POST /v1/videos"]
    D --> E["Save the returned video ID and destination"]
    C -->|Yes| F["Resume the original video job"]
    E --> F
    F --> G["GET status asynchronously"]
    G -->|queued / in_progress| G
    G -->|completed| H["GET content and persist the video"]
    G -->|failed| I["Return a row error"]
    H --> J["Return final Video metadata and file ID"]
    I --> K["Write result or error JSONL"]
    J --> K
    K --> L["Update request counts and release the slot"]
```

`queued` and `in_progress` are intermediate states. A successful row requires the video file and its output JSONL record to be saved. A backend failure or a terminal polling/content error uses the existing Batch row-error path. Output-persistence failures retain the execution record for the existing deferred/recovery path.

The serial path for inputs whose total is not yet known should call the same video executor. This proposal does not change that cursor protocol.

When using the gateway, the worker stores the returned public video ID and uses the same gateway and identity for status, cont

items.title: Runtime fails to launch an s3:// model: the downloaded path is a Path, and the launch log line raises TypeError
items.author: wguo7
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

`SubprocessEngineLauncher.launch()` gets the model path from `_resolve_model_path()` ([model_runtime.py#L898](https://github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/blob/f3300be0e65f81760ec3b0287aebbf1b638a4d1a/python/aibrix/aibrix/runtime/model_runtime.py#L898)). For an `s3://` or `tos://` artifact, that function returns whatever `download_model()` returns ([model_runtime.py#L1022](https://github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/blob/f3300be0e65f81760ec3b0287aebbf1b638a4d1a/python/aibrix/aibrix/runtime/model_runtime.py#L1022)). The downloader returns a `pathlib.Path` ([base.py#L254](https://github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/blob/f3300be0e65f81760ec3b0287aebbf1b638a4d1a/python/aibrix/aibrix/downloader/base.py#L254) and [base.py#L276](https://github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/blob/f3300be0e65f81760ec3b0287aebbf1b638a4d1a/python/aibrix/aibrix/downloader/base.py#L276)), even though `_resolve_model_path()` is annotated `-> str`.

The `Path` goes into `cmd` after `--model` (or `--model-path` for SGLang). Before `Popen`, the launcher logs the command with `" ".join(cmd)` ([model_runtime.py#L939-L945](https://github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/blob/f3300be0e65f81760ec3b0287aebbf1b638a4d1a/python/aibrix/aibrix/runtime/model_runtime.py#L939-L945)), and `str.join` raises `TypeError: sequence item 4: expected str instance, PosixPath found` (item 4 is the model path in the vLLM command). As a result, the weights are downloaded and the engine is never started. From reading the code, `activate()` then removes the model and re-raises ([model_runtime.py#L1781-L1789](https://github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/blob/f3300be0e65f81760ec3b0287aebbf1b638a4d1a/python/aibrix/aibrix/runtime/model_runtime.py#L1781-L1789)). The restart path calls the same launcher ([model_runtime.py#L1653-L1663](https://github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/blob/f3300be0e65f81760ec3b0287aebbf1b638a4d1a/python/aibrix/aibrix/runtime/model_runtime.py#L1653-L1663)), so it should fail the same way. The repro below calls `launch()` directly with S3. I did not run `activate()` or a restart. TOS goes through the same `BaseDownloader.download_model()`, which returns the same `Path`, but I did not run a TOS repro.

Local paths and `hf://` or `huggingface://` URLs are returned as strings, so they are not affected. The existing test `test_resolve_model_path_returns_the_downloaded_path` replaces `download_model` with a function that returns a `str`, so it does not catch this.

### Steps to Reproduce

The script stores one file under `s3://bkt/models/qwen3-0.6b` in an in-process S3 (moto), replaces `subprocess.Popen`, and calls `SubprocessEngineLauncher.launch()` with that URL. No engine and no network are used. Output on main (f3300be):

```
resolved model path type: PosixPath
launch raised: TypeError sequence item 4: expected str instance, PosixPath found
engine process started: False
expected: launch returns the pid and starts the engine with --model <local dir>/...
```

<details><summary>repro.py</summary>

```python
"""Run: PYTHONPATH=<aibrix>/python/aibrix python repro.py

SubprocessEngineLauncher.launch() with an s3:// artifact. _resolve_model_path()
returns the downloader's pathlib.Path, and the launch log line
" ".join(cmd) raises TypeError, so the engine is never started.

S3 is simulated in-process with moto, and subprocess.Popen is replaced so no
engine is started.
"""

import logging
import os
import subprocess
import tempfile

os.environ["AWS_DEFAULT_REGION"] = "us-east-1"
os.environ["AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID"] = "testing"
os.environ["AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY"] = "testing"
local_dir = tempfile.mkdtemp()
os.environ["DOWNLOADER_LOCAL_DIR"] = local_dir + "/"

import boto3  # noqa: E402
from moto import mock_aws  # noqa: E402

from aibrix.runtime import model_runtime as mr  # noqa: E402

logging.disable(logging.CRITICAL)  # keep the downloader's logs out of the output

popen_calls = []


class FakePopen:
    def __init__(self, cmd, **kwargs):
        popen_calls.append(cmd)
        self.pid = 4242


subprocess.Popen = FakePopen

with mock_aws():
    s3 = boto3.client("s3", region_name="us-east-1")
    s3.create_bucket(Bucket="bkt")
    s3.put_object(Bucket="bkt", Key="models/qwen3-0.6b/config.json", Body=b"{}")

    resolved = mr._resolve_model_path("s3://bkt/models/qwen3-0.6b")
    print("resolved model path type:", type(resolved).__name__)

    inst = mr.ModelInstance(model_name="qwen3-0.6b", port=18001, ipc_name="kvc_qwen3")
    try:
        pid = mr.SubprocessEngineLauncher().launch(
            inst, "s3://bkt/models/qwen3-0.6b", engine_config=None, additional_config=None
        )
        cmd = popen_calls[0]
        model_arg = cmd[cmd.index("--model") + 1].replace(local_dir, "<local dir>")
        print(f"launch ok, pid {pid}, --model {model_arg}")
    except Exception as e:
        print("launch raised:", type(e).__name__, e)
    print("engine process started:", bool(popen_calls))
    print(
        "expected: launch returns the pid and starts the engine with --model <local dir>/..."
    )
```

</details>

### Expected behavior

items.title: S3 storage stores only the tail of a large upload when a multipart part times out, and reports success
items.author: wguo7
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

`S3Storage.put_object()` sends data of 5 MiB or more (`multipart_threshold`) through `multipart_upload()`. That call sits inside a `try` whose `except (OSError, IOError, ValueError): pass` is meant only for the case where the size cannot be determined, as its comment says ([s3.py#L102-L122](https://github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/blob/f3300be0e65f81760ec3b0287aebbf1b638a4d1a/python/aibrix/aibrix/storage/s3.py#L102-L122)).

Several botocore errors subclass `OSError`, through the `requests` exception classes vendored in botocore. In botocore 1.43.115 these include `ReadTimeoutError`, `ConnectTimeoutError`, `SSLError` and `ProxyConnectionError`. When one of them is raised while a part uploads, `multipart_upload()` aborts the upload and re-raises ([base.py#L488-L495](https://github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/blob/f3300be0e65f81760ec3b0287aebbf1b638a4d1a/python/aibrix/aibrix/storage/base.py#L488-L495)), and `put_object()` swallows the error and falls through to a single PUT of `reader.read_all()` ([s3.py#L136](https://github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/blob/f3300be0e65f81760ec3b0287aebbf1b638a4d1a/python/aibrix/aibrix/storage/s3.py#L136)).

The reader has already been read up to and including the failed part, so the single PUT stores only the bytes after the failed part, and `put_object()` returns `True`. The Files API upload ([files.py#L205-L208](https://github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/blob/f3300be0e65f81760ec3b0287aebbf1b638a4d1a/python/aibrix/aibrix/metadata/api/v1/files.py#L205-L208)) then reports a successful upload of a file that holds only the data after the failed part. A batch input uploaded this way is missing every request up to the end of the failed part, and nothing reports an error.

S3 errors that are not `OSError` propagate as expected, for example `ClientError` (an HTTP 500 or AccessDenied on a part) and `EndpointConnectionError`. Open PR #3184 moves the multipart upload out of the same kind of `try` in `TOSStorage.put_object()`. It does not change `s3.py`.

### Steps to Reproduce

The script uses an in-process S3 (moto), makes `upload_part` raise `ReadTimeoutError` for part 2, and calls `put_object()` with 10,486,760 bytes: 5 MiB of `A`, 5 MiB of `B` and 1000 bytes of `C`. Output on main (f3300be):

```
put_object returned True (no exception)
stored 1000 bytes, starting with b'C'; the data had 10486760 bytes, starting with b'A'
expected: put_object raises the timeout and no object is stored
```

<details><summary>repro.py</summary>

```python
"""Run: PYTHONPATH=<aibrix>/python/aibrix python repro.py

S3Storage.put_object(): a read timeout on one part of a multipart upload is
swallowed, and the object is stored with only the bytes left after the
failed part.

botocore's ReadTimeoutError subclasses OSError, and put_object() wraps the
multipart path in `except (OSError, IOError, ValueError): pass`, which is
meant for "cannot determine size". It then falls through to a single PUT of
what the reader has left. S3 is simulated in-process with moto.
"""

import asyncio
import logging
import os

os.environ.setdefault("AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID", "testing")
os.environ.setdefault("AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY", "testing")
os.environ.setdefault("AWS_DEFAULT_REGION", "us-east-1")

import boto3  # noqa: E402
from botocore.exceptions import ReadTimeoutError  # noqa: E402
from moto import mock_aws  # noqa: E402

from aibrix.storage.base import StorageConfig  # noqa: E402
from aibrix.storage.s3 import S3Storage  # noqa: E402

logging.disable(logging.CRITICAL)  # keep the storage logs out of the output


async def main():
    with mock_aws():
        boto3.client("s3", region_name="us-east-1").create_bucket(Bucket="bkt-test")
        storage = S3Storage("bkt-test", region_name="us-east-1", config=StorageConfig())
        real_upload_part = storage.client.upload_part

        def flaky_upload_part(**kwargs):
            if kwargs["PartNumber"] == 2:
                raise ReadTimeoutError(endpoint_url="https://s3.example.com")
            return real_upload_part(**kwargs)

        storage.client.upload_part = flaky_upload_part
        part = storage.config.multipart_threshold  # 5 MiB
        data = b"A" * part + b"B" * part + b"C" * 1000  # 3 parts
        try:
            ok = await storage.put_object("out.jsonl", data)
            print("put_object returned", ok, "(no exception)")
        except Exception as e:
            print("put_object raised", type(e).__name__)
        try:
            stored = await storage.get_object("out.jsonl")
            print(
                f"stored {len(stored)} bytes, starting with {stored[:1]!r}; "
                f"the data had {len(data)} bytes, starting with {data[:1]!r}"
            )
        except FileNotFoundError:
            print("object not stored")
    print("expected: put_object raises the timeout and no object is stored")


asyncio.run(main())
```

</details>

### Expected behavior

`put_object()` raises the error from the failed part, and nothing new is stored under the key. Only an error from finding the size should fall back to the single PUT.

### Environment

- AIBrix version: main at f3300be
- Deployment environment: none. The repro uses `S3Storage` in-process against moto (macOS arm64, Python 3.12.15, botocore 1.43.115)
- LLM(s) being used: none

### Area

Batch

I have a fix with a test ready and will open a PR.

items.title: [Bug]: Two-model draft-target speculative decoding with sampling does not preserve the target distribution (1.2.1, PyTorch backend)
items.author: SeverinVisionary
items.body_excerpt:
### System Info

- GPU: NVIDIA L4 (SM89, 23 GB), driver 580.82.07, CUDA 13.0 (Google Colab)
- OS: Linux 6.6 x86_64, glibc 2.39; Python 3.12.3
- tensorrt-llm 1.2.1 (pip, NVIDIA index), torch 2.9.1+cu130, transformers 4.57.3
- PyTorch backend: `DraftTargetDecodingConfig(max_draft_len=3)`, `attn_backend="VANILLA"`, `disable_overlap_scheduler=True`, `disable_flashinfer_sampling=True`, `cuda_graph_config=None`

### Who can help?

_No response_

### Information

- [ ] The official example scripts
- [x] My own modified scripts

### Tasks

- [ ] An officially supported task in the `examples` folder (such as GLUE/SQuAD, ...)
- [x] My own task or dataset (give details below)

### Reproduction

I compared the output distribution of two-model draft-target speculative decoding with the same engine without speculation, on tiny Llama models (V = 8, 2 layers) where the whole output distribution can be counted. The script below needs only tensorrt-llm 1.2.1. It writes its own two random models (bf16), samples 20,000 sequences per arm (40,000 without speculation) from the prompt `[1, 2, 3, 1, 2]` with 4 new tokens, and compares the arms with a chi-square test. It also wraps `TorchSampler._process_draft_tokens_rejection_sampling` to count, per verification, the number of draft tokens K, the number of `py_draft_logits` rows R, and how many accepted draft tokens have probability 0 in their own `py_target_probs` row. The only patch to TensorRT-LLM is a workaround for a separate crash (described at the end).

```
python repro_draft_target.py --out ./repro_out      # about 10 min on an L4 after the install
```

<details><summary>repro_draft_target.py</summary>

```python
"""Standalone reproduction: TensorRT-LLM 1.2.1 two-model draft-target speculative decoding with sampling does not
preserve the target's output distribution.

    python repro_draft_target.py --out ./repro_out            # one GPU; about 10 min after the install

Needs only tensorrt-llm==1.2.1 (with the torch it pins), numpy, scipy and safetensors. The script:
1. writes two tiny random Llama checkpoints (V = 8, 2 layers, head_dim 32) with fixed seeds: a target and a draft;
2. samples N sequences from the prompt [1, 2, 3, 1, 2] (4 new tokens, EOS = 7) at temperature 1 and at top-k 3,
   in three arms, each in its own process (2N draws for `base`):
   - `base`: no speculation;
   - `spec`: `DraftTargetDecodingConfig(max_draft_len=3)`;
   - `spec_keeplast`: as `spec`, with `ModelDrafter._create_draft_request` passing
     `exclude_last_generation_logits=False`;
3. in the speculative arms, wraps `TorchSampler._process_draft_tokens_rejection_sampling` to record, per
   verification, the number of draft tokens K, the number of `py_draft_logits` rows R, the number accepted, and how
   many accepted draft tokens have probability 0 in their own `py_target_probs` row;
4. compares each speculative arm's sequence distribution with `base` (total variation and a chi-square test),
   next to `base` split in two halves as the noise floor.

The only change to TensorRT-LLM besides the `spec_keeplast` patch is a workaround for a separate crash: in 1.2.1,
`ModelDrafter.process_decoded_tokens` calls `generation_logits.squeeze_(0)` on an inference tensor outside inference
mode, which kills the executor thread when sampling with VANILLA attention. The script runs that method under
`torch.inference_mode()`. Nothing else is patched; the run is bf16 with stock kernels.
"""
import argparse
import collections
import json
import os
import pathlib
import signal
import subprocess
import sys
import time

V, EOS, MAX_NEW = 8, 7, 4
PROMPT = [1, 2, 3, 1, 2]
SETTINGS = {"T1": dict(temperature=1.0), "topk3": dict(temperature=1.0, top_k=3)}
N = 20_000
BATCH = 2_000
ARM_SEED = {"base": 1000, "spec": 2000, "spec_keeplast": 3000}  # TorchSampler seed, per arm and setting
FATAL = "[TRT-LLM] [E] Error in event loop"


def make_model(path, seed):
    """A tiny Llama with random weights; lm_head scaled up so the next-token distributions are not near uniform.
    Stored in bf16 with torch_dtype bfloat16: an fp32 checkpoint keeps fp32 activations even with LLM(dtype="bfloat16"),
    and FlashInfer's RMSNorm dispatches fp16/bf16 only."""
    import numpy as np
    import torch
    from safetensors.torch import save_file
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    hidden, heads, head_dim, inter, layers = 64, 2, 32, 128, 2

    def w(*shape, std=0.3):
        return (rng.standard_normal(shape) * std).astype(np.float32)

    sd = {"model.embed_tokens.weight": w(V, hidden, std=1.0), "model.norm.weight": np.ones(hidden, np.float32),
          "lm_head.weight": w(V, hidden, std=1.5)}
    for i in range(layers):
        p = f"model.layers.{i}."
        sd |= {p + "input_layernorm.weight": np.ones(hidden, np.float32),
               p + "post_attention_layernorm.weight": np.ones(hidden, np.float32),
               p + "self_attn.q_proj.weight": w(heads * head_dim, hidden),
               p + "self_attn.k_proj.weight": w(heads * head_dim, hidden),
               p + "self_attn.v_proj.weight": w(heads * head_dim, hidden),
               p + "self_attn.o_proj.weight": w(hidden, heads * head_dim),
               p + "mlp.gate_proj.weight": w(inter, hidden), p + "mlp.up_proj.weight": w(inter, hidden),
               p + "mlp.down_proj.weight": w(hidden, inter)}
    path.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    save_file({k: torch.from_numpy(v).to(torch.bfloat16) for k, v in sd.items()}, str(path / "model.safetensors"),
              metadata={"format": "pt"})
    cfg = dict(architectures=["LlamaForCausalLM"], model_type="llama", vocab_size=V, hidden_size=hidden,
               intermediate_size=inter, num_hidden_layers=layers, num_attention_heads=heads,
               num_key_value_heads=heads, head_dim=head_dim, hidden_act="silu", max_position_embeddings=64,
               rms_norm_eps=1e-6, rope_theta=10000.0, attention_bias=False, mlp_bias=False,
               tie_word_embeddings=False, bos_token_id=None,

comments.author: SeverinVisionary
comments.body:
A follow-up on newer versions. I ran the same script on 1.4.0rc1, where `DraftTargetDecodingConfig` goes through the one-model path (`DraftTargetOneModelWorker`). As far as I can tell, the distribution problem doesn't carry over. It looks limited to the 1.2.x two-model path, which #20869 targets.

What I checked, on an L4 with torch 2.14.0+cu130, bf16 and the same two tiny models:

- With `attn_backend="VANILLA"`, the engine fails during warmup:
  `AttributeError: 'VanillaAttentionMetadata' object has no attribute 'host_request_types'` at
  `_torch/speculative/draft_target.py:267`. I switched to the default TRTLLM backend for everything below.
- I tested both modes, default (`use_rejection_sampling=False`) and `use_rejection_sampling=True`. Each verification has as many draft-probability rows as draft tokens, and no accepted draft token has target probability 0.
- Compared directly with the non-speculative output, both modes differ by TV about 0.05. But on this fixture that's within bf16 noise: the non-speculative output is itself TV 0.037 from an fp64 reference. The speculative path computes the target logits in a multi-token forward, so I don't read anything into that number.
- So I tested something that doesn't depend on numerics instead. For every emitted position, I recorded the target probabilities the worker computed and checked the emitted tokens against them, about 58,000 verifications per mode and setting. All 12 goodness-of-fit tests pass (smallest Holm-adjusted p 0.85).

I haven't checked whether the target logits themselves match an fp64 forward beyond that, or anything on 1.3.x.

The VANILLA crash is a separate thing. I can open its own issue if that's more useful.

items.title: Non-persistent `triton_kernels.matmul` with a fused SwiGLU masks the MX output scales with the pre-activation `N` instead of `N // 2`, silently writing past each row's scales
items.author: Hughshine
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug


**TL;DR.** #8865 fixed the MX scale store mask of the persistent `triton_kernels.matmul` kernel to count scale blocks from the output width `yN = N // 2` of a fused SwiGLU instead of the pre-activation `N` ("there is a bug in mask_n_scale which should use yN (N // ACTIVATION_REDUCTION_N) instead N"), but did not change the same mask in the non-persistent kernel (`_matmul.py`), which still uses `N_MX_BLOCK = cdiv(N, 32)`. There, with an MXFP8 or MXFP4 output, the last output tile of a row also stores the scale blocks past the row's `cdiv(yN, 32)` (up to 3 bytes per row at the default `BLOCK_N = 256`, for example N = 576): onto the first scales of the next row, and past the end of the scale tensor for the last row. Possible fix: count from `yN` in the non-persistent kernel too, as #8865 does in the persistent one.

`test_matmul.py` checks this combination under "swiglu together with mxfp8 downcast", but only for the persistent kernel on Blackwell. The script below runs the non-persistent kernel with N = 576 (yN = 288, so 9 scale bytes per row; the output tile is 128 columns, 4 scale bytes) and leaves 3 spare bytes behind every row of the scale tensor, which nothing should write to. N = 512 is the control (yN is a multiple of the output tile):

```python
import sys

import torch
from triton_kernels.matmul import matmul, PrecisionConfig, FusedActivation, FnSpecs, FnName, Epilogue
from triton_kernels.matmul_details import opt_flags
from triton_kernels.numerics_details.mxfp import quantize_mxfp8_fn
from triton_kernels.swiglu import swiglu_fn

swiglu = FusedActivation(FnSpecs("swiglu", swiglu_fn, ("alpha", "limit"), reduction_n=2), (1.0, 1.0))
quantize = Epilogue(FnSpecs(FnName.QUANTIZE_MXFP8.name, quantize_mxfp8_fn, (), ()), (), ())
M, K = 64, 512
bug = False
for N in (512, 576):  # SwiGLU halves N; one scale byte per 32 outputs: 256 outputs = 8 scales per row, 288 outputs = 9
    n_scale = N // 2 // 32
    a = torch.randn(M, K, device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16)
    b = torch.randn(K, N, device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16)
    scales = torch.full((M, n_scale + 3), 0xA5, dtype=torch.uint8, device="cuda")  # 3 spare bytes after each row
    config = PrecisionConfig(out_dtype=torch.float8_e4m3fn, c_mx_scale=scales[:, :n_scale])
    with opt_flags.scoped_opt_flags_constraints({"is_persistent": False}):
        matmul(a, b, None, precision_config=config, epilogue=quantize, fused_activation=swiglu)
    written = int((scales[:, n_scale:] != 0xA5).sum())
    print(f"N={N}: {written} of {M * 3} spare bytes written (expected 0)")
    bug |= written > 0
sys.exit(1 if bug else 0)
```

Observed on main @6fe3348e6 (exit code 1):
```
N=512: 0 of 192 spare bytes written (expected 0)
N=576: 192 of 192 spare bytes written (expected 0)
```
Expected: 0 for both. Every row of N = 576 gets 3 stores at scale columns 9 to 11, which the row does not have. The stored bytes hold 119, the scale byte the epilogue computes for a block that is entirely padding: masked lanes enter the max as -1 ([_downcast_to_mxfp.py#L45](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/6fe3348e6e907584e07e593ab19a35caee95c37a/python/triton_kernels/triton_kernels/numerics_details/mxfp_details/_downcast_to_mxfp.py#L45)), and `-1 / 448` gives byte 119 in the rounding formula at [L55-L56](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/6fe3348e6e907584e07e593ab19a35caee95c37a/python/triton_kernels/triton_kernels/numerics_details/mxfp_details/_downcast_to_mxfp.py#L55-L56) (`-1 / 6` gives 125, the byte seen with an MXFP4 output). A caller passes a contiguous `[M, 9]` scale tensor, where column 9 + j of row r is column j of row r + 1: the stores overwrite the first three scales of the next row (wrong outputs, see below) and, behind the last row, fall outside the tensor. With the change below the script prints 0 for both sizes (exit code 0). On the 3.8.0 wheel with `triton_kernels` from the v3.8.0 tag the output is identical to main.

<details>
<summary>The same with a contiguous scale tensor and a torch reference (3298 of 18432 outputs wrong)</summary>

```python
import sys

import torch
import triton
from triton_kernels.matmul import matmul, PrecisionConfig, FusedActivation, FnSpecs, FnName, Epilogue
from triton_kernels.matmul_details import opt_flags
from triton_kernels.numerics_details.mxfp import quantize_mxfp8_fn, upcast_from_mxfp
from triton_kernels.swiglu import swiglu_fn

M, K, ALPHA, LIMIT = 64, 512, 1.702, 7.0
SENTINEL = 0xA5


def run(N):
    y_n, n_scale = N // 2, triton.cdiv(N // 2, 32)
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    a = torch.randn(M, K, device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16)
    b = torch.randn(K, N, device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16)
    swiglu = FusedActivation(FnSpecs("swiglu", swiglu_fn, ("alpha", "limit"), reduction_n=2), (ALPHA, LIMIT))
    quantize = Epilogue(FnSpecs(FnName.QUANTIZE_MXFP8.name, quantize_mxfp8_fn, (), ()), (), (), effective_itemsize=6.0)
    # the [M, n_scale] scales, followed by 64 bytes that nothing should write to
    scale_buf = torch.full((M * n_scale + 64, ), SENTINEL, dtype=torch.uint8, device="cuda")
    scale = scale_buf[:M * n_scale].view(M, n_scale)
    config = PrecisionConfig(out_dtype=torch.float8_e4m3fn, c_mx_scale=scale, c_microblock_size=32)
    with opt_flags.scoped_opt_flags_constraints({"is_persistent": False}):
        y = matmul(a, b, None, precision_config=config, epilogue=quantize, fused_activation=swiglu)
    got = upcast_from_mxfp(y, scale, torch.bfloat16, axis=-1).float()
    acc = a.float() @ b.float()
    g, lin = acc[:, ::2].clamp(max=LIMIT), acc[:, 1::2].clamp(-LIMIT, LIMIT)
    want = g * torch.sigmoid(ALPHA * g) * (lin + 1)
    wrong = (got - want).abs() > 0.15 * want.abs() + 0.1  # fp8 e4m3 rounding stays below 15%
    past_end = int((scale_buf[M * n_scale:] != SENTINEL).sum())
    print(f"N={N} (yN={y_n}, {n_scale} scale blocks per row): {int(wrong.sum())}/{wrong.numel()} output elements wrong, "
          f"{past_end} bytes written past the end of the scale ten

items.title: [interpreter] Debug mode is never actually set, so `tl.device_assert` and integer overflow checks silently do not fire as on the GPU
items.author: Hughshine
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug


With `TRITON_INTERPRET=1`, turning on debug mode (`TRITON_DEBUG=1`, `@triton.jit(debug=True)` or `debug=True` at launch) has no effect: the interpreter's options keep `debug=False`. So everything that only runs in debug mode, such as `tl.device_assert`, the integer overflow checks and `tl.expect_zero`, silently does nothing, while the same kernel on the GPU with `TRITON_DEBUG=1` asserts.

```python
import os
import sys

os.environ.update(TRITON_INTERPRET="1", TRITON_DEBUG="1")  # read when triton is imported

import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl


@triton.jit
def assert_kernel(x_ptr):
    x = tl.load(x_ptr + tl.arange(0, 4))
    tl.device_assert(x >= 0, "negative element")


@triton.jit
def overflow_kernel(x_ptr, y_ptr):
    offs = tl.arange(0, 4)
    tl.store(y_ptr + offs, tl.load(x_ptr + offs) + 1)


fired = 0
for name, run in [
    ("device_assert", lambda: assert_kernel[(1, )](torch.tensor([1.0, -1.0, 1.0, 1.0]))),
    ("int32 overflow check", lambda: overflow_kernel[(1, )](torch.full((4, ), 2**31 - 1, dtype=torch.int32),
                                                             torch.empty(4, dtype=torch.int32))),
]:
    try:
        run()
        print(f"{name}: did not fire")
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"{name}: {type(e).__name__}: {e}")
        fired += 1
sys.exit(0 if fired == 2 else 1)
```

Observed on main @23d6832c42 (exit code 1):
```
device_assert: did not fire
int32 overflow check: did not fire
```
Expected, as on the GPU (both kernels with `TRITON_INTERPRET=0` and `TRITON_DEBUG=1` print ``Assertion `negative element` failed`` and ``Assertion `int32 overflow detected for operation add` failed``), and as the interpreter prints once its debug flag is set by hand (`interpreter_builder.options = dataclasses.replace(interpreter_builder.options, debug=True)`):
```
device_assert: InterpreterError: AssertionError('negative element')
int32 overflow check: InterpreterError: AssertionError('int32 overflow detected for operation add')
```

**Root cause.** These checks are emitted only when `builder.options.debug` is set ([semantic.py#L1940](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/23d6832c426e79a9b269d6252b11f17041bd35b5/python/triton/language/semantic.py#L1940)). The interpreter's builder is created once with `InterpreterOptions()` ([interpreter.py#L408](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/23d6832c426e79a9b269d6252b11f17041bd35b5/python/triton/runtime/interpreter.py#L408)), whose `debug` is `False`, and `InterpretedFunction.run` ([interpreter.py#L1668-L1672](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/23d6832c426e79a9b269d6252b11f17041bd35b5/python/triton/runtime/interpreter.py#L1668-L1672)) never sets it, unlike `JITFunction.run` ([jit.py#L737](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/23d6832c426e79a9b269d6252b11f17041bd35b5/python/triton/runtime/jit.py#L737)). Since #4589 (v3.2.0), which moved the debug check into `device_assert`; in v3.1.0 the interpreter asserted.

**Possible fix.** Resolve the flag in `InterpretedFunction.run` as `JITFunction.run` does (`InterpreterOptions` is frozen, so replace and restore it):
```diff
--- a/python/triton/runtime/interpreter.py
+++ b/python/triton/runtime/interpreter.py
@@ -1671,2 +1671,8 @@ class InterpretedFunction(KernelInterface[T]):
         fn = self.rewrite()
-        return GridExecutor(fn, self.arg_names, grid, self.pre_run_hooks)(*args, **kwargs)
+        options = interpreter_builder.options
+        debug = kwargs.get("debug", self.kwargs.get("debug")) or triton.knobs.runtime.debug
+        interpreter_builder.options = dataclasses.replace(options, debug=debug)
+        try:
+            return GridExecutor(fn, self.arg_names, grid, self.pre_run_hooks)(*args, **kwargs)
+        finally:
+            interpreter_builder.options = options
```
Tested on main @6fe3348e6 with `test_debug.py` run under the interpreter (all pass with the change). With it, interpreter tests run with `TRITON_DEBUG=1` that deliberately overflow integers (for example some `test_bin_op` cases) now report the overflow, as they already do on the GPU in debug mode.


### Environment details

Triton: main @23d6832c42 (also 3.2.0 to 3.8.0)
GPU: NVIDIA L40S (the interpreter runs on the CPU; the GPU only for the comparison)
