shortlist.title: Misc. bug: Regression- draft-MTP over RPC split generation is 25-30% slower - drafter acceptance unchanged, dense decode unchanged
shortlist.author: mikicvi
shortlist.body_excerpt:
### Name and Version

./llama-server --version
version: 0.4.0-dev (build 254, commit 6a1a922)
built with GNU 13.3.0 for Linux x86_64


### Operating systems

Windows, Linux

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

llama-server, libllama (core library)

### Command line

```shell
# Linux server
cmake -B build -DGGML_CUDA=ON -DGGML_RPC=ON && cmake --build build --config Release -j$(nproc)

llama-server \
  --model Qwen3.8-27B-UD-IQ4_XS.gguf \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8081 \
  --ctx-size 98304 -ngl 99 \
  --spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-ngl 99 --spec-draft-n-max 2 \
  --cache-type-k q8_0 --cache-type-v q8_0 \
  --spec-draft-type-k q8_0 --spec-draft-type-v q8_0 \
  --flash-attn on \
  --rpc <windows-host>:50052 -dev RPC0,CUDA0 -ts 0.49,0.51 \
  --threads 8 --jinja -b 2048 -ub 1024

# Windows server
cmake -B build -DGGML_CUDA=ON -DGGML_RPC=ON -G 
cmake --build build --config Release

./ggml-rpc-server.exe -H 0.0.0.0 -d CUDA0 -p 50052
```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

After updating both ends from bb4caa7 (21-08-2026) to 6a1a922, generation with draft-mtp over an RPC tensor split dropped ~25–30%. Isolation measurements (same 1209-token prompt / 1024-token generation benchmark throughout)
| Config | `bb4caa7` | `6a1a922` |
|---|---|---|
| draft-mtp depth 2 (flags above) | 27–32 tok/s | 21.3 tok/s |
| draft-mtp depth 1, re-tuned split 0.52/0.48 | — | 22.6–24.4 tok/s |
| no MTP (raw dense decode, same split) | ~17–18 tok/s | 17.5 tok/s |
| draft acceptance (server stats) | ~0.68–0.80 | 0.737–0.832 |
| mean accepted length | ~1.7–1.8 | 1.74–1.83 |

Control point:  a 31B dense model (Muse Glimmer) (no speculative decoding) on the identical RPC split, flags, and both commits measures 17.66 tok/s before and after so that part seems fine to me. This should rule out the RPC transport for single-forward decode, the tensor split, and sampling.

Repro: run the commands above on both commits (both ends must be same-era due to the RPC protocol bump), generate 1k tokens, compare `eval time` in slot timings and the `draft acceptance` stats. 
- From what I can tell, acceptance and raw decode are unchanged, so i think the finger can be pointed at MTP changes. 
- Possibly related: graph/compute buffer sizing grew in the same window - ctx 98304 with `-b 2048 -ub 1024` loaded on `bb4caa7` on a 12GB device but fails graph reserve with CUDA OOM on `6a1a922` until the tensor split is re-tuned, or CTX made smaller.


I am happy to test/build any specific build/version.

Model: unsloth Qwen3.8-27B UD-IQ4_XS GGUF (14.25 GB) with embedded MTP heads. 
Hardware: Linux = i5-12600H, RTX A2000 12GB, 96GB DDR5 5600Mt; windows = RTX 3080 10GB, AMD 5800x3d, 32gb DDR4, 2.5GbE LAN between both.
Linux server is only used as AI server, windows desktop is used only to supplement gpu compute for dense models. 

### First Bad Commit

Not bisected-windows builds take over 30 minutes :( . Regression window is `bb4caa7` (21-08-2026 good) to `6a1a922` (05-09-2026 bad). 

Some candidates in the window, but I can't confirm yet.
- `2c6b141` 2026-08-22 `common : fix draft-mtp with embeddings (#26352, #27299)` this one touches the draft-MTP loop directly and the timeline fits
	- RPC protocol bump to 6.0.0 landed during this time and per-call overhead would be amplified by the speculative loop's higher exchange count
- `662a0b0` 2026-08-31 `spec : fuse the DFlash encoder into the KV cache injection (#27310)`

### Relevant log output

<details>
<summary>Logs</summary>

```console
# acceptance stats on 6a1a922 (healthy — regression is not acceptance-related)
slot print_timing: id  3 | task 0 | draft acceptance = 0.83154 (  464 accepted /   558 generated), mean len =  1.83
slot print_timing: id  3 | task 563 | draft acceptance = 0.73684 (  434 accepted /   589 generated), mean len =  1.74

# secondary issue: graph reserve growth (ctx 98304 loaded on bb4caa7 with identical flags)
E ggml_backend_cuda_buffer_type_alloc_buffer: allocating 1473.19 MiB on device 0: cudaMalloc failed: out of memory
E ggml_gallocr_reserve_n_impl: failed to allocate CUDA0 buffer of size 1544749568
E graph_reserve: failed to allocate compute buffers
```

shortlist.title: Performance comparison for dense shared prefix + block-diagonal local mask: custom mask in BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheWrapper vs MultiLevelCascadeAttentionWrapper
shortlist.author: catnanami
shortlist.body_excerpt: I am trying to evaluate the best way to implement an attention pattern with a dense shared/global prefix plus a local block-diagonal suffix. The mask pattern is shown below: I am considering two implementations: BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheWrapper with a custom mask MultiLevelCascadeAttentionWrapper Questions: 1. For this pattern, is cascade attention expected to be faster than paged prefill with a custom mask? 2. Or is this pattern better handled by a custom kernel/backend? My use case is speculative decoding, where all verification tokens share the same prefix KV, but each local block should only attend to its own block.

comments.author: VectorPeak
comments.body:
For the mask in the image - a dense shared prefix on the left plus independent block-diagonal local regions on the right - `MultiLevelCascadeAttentionWrapper` is usually the better fit than `BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheWrapper` with one large custom mask.

The reason is that the custom-mask prefill path does not really exploit this structure as well: it still treats the problem like one masked attention problem over the full layout, so the block-diagonal sparsity mostly becomes masking overhead. Cascade attention lets you model this as:

- shared/global prefix KV: attended by all verification tokens
- local suffix KV: split into independent blocks/requests
- final result: merge prefix-attention state with each local block’s attention state

For speculative decoding, this is exactly the kind of case where cascade can help, especially when the shared prefix is large and the local verification blocks are relatively small. Each local block can be represented as a separate batch item sharing the same prefix. If the local part also needs causal masking inside each block, use the normal causal/local mask for that per-block suffix attention.

shortlist.title: KV-Cache Persistence Issue with SSD Offloading
shortlist.author: LiuQW519
shortlist.body_excerpt:
**Description:**  
follow the SSD offload guide in :

> https://docs.lmcache.ai/kv_cache/local_storage.html

experimentation with vLLM  and LMCache, we observed that the KV-Cache offloading to SSD works partially but lacks persistence across server restarts.  

**Steps to Reproduce:**  
1. Configure vLLM server with SSD offloading for KV-Cache  
2. Run inference scripts with a specific prompt 
3. Observe 2.4GB `.pt` file generated in the SSD cache directory  
4. Restart the vLLM server process  
5. Query the same prompt again  
6. the kv-cache regenerated in SSD

**Expected Behavior:**  
The existing KV-Cache files should be reused, avoiding redundant computation and disk I/O.  

**Actual Behavior:**  
New identical KV-Cache files are regenerated instead of reusing the existing ones

This optimization would significantly improve latency for recurring queries in production scenarios. I would appreciate guidance on recommended methods to achieve proper KV-Cache persistence across server restarts in this workflow.

comments.author: ziruiliu
comments.body:
Which version of vllm and lmcache are you using? Can you show us sample of file names that regenerated time of time?

Latest lmcache has changed data type of hash from str to int and use seed from vllm's NONE_HASH. Such change results in the change of filename in local disk.
If PYTHONHASHSEED is not set, vllm's NONE_HASH changes every time.
see vllm's code
```
def init_none_hash(hash_fn: Callable):
    global NONE_HASH

    hash_seed = os.getenv("PYTHONHASHSEED")
    if hash_seed is None and hash_fn is sha256_cbor_64bit:
        logger.warning(
            "PYTHONHASHSEED is not set. This will lead to non-reproducible "
            "block-hashes when using sha256_cbor_64bit as the hash function."
            "Consider setting PYTHONHASHSEED to a fixed value for "
            "reproducibility.")

    NONE_HASH = (int.from_bytes(os.urandom(32), byteorder="big")
                 if hash_seed is None else hash_fn(hash_seed))
```

You can try to set PYTHONHASHSEED to a fixed value to see if file names are different once you restart vllm and re-query

shortlist.title: Vulkan: ~78% decode throughput cliff at 131072 context — suballocation fragmentation; fixed via GGML_VK_SUBALLOCATION_BLOCK_SIZE=4 GiB
shortlist.author: KEndlleas
shortlist.body_excerpt:
# Vulkan: ~78% decode throughput cliff at 131072 context window — default ~1 GiB suballocation fragmentation; fixed via GGML_VK_SUBALLOCATION_BLOCK_SIZE=4 GiB

## Environment

| | |
|---|---|
| GPU | AMD Radeon RX 7900 XTX (24 GB, RDNA3, gfx1100) |
| OS / Driver | Windows 11, AMD proprietary driver |
| llama.cpp | 0.2.0-dev (build **10603**, commit c060ca974), Vulkan backend (ggml-vulkan.dll) |
| Model | Qwen3.8-27B (hybrid linear-attention, 64 layers), `Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf` (16.35 GiB) |
| Context | 131072 · KV cache `q8_0`/`q8_0` · `-fa on` · 4 slots unified pool |

## Summary

Decode throughput collapses from **~40 tok/s to ~8.9 tok/s** when the context window is raised from 98304 to 131072. The cliff is caused by the Vulkan backend's default **~1 GiB suballocation block size** fragmenting the large KV/compute pool into **30+ separate VkBuffers**. Setting `GGML_VK_SUBALLOCATION_BLOCK_SIZE=4294967296` restores full throughput at 131072.

## Reproduction

```powershell
llama-server -m Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf --mmproj mmproj-F16.gguf `
  --ctx-size 131072 -fa on --cache-type-k q8_0 --cache-type-v q8_0 --jinja `
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080
```

Send a single-stream 1200-token completion (prompt ≈ 31 tokens), measure wall time.

## Results (same request, same binary, single GPU)

| ctx | KV dtype | suballoc block size | wall time | throughput |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 65536 | f16 | default (1 GiB) | ~30 s | **40.4 tok/s** |
| 98304 | q8_0 | default | ~29 s | **40.8 tok/s** |
| **131072** | q8_0 | default | **~145 s** | **8.9 tok/s** ← cliff |
| **131072** | q8_0 | **4 GiB** | **~30 s** | **40.3 tok/s** ← restored |

Note: `llama-bench -p 512 -n 128` (small actual KV usage) stays at 40.4 tok/s even with q8 KV, so the cliff is tied to **pool allocation size**, not KV dtype.

## Diagnosis (`GGML_VK_MEMORY_LOGGER=1`)

At 131072, total device allocation is **21.55 GiB — fully in VRAM, no sysmem fallback** (total host = 152 MiB). The largest individual allocations are ≈ **1018 MiB each**, i.e. the pool is split into 30+ sub-blocks. At 98304 the same split stays below a critical block count and performance is unaffected.

No `OOM` / fallback warnings in logs. Memory location is not the issue — fragmentation of the pool into many independent `VkBuffer` objects is.

## Root-cause hypothesis

Decode at batch=1 touches the full KV/compute pool every step. With 30+ separate ~1 GiB sub-buffers, each step incurs per-buffer descriptor binding / submission overhead (and likely suboptimal memory access locality across disjoint buffers), multiplying the per-token cost by ~4.5×. Raising the suballocation block to 4 GiB keeps the pool in contiguous large buffers and eliminates the overhead.

## Workaround

```
GGML_VK_SUBALLOCATION_BLOCK_SIZE=4294967296
```

(before launching llama-server / llama-bench)

## Suggestions for maintainers

1. Consider raising the default suballocation block size, or sizing it relative to the KV pool (e.g. grow block size when the requested buffer exceeds N GiB).
2. Alternatively, allocate the KV cache as one contiguous buffer when it fits in VRAM, instead of splitting through the suballocator.
3. This appears to be a sibling of other "cliff at specific sizes" issues in the same backend: #25356 (fixed 8-token MMV dispatch thresholds) and #16759 (compute buffer jumps at specific context breakpoints).

---

**AI disclosure:** This report was researched and drafted with the assistance of an AI assistant (opencode). All measurements were performed locally on the machine described above; the evidence chain (memory logger output, A/B benchmark table) is reproducible with the commands provided.

## Additional NVIDIA reproduction and profiling

I reproduced a **related block-size-sensitive Vulkan decode regression** on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5070 Ti 16 GB using llama.cpp commit `2cdae802`.

### Environment

| Item        | Value                                      |
| ----------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| GPU         | NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5070 Ti, 16 GB          |
| OS / Driver | Windows 11 / NVIDIA 576.02                 |
| Vulkan      | 1.4.303                                    |
| llama.cpp   | 0.3.0-dev, build 10714, commit`2cdae802` |
| Model       | `Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q2_K_XL.gguf`            |
| KV cache    | `q8_0/q8_0`, Flash Attention enabled     |

### Reproduction

```powershell
llama-server.exe `
  -m Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q2_K_XL.gguf `
  --mmproj mmproj-F16.gguf `
  -ngl 99 `
  --ctx-size 131072 `
  -fa on `
  --cache-type-k q8_0 `
  --cache-type-v q8_0 `
  --jinja
```

For the 4 GiB run:

```powershell
$env:GGML_VK_SUBALLOCATION_BLOCK_SIZE="4294967296"
```

The only changed parameter between the two short-prompt `ctx=131072` runs was `GGML_VK_SUBALLOCATION_BLOCK_SIZE`.

### Runtime results

| Context | Block size | Generation time |  Throughput |
| ------: | ---------: | --------------: | ----------: |
|  98,304 |      1 GiB |         29.38 s | 40.81 tok/s |
| 131,072 |      1 GiB |         49.92 s | 24.02 tok/s |
| 131,072 |      4 GiB |         33.24 s | 36.07 tok/s |

At `ctx=131072` with a short prompt, increasing the block size from 1 GiB to 4 GiB improves throughput from **24.02 to 36.07 tok/s**, about **50%**.

### Nsight Systems profiling

I also collected a control trace for `98304 / 1 GiB` and compared it with the two `131072` traces.

| Configuration   | `vkWaitForFences` total | Median wait |  Max wait |
| --------------- | ------------------------: | ----------: | --------: |
| 98,304 / 1 GiB  |                   3.496 s |     8.43 ms |  342.6 ms |
| 131,072 / 1 GiB |                   5.670 s |    10.00 ms | 1751.4 ms |
| 131,072 / 4 GiB |                   4.599 s |     8.03 ms |  613.5 ms |

The graph structure does not show a corresponding large increase in CPU-side submission work:

| Configuration   | `vkQueueSubmit` | `vkUpdateDescriptorSets` |
| --------------- | ----------------: | -------------------------: |
| 98,304 / 1 GiB  |             5,584 |                    351,009 |
| 131,072 / 1 GiB |             5,662 |                    352,214 |
| 131,072 / 4 GiB |             5,628 |                    351,009 |

All observed `vkWaitForFences` intervals longer than 1 ms overlap WDDM GPU packet activity, with both 3D and Copy queue activity visible during the waits.

This does **not** support a simple explanation based on:

- increased queue submission count;
- increased descriptor update count;
- or the CPU being blocked on fences while the GPU is completely idle.

The fence-wait data by itself does not account for the full runtime difference, so the exact location of the additional GPU/WDDM execution time still needs to be identified.

### Active-KV crossover

4 GiB is **not a general workaround**.

With approximately 52.4K prompt tokens at the start of decode, while keeping `ctx=131072`, the result reverses:

| Prompt tokens at decode start | Block size | Generation time |  Throughput |
| ----------------------------: | ---------: | --------------: | ----------: |
|                           ~31 |      1 GiB |         49.92 s | 24.02 tok/s |
|                           ~31 |      4 GiB |         33.24 s | 36.07 tok/s |
|                        52,442 |      1 GiB |         52.64 s | 22.80 tok/s |
|                        52,442 |      4 GiB |        230.05 s |  5.22 tok/s |

## Linux / RADV datapoint: the fragmentation reproduces exactly, but neither throughput regression does

Testing this on Linux with the same GPU as the OP, and got a result worth adding to the thread: **the ~1 GiB buffer fragmentation you describe reproduces almost character-for-character, `GGML_VK_SUBALLOCATION_BLOCK_SIZE` fixes it exactly as advertised — and decode throughput does not move, in either direction, at either short or long active-KV.**

### Environment

| | this report | OP (@KEndlleas) | @SG-Amadeus |
|---|---|---|---|
| OS | **Linux (Arch)** | Windows 11 | Windows 11 |
| GPU | RX 7900 XTX 24 GB | RX 7900 XTX 24 GB | RTX 5070 Ti 16 GB |
| Driver | **RADV / Mesa 26.2.3-arch1.1**, Vulkan 1.4.354 | AMD proprietary | NVIDIA 576.02 |
| llama.cpp | **b11065** (0.4.1-dev, `ce8caa6`) | 10603 | 10714 (`2cdae802`) |
| Context | **131072** | 131072 | 131072 |
| KV | **q4_0** | q8_0 / f16 | q8_0 |
| speculative | **MTP on** (`--spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-n-max 2`) | off | off |
| pool | **14.08 GiB device / 301 MiB host** | 21.55 GiB / 152 MiB | — |

Single slot (`-np 1`), `-fa on -dev Vulkan0`, `-t 16`, `GGML_VK_TILE_L=64:256:32`, Qwen3.8-27B IQ3_XXS + MTP.

### Method

Two things, both against `llama-server`:

1. **Allocation structure** via `GGML_VK_MEMORY_LOGGER=1`, parsing the `ggml_vulkan memory:` alloc/dealloc lines keyed by address and keeping only **net-alive** buffers (transients excluded).
2. **Throughput** via `POST /completion`, `n_predict=300`, `cache_prompt=False`, **3 reps per arm** (short KV) and **2 reps per arm** (long KV). Both arms launched with byte-identical cmdlines — the *only* difference is `GGML_VK_SUBALLOCATION_BLOCK_SIZE`.

That yields a **2×2**: `{1 GiB, 4 GiB} × {short KV, long KV}`, so the high-active-KV crossover you found could be tested too.

### Fragmentation: reproduces, and is deterministic

Both arms start at an identical `Total device: 14.08 GiB, total host: 301.07 MiB`, so only the block size varies. Both parsed at the same **startup-only** stage (before either saw probe traffic):

| metric | 1 GiB | 4 GiB |
|---|---|---|
| device buffers | **25** | **16** |
| buffers ≥ ~1000 MiB | **10** | **4** |
| **the ~1000–1024 MiB ring** | **10** | **0** |
| largest single buffer | **1020.52 MiB** | 4.000 GiB |
| distinct sizes | 22 | 14 |

1 GiB arm, largest device buffers:

```
1020.52  1017.51  1016.78  1016.73  1010.63
1009.50  1008.00  1008.00  1005.05  1001.85   MiB
 991.18   887.99   512.00   470.45   448.88   MiB
```

4 GiB arm:

```
4.000  3.990  2.250  1.340 GiB
887.99  512.00  448.88  260.28  248.10  200.02 MiB
```

You wrote *"the largest individual allocations are ≈1018 MiB each."* Here the top ten cluster at **1001.85–1020.52 MiB** — a match within ~2 MiB, on Linux, on RADV. And `GGML_VK_SUBALLOCATION_BLOCK_SIZE=4294967296` does exactly what you say: **the ring goes 10 → 0**, largest 1020.52 MiB → 4.000 GiB.

**It is also fully deterministic, not run-to-run noise:** two independent launches from different shells, 44 minutes apart, produced byte-identical top-3 device allocations (`1020.5 / 1017.5 / 1016.8 MiB`), the same 10-buffer ring, and the same `14.08 GiB` endpoint.

### Throughput: flat in all four cells

- **long KV (56,110 / 58,116 prompt tokens):** 72.93 vs 72.86 → **0.10% apart** (spread only 0.04 and 2.83 — much tighter than short KV)

shortlist.title: [Bug] unified_moe cuDNN BF16 reference-check failures recur on VR_NVL72
shortlist.author: yufeiwu-nv
shortlist.body_excerpt:
The official `unified_moe` benchmark again intermittently fails the shared reference check for `cudnn_grouped_gemm_bf16` on VR_NVL72 (SM107).

### Observed executions

Test: `unified_moe / cudnn / Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-BF16`; T=128, hidden=2048, intermediate=512, experts=256, top-k=8, Swiglu, BF16, autotune, seed 42. This is a synthetic benchmark case, not an end-to-end model test.

Of 12 matching completed executions across six revisions, two failed and ten produced a cuDNN result without this error:

- [`3b65505`](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/commit/3b65505f40e34d1bd08d9364811057242e3342fd), repetition 0: 4 / 262144 elements mismatched; greatest absolute difference 0.64453125.
- [`a3f2525`](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/commit/a3f2525e39dffc98dcad4ce50706641a580358f0), repetition 1: 21 / 262144 elements mismatched; greatest absolute difference 0.6953125.

The official BF16 check uses `rtol=0.03, atol=0.5`. The logged primary failure is:

```text
[ERROR] cudnn_grouped_gemm_bf16 failed the shared reference check
Tensor-likes are not close!
```

The other completed revisions were c1bcf70, 130dd24, 52fbbd0 and fc1790f, with two repetitions per revision. Passing repetitions, including the latest revision, are retained; this is an intermittent consistency failure, not a continuously failing test or a proven introducing-commit regression. All 12 executions belong to one environment sample.

### Reproduction

From `benchmarks/` at either failing revision, on VR_NVL72 with CUDA 13.4 and the cuDNN backend available:

```bash
python3 flashinfer_benchmark.py --routine unified_moe --backends cutlass cutile cudnn --quant-variant bf16 --num_tokens 128 --hidden_size 2048 --intermediate_size 512 --num_experts 256 --top_k 8 --activation-type Swiglu --input_dtype bfloat16 --autotune --refcheck --random_seed 42 -vv --generate_repro_command --case_tag "Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-BF16"
```

Repeat the command because the failure is intermittent.

### Scope and reference contract

The official architecture/configuration checks accepted the cuDNN BF16 runner, and it actually executed. The benchmark supplies seeded canonical BF16 inputs and valid precomputed routing to the selected backends. Its shared reference performs FP32 operations with BF16 precision boundaries. The canonical input generator, shared reference and check are unchanged between the two failing revisions.

The failure exceeds the benchmark's stated tolerance. This reports an observed consistency failure; the responsible implementation, root cause and introducing commit remain unverified. The shared reference is not an independently established full-precision ground truth.

### Historical context and evidence

The same test was previously reported in [#6935](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/issues/6935), then closed after an intervening 12-execution passing window. Both failures above occurred in a later completed CI execution after that closure. No exact Open issue was found; this report preserves the recurrence and the subsequent passing repetitions rather than treating the earlier passing window as proof of a permanent fix.

[Execution with repetition 0](https://nv/flashinfer-ci/-/jobs/504602698) · [Execution with repetition 1](https://nv/flashinfer-ci/-/jobs/504602699)
